note: Both epics open by going for refuge to the feet of the tirthankara: the Cintamani's red feet, this poem's feet of Nemi under the pindi.
teaches: Two Jain epics begin with the same act of going to the feet but name different lords, so the invocation is a convention and the chosen tirthankara tells which tradition the poem draws on.

note: Both poets defend flaws in speech by an image, the Cintamani's unwashed gem and this poem's lamp with smoke.
teaches: The apology for a flawed poem is a set piece of the Jain epics, but this poem argues from the lamp's worth and the Cintamani from the washing that cures the flaw.

note: The Neelakesi excuses its flaws with the moon's spot and this poem with the lamp's smoke, both asking the learned to keep the work.
teaches: The lamp is smoky yet bright and the moon spotted yet loved: the two images make the same plea for a work of mixed quality, which shows it was a stock gesture of the Jain poets.

note: The Naladiyar says the noble cannot bear one stain as the moon bears its spot; the poet asks that one smoky flaw not make the lamp be thrown away.
teaches: The ethics book sets the noble above forgiveness of their stain, while the poet, claiming no such standard, pleads that a stained thing still be kept.

gains.a: the poet's plea is seen to relax the Naladiyar's strict standard of stainlessness
gains.b: the quatrain's rule is shown to be a standard for character, which a poem may leave aside

note: The Naladiyar says an old deed seeks out its doer like a calf its mother; this verse says deeds already gathered can be shed in a moment.
teaches: The Tamil ethics book makes old deeds unavoidable, while the Jain epic's poet leaves a way to drop them at once, so karma is binding in one book and removable in the other.

gains.a: the Jain poem's claim is set against the stricter view that old deeds always find their doer
gains.b: the calf-and-mother image is shown to have an exit in the Jain account of karma

note: Both make the god the one to whom deeds do not cling; the king praises a lord who himself defeated hard deeds.
teaches: The Kural says worshippers are freed from deeds by praise, while the Jain king hymns a lord who won against deeds by his own conquest, so the same praise stands on different grounds.

gains.a: the king's hymn is seen to give a conquering lord, not a pure being to be reached, as the one praised
gains.b: the couplet's lord is shown to be read in a Jain way as one who defeated karma

note: This verse praises the lord who burned all old deeds by his own renunciation; Tirumular's sunstone burns the malas only when the Lord's sun appears.
teaches: Jain deliverance burns karma by the liberated one's own effort without a god, while the Saiva text burns it by presence and grace, so the two disagree on whether anything outside the soul does the burning.

gains.a: the Jain hymn is shown to stand against the Saiva view that grace is needed to burn deeds
gains.b: the Saiva image of grace burning bond is shown to be one answer to a question the Jain poet answers by effort

note: The Kural's எண்குணத்தான் (one of eight qualities) and the verse's இருநான்கு குணமுடைய இறைவன் (the lord with twice four qualities) are the same number.
teaches: The Kural's unlisted eight is matched by a Jain count of eight qualities, so a Jain poet can read the couplet as meaning his own liberated lord.

gains.a: the Jain poem is shown to use the eight-quality formula the Kural already uses
gains.b: the couplet's unlisted eight is given a Jain reading by a poet who also leaves the eight unlisted

note: The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; the verse says the lord has ended birth, old age and death.
teaches: The couplet makes ending birth the reward of reaching the feet, and this verse names the three things the lord himself has ended, so the poem tells what is meant by crossing the sea.

gains.a: the epic's hymn is shown to say what the crossing of the sea of births consists of
gains.b: the couplet's promise is shown to be read as freedom from birth, old age and death

note: Both name two kinds of deed; the Kural says they do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise, the verse names the two as what makes becoming, as something the lord taught.
teaches: The Kural states that the two deeds fall away from the devoted, and the Jain verse says it is the lord's own teaching of them that frees.

gains.a: the 'two deeds' are put in the Tamil devotional frame where deeds both good and bad are what binds, a reach the verse's own wording does not state
gains.b: the lord's praise gets a content: in the epic it is the lord's naming of the two deeds that the devotee takes up

note: Jayandhara falls in love with a painted woman who is real elsewhere; the Manimekalai prince sees the living girl as a painted image.
teaches: The two works run the same trope in opposite directions, so a reader sees that the poets use the picture to say a desire is shaped by a seen form before the person is known.

note: Prithidevi fears her senior co-wife will let her fall; the Silappathikaram lists a woman who reared her co-wife's child as her own as a type of pathini.
teaches: The epic sets the co-wife's presumed envy beside the Tamil ideal of the co-wife who cares, so the new queen's fear is read as a convention the other works already know and answer.

note: The Kural says envy ruins fortune and leads one to a bad place; the verse shows only a new wife's fear of envy and the retreat to the temple.
teaches: The Kural describes envy's results, and the verse shows how its mere expectation sends a wife to the god instead of to the rival.

gains.a: the fear in the verse gets a name and a moral cost from the Kural's chapter on envy, which the verse leaves unsaid
gains.b: the Kural's abstract envy is given a household: a co-wife whose envy is presumed and never shown

note: The Kural makes not killing the whole of virtuous action; the verse makes a lord of that vow the one whose worship cuts the evil birth.
teaches: The Kural sets non-killing as the rule, and the verse makes it the lord's own vow, so worship of him is worship of the rule kept to its end.

gains.a: the vow is set in the Tamil rule that killing brings all other deeds, so what the god is praised for has a reason
gains.b: the rule is made a person: the lord who kept it all the way and is the end of its path

note: Tirumanthiram 200 has those who give up killing, theft, lust and lying reach Siva's feet; the verse has worshippers of a lord who has kept non-killing reach release.
teaches: Both name feet and release for those who keep the vow, but the Saiva verse makes the worshipper the keeper of the vow and the Jain verse makes the lord the keeper.

gains.a: the worshipper's gain is set against a Saiva account where one's own giving up of killing is what earns the feet
gains.b: the Saiva list is shown to have a Jain counterpart in which the god, not the worshipper, is the one who has kept the vow

note: Soolamani 1 praises the one who conquered the sum of deeds, whose worshippers are freed; the verse praises the lord of non-killing whose worshippers cut off the evil birth.
teaches: Two Jain epics open with the same promise of release through the conqueror but name his victory differently, over deeds in one and in vow of non-killing in the other.

note: The Kural has the son's merit read back as the father's tapas; the verse has the sage promise a virtuous son when the queen asks for tapas.
teaches: The Kural reads a son as the proof of a parent's penance and the verse reverses it, making the promised son the answer to a request for penance.

gains.a: the sage's answer gets an ordinary Tamil frame in which a son is a fruit of tapas, which clears the odd turn from tapas to son
gains.b: the couplet's 'what penance did his father do' is given a scene in which the penance is asked for and a son promised

audit_text_issue: Sense of நற்றவம் ஆமோ is open.

note: The Kural says nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives first even when one plans against it; the verse bows to a lord who has conquered fate.
teaches: The Kural makes fate the strongest force and the Jain verse puts one who has beaten it in front of the worshipper, so release means the end of the thing the Kural says cannot be passed.

gains.a: the lord's conquest of fate is weighed against a Tamil saying that nothing is stronger than it
gains.b: the couplet's claim that fate cannot be beaten is shown to have a Jain exception, and the exception is the god

note: The sage says austerity will cut away the prince's heated deeds so that he reaches release; the quatrain says austerity drives sin out as a lamp drives darkness, and that evil settles in again when the good deeds that feed it run out.
teaches: The sage's promise of a final release by tapas is answered by a warning that austerity burns sin only while its good is kept up, so the prophecy needs the prince's own lasting effort.

gains.a: a limit on the prophecy: release by tapas has to be kept up and is not given once
gains.b: a story in which a lamp-like tapas is foretold of one person, with the end of deeds as its goal

note: The Jain sage says the son's own austerity will cut his deeds and end birth; Tirumular says austerity and virtue are a boat across the sea of deeds only because the Lord makes them fruitful.
teaches: The same word, tapas, ends karma by the doer's effort in the sage's mouth and by the Lord's grace in Tirumular's, so the release the two promise rests on opposite sources.

gains.a: a rival account in which release is not won by the ascetic's effort alone but by the Lord's help
gains.b: a case of austerity credited with ending karma with no god at all in the account

note: The queen's dream of a bull and a young sun is told as an omen with no meaning given; the sage's reading in 44 turns it into a son who is king, ascetic and freed.
teaches: The dream is not left as an omen: the sage's reading supplies its meaning, and the prince's whole later life is fixed in it before his birth.

note: The sage names the temple doors opening at the son's foot and a pond among the signs; verse 51 shows the doors swing open at the child's foot-touch and the boy fall into the pond.
teaches: The sign comes true as an ordinary accident of an outing, so the story shows the prophecy fulfilling itself without anyone seeking it.

note: The prince is named Pirathapan at birth; after he is found on the serpent's head the king gives him a second name, Naga Kumaran, which becomes the poem's title.
teaches: The infant's first name is replaced by one taken from the miracle, so the name the book carries marks what the serpent did, not what the king first chose.

note: The sage had foretold that the prince would curb the rut of a great elephant; verse 57 shows him doing so on the city's own mad elephant.
teaches: The sage's prophecy is not left as a promise: the city's real elephant is the first thing that proves it, so a reader sees the prince's prowess as the working of what was foretold.
audit_text_issue: 46: marked reading says curb pride, but மதம் is rut

note: The sage's dream-reading promised a son who would bear great austerity and cut off karma; verse 59 shows him grown in learning by the sage's teaching, the first step toward that end.
teaches: The prophecy of renunciation is paired here with a worldly rise, so the story shows the prince's skill as a stage on the way to release and not a rival to it.

note: The king's order to play outside the city becomes, in verse 73, his command to build the prince a city of his own and name it.
teaches: The expulsion is turned into an honour by the end of the chapter, so the sentence of exile never takes effect as a punishment.
audit_text_issue: 65 flagged uncertain; addressee and son unclear.

note: The king had ordered the prince's goods taken; in 72 the prince, enriched by dice, gives away all that he wins to the kings and his mother.
teaches: The order to strip the prince is answered not by revenge but by the prince's giving, so the seizure leaves him richer in standing than the king who ordered it.

note: Kovalan frees a Brahmin from a rogue elephant and tames it, and Naga Kumaran subdues a maddened elephant that has been wrecking the city: the same feat of a hero.
teaches: In the Silappathikaram the feat is an act of compassion for one man; in this epic it is a sign of a foretold destiny and a cause of royal suspicion.

note: The prince masters a rutting elephant; Tirumular's body holds five rutting elephants that will not come to the post of the Agamas' teaching.
teaches: The epic's taming is an outward feat of the body, and the Tirumanthiram carries the same image inward to the senses, so the story's word மதம் is read both as rut and as the pride the senses breed.

gains.a: The epic's elephant gains a second sense: its mastery is also a figure for the senses held in check.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's inner elephants gain a narrative picture, a man who actually stops a rampaging beast.

note: The prince mounts and rides a vicious horse through the streets; Tirumular tells the reader to hold the reins of the running horse firmly.
teaches: The ride of a hero is shown in the epic as skill before a crowd, and in the Tirumanthiram as the discipline of the mind that needs no show, so the two use one image for different ends.

gains.a: The prince's horse-taming gains a reading as the discipline of a restless will.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's running horse gains a visible rider and a crowd, a show that the verse tells its hearers to do without.

note: The prince wins at dice from the kings, as the Kural warns that what a gambler wins is like the hook's metal in the fish.
teaches: The Kural treats winning as the lure; the epic gives a winner who is not caught by it because he gives the winnings back, which shows the rule is about the winner's grip on the goods.

gains.a: The prince's win gains a measure: it is the keeping of the winnings, not the playing, that the couplet condemns.
gains.b: The couplet's warning gains a hard case, a winner who takes nothing, which tests whether the warning is about the game or the hunger.

note: The prince is accused through a lie told against him and keeps his bearing; the Naladiyar says the pure of heart are not shaken by cruel slander, like a lamp's flame.
teaches: The Naladiyar's steadiness under slander is shown in the epic as a prince who answers the false charge with a procession and with giving, not with protest.

gains.a: The verse gains a character who passes the Naladiyar's test of staying unshaken by false speech.
gains.b: The Naladiyar quatrain gains a story in which the slander is followed by exile and a city, so the cost and the outcome of steadiness are shown.

note: The sage tells the king that his sons will serve one man; in 81 Vyala meets Naga Kumara and calls himself the small one.
teaches: The prophecy names no master, so Vyala's self-lowering at first sight shows the foretold service beginning as a choice of bearing and not a forced bond.
audit_text_issue: 81: speaker and the forehead-eye clause uncertain

note: Sridharan arrives in anger and meets the prince in 83, and in 85 he is rebuked and withdraws in fear.
teaches: The threat built in 83 is ended not by a battle but by a minister's speech, so the epic makes counsel the thing that turns the king back.

note: The king in 78 leaves for forest austerity after crowning his sons, the move Kural 46 asks the householder to question.
teaches: The epic shows leaving for the outside way as a late step after the duty of rule is done, which narrows how far the Kural's rhetorical question reaches.

gains.a: The king's departure gains a test: it is not flight from household duty but follows its completion.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case of a ruler who goes outside the household way and loses nothing it names as virtue.

note: Naladiyar 21 says kings under umbrellas were carried off and called dead; in 78 the king leaves the throne alive and by his own act.
teaches: The same fall of royal pomp appears as chosen renunciation rather than death, showing impermanence can be met before it arrives.

gains.a: The king's retreat gains the Naladiyar's reason for giving up rank, impermanence, which the verse leaves unspoken.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king who acts on its warning instead of only being its example.

note: The hunter's cry and his wife's imprisonment in 93 are met in 95 by her release.
teaches: The prince's help answers the plea at once, so 93 and 95 show the hero's mercy as action rather than promise.

note: The city given by Vanaraja's sacrifice-gift of his daughter in 99 is repaid in 100 by the prince winning back a city for Vanaraja.
teaches: The marriage in 99 is returned by a kingdom in 100, so the gift of a wife is shown as an obligation the husband repays in arms.
audit_text_issue: 99 flagged uncertain; daughter's name lost from line 2

note: The prince wins a princess by defeating her at the vina; in the Cintamani the girl goes out to break her opponents with the yaazh.
teaches: Both epics make the vina contest the means by which a king's son wins his bride, so the motif is a standard marriage test rather than one poet's invention.

note: The Kural defines தவம் as enduring pain and not harming; 101 gives a king who loses his land and then takes up yoga to end old deeds.
teaches: The verse shows tavam taken up after loss and aimed at ending vinai, which the Kural's definition of endurance and non-harm does not say.

gains.a: the Kural fixes what the sage's austerity must mean, an endurance of pain without harming
gains.b: the couplet gets a worked case in which a man chooses austerity after losing a throne

note: Tirumular's Siva-yoga ends in the Lord's abode, given by Nandi; Somaprabha guards his yoga so that his own deeds end, with no god named.
teaches: The two texts use the word yoga for a discipline of release but one gives the release to the Lord's grace and the other to the ascetic's own guarding, so grace and effort part on the same practice.

gains.a: the epic's yoga is set beside a text where the same practice is a gift of grace, showing what the Jain ascetic does not invoke
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's grace claim meets a case where the same discipline of release is held up without a god

note: The king asks whether his two sons will rule or serve; at 109 the two come to Naga Kumara and become his servants.
teaches: The ascetic's foresight is shown to be exact, so the story makes the sons' loss of the kingdom a matter of fate that no choice of the king's undoes.

note: The hymn's three verses promise rule on earth and in heaven (118), Indra's rank (119), and release (120).
teaches: The hymn arranges worship's rewards as a ladder, so release comes as the last step above the worldly kingship the prince himself holds.

note: Naladiyar says even kings on elephants under the moon-bright umbrella are carried off and spoken of as dead; Jayavarma lays down his kingdom while living.
teaches: A king's leaving rule by his own act, before it is taken from him, is the story's answer to the impermanence the Naladiyar says no king escapes.

gains.a: the abdication is seen as a chosen answer to the loss of rule that the Naladiyar says death forces on every king
gains.b: the Naladiyar's lament over fallen kings is given a king who acts on the lesson while still ruling

audit_text_issue: naga_kumara_kaviyam:106 செவ்வினை and the subject of நின்றனர் are not fixed.

note: Kural 3 places the god on a flower and says those who reach his feet live long on the earth; the hymn has the lord seated on a lotus and promises Indra's rank to those who worship his feet.
teaches: Both couplet and hymn set the god on a flower and promise a reward for reaching the feet, but the hymn's reward is rank in heaven while the couplet's is long life on earth.

gains.a: the hymn's lotus-seated lord is seen as a Jain case of the flower-borne god of the Kural's opening
gains.b: the couplet's reward of long life on earth is set beside a hymn that pays in heaven's rank

note: Kural 10 says only those at the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; the hymn says those who bow to the lord on the lion throne become gods and then reach release.
teaches: The hymn makes the crossing of births a graded gain, gods first and release after, where the couplet states it only as a crossing for those who reach the feet.

gains.a: the hymn's promise of release is read as the Kural's crossing of births with a stage of divine rank before it
gains.b: the couplet's one-step crossing is given a sequence of worlds the worshipper passes through

note: Both name the star Arundhati as the measure of a woman's chastity: Mrigalochana is like her, and in the Cintamani a woman is said to put her aside.
teaches: Two Jain epics use the same star as the yardstick of wifely chastity, one saying a queen is equal to it and the other that a woman surpasses it.

note: In both a sage's saying about who will rule or serve is fixed as a prophecy: here the sons will serve the conqueror, there the hearers affirm the prophecy that one will protect the world under one umbrella.
teaches: Jain epics let a sage's sight settle a future rule and the later scene confirm it, so succession is told as fate foreseen, not as a contest.

note: The hero kills Vayuvegan to avenge a father's murder; the couplet makes not killing the whole of virtuous action.
teaches: A Jain-framed epic lets its hero kill a usurper without comment, so the couplet's absolute not-killing meets a case where the story itself counts killing as justice.

gains.a: the hero's killing is seen against a rule the poem's own faith holds
gains.b: the couplet is shown meeting a hard case of vengeance for murder

note: Vayuvegan kills a king and seizes his land; the hero kills him, as the king's weeding of the cruel in the couplet.
teaches: The couplet puts the punishment of the cruel in a king's hand; here a wandering prince does it, so the story shows the same duty fallen to whoever happens to be there.

gains.a: the hero's killing is read as the weeding-out of a cruel man
gains.b: the couplet's weeding is shown done by a prince with no throne

note: The hero takes five hundred princesses by the mantra-rite; the couplet praises the man who does not look at another's wife.
teaches: The couplet bars only another's wife, and the poem's heroes win unmarried women, so the epic's polygamy sits outside what the couplet forbids.

gains.a: the hero's many marriages are measured against the couplet's one fixed limit
gains.b: the couplet's limit is shown to leave room for many wives who are unmarried

note: The merchant could not say why five hundred women sing daily at the temple; Dharanisundari gives the cause.
teaches: The merchant's wonder is only a wonder until the women speak, showing the poem makes a marvel into a wrong that the hero is to put right.
audit_text_issue: 137 line 3 loosely joined; மருகன் ambiguous | 137 line 3 is loosely joined (வரதிரட்சகனேமர்)

note: Just after the hero takes his pleasure with Ilakkanai, sages arrive and he asks them about it.
teaches: The sage's coming in the same breath as the marriage shows the poem placing the hero's pleasures under the teaching that follows them.

note: The couplet calls even the body excess for those who would cut off births; Nagadattan lets go of the body by fasting.
teaches: The couplet calls the body surplus for one bent on ending births, and the story shows that a householder who lets the body go by fasting is rewarded with a god's birth, so the Jain fast does not by itself end births.

gains.a: the fast is read as the couplet's 'body is excess' acted to the end
gains.b: the couplet's claim gets an actual practice, and a limit: the first reward is a heaven, not the end of births

note: The quatrain praises those who hold their vows through unbearable trouble; here the trouble of hunger is the vow itself.
teaches: The quatrain sets trouble as the test of a vow, but the fast makes the trouble a part of the vow, so holding firm means keeping a hunger that ends the keeper's life.

gains.a: the hunger of the fast is seen as the very trouble the vow-keeper is told to bear
gains.b: the quatrain's trial is given an extreme case in which holding on ends in death

note: The couplet likens death to sleep and birth to waking; here the death by fast is followed at once by waking as a god.
teaches: The couplet's sleep-and-waking comparison is made literal, and the waking place depends on how the sleeper died.

gains.a: the death in meditation is read as a sleep that ends in a chosen waking
gains.b: the couplet's comparison is shown with a destination fixed by the way of dying

note: In both works a former birth's vow explains what happens in this one: a broken vow there, a kept vow here.
teaches: The same cause by a vow of a past birth explains a loss in one work and a gain in the other, so the epics do not tie past deeds to suffering alone.

note: The verse says a vow, worship and gifts conquer the binding deed; the Tirumanthiram says the Lord made the bond that fastens the soul to what went before.
teaches: One text lets the soul loosen its own bond by vow and giving, while the other makes the bond the Lord's work, so the question of who can undo the bond divides them.

gains.a: the vow-and-gift path to conquering the bond is set against a view in which the bond is not the soul's own doing
gains.b: the Saiva verse's bond meets a rival claim that effort alone can undo it

note: The Tirumanthiram says only the vows kept and the knowledge gained go with the dead; the verse lists what the vow buys after death.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram names the vow as what travels past death, and the epic adds a ledger of what it buys: Indra's rank, kingship, then the end of deeds.

gains.a: the vow's journey after death gets a stated ladder of rewards
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's bare claim is given a worked sequence that the Jain epic fills in

note: The couplet says to renounce while there is time; the king crowns his son first and then renounces.
teaches: The couplet gives only the timing, and the story adds that a king's renouncing in time includes installing his heir first.

gains.a: the king's exit is read as renunciation in time, with the succession first
gains.b: the couplet's time gets a king's duty: the throne is handed on before it is left

audit_text_issue: Kural 342 sense uncertain; the 'time' reading is commentary

note: The sage foretold that the son would bear austerity and reach release; here the father renounces and the son is crowned.
teaches: The prophecy of the son's austerity is not yet kept; the father takes the sage's way first, so the work leaves the son's renunciation for later.

note: A queen leaves her son for the nun's life and is rewarded in heaven, while the couplet asks what a householder gains by going to the outside way.
teaches: The story answers the Kural's question by showing a woman rewarded for leaving, so the couplet's praise of the householder is met by a Jain ideal that holds the opposite.

gains.a: the queen's leaving is set against a rule that makes the home the greater path
gains.b: the couplet's challenge is met by a case where leaving is rewarded, not wasted

note: A king on his throne turns from rule at the sight of a vanishing cloud, as the quatrain's best of people see home, youth and wealth fail and renounce.
teaches: The quatrain gives renunciation as a conclusion of reasoning; the story shows the same turn as a sudden sight on a throne after the heir is crowned.

gains.a: the king's turn is shown as the reasoned choice of the best the quatrain names
gains.b: the quatrain's argument gets a figure who acts on it at the height of his splendour

note: The king gives up kingship at the height of his state and takes austerity, as the couplet urges renouncing while there is time.
teaches: The couplet urges haste in the abstract; the king's act shows what haste costs, a throne handed to a son, and what it is paid for.

gains.a: the king's going forth is shown as renouncing in time, not in old age
gains.b: the couplet gains a prince who leaves a throne, a cost it does not state

note: The hero asked the sage about his pleasure and heard dharma; here he follows that teaching to its end, by conquering karma and reaching siddhi.
teaches: What the hero hears in the earlier grove scene is the cause of the choices he makes here, which shows the poem's plan: hearing dharma comes before renouncing.

note: The monk conquers both deeds by his own austerity, where the couplet says the two deeds do not cling to those who praise the Lord.
teaches: The couplet places freedom from both deeds in devotion to a Lord; the story gives the same freedom through a man's own austerity and no god, so the same result has two causes.

gains.a: the hero's liberation is set against a rule that places it in devotion
gains.b: the couplet's route is shown to have a Jain rival that reaches the same end by effort alone

note: The brothers destroy both deeds by meditating on the soul, where Tirumular says the worshipped fire burns up deeds.
teaches: The two accounts reach the same freedom from deeds by different agents, the practitioner's own meditation against a fire that burns them, so the dispute is over who does the burning.

gains.a: the brothers' liberation is set against a view that gives the work to a worshipped fire
gains.b: Tirumular's fire is shown to have a rival account in which no fire is needed

note: Austerity and yoga bring the brothers perfection and the rest heaven, as Tirumular says austerity and virtue together are a boat over the sea of deeds.
teaches: The story shows austerity giving two different ends for two sets of people, which the single boat in Tirumular's line does not.

gains.a: the story's two ends are seen as a way to read the one boat of the verse
gains.b: the verse's boat gains a case where the same austerity reaches two shores

note: The closing sermon says nothing helps the soul but virtue and nothing harms it but vice; the couplet says no gain surpasses virtue and no ruin surpasses forgetting it.
teaches: The couplet's ruin is forgetting virtue, while the sermon's is positive vice (maram), so the story hardens the Kural's lapse into a deed that harms the soul.

gains.a: the sermon's rule is seen as a hard form of a rule the Tamil tradition already held
gains.b: the couplet's ruin of forgetting is made sharper by a vice that actively harms

note: The sermon says to fear a bad rebirth and leave vice; the quatrain gives the bad rebirth as the fruit of wronging others' wives.
teaches: The sermon names fear of an evil birth without a case, and the quatrain supplies one, so the fear gets a concrete deed and fruit.

gains.a: the sermon's fear of an evil birth is given a concrete deed behind it
gains.b: the quatrain's penalty is shown as the ground of a whole poem's moral

note: Both invocations make knowledge the mark of the god: the Kural's வாலறிவன் (one of pure knowledge), the Neelakesi's எல்லாம் உணர்ந்தான் (one who knows all).
teaches: The Kural's unnamed pure knower is open enough that a Jain poet can fill the same slot with a god defined only by omniscience and freedom from birth, with no creating role.

gains.a: the Jain invocation is seen standing in a shared Tamil form of praising the god as knower
gains.b: the couplet's sectless epithet is shown being read in a sectarian sense by a debate poem

note: Both honour the feet of one who walked on the flower: மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் in the Kural, தண்டாமரைமேல் நடந்தான் in the Neelakesi.
teaches: An avowedly Jain poet uses the flower-walking epithet for his god, so the Kural's disputed epithet was current in Jain praise and not only open to other readings.

gains.a: the dream-apology is anchored in a known image of the god's feet
gains.b: the couplet's contested epithet gains a sectarian witness for one of its readings

note: Both use the moon's spot: the Naladiyar to say the noble cannot bear one stain as the moon does, the Neelakesi to say a work, like the moon, may carry a fault and still be loved.
teaches: The same image yields opposite counsel: for a person's character a single stain is unbearable, but for a poet before an assembly an acknowledged fault is excusable.

gains.a: the poet's apology is seen to lower the standard the ethics books set for the noble
gains.b: the quatrain's rule is shown to be about moral stain, not every imperfection

note: The Kural says a fault in the well-born shows like the moon's spot; the Neelakesi says the moon's spot does not stop the world loving it.
teaches: Read together, the moon's spot is both what makes a high fault visible and what proves the loved and high are never spotless, so visibility is not the same as rejection.

gains.a: the apology answers the worry the couplet raises, that a fault in a high place is seen by all
gains.b: the couplet's warning is softened by a case where the visible spot is forgiven

note: The invocation says she took the great one's dharma and her dark heart turned; at the end of the sermon she says she has taken the clear knowledge and asks for atonement for the wrong she did.
teaches: The prologue's single word of conversion becomes, in the story, a confession and a request for expiation, so the turn is shown as moral repair and not only a change of belief.

note: The invocation's demons who lost their god's refuge are, in the story, the demons who complain to Neelakesi that the sage stopped their offerings.
teaches: The phrase 'removing refuge in the god' turns out to mean ending blood offerings, so the demons' grievance is the loss of sacrifice, the poem's first act against killing.

note: The invocation's 'unable to disturb his penance' is told at length when her terrors fail and she gives up, fearing his penance will burn her.
teaches: The story makes the sage's penance an active power that the demoness fears, which the prologue's bare statement of her failure does not convey.

note: The invocation announces the debates 'beginning with the view that accepts flesh'; in the Kundalakesi debate Neelakesi charges the Buddha's path with not calling flesh-eating a fault.
teaches: The prologue names the Buddhist teaching by its tolerance of flesh, showing that the poem's first and framing charge against a rival school is ethical before it is metaphysical.

note: The shrine set up for the demon-mother among flesh-eating hosts is where, in 35, people come to cut a lamb's head for the goddess and the sage forbids the killing.
teaches: The description of the shrine as a place of demons who eat bodies is the moral setting of the first act: the sage's reform begins by ending blood offering at that very shrine.

note: 33 likens the sage to the earth in patience and Meru in strength; in 49, as Neelakesi prepares her terrors, he resolves to let her frighten him as she will and to teach her.
teaches: The epithet of patience becomes the sage's whole strategy against the demoness: he does not resist her terrors but outlasts them, and turns the trial into a chance to teach.

note: Both put the renouncer in the burning ground with the same verb: காட்டகத் துறைவான் in the Neelakesi, உறைவது காட்டகம் in the Tirumanthiram.
teaches: The burning ground was the renouncer's accepted dwelling across sects, but for Tirumular its dweller is Siva himself, whom renouncers imitate, while the Jain sage enters it as a stranger in a goddess's shrine whose offerings he will end.

gains.a: the sage's choice of dwelling is seen as a recognised mark of the renouncer, not only a test of courage
gains.b: the verse's image of the god in the burning ground is shown claimed by a rival tradition that gives the place no divine owner

note: The Naladiyar calls the meat-eater's belly a burning ground for beasts and birds; the Neelakesi places its flesh-eating demon hosts and a goddess's shrine inside a real burning ground.
teaches: The quatrain's metaphor joining flesh-eating and the cremation ground becomes the Neelakesi's literal scene, so the epic's first quarrel over flesh is staged where eating bodies and burning them meet.

gains.a: the burning-ground description is shown to carry an ethical charge against eating flesh, not only horror
gains.b: the quatrain's figure is shown worked out as a setting for the doctrinal fight over offerings

note: The Kural asks what a virtuous householder would gain by going the outside way; the Neelakesi's ideal land has virtuous householders and also those who leave home's troubles to wear away their deeds.
teaches: The Jain poet answers the couplet's question by naming a gain the household cannot give, the wearing away of deeds already done, while still praising the household's gifts and conduct.

gains.a: the verse's two kinds of people are seen as a reply to a known Tamil challenge to renunciation
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question is given a specific answer that it does not consider

note: The Neelakesi praises those who strive (முயல்வார்) with knowledge to wear away their deeds; the Tirumanthiram says deeds end when grace comes as the guru and one's own doing ceases (தன்செயல் அற்றால்).
teaches: Both make knowledge the solvent of deeds, but they disagree on whose act it is: for the Jain land it is the striver's own effort, for Tirumular the end of one's own agency under grace; the tension holds if முயல்வார் is read as self-reliant effort.

gains.a: the passing praise of strivers is shown to carry the Jain view of self-wrought release
gains.b: the verse's stress on the end of one's own agency stands out against a tradition that makes that agency the means

audit_text_issue: Line 3 division (கானமொடு கல்லடரு ளில்லிடரு நீங்கி) is uncertain.

note: The Kural says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the work one does; the Neelakesi praises a land where the four varnas each keep the path given to them.
teaches: A Jain poet could honour the Kural's ethics and still count the hereditary varna order as a land's virtue, so the couplet's levelling of birth was not read by him as rejecting the order, only as asking each to keep its duty.

gains.a: the verse's praise of varna order is seen against a Tamil claim that ranks by deeds, not birth
gains.b: the couplet's ambiguous செய்தொழில் is shown open to the reading of a fixed hereditary duty

note: Thirikadugam names three seeds of the month's three rains: the priests' virtue, the king's just rule, and the wife who follows her husband; the Neelakesi gives its land three rains a month from its own known goodness.
teaches: The three-rains formula, which Thirikadugam ties to the conduct of priest, king and wife, appears in the epic as a landscape convention that explains away the missing palai tinai, its moral causes left unspoken.

gains.a: the epic's claim of three rains is seen to carry an implied moral order the verse does not state
gains.b: the quatrain's formula is shown travelling into poetic description, where it serves the tinai scheme rather than ethics

note: Both give an account of where a child comes from: the Neelakesi's sage assigns the body to the parents' blood and the life to its own former deeds, leaving the deity nothing to give; Tirumular has the Lord sit in the womb and form the embryo, knowing what it will become.
teaches: On the same question, the making of a child, the Jain sage removes every divine agent while Tirumular puts the Lord inside the womb, so karma alone and karma shaped by the Lord are opposed answers, not one view in two idioms.

gains.a: the sage's denial is seen to cut against a Tamil theology in which a god does make the child, not only against a village vow
gains.b: Tirumular's embryology is seen as a position a rival school in Tamil openly argued against

note: The Kural sets abstaining from one killing above a thousand fire sacrifices; the Neelakesi's sage does not ask the worshippers to drop their vow but to offer a clay goat in its place.
teaches: Between the Kural's flat preference for not killing over ritual and outright refusal of the rite lies a third course the epic shows a teacher using: keep the vow, replace the victim with an image.

gains.a: the clay-goat advice is seen as a practical form of a principle the ethics books already state
gains.b: the couplet's comparison is shown applied to a vowed village offering, where giving up the rite has a social cost the couplet does not weigh

audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 38 lines 1-2 do not construe securely; the link rests on the plain line 3.

note: The Kural ranks not killing first and not lying second; the sage lists killing, lying, theft, going to others' wives and craving for wealth, and promises the world of the gods.
teaches: The Kural's ranking of not killing above not lying is the head of a fixed Jain list of five householder abstentions, which the epic gives whole with a heavenly reward rather than release.

gains.a: the sage's list is seen keeping the same order of the first two goods that the Kural argues for
gains.b: the couplet's two-term ranking is shown as the opening of a longer five-part code

audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 40 was rejoined from half-lines; the sense is clear.

note: Both list the same abstentions, killing first, then lying and theft; the Siddhar asks the Lord of Chidambaram to grant him a life without them, while the sage tells householders that keeping them wins the world of the gods.
teaches: The same list of abstentions is a gift begged of the Lord in the Siddhar and the householder's own work with a self-acting reward in the Jain sermon, which is the grace-against-effort divide in miniature.

gains.a: the sermon's silent assumption, that the hearer can keep the vows unaided, is brought out by a text that asks for them as grace
gains.b: the Siddhar's petition is seen against a rival ethic that needs no giver for the same virtues

note: The Silappathikaram's hunters offer the goddess blood as the price (விலை) of the victory she gives; the Neelakesi's worshippers offer a goat for the child she gave, and the sage denies that she gave anything.
teaches: Both epics show worship to the fierce goddess as an exchange of blood for a boon; the Jain sage attacks the exchange at its first term, the boon, which the hunters' song takes for granted.

gains.a: the sage's argument is seen to strike at the logic of a widespread kind of worship, not at one family's vow
gains.b: the hunters' price-for-victory is shown to rest on a premise another epic set out to deny

note: The Kural says penance can crush one's foes if one so intends; the sage, attacked by Neelakesi, intends instead to make her see her powerlessness and come to the dharma.
teaches: The power the Kural grants penance against enemies is here held back and turned to converting the enemy, which is what the Kural's 'if one so intends' leaves open.

gains.a: the sage's restraint is seen as a choice not to use a power the Kural says penance has
gains.b: the couplet's condition எண்ணின் gains a case where the ascetic, able to destroy, chooses not to

note: The Kural pictures penance as pain burning the ascetic as fire burns gold; Neelakesi fears that the fullness of the sage's penance will burn her.
teaches: The fire of penance faces two ways: inward in the Kural, where it purifies the one who bears it, and outward in the epic, where the assailant feels it as a fire that would consume her.

gains.a: her fear is seen to rest on the same fire that the Kural says the ascetic has passed through
gains.b: the couplet's inward fire is shown to be imagined by others as a danger to them

note: The sage foresees that Neelakesi, once she learns the arts of meaning, will come to the path of dharma; the invocation says she took the great one's dharma and turned the world from violence.
teaches: The invocation's report of her conversion is planted in the story as the sage's own foreknowledge at the moment of her attack, so the conversion is his aim from the start, not a later turn.

note: The sage resolves to make her understand her own powerlessness (திறமின்மை); she ends by confessing she cannot touch him.
teaches: His plan is carried out without any act of his: her own failed terrors teach her the powerlessness he meant her to learn.

note: Both set the ascetic's ஆற்றல் against கூற்றம்: the Kural says those who gain the power of penance can leap even Death; here a demoness likened to Death owns that the fire of the sage's penance would destroy her.
teaches: The couplet's abstract boast that penance outruns death becomes a scene in which Death's likeness itself gives up the fight, and the victory comes without the ascetic acting at all.

gains.a: the demoness's surrender is read as the outcome the Kural promised for true penance
gains.b: the couplet's claim gains a dramatised instance in which the threat is a being, not the end of life

note: Verse 58's plan that the sage will drop his vow once she breaks his restraint in a woman's form meets its answer in 72, where every wile draws only the question of what these are to him.
teaches: Holding the plan beside its failure shows that the epic places the vow's safety in the sage's inner containment, the very மனநிறை she meant to break, not in avoiding the temptress.

note: Both heroines of the debate epics take another woman's form: Neelakesi takes a princess's shape to break a sage's vow, Manimekalai took Kayachandigai's shape to teach her former husband birth and death and end his karma.
teaches: The Jain and Buddhist epics use the same device of a borrowed body to opposite ends, one to bind a man in desire and one to free him from it, so the borrowed form itself is neutral and the intent decides.

note: The Kural calls the tie of body and life a friendship that ends as a bird leaves its nest; the Neelakesi's sage knows a scripture that cuts the deeds entangled in the soul's oneness with and difference from the body.
teaches: Set beside the Kural, the Jain verse turns the body-soul tie from a bond death simply ends into a knot of deeds that a discipline can cut while one still lives.

gains.a: the sage's knowledge is placed against the Tamil commonplace of body and life as passing companions
gains.b: the couplet's bird-and-nest friendship gains a doctrinal account of what holds the two together

audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 64 is printed with the number 6, and line 3 is obscure. | line 3 (பணிந்தவரட் காசிடை) is obscure; the verse number is reconstructed (printed as 6)

note: Both picture life in a house: the Kural asks whether life, a lodger in the body, has no home of its own; the Neelakesi's sage likens beings across the states of birth to people who live together in one house and do not fear each other.
teaches: The same lodging image serves the Kural to make the soul homeless and the Jain sage to make all souls housemates, so it can teach unrest or fearlessness depending on whether one looks at one body or at all lives.

gains.a: the sage's housemates image is seen to rework a known Tamil figure of the soul as a lodger
gains.b: the couplet's lonely lodger gains a counter-image in which every being shares the house

note: The Naladiyar answers a beautiful woman's appeal by dissecting the body into entrails, blood and bone and asking which part is she; the Neelakesi's sage meets a full display of wiles with one question, what are these to us.
teaches: The Naladiyar's dissection is a method for one still tempted, while the sage needs no method; and since this beauty is a demoness's borrowed shape, the Naladiyar's question of where the woman is in the body has, here, a literal answer: nowhere.

gains.a: the sage's bare dismissal is shown to stand where a quatrain needs a whole argument
gains.b: the quatrain's rhetorical question gains a scene in which the alluring body truly belongs to no woman

note: Both call birth a sickness with a medicine: the Neelakesi's sage names the medicine as dharma that cuts the diseases of birth; Pattinathar names it as never forgetting the lotus feet of the Lord of the Tillai hall.
teaches: The two traditions agree on the diagnosis and part on the cure: the Jain medicine is a dharma one takes up oneself with no god named, while the Siddhar's medicine is remembrance of the Lord's feet.

gains.a: the Jain sermon's medicine is set against a Saiva one, showing that it names no saviour
gains.b: the Siddhar's medicine of the feet is seen as one answer among rival cures for the same disease

note: The Neelakesi's sage counts four states of birth (நாற்கதி); Aravanar in the Manimekalai counts six kinds of living beings: humans, gods, Brahmas, hell-beings, animals and ghosts.
teaches: The rival epics disagree even on how many destinies there are, so a reader comparing their karma teaching must first map the Jain four gatis onto the Buddhist six realms.

note: The Neelakesi's sage says the hells are seven (ஏழாய்) and spread into eighty-four hundred thousand dwellings; the Manimekalai's goddess summons the eight kinds of hell-beings (எண் வகை நரகர்) within the Chakravala.
teaches: The two epics count the hells differently, seven earths stacked below the world against eight kinds of hell-dwellers within one world-system, so hell's shape is itself a point of sectarian difference.
audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 76 lines 3-4 (முழுச்செவி கிண்ணர்கள், முவ்வாதம்) are hard to construe.

note: In 64 the sage sees privately that the woman before him is a demon's daughter, not a princess; in 88 he lets it show in one word, நுமர் (your kin), among the demon class of the Vyantara gods.
teaches: The sage's knowledge of her true form, held silent in 64, becomes a tool of teaching: he names her kind inside a list of gods, so the cosmology itself unmasks her, and then defers it to keep her listening.
audit_text_issue: 64 is printed with the number 6; line 3 is obscure.

note: 83 denies that great penance raises the humans of the small islands; 86 says penance frees the humans of the land of deeds.
teaches: Penance is not a power that works anywhere: in this sermon its fruit depends on the land of one's birth, so the same act frees in one land and fails in another.

note: In 74 the sage promised to tell birth, its disease, and the medicine that cuts that disease; 86 names the medicine as penance that drives out the dark karma.
teaches: The promised medicine for birth turns out to be penance, and it is offered only to humans of the land of deeds, so the cure is narrower than the promise first sounded.

note: The sermon's hell names 'the sin of eating flesh' beside 'the sin of killing'; in 163 Neelakesi's first charge against the Buddha's way is that he does not call eating flesh a fault.
teaches: The hell scene supplies the doctrinal ground for the first debate: because eating is a sin apart from killing, a school that permits meat not killed by the eater stands accused before any metaphysics is argued.

note: Kural 255 says hell will not open its mouth to release the flesh-eater; Neelakesi 97 shows the flesh-eater burning inside the fire's mouth, crying out.
teaches: The couplet's closed mouth of hell, read beside the epic, becomes a place one is held and burned in, and the epic shows that the Kural's verdict falls on the eater as a sinner in his own right, not only on the killer.

gains.a: the epic's charge against eating flesh gains the Kural's warrant that eating, not only killing, keeps one in hell
gains.b: the couplet's bare image of a mouth that will not open gains a picture of what is suffered inside it

note: Tirumular puts in fire-mouthed hell those who said 'kill, stab'; the Neelakesi puts there those who ate the flesh as well as those who killed.
teaches: A Saiva and a Jain text each carry the guilt of a killing beyond the hand that strikes, one back to the man who ordered it and the other forward to the man who eats, so between them the whole chain around a death is held to account.

gains.a: the Jain charge against the eater is seen as one case of a wider rule of shared guilt that a Saiva text also holds
gains.b: Tirumular's extension of guilt to the speaker gains its counterpart in the consumer, which he leaves to his next verse on flesh

note: The Neelakesi's hell has no one to relieve the sufferer (பரிபவரும் இல்லையே); Arunagirinathar asks Murugan to come at speed when Death would drop him into the seven hells, so that his sins go.
teaches: The two answer opposite ways whether anyone can stand between a sinner's deeds and hell: the Jain sermon says no one can, the Murugan song asks that the god do exactly that; the conflict holds if பரிபவர் means one who relieves or rescues.

gains.a: the Jain hell's lack of a rescuer is seen as a stance against the hope of divine rescue that Tamil devotion voices
gains.b: the devotee's plea is seen against a doctrine for which such a plea has no one to hear it

audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 1244 has several corrupt words and is flagged uncertain.

note: Naladiyar 37 says the gains of human birth are many and should be used for the world beyond; Neelakesi 86 says only the humans of the land of deeds can reach bliss by penance.
teaches: The quatrain treats human birth as one opportunity, while the epic splits humanity by land and says the gain of release belongs only to those born where deeds and penance are possible.

gains.a: the epic's cosmological sorting of humans gains an ethical point: it matters where one is born because only there can the human gain be used
gains.b: the quatrain's general 'gains of human birth' gains a limit it does not state, that not every human birth carries them

audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 86 line 1 'ஆவிதையம்' is unclear and may be corrupt. | 86 flagged uncertain; ஆவிதையம் may be corrupt.

note: The invocation praises the god whose word removes the suffering of souls; the sermon names that word's content as a medicine of three parts the soul takes.
teaches: The invocation's claim that the god ends suffering by his word, not by intervening, is made concrete here: the cure is a discipline the hearer takes, so the god's role stays that of teacher.

note: The invocation says Neelakesi was a demoness of harm whose heart turned; the teacher, describing demons as fire to all, exempts her from her own kind.
teaches: Her conversion is acknowledged inside the sermon itself, which uses her former kind as its example of harm while addressing her as one already changed.

note: The sermon lists killing for spirits and gods among the beasts' deaths; in the Veda debate Neelakesi tells the Vedic disputant that killings for the Vasus, Rudras and ancestors bring hard karma on the killers.
teaches: The sermon counts the sacrifice from the victim's side and the later debate from the sacrificer's, so the Jain case against the rite is made twice: the beast suffers, and the deed returns on the one who kills.

note: The Kural ranks abstaining from one killing above a thousand sacrifices; the Neelakesi lists the Vedic sacrifice among the deaths that make a beast's birth a suffering.
teaches: The couplet weighs sacrifice and abstention as merits for the actor and leaves the rite standing as a lesser good; the Jain sermon removes it from the scale of merit by counting it as a harm to the slain beast.

gains.a: the sermon's charge is seen as a sharpening of an older Tamil ranking that already put non-killing above the rite
gains.b: the couplet's comparison is shown to be open to the harder reading that sacrifice is itself a killing, which a Jain teacher draws

note: The Naladiyar's fool hails a pot of filth as a woman because of its skin; the Neelakesi's men perish for a filthy body worm-filled under its cover.
teaches: The quatrain rests its case on disgust alone, while the sermon sets the same disgust beside the evil rebirth and the stained lineage, so the impure body becomes one of three reckonings a restrained man makes rather than the whole argument.

gains.a: the sermon's compressed image of the covered body is explained by the quatrain's fuller picture of skin hiding the openings
gains.b: the quatrain's single argument from the body's foulness is placed within a teaching of rebirth and family honour it does not state

note: The Kural says pain perishes when the names of desire, anger and confusion perish; the Neelakesi names anger, pride, deceit and attachment as the very pains of the unrestrained.
teaches: Both make the passions the root of suffering, but they count them differently: the Kural's three (desire, anger, confusion) against the Jain four (anger, pride, deceit, attachment), so pride and deceit, absent from the couplet, are for the Jain teacher as basic as anger.

gains.a: the Jain list is seen against an older Tamil triad and shows what it adds, pride and deceit
gains.b: the couplet's triad is shown to be one count among rival counts of the passions, not the only Tamil one

note: Both call the cure of the soul a medicine that leaves it clear: in the Neelakesi the soul takes the three remedies of knowledge, clear faith and conduct; in Tirumular the mind becomes clear when Nandi gives grace, like a madman cured by medicine.
teaches: The shared image of medicine and clarity hides opposed accounts of who heals: for the Jain sermon clarity is one of the remedies the soul swallows itself, for Tirumular it is the effect of the Lord's grace, and on the Jain reading no giver of grace is needed.

gains.a: the sermon's godless remedy is seen as a real alternative to a Tamil account of release by grace that uses the same image
gains.b: the verse's claim that clarity is given, not achieved, is sharpened by a rival who makes clarity something the soul takes

note: The Kural tells the healer to find the disease, its source and the means that subdue it; the Neelakesi sermon classifies suffering as disease in 109-113 and then names its remedy.
teaches: The sermon follows the physician's order the couplet sets down, diagnosis by kinds before the cure, and applies it to the disease of birth, so the Kural's medical rule serves as the shape of a religious argument.

gains.a: the sermon's long classification of harms is seen to have a purpose, the diagnosis that must precede the remedy
gains.b: the couplet's method is shown at work outside medicine, governing how a teacher reasons about suffering itself

note: The Vedic logician in the Manimekalai defines perception as fivefold sense knowledge; the Neelakesi's teacher counts as perception also avadhi, manahparyaya and kevala, knowledge without the senses.
teaches: The two epics define the same first means of knowledge incompatibly: for the logician perception ends at the five senses, for the Jain it reaches up to omniscience, which is what lets the Jain claim an all-knowing teacher as a source of valid knowledge.

note: The Manimekalai's Vedic logician lists comparison, scripture, presumption and other means beside perception and inference; the Neelakesi's teacher lists memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and scripture.
teaches: Both lists keep inference and scripture, but the Jain list admits memory and recognition as valid knowledge and leaves out comparison and presumption, so the count of means is itself a point of difference between the schools the epics stage.

note: The Kural asks what a householder living in dharma gains by taking the outside way; the Neelakesi grades conduct as complete or partial.
teaches: If the partial conduct is the householder's, as Jain usage suggests, the sermon accepts the household as a path of dharma but ranks it below renunciation, which is just the ranking the couplet's question refuses.

gains.a: the sermon's bare division into two grades is seen to answer a Tamil claim of the householder's equal standing
gains.b: the couplet's rhetorical question is shown meeting a rival that grants the household dharma yet calls it incomplete

note: At 63 she bears a form made to be desired so as to shake his penance; at 128 the sage answers that the same limbs are three different things to the lustful, the ascetic and the jackal.
teaches: The sermon on the body is a direct reply to the disguise: the form chosen to excite desire is answered by showing that desirability lies in the seer, so the trick fails at its root.

note: Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, blood, bone and skin and asks which of these is the garlanded woman; Neelakesi 128 lists the woman's beauties and says lovers, ascetics and jackals each see something else in them.
teaches: The quatrain dissolves the beloved into parts, while the epic keeps the parts whole and moves the difference to the viewer, so the two give two routes to the same detachment: analysis of the object and analysis of the gaze.

gains.a: the sage's three viewers gain the anatomical list that says what the ascetic and the jackal actually see
gains.b: the quatrain's question gains a speaker and an addressee, a sage telling it to the woman herself

note: Manimekalai shows the prince an old woman's body and says flowers, sandal, cloth and jewels hide its flesh; the Neelakesi's sage tells the adorned woman herself that her bath, scents, jewels and garlands only cover filth with skin.
teaches: The Buddhist and Jain epics use one argument with the roles reversed: in the Manimekalai a woman ascetic cures a man's lust, in the Neelakesi a male ascetic rebuffs a woman's, and here the body he unmasks is itself a borrowed disguise.

note: Both speakers refuse to be swayed by praise of a woman's beauty because they have seen bones in the burning ground: the Naladiyar's speaker has seen the scattered teeth, the Neelakesi's sage lives among the bones.
teaches: The quatrain's resolve rests on having once seen the burning ground; the sage's rests on dwelling there, so the pair shows the same defence held as a memory and as a way of life.

gains.a: the sage's boast gains the quatrain's precise point that beauty praised as jasmine and pearl ends as scattered teeth
gains.b: the quatrain's resolve is shown put to a real test, a supernatural temptress who chose the burning ground's own sage

note: At 59 she takes the form of the princess Kamalekai to tempt the sage; at 134 she casts off that illusory form, takes her own, and asks pardon as a demon.
teaches: The disguise put on to break his vow is the first thing she gives up, so conversion begins with the end of deception and confession of her real nature, before any doctrine is taken.

note: Kural 579 calls it the highest disposition to show kindly regard to and bear with even those whose way is to hurt one; the Neelakesi's sage is likened to a mother who in excess of kindly regard (கழிகண்ணோட்டம்) suckles the infant that hurts her.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's high virtue an image and a result: the forbearance is maternal, and it converts the one who came to harm, which the couplet's rule does not promise.

gains.a: the mother simile gains a name in the ethics books, கண்ணோட்டம் extended to those who harm
gains.b: the couplet's virtue is shown working on an attacker who then gives up her violence

note: At 55 the narrator tells how her terrors of elephant, tiger and lion failed to frighten him and she gave up; at 137 she herself sings that he stayed unshaken when she made the forest rise against him.
teaches: The failed assault becomes, in the attacker's own mouth, a title of praise, so the story's earlier defeat is retold as the ground of her devotion.

note: Kural 314 says the punishment for those who hurt you is to shame them by doing them good; Neelakesi 138 says the sage made her, who came to kill him, bow by his virtues alone.
teaches: The epic shows the couplet's punishment by goodness carried through to its end: the would-be killer is not only shamed but turned into a worshipper and, two verses later, an advocate.

gains.a: her confession gains the couplet's frame, in which his forbearance is a form of punishment and not passivity
gains.b: the couplet's counsel gains a case in which the wrongdoer was a deadly enemy and the result was conversion

note: The Siddhar verse names the Lord as the one who opened his fire-eye and burned Kama; the Neelakesi's hymn says the sage in anger reduced Ananga to white ash.
teaches: A Jain hymn takes the Saiva god's signature deed and gives it to a human ascetic, so the victory over desire that the Saiva texts reserve for the Lord is claimed as something a man achieves by penance.

gains.a: the Jain epithet is seen as a borrowing from the Saiva stock of praise, pointed against it
gains.b: the Siddhar's image of the Lord is shown contested by a school that gives his deed to the ascetic

note: Kural 340 asks whether the life lodging in the body has no home of its own; Neelakesi 140 praises the sage who, while rain beat on him and poisonous creatures crawled over him, knew himself to be other than the body.
teaches: The couplet's doubtful question about the soul's lodging becomes in the epic a settled conviction that is practised: knowing the self is other than the body is what lets the ascetic bear the body's torments.

gains.a: the sage's endurance gains the couplet's image of the soul as a lodger, which explains why bodily suffering does not touch him
gains.b: the couplet's question gains an answer from a school that holds soul and body distinct and turns that into discipline

note: Pattinathar searches hair, skin, blood, bone and worms for the 'I', finds it nowhere, and says that only when the Lord's grace came did he see himself; the Neelakesi praises an ascetic who knows himself other than the body by his own steadfast penance.
teaches: Both hold that the self is not the body, but the Saiva poet reaches that knowledge only by grace while the Jain sage reaches it by enduring, so the shared insight hides a disagreement about how it is won.

gains.a: the Jain claim gains a sharp contrast that shows it needs no god for the knowledge of the self
gains.b: the Siddhar's turn to grace is shown to be a choice, since another school claimed the same insight without it

note: Tirumanthiram 1616 makes Siva the renouncer who dwells in the burning ground and cuts off the births of those who renounce; Neelakesi 141 praises the ascetic who in the burning ground uprooted all his own karmas.
teaches: The same dwelling place holds two answers to who ends rebirth: in the Saiva verse the god of the burning ground cuts the renouncer's births, in the Jain hymn the renouncer there uproots his karma himself, a disagreement that turns on reading பல்வினையும் பறிப்போய் as his own karma.

gains.a: the hymn's self-won release is set against the Saiva alternative it implicitly excludes
gains.b: Tirumular's burning-ground renouncer-god is shown to answer a rival model in which no god is needed

note: Kural 10 says those who reach the Lord's feet swim the great sea of births; Neelakesi 147 says souls sunk in the sea of sorrow, born among beasts and in hells, should take refuge in the guileless great one.
teaches: The epic names what the couplet leaves open: the sea is filled with the births of beasts and hells, and the feet are those of the Jina, so a Jain teacher reads the Kural's refuge as his own.

gains.a: the sage's call to refuge gains the Kural's image of crossing, which shows refuge as escape from rebirth
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord is given a sectarian identity and its sea a list of states

note: At 148 the sage gives as her atonement the task of making the Jina's path clear; at 163 she chooses the Buddha's path, which does not call flesh-eating a fault, as the first to subdue.
teaches: The debates of the rest of the poem are her penance: the commission given as expiation for her violence is carried out first against the school she charges with tolerating killing for food.

note: Purananuru 34 cites dharma as granting expiation (கழுவாய்) for killing cows, destroying unborn children and wronging elders, but none for ingratitude; in Neelakesi 148 the demoness asks expiation for her sins and is told to teach the Jina's path.
teaches: Both assume that grave wrongs admit expiation, but the Sangam maxim treats it as a provision of dharma with exceptions while the Jain sage turns it into a lifelong mission of persuasion.

gains.a: the sage's command gains the older Tamil idea of a fixed expiation, against which its novelty shows
gains.b: the maxim's list of expiable wrongs is shown to admit a case, killing and the will to kill, met by teaching rather than rite

note: Both use the sea of births: the Kural's பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல், crossed by reaching the Lord's feet; the Neelakesi's sea of the souls' own evil deeds, crossed on a raft the Jina made.
teaches: The Jain hymn fills in what the couplet leaves open: the sea is made of the swimmer's own deeds, and the Lord's part is to build the raft, not to hold the swimmer.

gains.a: the hymn's raft is seen answering a Tamil formula in which reaching the god is the only way across
gains.b: the couplet's bare verb 'reach the feet' is shown to admit a reading in which reaching means following a path one must travel oneself

note: Both say that the two kinds of deed, good and evil, leave the soul: in the Kural, for those who love the Lord's true praise; in the Neelakesi, by the way the Jina taught under the asoka tree.
teaches: Sung in the middle of Neelakesi's own praise, the verse credits release from both deeds to the teaching the Jina gave, not to the praise itself, which the couplet makes sufficient.

gains.a: the hymn's claim that merit too must go is matched by an older Tamil statement that both deeds are bonds
gains.b: the couplet's 'true praise' (பொருள்சேர் புகழ்) is shown being read as praise of a teaching to be followed

note: Both speak of the two deeds (இருவினை) and their ending: the Jina taught the way they part; Tirumular says that when they balance, grace-power comes as the guru and one's own doing ends.
teaches: On the same pair of deeds the Jain hymn gives the teacher only the role of telling the way, while Tirumular makes the guru a descent of grace that ends the soul's own agency.

gains.a: the hymn's silence about grace becomes visible as a position once set beside a text that makes grace the agent
gains.b: the Saiva doctrine of the balanced deeds is seen against a release in which no power descends and the soul does the work

note: Both praise the highest being as victor over Death: Siva kicked Death and became king of the south; the Jina passed beyond Death (காலனைக் கடந்தாய்) along with desire, aging and birth.
teaches: The same victory over Death means a deed of force against another being in the Saiva invocation and a leaving-behind of one's own mortal condition in the Jain hymn.

gains.a: the hymn's war imagery is seen as borrowed from a praise tradition that told the victory as combat
gains.b: the kick of the invocation is set against a victory that requires no enemy outside the self

note: Neelakesi's first charge against the Buddha is that he does not count eating flesh a fault; the couplet argues that flesh is sold only because people eat it.
teaches: The couplet supplies the reason a Jain debater can blame the flesh-eater who kills nothing: the eating is what causes the killing, so silence on eating is silence on killing.

gains.a: the bare charge in the verse gains the argument by which it is pressed later in the Neelakesi
gains.b: the couplet's market argument is seen aimed at a school's actual position in Tamil debate

note: Neelakesi charges that the Buddha does not count enduring austerity a vow; the Kundalakesi fragment calls bodily mortifications, nakedness among them, mere words, and puts tapas in restrained living.
teaches: The Buddhist fragment confirms the position the Jain debater attacks but shows it as a relocation of austerity into conduct, not the plain denial of austerity the charge describes.

gains.a: the Jain charge is seen against the opponent's own words
gains.b: the fragment's list of empty practices is shown to have a Jain target that the Neelakesi takes up

audit_text_issue: kundalakesi:4 line 4 reading uncertain; fragment speaker unnamed

note: Neelakesi sets out to debate in order to do compassion (தயா செய்தற் பொருட்டாக); in the debate she asks whether one who let his own calf die has compassion (தயா) for others.
teaches: The debate is a contest over who owns compassion: the Jain debater's mission is framed as தயா, and her attack denies the Buddha the same virtue.
audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 165 runs on into 166, and its city and pearl seat are unclear.

note: Kundalakesi will not speak without a great prize for the winner; in 230 the winner, Neelakesi, refuses every gift the king offers and asks only that he keep to dharma.
teaches: The stake Kundalakesi demanded turns against her twice: she suffers the loser's penalty, and the victor shows by refusing the prize that the Jain side did not argue for gain.

note: The king pledges to drive out the losers that day; in 228 the beaten Kundalakesi is drummed out of the city gate.
teaches: The penalty the debaters agreed to at the start is carried out exactly, so the debate is framed as a binding royal trial and not a mere exchange of views.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:174 line 4 is garbled at its opening (கிறப்பவும் பெருதுவந்தார்); the link does not rest on it.

note: The invocation praises as god only the one who knows all (எல்லா முணர்ந்தான்); verse 193 denies that the Buddha knew without remainder (ஒழிவின்றி யுணர்கலான்).
teaches: The invocation's definition of god by omniscience is not only praise but the premise of the debate: it becomes the test by which the rival teacher's book is ruled out as scripture.

note: The Buddhist teacher in the Manimekalai accepts only two means of knowledge, perception and inference; Neelakesi says a teacher who knew only through the senses and reasoning lacks subtle knowledge and his word is no scripture.
teaches: The same restriction to perception and inference that the Buddhist offers as rigour is, from the Jain side, the proof that its founder was not omniscient and so cannot ground a scripture.

note: The Manimekalai names the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness); Neelakesi says three of them are modes of knowing, leaving two.
teaches: Set beside the Buddhist's own list, the Jain attack is seen to aim at the split of consciousness from feeling, perception and volition, collapsing the person into a knower and form, which is the Jain soul and matter by another route.

teaches: The Buddhist offers the lightning-flash mind as a manner of speaking about what has no lasting being, while the Jain treats it as a claim about a knower and asks who is left to witness the flash's end.

teaches: A homely image of borrowed fragrance served Tamil writers for transmission without identity, and the Jain debater shows that the image cuts both ways, since a scent that outlives its flower can be claimed for an enduring soul.

note: The Kural says the loving belong to others even to their bones; Kundalakesi lists the Buddha's literal gifts of eyes, body, wife and child as proof of his compassion.
teaches: The couplet's figure of giving one's bones becomes in the birth-stories a literal record of bodily gifts, and the pairing shows where the figure turns contestable: once it includes wife and child, the Jain opponent can call it madness rather than love.

note: The Kundalakesi invocation praises its lord as one who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good; Neelakesi calls the stories of the Buddha's self-giving the doings of the deluded and possessed.

note: Purananuru 43 praises a Chola as descendant of the king of limitless giving who entered the scales to save a dove from a hawk; Neelakesi says no living person asks for another's flesh, eyes or head.
teaches: The gift of one's own flesh to a creature in distress, a dynastic boast in Sangam praise and a credential of compassion for the Buddhist, is denied any worth by the Jain debater's test of need, so Tamil tradition did not hold it as a settled virtue.

gains.b: the poem's ancestral boast is shown to have met a reasoned challenge in a later work

note: The Kundalakesi's invocation praises its lord as one who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good (பிறர்க்கே உறுதிக்கு உழந்தான்); Neelakesi 222 mocks the monkey-king's self-offering, which saved no one, as no greatness.
teaches: The dispute is not whether the Buddha gave himself away but whether labour for others counts when, as the Jain argues, it profits no one; the Buddhist praise rests on intention, the Jain rebuttal on result.
