note: Flesh eaten by birds: the Kundalakesi fragment shows vultures and dogs tearing the desired body; Neelakesi 214 says flesh cut off as a gift feeds only crows.
teaches: The same carrion image serves the Buddhist as a reason to stop desiring the body and the Jain as a reason not to throw it away, so contempt for the body and refusal to waste it come from one picture.

note: Kural 221 defines giving as giving to those who have nothing; Neelakesi 214 argues that a gift of flesh or an eye cannot become the receiver's and so fills no lack.
teaches: The Kural fixes a gift's worth by the receiver's want; the debate adds that the gift must also be usable by the receiver, which rules out the heroic gifts of the body.

gains.a: the Jain objection gains a recognised Tamil definition of giving to argue from
gains.b: the couplet's want-based test is extended to what is given, not only to whom

note: Kural 230 says death is sweet when one can no longer give; Neelakesi 218 says a death known to achieve nothing is no virtue, and draws the wife on the pyre as the absurd consequence.
teaches: The Kural's rank of giving above life is hyperbole about value; the Jain argument shows where taking it literally leads, and limits the praise of self-loss to a death that does something.

gains.a: the epic's limit on self-sacrifice is seen answering a Tamil maxim that ranks giving above living
gains.b: the couplet's hyperbole is shown needing a boundary once epics told of givers who literally died

note: Perunkoppendu argues for her place on her husband's pyre against the elders who hold her back; Neelakesi 218 cites the wife who burns with her guardian husband as the futile death no one should call virtue.
teaches: The Sangam queen gives the pyre a reason, escape from the widow's diet and gravel bed, that the Jain reductio ignores when it calls such death one that achieves nothing; the two disagree on what the wife's death is for.

gains.a: the epic's 'nothing comes of it' is tested against a widow who says exactly what comes of it
gains.b: the queen's choice is seen being cited later as the standard case of a death a moral argument rejects

note: Aathirai enters the pyre to go where her husband's deeds have carried him, but the fire will not touch her and a voice says he lives; Neelakesi 218 names the wife's death with her husband as the absurd end of praising futile death.
teaches: Neither epic lets a wife's death on the pyre stand as achieved virtue, the Jain by argument and the Buddhist by a fire that refuses her, yet the Manimekalai gives the karmic motive the Neelakesi's reductio leaves out.

note: Kundalakesi lists her lord's gifts of eyes, flesh, body, wife, land, child and heaven (205); the king's verdict in 224 calls those birth-tales fabrications of a one-sided teacher.
teaches: The debate is settled not by refuting each gift but by the king reclassifying the whole catalogue as fiction, so the Buddhist's chief proof of compassion is turned into the proof of one-sidedness.

note: Before the debate the king promised to send the loser out with shame (174); in 228 the townspeople drive Kundalakesi out of the gate with drums and insults.
teaches: The expulsion is the execution of a stake both debaters accepted with joy beforehand, so the shame is the contract of the debate rather than the mob's cruelty.

teaches: Each defeat in the Neelakesi names the next opponent, so the chain of debates is built by the losers' own testimony of who taught them.

teaches: The visitor who turns a king's favour into counsel persists from bardic to religious poetry, but the counsel shifts from ruling with grace to following a doctrine, and the refusal of gifts becomes a renouncer's mark.

gains.a: Neelakesi's scene is seen as a known Tamil form, the counsel given in place of a gift
gains.b: the Sangam form of counsel to a king is shown carried into a sectarian epic where the adviser wants nothing

note: 242 announces that Arkkachandra should hear the deceits (சலம்) bound up with the Buddhist vows; 249 ends the list by asking whether such a rule is not deceit (சலமதோ).
teaches: The frame word shows that verses 243 to 249 are one indictment, so obscure items like the courtesan and Simhadatta verses belong to a single charge of sophistry rather than to separate anecdotes.

note: 246 sets out the no-soul doctrine against the Buddhist talk of a being who relieves pain and wins release; 248 cites a Buddhist assembly that recites that a person exists.
teaches: Neelakesi answers the no-soul claim not with Jain doctrine but with a split inside Buddhism, so the debate uses the opponent's own schools as witnesses.

note: Aravana Adigal teaches that seeing that no thing has a self (எப்பொருளுக்கும் ஆன்மா இலை) is the nature of release; Neelakesi asks how release and relief of pain fit a teaching that there is no soul.
teaches: The Buddhist epic makes no-self the content of release, while the Jain epic treats the same doctrine as making release impossible, since for it someone must be freed; the two verses disagree on whether release needs a subject.

note: The Kundalakesi praises the Buddha as one who kept nothing for himself and toiled only for others; Neelakesi takes the bodhisattva's gift of himself and his wives as proof of a man bound by nothing.
teaches: The same total self-giving is the Buddhist invocation's ground of worship and the Jain debater's first charge, which shows the quarrel was over whether others (a wife) can be given as one's own.

note: The Kundalakesi calls covering or stripping the body, ash, cold, fire, alms and matted hair mere words, and true tapas a subdued life; Neelakesi asks whether the Buddhist rules of eating, shaving and kohl are dharma.
teaches: Both schools use the same test, that outward discipline is not the path, and each turns it on the other: the Buddhist verse includes the Jain's nakedness among empty forms, and the Jain debater counts the Vinaya's grooming among them.

gains.a: the debater's objection is shown to rest on taking the void as mere absence, which another Tamil tradition denies
gains.b: the Siddhar's call to cling to the void is set against the strongest objection to it, that no one desires an empty release

teaches: The debate turns on the source of authority: the Buddhist attacks the categories by their origin in one mind, and the Jain defends them by the teacher's nature, so neither touches the categories themselves.

teaches: The Jain categories circulated as a fixed formula that both sects' epics quote; the Buddhist epic lets a Jain recite it and moves on, while the Jain epic puts it in a Buddhist's mouth so that its defence can follow.

note: The Kural says neither shaving nor matted hair is needed if one avoids what the world condemns; Mokkalan grants the robe only the small use of making the monk known, and Neelakesi asks what such a sign is for.
teaches: The Kural's dismissal of ascetic marks becomes a live weapon between sects: the Jain debater uses it against the Buddhist robe, while her own tradition's nakedness is a mark of another kind.

gains.a: Neelakesi's question about the robe is seen to rest on an accepted Tamil maxim that outward marks are not the test of renunciation
gains.b: the couplet's general maxim is shown being turned by one order against another's dress, a use it does not foresee

note: The Kural says outer purity (புறந்தூய்மை) comes by water and inner purity by truth; Neelakesi lists water, betel and the tooth-stick and says that if outer cleaning purified the mind, courtesans would be the purest.
teaches: The couplet's two-part rule is turned into a reductio: Neelakesi supplies the absurd case that proves outer and inner purity are separate, and aims it at monks who tend their robes.

gains.a: Neelakesi's jibe gains a recognised rule behind it, so the courtesan example reads as proof rather than insult
gains.b: the couplet gains a counter-example that shows why water cannot reach the mind, which it states without argument

note: Tirumular keeps the body because without it true knowledge cannot be won; Neelakesi cites as common knowledge that the body lives by food and awareness by the body.
teaches: The same chain, food to body to knowledge, serves opposite ends: Tirumular uses it to justify cultivating the body, while Neelakesi uses it to say the renouncer needs food and nothing more.

gains.a: Neelakesi's proverb is shown to be a premise other traditions also build on, not her private argument
gains.b: Tirumular's case for nurturing the body is shown limited by a rival use of the same premise, where it licenses only bare food

note: Sivavakkiyar mocks the ochre-wearers with matted hair, water-pots and yoga staffs who leave their wives and beg from house to house; Neelakesi mocks the monk who boils and dyes his cloth as though he had only given up cooking rice.
teaches: Jain and Siddhar both ridicule the ochre-robed renouncer, but for opposite failings: Sivavakkiyar faults him for abandoning home duties, Neelakesi for carrying them on in the monastery.

gains.a: Neelakesi's joke is seen to belong to a wider Tamil satire of the ochre robe, aimed here at its labour rather than its begging
gains.b: Sivavakkiyar's charge that the renouncer abandons home is set against a charge that he never left it

note: The Kural says that one who restrains the five senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs is protected through seven births; Neelakesi says the monk should guard the eyes that stir the mind instead of covering his limbs.
teaches: The tortoise image of drawing in the limbs is exactly what Neelakesi denies is restraint when done with cloth: she moves the Kural's withdrawal from the body to the senses, against the robe.

gains.a: her charge gains a standard of restraint the Buddhist side would also grant, so the robe can be judged by it
gains.b: the couplet's figure is shown to need a reading, since hiding the limbs literally is what she calls weakness

note: The Manimekalai's Jain speaker says dharma pervades everything and makes things move (பொருள்களை நடத்தும்); Neelakesi calls the reading 'we move by dharma' a quibble and says dharma lets things move as the sea lets a ship go, without pushing.
teaches: A Jain debater rejects as a misreading the very wording a Buddhist epic puts in a Jain's mouth: dharma is a condition of motion, not a mover, a distinction the Buddhist report blurs.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain says time makes the short occurrence called கணிகம் and the long one of கற்பம்; Neelakesi throws the same two words at the Buddhist who denies time while using them.
teaches: The pair கணிகம் and கற்பம் was the Jain definition of time, so when Neelakesi mocks the Buddhist for speaking of moments she is pointing out that the word for his momentariness belongs to a doctrine of time he rejects.

note: Both give the Jain doctrine that a thing persists in kind while its form arises and perishes: the Manimekalai's Jain with gram cooked into a dish and the sprouting neem, Neelakesi with a gold pot remade as a crown, applied to the soul passing from man to god.
teaches: On arising, persistence and destruction the Buddhist epic's report of the Jains matches a Jain debater's own illustration, so here the polemical account is one the school would accept, and the Neelakesi shows it was aimed at the soul's rebirth.

note: Neelakesi says the Buddhist has no space of measureless extent; the Manimekalai's teacher of logic names both 'one who says space is unreal' and 'one who says it is real' as parties to an argument, without taking a side there.
teaches: The Buddhist manual treats the reality of space as a disputed thesis between parties, while the Jain debater fixes the denial on the Buddhist and draws its cost, that the world then has no edge.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher says the first Jina (in Buddhist usage, the Buddha) taught only two means of knowledge, perception and inference; Neelakesi answers that on that rule there could be no medical treatise that cures disease.
teaches: The Buddhist rule of two means of knowledge, stated as doctrine in one epic, meets in the other a counter-case from medicine, showing that the dispute over scripture as a means of knowledge was argued in Tamil from practical knowledge, not only from revelation.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness) as what is spoken of as a person; Neelakesi names feeling, cognition, perception and action (உழப்பு, அறிவு, குறி, செய்கை) and says they belong to one being.
teaches: The Jain debater accepts the Buddhist list of the four mental aggregates term for term and disputes only whether they have one owner, so the quarrel over the self is about ownership of the aggregates, not about what they are.

note: In the opening sermon the sage tells the worshippers that a child's body comes from blood and its life from former deeds; here Neelakesi explains how the soul takes up the father's seed and the mother's blood and grows within the body.
teaches: The sage's bare division between a body from the parents and a life from former deeds is filled in by the debate with the mechanism of conception that lets the Jain deny any god a part in it.

note: Neelakesi says that if only perception and inference counted there could be no medical treatise; the Kural's chapter on medicine states the three humours on the authority of the learned in the books (நூலோர்).
teaches: The Kural's deference to the medical books for the three humours is just the kind of text-borne knowledge the Jain debater cites: neither the patient's sight nor his inference gives it.

gains.a: the debater's appeal to medicine gets a Tamil instance in which a moral book takes medical doctrine on its authors' word
gains.b: the couplet's passing reference to நூலோர் is seen to carry a view of knowledge that a rival school in Tamil denied

note: Neelakesi rejects the Buddhist rule that the sin of killing attaches only where there is intention; the Kural argues that if none killed to eat, none would sell flesh for a price.
teaches: The Kural's buyer-and-seller argument is the reply the intention defence needs: the eater need intend no killing for his eating to cause one, so a rule that weighs only intention misses the chain from buyer to slaughter.

gains.a: Neelakesi's bare charge that the sin reaches the eater gets a causal argument behind it
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed opponent is identified as a live doctrine, that sin requires the intent to kill

note: The objection in Neelakesi 316 is that if pleasure and pain are the fruit of deeds, the pain of penance is too; the Kural defines penance as bearing the pain that comes and harming no life.
teaches: The Kural's definition of தவம் as bearing the pain that comes takes away the force of the objection: if penance is endurance of what arrives, it does not matter that the pain is old karma's fruit.

gains.a: the epic's objection meets a Tamil definition of penance that already answers it
gains.b: the couplet's உற்றநோய் is shown to bear on a live dispute about whether penance's pain is only karma ripening

audit_text_issue: 316 line 4 is corrupt; sense of the verse uncertain.

note: Neelakesi says deeds move the soul to its next birth as the wind turns a whirligig; Tirumular says the subtle breath in the soul carries it as wind carries a flower's scent.
teaches: Both answer what carries a soul between bodies with an image of wind, but for the Jain the wind is the deed itself, needing no other mover, while for Tirumular it is the vital breath at the appointed moment, so the same image names karma in one and breath in the other.

gains.a: the whirligig image is set against a Tamil alternative it leaves out, breath as the carrier
gains.b: Tirumular's image is seen as one answer to a question a rival school answered with deeds alone

note: Neelakesi's fiery body enters another body like a shadow; Tirumular's light born in the womb spreads through the earthly body like a bubble in water, a shadow, and the eight take hold.
teaches: Writers of opposed schools both picture the subtle body that passes into a new one as a shadow, which shows they agreed rebirth needs a subtle carrier and differed only on what it is made of, the Jain fiery and karmic bodies or Tirumular's eight.

gains.a: the Jain doctrine of the subtle bodies is seen to have a Saiva counterpart, so the debate does not turn on whether a subtle body exists
gains.b: Tirumular's obscure bubble-and-shadow line gets a plain statement of a shadow-like body entering another

audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 309 line 4 begins டேயுடம்பு, where தேயுடம்பு is expected; Tirumanthiram 472 காவுடைத் தீபம் is obscure.

note: In 238 Neelakesi hears the Vinaya rule of how to shave the head recited in Arkkachandra's monastery; in 318 she cites the same tonsure (தலைமழி) against Mokkalan's claim that bodily hardship is a fault.
teaches: The Vinaya rules she overheard as ritual detail at Ujjain become her evidence that the Buddhist middle way still imposes discipline on the body, so the earlier scene was gathering ammunition.

note: The Manimekalai's drunk pleads with an unwashed Jain ascetic (மண்ணா மேனியன்) that his soul should not suffer in a filthy body; the Neelakesi answers that dirt on the body is nothing to correct, since adornment hinders meditation.
teaches: The unwashed Jain ascetic was a stock target in the Buddhist-Jain quarrel: the Buddhist epic mocks it through a drunkard's pity, and the Jain epic gives the reply, that the filth is the body's own and attending to it is the real distraction.
audit_text_issue: manimekalai:3:82-103 is a merged unit; line 101 கையுதிர்க்கொணம் is a rare form.

note: The Kundalakesi fragment says filth pours from every opening of the body, so no fragrance is to be found in it; the Neelakesi says dirt on the ascetic is simply the human body's nature.
teaches: The Buddhist poet's own premise, that the body is filth through and through, is the ground of the Jain reply: if the body is foul by nature, washing it cannot make it clean, and mocking the unwashed ascetic contradicts the Buddhist's teaching on the body.

note: The Kural asks what other ties (தொடர்ப்பாடு) can remain for those cutting off birth, when even the body is excess; the Neelakesi defends those who teach that at death every tie, even to dharma (அறத்தொடர்ப்பாடு), must go.
teaches: The Kural's list of ties ends at the body, while the Jain teaching carried into the hour of death adds dharma itself to what must be let go, so renunciation's last step is dropping the merit that led there.

gains.a: the Jain teaching of letting go at death is seen to extend a rule the Tamil ethics book already states for the renouncer
gains.b: the couplet's 'further ties' is given a hard case it does not name: the tie to dharma, and a moment, the time of dying

audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 321 line 2 is obscure; the அற/அறம் division in line 1 is ambiguous.

note: 327 promises to establish that refusing flesh is a good deed; 331 completes it by turning the Buddhist view that image-makers and worshippers share merit into the view that killers and eaters share sin.
teaches: Neelakesi's proof against meat is built from the opponent's own devotional practice: once merit can pass to those who stand at a distance from the act, sin can too, and the eater cannot claim to stand clear of the killing.

note: The Kural asks how one who eats another's flesh to swell his own can hold to compassion (அருள்); Neelakesi asks a monk who eats flesh so that his body thickens whether he has any compassion (அருள்).
teaches: The couplet's question, put to anyone, becomes in the debate a charge against a school that makes compassion its centre, so its force is to expose a contradiction inside a teaching rather than to state a general rule.

gains.a: the taunt draws on a rule Tamil readers already held, so it reads as a common standard and not only a sectarian one
gains.b: the couplet is shown aimed at a real opponent who claimed compassion while eating meat, which the couplet alone does not name

note: The Kural says no one would bring meat to sell if the world did not kill to eat; Neelakesi tells the monk who calls buying meat fair that by paying the fishermen daily he wants killing always.
teaches: The couplet's market argument is turned on a particular defence, that meat bought or given is clean of killing, and shown to cover the buyer who pays day after day, so steady demand makes him a party to each killing.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument is seen to rest on a principle already stated in the Tamil ethical canon
gains.b: the couplet's general demand-and-supply claim is applied to the Buddhist rule of meat accepted from others, a case it does not name

note: In 163 Neelakesi resolves to bring down the Buddha's path because he does not call eating flesh a fault; in 335-337 she argues it point by point against Mokkalan.
teaches: The charge stated in one line at the outset of her debates turns out to need a long argument against particular defences, that the killer was hidden, the animal not marked out, and the meat paid for.

note: Saathuvan tells the Naga chief that the faultless forbade liquor and the killing of living beings; Neelakesi argues that those who shun toddy should for the same reason shun flesh.
teaches: The Buddhist epic's own ban joins liquor with killing, not with eating meat, and the Jain debater exploits exactly that gap, asking why the reasoning that forbids toddy stops before flesh.

note: Saathuvan lets the chief stop killing yet still eat beasts that die of old age; Neelakesi holds that flesh is itself a fault and that its renunciation by all would end the killing.
teaches: For the Buddhist story the wrong lies in the killing, so meat from a natural death is allowed, while for the Jain debater eating is wrong in itself because it is what keeps killing going; the two epics draw the line at different acts.
audit_text_issue: manimekalai:16:116 is of uncertain construction, and the sentence runs on to 117.

note: Kural 256 says no one would sell flesh if the world did not kill to eat; Neelakesi says that if all renounced flesh no one would go near killing, and that the teacher who teaches dharma earns its merit.
teaches: The couplet blames the eating world for the killing; the debate adds that a world's eating follows its teachers, so a teacher who permits flesh carries the demand argument's guilt.

gains.a: Neelakesi's bare 'if all renounced it' gains the Kural's market reasoning that links each buyer to the killing
gains.b: the couplet's faceless 'world' gains a concrete cause of its habits, the teacher whose word makes flesh-eating dharma

note: In 260 Neelakesi tells Arkkachandra that the eater shares the butcher's karma whatever his mind; in 344 she meets Mokkalan's same plea of innocent intention with the seller who kills for the price.
teaches: Against two Buddhist teachers the Jain debater answers the defence by intention in two ways, by the butcher's act and by the merchant's motive, so the epic builds a consistent case that the buyer's purpose is the cause.
audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 260 இல்லில்வாழ்பேய் and 344 line 3 ஓவெனு முன் are obscure.

note: The Kundalakesi fragment lists exposure, fire, cold, begging and matted hair as mere words and calls living subdued the true penance; Mokkalan lists sun, rain, fasting and sleeplessness as profitless.
teaches: The Buddhist dismissal of mortification, stated in the fragment as a positive ideal of restraint, appears in the Jain epic only as a negative charge that it can then answer, so the Neelakesi keeps the attack and drops the Buddhist alternative.
audit_text_issue: Kundalakesi 4 is a fragment with an unnamed speaker; the marker flagged its last line uncertain.

note: Pattinattar lists the five fires, lying in water, plucking hair and going without food and says his devotees reached release without them; Mokkalan lists sun, rain, fasting and sleeplessness as bringing no gain.
teaches: Buddhist debater and Saiva poet reject the same austerities for opposite reasons: for Mokkalan pain has no power to free, for Pattinattar the god's name frees without it, so a shared rejection hides a disagreement about what does the freeing.

gains.a: Mokkalan's attack is seen to belong to a wider Tamil rejection of mortification, not only to anti-Jain polemic
gains.b: the poem's list of austerities, which includes plucking the hair, is seen as the Jain practice a Buddhist also attacked, so its claim of a better way enters an existing quarrel

note: Mokkalan says exposure, fasting and sleeplessness bring nothing; Neelakesi replies that the Buddha's own perfections and ascetic rules bring many hardships.
teaches: The Buddhist attack on Jain penance is met not by defending pain but by showing the Buddhist path also prescribes sleeping in the open and eating once, so the quarrel becomes one of degree rather than of principle.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:357 line 2 does not construe cleanly

note: In 282 Neelakesi herself says the body lives by food and awareness by the body; in 357 she mocks the Buddhist claim that cold, heat and hunger keep dharma out of the mind.
teaches: The Jain debater grants that the mind needs a fed body but not that it needs a comfortable one, so her two arguments mark a line between sustaining the body and sparing it.
audit_text_issue: 357 line 2 and 282 line 4 do not construe cleanly.

note: Kural 261 makes bearing pain one half of penance; Mokkalan argues that if wasting the body were good, burning or wasting with disease would also be penance.
teaches: The reductio bites only if the couplet's pain is pain one inflicts on oneself; if it is the pain that comes unsought, the Kural and the Buddhist agree, so the pairing shows that the couplet's word உற்ற decides which side it is on.

gains.a: Mokkalan's argument gains a precise target: a definition of penance in which enduring pain is half the whole
gains.b: the couplet's ambiguity about whose pain is meant is shown to matter, since a rival school's objection falls on one reading and not the other

note: Tirumular says that even burning one's bones as firewood and frying one's flesh does not reach the Lord without melting love; Mokkalan says cutting wounds and leaping from mountains serve no purpose.
teaches: Both reject bodily extremity as the way, but Tirumular keeps it as a measure that love surpasses while Mokkalan declares it simply useless, so the Saiva verse still honours the ascetic's pain where the Buddhist does not.

gains.a: Mokkalan's list gains a Saiva witness that self-torment was a recognised extreme to be gone beyond
gains.b: Tirumular's hyperbole is seen against a debate in which such acts were literally practised and literally attacked

note: Mokkalan says that if self-torment were dharma, mutilation and impalement would be excellent; Neelakesi answers that he praises the bodhisattva for enduring having his flesh cut and his body split.
teaches: The Buddhist's own hero stories contain the very bodily sufferings he ridicules, so the reductio is turned on him: either the bodhisattva's endurance was folly or the Jain's is not.

note: In 214 Neelakesi argues that a gift of flesh or an eye cannot join another's body and so helps no one; in 360 she argues that the gift of the body to a beast kills the many lives within it.
teaches: The Jain case against the bodhisattva's self-giving has two prongs across the debates: the gift is useless to the receiver and murderous to the small lives in the giver, so it fails both as charity and as non-harm.

note: The Kundalakesi fragment calls the body a deed-made thing where swarms of worms small and grown feed and live; Neelakesi says the many lives within the bodhisattva's body die when he gives it to the beast.
teaches: The Buddhist verse uses the body's teeming worms to teach disgust for it, while the Jain debater uses the same teeming body to charge the Buddhist hero's gift with mass killing, so one image serves renunciation on one side and non-harm on the other.

note: The sermon told Neelakesi the fixed beings are of five kinds; here she defends that teaching against a Buddhist by calling trees fixed beings (தாவரம்) that everyone knows to be such.
teaches: The doctrine she received as a convert's lesson becomes the first ground she must hold in open debate, and she defends it by appeal to common usage rather than to the sage's authority.

note: In the Arkkachandra debate she named the felling of living trees among sins that bring hell; here she argues against Mokkalan that trees really are alive.
teaches: The earlier charge that felling a tree is a sin rests on a premise the Buddhists deny, and this passage supplies the argument for it: healing, feeding and withering show the tree to be a soul one can wrong.

note: Both use gram cooked into a mash (கும்மாயம்) as the Jain example of a kind that persists while its form passes; the Manimekalai lets the Jain state it unanswered, the Neelakesi puts it under a Buddhist's attack.
teaches: The same stock example served the two traditions differently: the Buddhist epic records it as the Jain's own illustration and moves on, while the Jain epic has a Buddhist demand to be shown the persisting thing, so the example's weak point is named by the side that wrote it down.
audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 388 line 1 (பயற்றியல்டே) is corrupt. | 388 line 1 பயற்றியல்டே is corrupt.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists impermanence, suffering, no-self and impurity as marks to contemplate in order to cut attachment; Neelakesi names the same four as qualities the Buddhists lay on the aggregates.
teaches: The four marks the Buddhist teacher gives as a meditation for release are read by the Jain debater as predicates of a bearer, so the Buddhist list is turned into evidence for the substance-and-quality relation Mokkalan denies.

note: Mokkalan says that to declare a thing inexpressible is self-contradiction; the Manimekalai's Buddhist teacher counts keeping silent before an ill-formed question as a proper kind of answer.
teaches: The Buddhist in the Jain epic attacks the Jain mode of the inexpressible with an argument his own school, as the Manimekalai presents it, would have to face, since it too treats not saying as an answer.

note: Mokkalan demands that substance and quality be declared either one or different; the Manimekalai's teacher gives a naya of oneness and a naya of difference as two valid ways of seeing cause and effect.
teaches: Mokkalan's either-or is stricter than the Buddhist doctrine the Manimekalai sets out, which itself allows a thing to be viewed as one with its cause under one naya and as different under another, close to the Jain answer he rejects.

note: The Kural likens men without kindly regard to trees fixed in the soil; Neelakesi argues that trees feel heat and cold and change as living bodies do.
teaches: Read with the Jain argument, the couplet's tree is not a dead thing but a living being that feels by touch yet has no eye to look with, which makes the comparison exact for a man who has eyes and does not use them kindly.

gains.a: the Jain claim that trees feel is seen against a Tamil commonplace that used the tree as the very type of the unfeeling
gains.b: the couplet's simile gains a precise sense under the Jain scale of senses: the tree lacks sight, not life

note: The Kural calls it the lowest folly to take what does not last for what lasts; Mokkalan and Neelakesi dispute whether a thing can both last and not last.
teaches: The couplet assumes things fall cleanly into the lasting and the passing, and the debate shows that division itself was contested, the Jain holding one thing lasting in substance and passing in its modes.

gains.a: the debate's technical question is tied to a Tamil moral warning about mistaking the passing for the lasting
gains.b: the couplet's simple contrast is shown to stand on a metaphysical choice the schools did not share

audit_text_issue: The detail of Neelakesi 377 line 2 is unclear. | Neelakesi 377 line 2 காயத்தின் றன்மைய is unclear. | 377 flagged uncertain

note: The Jain in Manimekalai 27 gives gram cooked into கும்மாயம் as his example of a kind that persists while a form passes; in Neelakesi 390 to 391 the Buddhist attacks that very example and Neelakesi defends it.
teaches: The cooked-gram example is shown to be a fixed Jain teaching case known to both sides, so the Buddhist epic's report of Jain doctrine matches what the Jain epic itself has to defend.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:391 line 1 (பாவியுண்டா) is hard to construe

note: Manimekalai's Jain states that every thing takes on origination, persistence and destruction in each instant; Neelakesi 392 has the Buddhist ask what bears those three if they are qualities.
teaches: Manimekalai lets the Jain triad stand unanswered, while the Jain epic shows the Buddhist's actual objection to it, the missing bearer, and the Jain reply in 393 that quality and bearer are one and different.

note: The Vaisheshika in Manimekalai 27 lists substance and quality as separate categories, substance bearing quality; Neelakesi says the quality is the qualified substance itself and the two are both different and one.
teaches: Against the Vaisheshika separation of substance and quality, the Jain refuses both their separateness and their simple identity, so the two schools disagree on whether a quality can be counted apart from its bearer.

note: Manimekalai's Jain says only that the atom, matter (புற்கலம்), is the outward form of things; Neelakesi 395 to 397 defends how atoms become form against the objection that touching atoms must have parts.
teaches: The bare formula in the Buddhist epic hides a live problem, how indivisible atoms can join, which the Jain epic answers with many atoms sharing one place.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:397 flagged uncertain; line 3 comparison with அறிவு obscure

note: Manimekalai's Buddhist teacher gives the hare's horn as the case of what has no arising at all; Neelakesi's Buddhist uses the hare's and donkey's horns to show that some things are non-existent outright.
teaches: The Jain epic's Buddhist argues with the same stock example the Buddhist epic teaches, so here the polemic reproduces Buddhist doctrine fairly before Neelakesi answers it in 405.
audit_text_issue: Why கன்று appears in Neelakesi 404 line 1 is unclear. | Neelakesi 404 line 1 lists கன்று, which is unexplained.

note: Manimekalai's teacher lists modes of usage that rest on what is not (இல்லது சார்ந்த வழக்கு), and pairs cognition with the hare's horn; Neelakesi's Buddhist insists that names and cognitions occur for what does not exist.
teaches: Holding the two together shows the Buddhist claim in 412 rests on a worked-out doctrine of usage, which is what Neelakesi's reply in 413 must deny by appeal to scripture.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:412 line 3 repaired from TSCII; sense uncertain

note: In 243 Neelakesi charges that the bodhisattva gave away his wives and took that as dharma; in 398 the narrator names the Buddhist debater as great in the dharma that gives away women.
teaches: A charge made once in argument has become the narrator's standing epithet for the Buddhist side, so the poem's narration takes Neelakesi's part even in describing the speaker.

note: 392 asks what bears arising, persisting and perishing; 403 applies the answer to the calf and the bull, whose horn arises while the substance persists.
teaches: The abstract triad of 392 to 393 is turned into a test case in 403, which shows what the Jain means by persistence: the animal's substance, not its horn.
audit_text_issue: 403 is uncertain throughout and line 4 'கலைக்கு' is unclear. | 403 flagged uncertain; கலைக்கு (line 4) unclear and the horn is supplied by the marker.

note: Tirumular says the wise gave up disputation (தர்க்க வாதம்) and gained release by reciting the Veda; Neelakesi appeals to the Apta's scripture as what leaves nothing unknown, but does so as a move in a debate.
teaches: Both rest final authority on a scripture, but the Saiva verse sets scripture against argument while the Jain debater uses scripture as the ground of argument, so the two disagree about whether debate serves the scripture.

gains.a: the Jain appeal to scripture is seen as one way to end a dispute, which a rival tradition takes as reason to give up disputing
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of argument is seen as a choice, since another scriptural tradition put argument at the centre of its practice

note: Naladiyar 313 describes people who rush to debate on the strength of a word, talk at length and do not know when they are beaten; Neelakesi tells the Buddhist he does not know words and prattles many words like a ghost.
teaches: The Naladiyar's type of the endless talker becomes a charge thrown by one debater at another, which shows the description used as a weapon in debate as well as a moral portrait.

gains.a: Neelakesi's insult is placed within a known ethical type, the speaker who does not know when he is beaten
gains.b: the quatrain gains a scene where its charge is made by a party to the dispute, which shows that calling the other side a prattler is itself a debating move

note: The Kural says giving alone is good even if there were no higher world; in 416-417 both debaters take the giver's reaching heaven as what makes giving worth doing, and Neelakesi calls the identity of giver and god the truth of giving (தானத்தின் உண்மை).
teaches: The Kural's 'even if there were no higher world' is a position neither the Jain nor the Buddhist debater will hold here, since both stake the worth of alms on a rewarded doer.

gains.a: The epic's grounding of giving in reward is shown to be a choice that another ethics declined.
gains.b: The couplet's hypothetical is seen against a real debate in which a giver without a future was taken to make giving void.

note: The Kural likens the body-life bond to a bird leaving its nest; Neelakesi holds the soul joined with the body it has taken and makes it the one who sees and knows there.
teaches: The Kural's bird stresses how loosely the life sits in the body, while the Jain debater insists the soul fills and works the body as its knower, so the same separability is put to opposite uses.

gains.a: The verse's soul is set against a familiar image of a life that merely lodges in the body and leaves.
gains.b: The bird-and-nest image is shown to leave open what does the knowing while the bird is in the nest, which the debate answers.

note: Against Kundalakesi (201) Neelakesi used the thread running through a garland for what carries knowledge from moment to moment; against Mokkalan (419) she says the soul's being stays through austerity, vows and divine birth.
teaches: The continuity argued against Kundalakesi for memory within one life is here stretched across births, because the reward of penance needs the same soul to arrive in heaven.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain debater says each thing is both lasting and passing and takes on origination, persistence and destruction in every moment; in 420-421 Mokkalan calls this self-contradiction (milk becomes curd), and Neelakesi answers that change runs only by a thing's own causes.
teaches: The Buddhist epic sets out the Jain both-lasting-and-passing doctrine unanswered, while the Jain epic shows the Buddhist charge against it and the reply, so together they show the doctrine and where it was attacked.

note: In 202 Neelakesi grants that the pathiri scent stays in the new pot after the flower decays, to argue a soul outlasting the body; in 422-423 Mokkalan cites the scent in the sherd as a quality leaving its substance, and she answers that the flower's particles stay and carry it.
teaches: The same pot-and-scent example cuts both ways in the Jain debater's hands: against Kundalakesi it shows something that endures, against Mokkalan she must deny that the scent ever left its substance.
audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 202 line 4 can also be read as a question that reverses the point.

note: Neelakesi says the Buddha himself spoke of six kinds of destinies; in the Manimekalai Aravanar teaches that beings are of six kinds (humans, gods, Brahmas, hell-beings, animals, ghosts), born by good and bad deeds.
teaches: Neelakesi's retort works because Buddhists did teach six realms on their master's word, as the Buddhist epic confirms, so her appeal to scripture for the place of release matches their own practice.

note: The Kural says those who have learned and seen the true thing reach the path of not coming back here; Mokkalan asks what makes non-return final, and Neelakesi answers that karma returns only through yoga activity, which the freed soul lacks.
teaches: The Kural names the path of no return without saying what keeps it closed, and the debate supplies a mechanism: return needs the inflow of karma through activity, which release has ended.

gains.a: The Jain answer is set against the general Tamil promise of a path of no return, showing which part of that promise it explains.
gains.b: The couplet's 'not coming back' is tested by the objection that a lasting freed self could be bound again.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain debater says release is blocking the way good and bad deeds come in and wearing out past deeds; Neelakesi names that way as yoga activity and uses it to deny that a freed soul could be rebound.
teaches: The inflow that the Buddhist epic's summary only mentions becomes, in the Jain epic, the answer to the charge that a released soul could fall back into bondage.

note: The narrator in 48 says the sage Munichandra knew without limit the things of the three times; in 435 Neelakesi argues that if virtuous gods can show the three times, the Lord must know them.
teaches: Her a-fortiori argument for the Lord's knowledge of the three times rests on lesser knowers the epic had already shown, including the human sage who converted her.

note: Tirumular says the undiscerning take the moon in clouds and in a pot of Ganga water as many, though it is one; Neelakesi asks who ever said the moon differs in each water, to show the Lord's one knowing present to all things.
teaches: Both use one moon in many waters, but the Saiva verse makes the many appearances one reality, while the Jain keeps the many things real and makes only the knowing single.

gains.a: The Jain image is seen to stop short of the oneness the same figure carries in Saiva teaching.
gains.b: Tirumular's moon is shown to be a shared figure the Jains used for knowledge, not only for the one Lord in many bodies.

note: Mokkala argues that infinite things cannot be known to their end; the hymn answers that the Lord's knowledge is not sensory and does not go in order (முறைபடும் அறிவிலன்).
teaches: The infinity objection assumes knowing means counting through objects one by one, and the hymn's answer is to deny that the omniscient's knowledge is sequential at all, which shows where the two sides really part.

note: 445 defines the Lord by the burning of the eightfold seeds; 458 uses the burnt seed that never sprouts to explain why the released soul is never reborn yet remains.
teaches: The same image does two jobs: first it defines what made the Jina Lord, then it answers whether release is extinction, so the seed shows that what is destroyed is karma while the soul persists.
audit_text_issue: 445 lines 3-4 are loose in syntax; the link rests on line 2, which is clear.

note: Arkkachandra, defeated, named Mokkala, the Buddha's first disciple, as his teacher; Mokkala, defeated, names the one in Kapilapuram who first gave him his delusion.
teaches: Each defeated Buddhist names the teacher above him, so the debates climb a chain of transmission from Kundalakesi to the Buddha himself, and the epic's route is the lineage read backwards.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher describes release as the reverse chain in which birth and all its sorrow cease; Neelakesi says the released soul, like a burnt seed, never sprouts but abides eternally with eight qualities.
teaches: Both epics define release as the end of birth, but the Buddhist account has nothing that remains while the Jain account insists a soul abides, which is exactly what Mokkala's question in 457 asks.

note: The Kural defines a land as one free of severe hunger, unceasing disease and destructive enemies; the hymn says hunger, disease and enmity perish wherever the Jina goes.
teaches: The three ills the Kural treats as a test of a well-governed land are, in the Jain hymn, ended by the presence of a saint rather than by the king, so the pairing moves the source of a land's welfare from rule to holiness.

gains.a: the hymn's list of marvels is seen to answer a standard Tamil measure of a good country, not just to praise
gains.b: the couplet's measure is shown being claimed by religious polemic for the Jina's presence

audit_text_issue: Line 4 names சுகதன், usually the Buddha's title; whether the hymn claims it for the Jina is unsettled, so 'the Jina goes' is a reading.

note: The Kural says the two kinds of dark deed do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise; Neelakesi says those who strew flowers and hymn the Aptha lose both kinds of deed and reach the state of Siva.
teaches: The couplet leaves its Lord unnamed and its reward unstated, and the epic fills both, naming the Aptha by the marks just argued for and calling the reward release, which shows how a sect could read the Kural's opening chapter as its own.

gains.a: the verse's claim that worship removes both kinds of deed is seen to rest on a widely known couplet, not on Jain doctrine alone
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed Lord and unstated outcome are given one concrete reading in a sectarian debate

note: Tirumular says that saying Siva Siva makes evil deeds die and brings the state of Siva (சிவகதி); Neelakesi says that praising the Aptha destroys both kinds of deed and brings the undivided state of Siva (சிவகதி).
teaches: The two verses share the formula of praise, deeds destroyed and சிவகதி, but for Tirumular the word names Siva and only evil deeds must go, while for the Jain hymn it names a godless auspicious state and good deeds must go too.

gains.a: the hymn's Saiva-sounding vocabulary is seen as a contest over shared words, not a borrowing of Saiva belief
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's சிவகதி is shown to be a term a rival school used for release without a creator god

note: Idaikkadar says a roasted seed will not sprout and those without devotion will not reach the goal; Neelakesi says a burnt seed never sprouts and so the released soul is never born again.
teaches: The same roasted seed is failure for the Siddhar, the soul without devotion that cannot grow toward release, and success for the Jain, the soul whose karma is burnt so it cannot grow into rebirth, so the image's meaning depends on whether sprouting is birth or attainment.

gains.a: the Jain verse's image is seen to have a rival use in which not sprouting is a loss
gains.b: the Siddhar's terse image is set against the older doctrinal use it inverts

note: Kural 256 says no one would sell flesh for a price if the world did not kill to eat; 471 makes the market's beasts say the buyers' money sends the netter out to kill them.
teaches: The couplet's demand argument is given a voice and an opponent: in the Buddha's own town the dead animals accuse the buyer, so the rule becomes a charge against a monastic order that buys rather than kills.

gains.a: the verse's picture of the protesting beasts gets the Kural's general law of price and killing behind it
gains.b: the couplet's abstract buyer becomes a named religious community, which shows whom the argument was useful against

note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh to swell his own can hold to grace; 472 grants the Buddha the greatest self-giving, even of his wife, and still faults him for not forbidding flesh.
teaches: Grace in the Kural is lost by the eater; the Neelakesi adds a teacher's grace lost by silence, so that a life of total giving can still fail the test if it leaves others free to eat flesh.

gains.a: the charge against the Buddha gets the Kural's rule that grace and flesh-eating cannot go together
gains.b: the couplet's test is extended from the one who eats to the one who teaches and does not forbid

note: Kural 255 says hell does not open its mouth to release one who eats flesh; 473 says the Buddha, by permitting flesh, will lead himself and his disciples into the burning hell.
teaches: The Kural's hell takes the single eater; the Jain polemic widens it to a teacher and his whole following, so a permission given in doctrine becomes a collective path to hell.

gains.a: the ironic praise of the Buddha's 'kindness' gets the Kural's plain sentence on where flesh-eating leads
gains.b: the couplet's punishment is shown to reach the teacher who permits as well as the one who eats

note: Thirikadugam 36 names among the self-deceived the one who eats flesh and claims compassion and the one who says the deed is done without his consent; 474 answers that defence with the middleman who profits from a trade he does not perform.
teaches: The Thirikadugam only lists the excuse 'it was not done with my consent'; the Neelakesi gives the reason it fails, since the eater stands to the killing as a middleman to a sale, profiting from both sides.

gains.a: the attack on the monk's threefold excuse is shown to be a known type of self-deception in the ethical manuals
gains.b: the verse's bare list gets an argument and a target, the Buddhist rule of meat not killed for the eater

audit_text_issue: முத்துரைத்து as the threefold rule is a likely reading

note: Sirupanchamoolam 69 binds the sin of a killing on five: the killer, the one who consented, the one who took the carcass, the cook and the eater; 475 mocks a master who sorts sin so that the killer bears it and the eater does not.
teaches: Held together, the two show the Jain account of shared guilt as a deliberate counter-rule: the Sirupanchamoolam's five sharers are the answer to the very division of guilt the Neelakesi's Buddha is said to make.

gains.a: Neelakesi's mockery gets a full rule of who shares a killing, which the verse only implies
gains.b: the manual's list of five is shown to be aimed at a rival doctrine that confined guilt to the killer

note: 251 charged the monk Arkkachandran with preaching compassion while eating fish and flesh; 470 brings the same charge to the Buddha's own town and its market, before the teacher himself.
teaches: The flesh charge moves from the disciple's conduct to the master's city and then (472-473) to the master's teaching, so the poem traces a monk's fault back to the rule that permits it.

note: In 177 Kundalakesi reports that her teacher first taught the three scriptures and the five aggregates; in 477 the Buddha himself is shown dividing his teaching into Sutra, Vinaya and Shastra and then the aggregates.
teaches: The Neelakesi climbs from report to source: the doctrine Neelakesi first met second-hand from a nun is now spoken by the Buddha in person, so the debate that follows is staged as a refutation at the root.

note: In 203 Neelakesi argued that a power passing across the moments would be a sixth thing beside the five aggregates; in 478 and 480 the Buddha's teaching posits a person (pudgala) besides the aggregates.
teaches: The 'sixth thing' that Neelakesi forced on Kundalakesi as an absurd consequence turns up as the master's own tenet, the person, so the earlier argument becomes the charge of contradiction here.
audit_text_issue: 480 line 3 differs from 478 line 3 (போதியால் / புந்தியால்); one reading is likely a copyist's slip. | 480 line 3 has போதியால் where 478 has புந்தியால்; one is likely a slip.

note: In 194 Neelakesi argued that feeling, perception and formation are not other than knowing, so the five aggregates collapse; in 481 the Buddha concedes that many of his divisions of the five do not fit but holds the aggregates real.
teaches: The objection made against the disciple is half admitted by the master, which lets the poet show the Buddhist defence retreating from the five divisions to a bare claim that the aggregates exist.
audit_text_issue: 194 line 2 (சிங்குந்தன்) is obscure, so which three are merged is uncertain.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher names the five aggregates simply (form, feeling, perception, formation, consciousness); the Neelakesi's Buddha gives them with numbered subdivisions, three feelings, six consciousnesses and twenty formations.
teaches: The Buddhist epic gives the aggregates as a short list within the four truths; the Jain epic's Buddha gives a scholastic count, so the polemic attacks a more technical Abhidharma than the one the Buddhist epic chose to teach.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:484 line 2 does not divide with certainty

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika gives earth as hard, water cool, fire burning and wind moving, borne by eternal atoms; the Neelakesi's Buddha gives the same four marks with functions, borne by octads of momentary form (478, 485).
teaches: Across two polemical epics the marks of the elements are common ground; what the schools dispute is the bearer, eternal unchanging atoms for the Ajivika against momentary eight-fold clusters for the Buddhist.

note: 491 says the five aggregates arise together in one moment; 506 gives them an order in which cognition makes activity and activity makes feeling.
teaches: Neelakesi uses the Buddhist's own causal chain against his doctrine of simultaneity: if one aggregate produces another, they cannot all be born and die in the same instant.

note: The Buddha calls the five aggregates a soul only as five fingers are called a hand; Neelakesi says the fingers' unity needs a bearer, or else they are five things.
teaches: The Buddha's chosen example becomes the Jain's evidence: an analogy for a mere name is turned into a case of qualities that need one substance.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:495 says முட்டி (fist) where 492 says கை (hand)

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives the collective name (body, water, country) as a Buddhist mode of speech; the Neelakesi's Buddha calls the soul such a name, like 'hand' for five fingers.
teaches: The Jain poet gives his Buddha a doctrine the Buddhist epic itself states, so here the polemic reports Buddhist teaching recognisably before answering it.

note: The Neelakesi's Buddha calls impermanence, suffering, impurity and no-soul his four truths; the Manimekalai's teacher gives the four truths as suffering, its cause, release and release's cause.
teaches: Holding the two lists together shows the Jain epic replacing the Buddhist's path of cause and cure with four bare marks of things, so that release seems to follow from seeing alone; this depends on reading நான்மை in 493 as the four truths.

note: The Buddha says those who know the four truths reach release whatever they do; the monk in 259 says only the mind counts and evil conduct is not evil karma.
teaches: The monk's excuse in the earlier debate is given a source in the Buddha's own words here, so the poet makes the founder answerable for the disciple's conduct; this rests on reading எவையே செய்தும் as 'whatever they do'.
audit_text_issue: 493 line 2 (நாட்டிலங்காட்டமிலை) is hard to divide; the marker flagged the sense. | 493 line 2 is hard to divide; the marker flagged the sense.

note: Kundalakesi praised her teacher as one who suffered only for others; Neelakesi addresses the Buddha as the compassionate one who toiled for others through every aeon, in a verse that charges him with contradiction.
teaches: The Buddhist's chief title of praise returns in the Jain's mouth as an ironic address, so the founder's compassion is set beside the incoherence of his doctrine.

note: Against Kundalakesi, Neelakesi folded feeling, perception and volition into knowing; against the Buddha she folds feeling into activity.
teaches: The Jain reply to the five aggregates is the same in both debates: reduce them until only knowing and form remain, which is the Jain pair of soul and non-soul.
audit_text_issue: both verses obscure: 194 line 2 சிங்குந்தன், 505 line 2

note: The Buddha counts six cognitions at the six doors; Neelakesi asks how the five not occurring can be known to exist, and says their hidden existence licenses a soul.
teaches: Counting six kinds of cognition already assumes something that holds the unused ones, so the Buddhist's own enumeration is made to imply the abiding knower he denies.

note: Against Kundalakesi, Neelakesi said that if nothing of one moment is in the next, knowing and speaking are impossible; against the Buddha she says that if will perishes at each arising, knowledge cannot grow.
teaches: The argument against momentariness moves from memory to learning: the first debate asked how anything is known, this one how anything is learned.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain says gram keeps its nature when cooked into a dish; the Neelakesi's Jain asks how milk, curd and buttermilk could fill the vessels if nothing lasts.
teaches: Both epics give the Jain the same proof from the kitchen, a substance that persists through its changes; the Buddhist epic reports it unanswered there, and the Jain epic aims it at the Buddha's momentariness.

note: In 263 Neelakesi grieves for the Buddha who taught a void release; in 512 she argues that his account of will ends in the void through infinite regress.
teaches: The void is charged twice, once as a goal no one could want and once as the end of a regress, so the Jain treats Buddhist emptiness as both a bad hope and a failed argument.

note: Neelakesi says the Buddha's reasoning collapses into the void; the Siddhar tells his listener that all arising deeds are seen to be void, appearing without appearing in pure space.
teaches: For the Jain debater reaching the void is a reductio, for the Siddhar it is the seeing that frees; the same word marks defeat in one tradition and insight in the other.

gains.a: the Jain charge gains a witness that some Tamil teachers embraced the void as a goal, so the charge is aimed at a live position, not a straw one
gains.b: the Siddhar's void gains the objection it must meet, that a void reached by regress leaves nothing to know or hold

note: The Kural says understanding is seeing the true thing in whatever thing, of whatever nature; Neelakesi says no thing has ever been made clear except through its qualities.
teaches: The Jain makes the couplet's 'whatever its nature' into a method: the true thing is reached through its qualities, not by stripping them away, which is why she can claim the soul is known by knowing and seeing.

gains.a: the debater's rule about qualities gains the Kural's claim that seeing the real thing is what understanding is for
gains.b: the couplet gains an answer to how the true thing is to be seen, which it leaves open

note: In 203 Neelakesi told Kundalakesi that a power carried from moment to moment would be a sixth thing beyond the aggregates; in 513 she says the Buddha's store of consciousness is the soul under another name.
teaches: Across two opponents the Jain argument has one shape: any carrier the Buddhist adds to explain memory and continuity is called a soul, so the store-consciousness is met with the charge first made against Kundalakesi.

note: 201 argues that if nothing of the first moment remains in the next, knowing is impossible; 518 tests this on hearing a word letter by letter.
teaches: The general continuity objection becomes a concrete test the opponent cannot dodge: no one could even understand the word 'Buddha' if each letter's knower perished before the next.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives the joined name as a valid mode of speech: many letters coming together appear as a word; 518 says a momentary mind could never put the letters together.
teaches: The two epics take the same example, a word made of letters, to opposite ends: the Buddhist treats it as a correct conventional name, the Jain as proof that something must last to join the letters.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher counts the collective name (the body, water, a country) as a true mode of speech; 533 says naming collections one holds unreal makes every such word a lie.
teaches: The Jain charge of lying presupposes that a name must match one real thing, which is the very premise the Buddhist account of conventional naming in the Manimekalai rejects.

note: The Manimekalai names the mind's three bad deeds as coveting, anger and wrong view; 529 says pride, deceit and greed are as evil as anger and the Buddhists leave them uncondemned.
teaches: Set against the Buddhist epic's actual list, Neelakesi's charge turns out to be a clash of classifications: she measures a list of ten deeds against the Jain four passions, anger, pride, deceit and greed.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives exactly four bad deeds of speech in a closed list of ten; 535 says there are many more, such as talking alone with a woman.
teaches: Neelakesi quotes the Buddhist list faithfully and attacks its closure, not its content: her additions come from a renouncer's code of conduct, which a list of ten deeds for all people does not try to cover.

note: Kural 35 sets aside envy, craving, anger and harsh words as the four that virtue avoids; 529 names anger, pride, deceit and greed as the faults of the mind.
teaches: Both make anger and greed central, but each completes the list from its own school: the Kural adds envy and a fault of speech, the Jain debater pride and deceit, so the shared pair is common ground and the rest is sectarian.

gains.a: the Jain list of passions is shown to share its core with a widely accepted ethical rule, which strengthens her charge that the Buddhists left faults out
gains.b: the couplet's list is shown not to be the only fourfold reckoning; a Jain debater would count pride and deceit where it counts envy and harsh speech

note: 533 holds that naming a thing one thinks unreal is a lie; Kural 292 holds that even a falsehood stands as truth if it yields faultless good.
teaches: Neelakesi's charge only works on a test of truth by match with things; on the Kural's test by effect, the Buddhist's conventional names, harming no one, would not be lies at all.

gains.a: the verse's assumption about what truth is becomes visible as an assumption, one a widely read ethics book does not share
gains.b: the couplet's measure of truth by its fruit is shown to settle a philosophical dispute about speech that it never names

note: Kural 91 defines sweet words as moist with love and free of deceit; 536 argues against a rule that gentle speech is good by citing the soft-spoken plotter.
teaches: The Kural's definition already builds in the guard Neelakesi says the Buddhist rule lacks: speech counts as sweet only when it is without deceit, so her gentle conspirator would not qualify under it.

gains.a: the objection gets a ready answer in an older definition, which shows the rule can be repaired rather than discarded
gains.b: the couplet's clause படிறிலவாம் is shown to do real work, excluding exactly the soft-spoken plotter a debater raised

note: 534 mocks the teacher who calls earth, water, fire and city false; Pambatti Siddhar bids the reader be clear that the world is false and dance.
teaches: The Jain realist's retort, that one who calls all things false leaves no ground for his own truth, falls on the Siddhar's world-is-false as much as on the Buddhist's, though the Siddhar makes it a release-giving insight, not a doctrine to defend.

gains.a: the verse's attack is shown to reach beyond Buddhism to a Tamil Saiva-Vedantic saying that also calls the world false
gains.b: the Siddhar's flat statement meets the objection it never answers: how one who calls the world false still claims his own words are true

audit_text_issue: 534 line 4's exact turn is uncertain. | 534 line 4 turn is uncertain.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists killing, theft and lust as the three evil deeds that arise in the body; 539 takes that very grouping and asks who does them if the mind is not there.
teaches: The Buddhist epic sorts deeds by the door they go out through and counts the mind's three faults separately, so the Jain objection works only by reading a classification of doors as a claim that the body acts without mind.

note: In 259 the monk says nothing exists but the mind and evil conduct is not evil karma; 541 states the Buddhist rule that a killing needs knowledge and intention as well as a death.
teaches: The earlier boast that only the mind counts becomes a precise five-part rule here, and the precision is what lets Neelakesi build cases of mistaken identity in which a man dies and no killing is counted.

note: Kural 282 says even thinking of stealing another's goods is wrong; 547 holds that the burglar, the would-be killer and the would-be adulterer carry the karma of their intent even when the act fails.
teaches: Read beside a debate that also condemns the unintended killing, the couplet's thought-crime proves to be only half of the Jain position, which binds karma both to the intent without the deed and to the deed without the intent.

gains.a: the verse's claim that a failed intent binds finds a rule in the Kural that gives the same verdict on theft without any doctrine of karma
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'thinking is wrong' is set inside an account of why: the intent itself binds karma, and a deed done in error binds it too

audit_text_issue: Line 4 (சொல்லு வானோ டுலகமுஞ் சுற்றமே) is unclear.

note: 553 argues that if all is suffering there cannot be four truths; the Manimekalai's teacher gives four truths in which the fourth is joy, which is release caused by not clinging.
teaches: The reductio holds only against a Buddhism that calls everything suffering without exception; the Buddhist epic's own fourth truth (இன்பம் வீடே) is the exception, which shows the Jain argument aimed at a version the Buddhist teacher would not accept.

note: 256 mocks 'all is suffering' as a greedy monk's complaints; 556 draws its practical consequence, that with no joy anywhere one may as well walk into fire.
teaches: The poet attacks the first truth twice in two tones, as a lazy monk's grumble in the Arkkachandra debate and as an argument against the Buddha himself that the doctrine would remove every reason for conduct.

note: Naladiyar 48 says those who praise sandal paste and garlands have not seen what the body is; 557 treats 'those who wear garlands and sandal have not found the path' as the absurd outcome of the Buddhist claim that nothing is pure.
teaches: A Jain anthology and a Jain epic part ways on impurity: the Naladiyar finds it in the body and condemns the garland, while the Neelakesi attacks the Buddhist 'nothing at all is pure' because extended to everything it erases the difference between path and no path.

gains.a: the epic's reductio is shown to aim at the word 'all', since its own tradition accepts the body's foulness in the same image of sandal and garland
gains.b: the quatrain's contempt for adornment is marked as a claim about the body, which the Jain debater would not let grow into a claim that everything is impure

note: 252 says the monks call all things impure yet bow at their own defiled master's feet; 558 says they call their own recitation, conduct and food pure.
teaches: The charge of inconsistency grows from the monks' worship of their teacher to their whole daily practice, so the 'all is impure' doctrine is shown to exempt everything its holders do.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:252 lines 2 and 4 do not divide with certainty

note: Sivavakkiyar mocks those who bathe daily crying 'pollution', since the body itself took form from pollution; 561 tells those who hold all things impure to bathe in the gutter, as if that conclusion were absurd.
teaches: The Siddhar draws the very conclusion the Jain debater uses as a reductio: if everything is born of impurity, the ritual bath is pointless, so the same premise ends in mockery of ritual in one text and in mockery of the premise in the other.

gains.a: the epic's reductio meets a poet who accepts its consequence, showing that the argument holds only for one who still values the clean over the foul
gains.b: the Siddhar's attack on bathing is seen to rest on a premise a Jain epic thought no sane teacher could hold

audit_text_issue: 561 line 3 is obscure; Siddhar 1429's last line is uncertain.

note: 196 asks how perishing can be known if the mind perishes wholly with its objects; 562 asks how a teacher who says nothing stays can establish any thesis, the four truths included.
teaches: Neelakesi uses one argument against momentariness in both debates, first against the knowing of perishing and here against the stating of doctrine, so the self-refutation of the momentary becomes the Neelakesi's standing reply to Buddhism.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:562 line 3 (எல்லாந் தானே யென்றலி னேன் விழவெய்தி) insecure

note: The Buddha of the Neelakesi offers seed, sprout and branch as a continuity in which release lies; the Manimekalai's teacher uses seed, sprout and stalk as the example of the continuity name, one word for a series.
teaches: The Buddhist epic uses the seed series as a rule of naming, while the Jain epic puts it in the Buddha's mouth as an account of what passes on to release, which is the stronger claim its heroine can then attack.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:573 line 3 வெத்தவ looks corrupt, probably வெந்த அவ் (burnt seed); the reading changes what is said of release

note: The Buddha here says deed and fruit exist but no doer; Manimekalai 30's teacher says the chain has no maker, no I and no mine, and is itself deed and fruit.
teaches: Set against the Buddhist epic's own teaching, the Jain poem's Buddhist thesis turns out to be stated fairly, so Neelakesi's reply in 575 attacks a view the school holds, not a straw figure.

note: The Buddha denies any doer behind the deed; the quatrain says an old deed seeks out the very one who did it, as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
teaches: The quatrain's comfort that a deed finds its own doer depends on there being a doer who lasts, which is exactly what the Buddha's thesis denies, so the proverb takes a side in the Jain-Buddhist debate.

gains.a: the Buddha's thesis gains an everyday image of the persisting owner it rejects, showing what ordinary moral talk would lose under it
gains.b: the quatrain gains an opponent who makes explicit that its calf image assumes a lasting self

note: In 203 Neelakesi told Kundalakesi that a power passing between moments is either a sixth thing beyond the five aggregates or total destruction; here she tells the Buddha the lac is a further thing, and the aggregates have none.
teaches: The same dilemma defeats the disciple's power and the teacher's lac, which shows Neelakesi's case is one argument: every Buddhist carrier of karma is either a soul under another name or nothing.

note: Kundalakesi gave the Buddha's gifts of wife and child as proof of his compassion; Neelakesi tells the Buddha that those who take such gifts cannot be shown not to be thieves.
teaches: The gift offered as proof of compassion is answered not only as the giver's folly, as in 207, but as a wrong done through the receiver, since a wife and children were never the giver's to give.

note: The couplet defines a gift by its receiver: what goes to those who have nothing. Neelakesi tests a gift by what is given: persons handed over as alms make their taker a thief.
teaches: A gift can satisfy the couplet's test of the receiver's want and still fail, because the thing given must be the giver's own, which the couplet takes for granted.

gains.a: Neelakesi's objection gains a householder's definition of giving that does not mention property, showing her test adds a condition
gains.b: the couplet gains a limit it leaves unstated: one may give only what is one's own, and persons are not

note: Kundalakesi's invocation praises the lord who kept nothing for himself and laboured only for others' good (பிறர்க்கேயுறு திக்கு ழந்தான்); 587 tells the Buddha that because he laboured for others (பிறர்க்கே உழந்தாய்), by his own rule that a pain-bringing deed is evil, he must himself suffer those deeds.
teaches: The Jain epic lifts the Buddhist poem's central praise almost word for word and recasts it as a karmic debt, so the same self-giving reads as perfection in one sect and as a self-inflicted evil deed in the other.
audit_text_issue: 587 line 2 is compressed and the verse is flagged uncertain.

note: The Kural says all pains rest on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்); Neelakesi applies the rule to the Buddha's pain-bearing gifts and says he must himself suffer what they caused.
teaches: Applied without limit, the rule that pain returns to its causer condemns even the giver who bears pain for others, and only a theory of what makes a deed evil can stop that.

gains.a: Neelakesi's charge rests on a maxim Tamil readers already accept, so it reads as consequence rather than spite
gains.b: the couplet meets a hard case it does not consider, pain caused in the act of helping others, which forces a choice about whether intention excuses it
