note: In 313 Neelakesi rejects the Buddhist rule that sin joins only where there is intention, using meat-eating; in 595 she argues in general that wherever mind is there action is, so action cannot be left out of karma.
teaches: The particular quarrel over the meat-eater's guilt rests on a general thesis about intention and act, which the Jain debater states only when she faces the Buddha himself.

note: The Kural says to be spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and all else is show; Neelakesi denies that the mind alone is the deed and argues that action always goes with it and is karma too.
teaches: A mind-first ethic that the Kural states as praise of sincerity becomes, between Buddhist and Jain, a disputed claim about where karma lies, and the Jain side refuses to let the act fall away.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument is seen to cut against a widely accepted Tamil maxim, not only against Buddhist doctrine
gains.b: the couplet's stress on the mind is shown to carry a doctrinal risk, the excusing of the act, that the Kural does not address

note: In 583 Neelakesi objects that the lac colour put on the seed does not reach even the sprout, yet the Buddha says it settles in the flower; in 601 the Buddha replies that the power hides in between, hard to see, and appears in the flower.
teaches: The Buddha's defence of karmic transfer rests on an unseen passage, which is exactly what Neelakesi's empirical objection denied, so the dispute becomes one over whether what cannot be seen may be posited.
audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 583's turn to Angulimala (அங்குலி மாரனை) is unclear.

note: The Naladiyar says an old deed seeks out the one who did it (தற்செய்த கிழவனை) as a calf finds its mother among many cows; the Buddha in 602 says the doer has perished and the continuum running on from him receives the fruit.
teaches: The quatrain's image needs a doer who is still there to be found, while the Buddha's answer removes him, so the pair shows that the Tamil ethical common sense about karma assumes a lasting self.

gains.a: the Buddha's continuum is seen against the common Tamil picture of a deed finding its owner, which it has to replace
gains.b: the quatrain's calf-and-mother image is shown to carry an assumption, a persisting doer, that a Buddhist would deny

note: In 199 Neelakesi says Kundalakesi's two kinds of continuum destroy her own case; in 603 she presses the Buddha on what a feeble continuum can do once the aggregates have wholly perished.
teaches: The epic makes the same objection to continuity defeat the disciple first and the master later, so the Buddhist doctrine is shown failing at one point from both its spokesmen.
audit_text_issue: 199 line 4 and 603 line 2 are obscure; the marker flagged both. | Both verses are flagged uncertain; 199 line 4 and 603 line 2 are obscure.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher says the Buddha came down leaving the Tushita world (துடிதலோகம் ஒழியத் தோன்றி); Neelakesi asks how the ascetic who perished could be a god in the Tushita palace at all without a self to carry him.
teaches: The Buddhist epic tells the Tushita descent as sacred history, and the Jain epic takes the same episode as its test case against rebirth without a self.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher gives seed, sprout and stalk all called paddy as the example of naming by continuity (தொடர்ச்சி); Neelakesi grants seed-to-flower continuity only because a long branch joins them without a gap.
teaches: The Buddhist example of continuity works only where the stages touch, and Neelakesi uses that condition to deny that it reaches across death to a new body.
audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 610 lines 3-4 (மடியிலார் செய்த மானுயர் தெய்வப் படி) are uncertain, and so is the matching of examples to modes at Manimekalai 30:208-213.

note: Earlier the Buddha likened the aggregates, arising and perishing in one moment, to the tip of a lamp's flame; here Neelakesi refuses the flame as an example of continuity because two real things are in it.
teaches: The flame the Buddha offered as the very picture of momentary arising is claimed by the Jain for her own side, since a lamp shows a lasting fuel beside its passing tip, so one image serves both doctrines depending on which of its two parts is looked at.

note: The Buddha said the deed exists and its fruit exists but there is no doer; Neelakesi answers that if the fruit comes later down the line, the deed itself must last until then.
teaches: Granting deed and fruit while denying a doer moves the lasting thing from the agent to the deed: the Jain shows that the Buddha's karma needs a persistence somewhere, and the debate is over where to put it.

note: The pathiri scent left in a new pot appears in the Kundalakesi debate, where Neelakesi used it to argue a soul outlasts the body, and here as the Buddha's own example of the trace.
teaches: The same pot of scent is read two ways in one epic: against Kundalakesi Neelakesi took the lingering scent as proof that something outlasts its source, and against the Buddha she denies it can show a trace passing between moments that never coexist.
audit_text_issue: 202 line 4 can be read as a question reversing the point.

note: Against Mokkalan she said the scent in the sherd belongs to the flower, whose particles stay there and carry it; here she grants pot and flower coexist but denies that successive moments do.
teaches: Her earlier answer explains why the pot example cannot help the Buddha: the scent passes only because flower-matter is physically present with the pot, and no such co-presence exists between a perished moment and the next.

note: Against Kundalakesi she argued that if nothing of the first moment is in the next, knowing fails, and if something is, it is a soul; here she shows the two moments never exist together for a trace to pass.
teaches: The dilemma put to Kundalakesi about what a trace carries is sharpened into a point about time: before asking what the trace holds, the Jain asks when it could cross, and finds no instant shared by the two moments.

note: The Naladiyar's new pot gives its water the scent of pathiri flowers, an image of the unlearned gaining sense from the learned; Neelakesi attacks the same image as the Buddha's proof of a trace that outlives the flower.
teaches: The ethical image of borrowed fragrance only works if the scent has a lasting bearer, the flower-dust in the pot, so the Jain debater's demand to know whose the scent is shows what the Naladiyar's figure quietly assumes about company and influence.

gains.a: the debate verse is seen to be contesting a well-worn Tamil figure, not a stray example, which explains why the Buddhist chose it and why the Jain must dismantle it
gains.b: the quatrain's simile of good company is shown to rest on a theory of how a quality passes, which the epic makes an open question between schools

audit_text_issue: 622 line 3 (ஓதன கந்தம்) is unclear; the marker flagged the sense. | 622 line 3 ஓதன is unclear; the marker flagged the sense.

note: Mokkalan argued that on the Jain view an ascetic's soul would not exist in the time to come and keeping the precepts would be wasted toil; here Neelakesi argues that on the Buddha's view nirvana comes alike to the ascetic and the vicious.
teaches: Each side charges the other's metaphysics with making austerity pointless, which shows that in these debates a doctrine of time and persistence was tested by whether it could still reward discipline.

note: The Buddha said continuity arising from a seed by potency is change, and that release is not other than this; Neelakesi replies that if each moment perishes entirely, release is that perishing and needs no austerity.
teaches: The Buddha's own phrase that release is not other than the change of the series is what lets the Jain equate nirvana with every moment's end, so the Buddha's wording supplies the premise of her reductio.
audit_text_issue: 573 line 3 வெத்தவ is probably வெந்த அவ் (the burnt seed); the marker's reading drops it.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher makes release the seeing that the links are sorrow, unstable and without self; the Neelakesi's Jain argues that momentariness would make release the mere perishing of each moment.
teaches: Set beside the Buddhist epic's own account, the Jain charge is seen to aim at a version of Buddhism the Buddhist teacher would not own, since there release is an insight gained by those who see impermanence, not the impermanence itself.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher says there is no arising for a hare's horn, the mode of denial resting on what is not; Neelakesi says there is no perishing for what does not exist, as there is no size to a crow's tooth.
teaches: Both schools grant the same rule for the non-existent, and the Jain uses it against the Buddhist: if a perished moment is as unreal as a hare's horn, it cannot also be the thing whose perishing gives rise to the next.

note: In 574 the Buddha said deed and fruit exist but there is no doer; asked now who reaps, he gives a fourfold denial: not the doer, not another, not both, not no one.
teaches: Pressed on the reaper rather than the doer, the no-doer thesis has to become a tetralemma, so the denial of a self costs the Buddha the power to name who receives karma.

note: In 574 the Buddha denied any doer; here he says the doer is the doer and the reaper the reaper.
teaches: Neelakesi's pressure forces the Buddha from 'no doer' to 'the doer is the doer', which is the point at which she can make the doer the reaper and he falls silent.

note: The Buddha offered paddy and sugarcane as a continuity that is neither same nor other; Neelakesi answers that paddy never comes from cane's line, so the example shows each kind giving only itself.
teaches: The seed example cuts both ways: what the Buddhist uses to show change without identity the Jain uses to show a kind that persists, so the dispute is over which feature of the seed counts.

note: The Neelakesi's Buddha says the reaper is neither that nor other; the Manimekalai's teacher draws from the nayas a middle that is 'neither that nor what is not that' (அதுவும் அன்று அது அலாததும் அன்று), and that there is no doer apart from the doing.
teaches: The formula the Jain poem gives the Buddha is the one the Buddhist epic itself teaches, so Neelakesi's excluded-middle reply in 645 strikes the school's own middle way, not a caricature.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher calls 'paddy seed gives paddy sprout' the naya of own-nature; Neelakesi uses the same fact, that paddy gives only paddy, to argue that the Buddha's example proves sameness of kind.
teaches: One observation serves the Buddhist as a law of causes without a self and the Jain as proof of a persisting kind, so the two epics agree on the fact and differ on what it shows.

note: Kundalakesi listed the Buddha's gifts of eyes, flesh, wife and body as his glory; here Neelakesi lists the same gifts to ask how, on his doctrine, he could ever reap them.
teaches: The Jataka gifts are turned from praise into a refutation: if no doer reaps, the Bodhisattva's sacrifices were made for a fruit his own teaching denies him.

note: Mokkalan raised the faults of holding a thing both to stand and to perish; the Buddha now makes the same objection, and Neelakesi calls it one-sided.
teaches: The same objection recurs from the disciple to the master, and the reply sharpens from 'each in its respect' (378) to the charge of ekanta, naming the error the Jain sees in every Buddhist objection.

note: In the Manimekalai the Jain's account of things as lasting and passing at once is heard and left among the doctrines Manimekalai sets aside; in the Neelakesi the Buddha himself is made to praise that account.
teaches: Each epic stages the same Jain doctrine before the other side and gives it the opposite fate, so the debate scenes show how each school wanted the meeting to end.

note: The opening called Neelakesi a demoness who took the great one's dharma and turned from violence; her last words say those of any form who understand the Lord's scripture reach release.
teaches: Her closing claim generalizes her own story: a demoness who learned the scripture is the proof that form and birth do not bar release.
audit_text_issue: 658 carries five TSCII repairs and is flagged uncertain; who says செல் in line 4 is unstated.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Neelakesi makes 'the doers themselves reap' the point that silences the Buddha.
teaches: The proverb that a deed finds its doer turns out to presuppose a doer who lasts until the fruit comes, which is exactly what the Buddhist no-self denies and what Neelakesi defends.

gains.a: the debate's decisive answer gets a common-sense image of karma that ordinary hearers already trusted
gains.b: the quatrain's untroubled image is shown to carry a metaphysical premise, a persisting self, that one school rejects

note: Kural 319 says hurts done to others in the forenoon come back to oneself in the afternoon, of themselves; Neelakesi argues that the fruit of deeds falls to the doers themselves (செய்தார்கள் தாம்).
teaches: The couplet's 'to oneself' (தமக்கு) is set within one day of one life, while the debate asks whether the same self is there across births to receive it.

gains.a: Neelakesi's claim gets an ethical rule everyone grants, so its denial looks like a denial of morality itself
gains.b: the couplet's returning harm is stretched across births, where the identity of the one it returns to becomes a question

note: Kural 356 says those who have learned and seen the true thing reach the path of no return; Neelakesi says those of any form who understand the Lord's scripture reach release in due order.
teaches: Both make understanding the road to release, but the epic names whose scripture it must be and adds that any being, even a demoness, may walk it, by stages.

gains.a: the epic's sectarian claim is set beside a general rule that learning and seeing truth free one from birth
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed 'true thing' is claimed by one school's scripture, and its learner is opened to beings of any form

note: Tirumular says souls that know what truly is go to grace and release is becoming one with Siva; Neelakesi says understanding the Lord's scripture brings release in due order, with no grace and no union.
teaches: Both put knowledge first, but in the Saiva verse knowledge leads to grace and union with God, while in the Jain verse the Lord gives only the scripture and the soul reaches release by its own understanding.

gains.a: the Jain claim is sharpened by a rival account that needs grace and union where it needs neither
gains.b: the Saiva sequence of knowing, then grace, then union, stands out against a release reached by knowledge without a giver

note: In the Kundalakesi debate Neelakesi said the Buddha knew only by seeing, hearing and reckoning (எண்ணியும் உணர்தலால்); her hymn now praises the Jina as the one who knew without reckoning (எண்ணாது உணர்ந்தான்).
teaches: The epithet in the hymn is a debating point turned into praise: the Jina is defined by exactly the mode of knowing she denied the Buddha, so the hymn carries the earlier argument into worship.

note: The king of Kampili asked the debaters for their first teacher, his scripture, its matters and their workings; Neelakesi now puts the same heads (ஆத்தன், நூல், பொருள், நிகழ்ச்சி) to the Ajivika.
teaches: The heads that a king imposed on the first debate have become Neelakesi's own method, so the epic shows the convert taking over the judge's role as well as the debater's.

note: Manimekalai asks the Jain for his lord, his categories, their workings, and bondage and release; Neelakesi asks the Ajivika for his teacher, scripture, categories and their workings.
teaches: Both epics question rival schools by nearly the same heads, but the Jain examiner puts scripture in place of bondage and release, and her first attack (680) falls on the scripture, so the choice of heads already aims the refutation.

note: Manimekalai's Ajivika spokesman, Puranan, gives as god a knower without limit present everywhere, and five categories, soul and four atoms; Neelakesi's Puranan gives Makkali as god, the nine Kathir books as scripture, and five categories.
teaches: A Buddhist and a Jain polemic agree on the Ajivika spokesman's name and the five categories, which points to the Ajivikas' own teaching, but only the Jain account makes Makkali the god, which sets up its attack on a silent omniscient whose books no one heard.

note: Manimekalai's Ajivika says atoms never enter one another (ஒன்று ஒன்றில் புகுதா); Neelakesi's says they combine and part but one does not enter another.
teaches: Two hostile accounts state the same tenet in nearly the same words, so it is likely the Ajivikas' own, and the Jain debater singles it out for attack (698) where the Buddhist narrator lets it pass.

note: Puranan says the Lord kept silent because speaking would cast him back into wandering; Neelakesi repeats his words and turns them, so that silence would make any silent man a lesser Lord.
teaches: The refutation works by repeating the opponent's own verse almost word for word, so the reader sees how a Neelakesi debate argues: the rival's premise is restated and pushed to an absurd consequence.
audit_text_issue: Both verses are compressed; the last line of 682 is a reading.

note: The hymn in the Kundalakesi sarukkam says the Lord never says 'I will speak' yet has a voice like a drum, and has no mind to harm; the Ajivika holds that a knower who speaks falls into longing and anger.
teaches: The hymn's paradox of a Lord who speaks without willing to speak turns out to be the Jain answer to the Ajivika's dilemma, so a line that reads as devotion is doctrine aimed at this debate.
audit_text_issue: 682 line 4 is compressed and its turn is the marker's reading.

note: Kural 4 sets the Lord apart as one without liking or aversion; Puranan argues that a knower who speaks must fall into longing and anger, and Neelakesi denies that speech implies them.
teaches: The Kural defines its Lord by the absence of liking and aversion without asking whether such a Lord can teach; the Ajivika debate shows that the absence was contested, since a rival held that any speaking Lord must have them.

gains.a: the epic's debate gains a well-known Tamil statement of the passionless Lord that Neelakesi's position needs and the Ajivika's denies
gains.b: the couplet gains a live dispute over whether its Lord could speak at all without losing the very freedom from liking and aversion it praises

audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 682 line 4 is compressed; its turn is a reading.

note: Tirumular tells the devotee to take refuge in the shade of the one God's feet so that the sea of deeds will not reach him; Neelakesi, a Jain convert, prays at the Jina's feet that her old deeds may end.
teaches: A Jain convert and a Saiva poet both bring their deeds to a Lord's feet in prayer, so the difference between Jain release by wearing deeds away and Saiva release by grace is not visible in the act of worship but only in the doctrine behind it.

gains.a: the epic's prayer gains a Saiva statement of what refuge at the feet is supposed to do, against which the Jain hymn's silence about how the feet end deeds stands out
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a rival tradition that uses the same act of refuge at the feet without his one all-pervading God

note: Puranan likens the Lord's unseen form to a rainbow that no bound contains; Neelakesi answers that a rainbow is made when sunlight falls on rain-cloud.
teaches: The simile chosen to set Makkali beyond causes is turned into an example of a thing produced by conditions, so the Ajivika's own image testifies against a Lord without cause.

note: Neelakesi first argues that a silent omniscient leaves his books without authority; in 685 she adds that if silence proved full knowledge, children, trees and mountains would share it.
teaches: The attack on the silent Lord has two steps: silence cuts off the scripture, and silence cannot serve as evidence of knowledge, so the Ajivika is left with neither a speaking teacher nor a proof of his teacher.
audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 685 line 2 (னற்ற மகலவென் றானீ) is hard to divide.

note: Puranan likens his Lord's ungraspable form to the rainbow; Neelakesi makes the rainbow the type of a caused thing, born of sun on rain.
teaches: The same rainbow serves the Ajivika as a sign of a form beyond grasping and the Jain as proof that such a form is produced, so the simile decides nothing until its cause is asked.
audit_text_issue: Both verses flagged uncertain; 684's சாதகன் and line-4 division are guesses.

note: 673 praises a Lord who neither ages nor greys; 694 answers with a sickness hotter than fire that came upon the god.
teaches: Against a portrait of a Lord without wrinkle or grey hair the Jain debater sets a single bodily event, showing that the debate tests a doctrine by its founder's body as well as by argument.
audit_text_issue: both verses flagged uncertain by the marker

note: The Kural likens the learned who cannot unfold their learning to scentless flowers; Neelakesi ranks a silent omniscient below any man who tells the good he sees.
teaches: The couplet faults those unable to expound, and the verse extends the fault to one who could speak and chooses not to, turning a rule about scholars into a test of a god.

gains.a: the verse's mockery gains a recognised Tamil norm that knowledge counts only when it is passed on, which the debate itself never states
gains.b: the couplet, which speaks of inability, gains a case of deliberate silence and a use of its standard in judging a religious founder

note: Tirumular says silence of speech alone is mere muteness, true silence being the stilling of mind; Neelakesi says silence of speech proves nothing, since trees and mountains are silent.
teaches: Both deny that outward silence shows attainment, but they move the test in opposite directions: Tirumular inward to a stilled mind, the Jain debater outward to the teaching a knower must give.

gains.a: the verse gains a contrast showing that its attack on silence touches only silence of the tongue, not an inner stillness it never discusses
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's distinction gains a debater who uses the same point against a rival's mute Lord, showing that mere muteness was a live charge between schools

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika gives water its own coolness and taste and fire its burning; the Neelakesi's gives every sensible quality but sound to earth alone, and Neelakesi argues the other elements would then be imperceptible.
teaches: Set beside the Buddhist report, the Jain objection is seen to strike the version of the doctrine that gives the senses' objects to earth alone; the Manimekalai's Ajivika, who gives water a taste, would be harder to hit.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says the atoms never enter one another, yet move, sink and rise; Neelakesi takes the same premises and demands the cause of sinking and rising.
teaches: The two polemics report the same Ajivika premise, atoms that never enter one another and yet sink and rise; the Buddhist leaves it, while the Jain shows it leaves motion without a cause.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says gain, loss, birth and death are mixed in at conception and the fate laid down before brings what follows; Neelakesi tests this with the infant girl whose womanhood must then already be present.
teaches: The Buddhist epic records the claim that a life's course is fixed at conception and walks away from it; the Jain epic answers it with a concrete reductio, the grown woman's features absent from the infant.
audit_text_issue: 706 was printed as 7096; line 1 (துறவாளவளும்) and line 3 are unclear.

note: The Kural asks what is stronger than fate, which comes first whatever one devises; Neelakesi attacks a fixity that sets in advance what comes, how, how much and when.
teaches: The couplet claims fate outruns human contrivance, but the Jain attack shows that the vulnerable step is the further claim that every particular of an outcome is already fixed, which the couplet does not make.

gains.a: the verse gains a contrast showing that its target is the total fixity of every detail, not every Tamil teaching of fate's strength
gains.b: the couplet gains a measure of how far its claim stops short of the Ajivika determinism that the Jain debater thought refutable

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says gain, loss, birth and death are all mixed in at conception and the fate laid down before makes what comes; 707 tests that claim on breasts, teeth, hair and nails that a newborn lacks.
teaches: The Buddhist epic lets the Ajivika's 'all is set at conception' stand and walks away; the Jain epic takes it as a claim about the body and refutes it by the parts that visibly appear later.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:707 line 3 (நிலையில் லமையு மிலதா மெனினே) is compressed; the reading 'not existing beforehand' is tentative.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika puts all of a life into the moment of conception; 709 shows that this would put a woman's daughter's daughter, and so on, into the first womb.
teaches: Holding the two together shows what the Jain thinks the doctrine costs: if a life is complete at conception, so are all lives to come from it, an infinite nesting the bare report never faces.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says atoms never enter one another; in 713 the Jain's Ajivika says the same of souls, each with its own length and breadth.
teaches: The rule of non-penetration that the Buddhist account gives for atoms is, in the Jain account, also a rule for souls, and only there does it meet the objection of crowded bodies.

note: Both epics give the Ajivika fire rising, water sinking and wind moving; 717 adds that the soul rises with fire, and 718-720 attack the whole scheme.
teaches: Two hostile witnesses agree on the Ajivika theory of natural motions, which makes it likely a real doctrine; the Jain adds the soul to it because a rising soul is what he can refute.

note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika counts the soul as a category apart from the four atoms, the one that knows; 715 presses an opponent who gives the soul form.
teaches: The Buddhist report keeps the Ajivika soul apart from matter, so the Jain's charge that it has form and can be sliced like a pumpkin is aimed at a version the other report does not give.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain lists dharma, adharma, time, space, soul, atoms, deeds, bondage and release; 729 has the Jain debater close by giving the three-times-three categories.
teaches: A Buddhist's account of Jain doctrine mixes substances with the path, while the Jain epic hands the convert the nine categories as one fixed count, which shows how each side reckoned the Jain list.

note: In 127 the sage gives Neelakesi the nectar of dharma as the medicine for birth; in 722 she tells the Ajivika she was a demon until a great one gave her that medicine.
teaches: The cure first given to the demoness becomes the debater's own credential: she argues not only from doctrine but from her own conversion, offering the opponent what she was given.

note: 116 names the triple discipline as the medicine for the diseases of birth; 724 names birth as the disease, bad deeds as its cause and true understanding as its cure.
teaches: The sermon's medical scheme is not left in the opening: at the close of a debate it is the frame in which the defeated opponent is offered treatment rather than condemnation.

note: Kural 948 tells the physician to find the disease, then its root, then the remedy, and act; 723 says the teachers' instruction does the same for the suffering of many beings.
teaches: The Kural's method of the physician becomes, in a Jain debate, the method of the religious teacher, so that a rival doctrine is treated as a disease to be diagnosed rather than an enemy to be beaten.

gains.a: the debater's appeal to teachers gains a known, stepwise method that any listener can check her diagnosis of the Ajivika against
gains.b: the couplet's clinical rule is shown to carry over to the cure of births, a reach its place in the chapter on medicine does not claim

note: Kural 358 says understanding is seeing the excellent so that the folly called birth departs; 724 calls birth a disease, names bad deeds eaten as its cause, and makes true understanding the cure.
teaches: Both make birth the evil and understanding the cure, but the Jain verse inserts the deed as the cause between them, so understanding ends birth only by ending the eating of past deeds.

gains.a: the Jain claim is seen to share its end and its means with a widely held rule, which strengthens its offer to the opponent
gains.b: the couplet's 'folly called birth' is given a causal account it does not state: births go on because bad deeds are being eaten

note: Tirumular says that as a madman is cleared by medicine, he was made clear when Nandi gave grace; Neelakesi says she, once a demon, was made clear by the dharma a teacher gave her.
teaches: Both use the same image of madness cured, but the cure differs in kind: for the Saiva it is the Lord's grace that stops his doing, for the Jain a teaching she must take in and keep.

gains.a: the Jain convert's cure is shown to be teaching without a gracious god, which is what sets it apart from the nearest Saiva parallel
gains.b: Tirumular's grace-as-medicine is seen against a rival in which the medicine is doctrine and the patient does the work

note: Both epics give the Sankhya twenty-five, but the Neelakesi counts the unmanifest and the five subtle elements while the Manimekalai counts the five sense objects and thought (சித்தம்) and leaves primal nature outside the list.
teaches: Two rival polemics hand down different lists under the same count of twenty-five, so the Tamil reports of Sankhya were not one fixed table and neither epic's list can stand for the school by itself.

note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya soul is the knowing awareness, without the three qualities, one, pervading and eternal; the Neelakesi's has the same marks but adds that it does nothing and yet experiences.
teaches: The Buddhist and the Jain reports agree on the soul's marks, but only the Jain report foregrounds the pair 'does nothing' and 'experiences', which is exactly the pair it then sets against each other in 740-745.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:736 line 2 is hard to divide

note: 741 quotes 736's words எத்திறத்தின்னுஞ்செய்யான் and turns them on the teacher: a soul that does nothing cannot be the master who teaches.
teaches: The refutation works by quotation: the Sankhya's description of the soul, repeated word for word, is shown to cancel the act of describing it.

note: The Manimekalai's teacher lists a thesis that goes against one's own words (சுவசன விருத்தம், 'my mother is barren') among the false theses; 743 says the Sankhya's admission of acting souls destroys his own thesis (மேற்கோள்).
teaches: What the Buddhist manual gives as a textbook fault with a toy example, the Jain debater springs in a live debate, showing how the logicians' catalogue of faults was used as a weapon between schools.

note: In 302 Neelakesi asked the Buddhist how formless consciousness could touch or be bound to a body with form; in 745 she asks the Sankhya how a formless soul with no contact with nature can see or experience.
teaches: One Jain objection, that the formless cannot touch the formed, is aimed at two opposite opponents, the Buddhist who denies a soul and the Sankhya who makes it untouched, which shows the Jain body-sized soul is meant as the middle that both lack.
audit_text_issue: 745 line 3 carries a repaired TSCII leftover (தேரின்). | 745 line 3 carries a repaired TSCII reading (தேரினி).

note: In 307 Neelakesi answered that deeds carry the soul between births as wind turns a whirligig; in 748 she tells the Sankhya his soul, whether it goes or not, cannot be carried, and that its twofold deeds are its companion.
teaches: The image of deeds moving the soul that answered Mokkalan becomes the dilemma that sinks the Sankhya: only a soul that acts and is acted on can be carried by its own deeds from birth to birth.
audit_text_issue: neelakesi:748 line 4 is compressed; the sense of எல்லும் is uncertain

note: Neelakesi asks what could bind a soul that is pure and changeless; the Tirumanthiram makes soul and bond both beginningless, so the soul was never first pure and then bound.
teaches: The Jain question to the Sankhya, what first bound a pure soul, is the question the Saiva verse avoids by making bondage as old as the soul, at the price of a soul that was never pure until the Lord draws near.

gains.a: The Neelakesi's question gains a known school's answer, showing that one reply to it is to deny the soul ever had a pure beginning.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's 'beginningless' gains a reason: it closes off the debating question of how a pure, unchanging soul could fall into bondage.

note: Kural 706 has crystal show the colour of what is near it, as the face shows the heart; the Sankhya, in Neelakesi's report, uses crystal beside a coloured thing for a soul that only seems changed.
teaches: The same crystal runs opposite ways: in the Kural its borrowed colour is a true sign of what lies within, in the Sankhya it is a mere appearance over a soul untouched, which is why Neelakesi can call the image an evasion.

gains.a: The Neelakesi verse gains a common Tamil use of the crystal image, in which borrowed colour reveals rather than hides, against which the Sankhya use looks like special pleading.
gains.b: The Kural couplet gains a sense of the image's other use, where crystal's colour is denied any truth, showing that its own reading of the face as a reliable sign is a choice.

note: The Sankhya of 735 counts twenty-five principles that need no maker; Tirumular's Lord makes the twenty-five within the womb for each birth.
teaches: The Saiva verse keeps the Sankhya tally of twenty-five but puts a maker over it, the one element both the Sankhya and its Jain critic do without.

gains.a: The Neelakesi list gains evidence that its twenty-five were common coin in Tamil doctrine, later taken up into a theistic account of embodiment.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's bare 'twenty-five' gains its named members and its Sankhya origin, so a reader can see what the Lord is said to assemble.

note: In 516 Neelakesi tells the Buddha that sound travels until it reaches the ear; in 760 she tells the Sankhya that sound has form and so cannot belong to space.
teaches: The same Jain premise, that sound is matter, does the work against two opponents: it makes sound travel against the Buddhist and keeps it out of formless space against the Sankhya.

note: 295 says that without dharma and adharma the room of souls and matter would spill past the world's edge; 759 says space itself runs on through the world into the non-world.
teaches: Read together, the two verses show why the Jain account needs a limit beyond space: space has no edge, so the world's bound must come from the conditions of motion and rest.

note: In 736 the Sankhya says the soul does nothing, has no quality, is eternal and present everywhere; in 765 Neelakesi uses that all-presence to deny that soul and nature ever newly join.
teaches: The opponent's own praise of the soul as everywhere present becomes the premise that undoes his account of creation by union, since a thing never absent cannot newly arrive.
audit_text_issue: 765 opens with an obscure 'இல்லுளி', and 736 line 2 is hard to divide; the argument of lines 1-2 of 765 is clear enough to carry the link. | Both verses flagged uncertain: இல்லுளி (765.1) is obscure and 736.2 is hard to divide.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain speaker says space gives room to all things; Neelakesi says space is one, formless, non-sentient and extends through world and non-world.
teaches: The Buddhist epic's report of Jain space matches the Jain epic's own voice on its function, while only the Neelakesi adds the non-world beyond the world, the part an outside report left out.

note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker derives the ear and sound from space (line 214); 760 says sound has form and cannot belong to formless space.
teaches: The derivation the Buddhist epic lets the Sankhya state unanswered is the very step the Jain epic attacks, so the two polemics differ less in what they report of Sankhya than in what they choose to contest.

note: The Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker counts speech, hands, feet and the two excretory organs among the twenty-five principles; 756 denies these are organs, since they have no object and no knowing.
teaches: Set beside the plain Sankhya list in the Manimekalai, Neelakesi's mockery shows exactly which item of the count she treats as weakest: the organs of action, which fail her test that an organ must know something.

note: Tirumular says the soul reaches the saving state by seeing through the twenty-five principles, prakriti and maya; 763 says listing the principles can do nothing for a soul that never changes.
teaches: The pair shows what the Saiva use of the twenty-five needs and the Sankhya lacks: a soul that can be bound and freed, so that seeing through the principles is a real change of state.

gains.a: The Neelakesi verse gains a case where the twenty-five lower principles are in fact used as a path to release, which is the use its objection says is impossible.
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a pointed objection it must meet: that seeing through the principles changes nothing if the soul who sees is unchangeable.

audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 2294 is flagged uncertain; ஐஐந்து as the twenty-five tattvas is a construal.

note: Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker lets primal nature unfold and withdraw by itself and names no creator; in the Neelakesi's Sankhya sarukkam the opponent defends a Lord of five acts, with the dance first.
teaches: The two polemical epics give the same school different shapes: the Buddhist account keeps Sankhya godless, while the Jain account hangs a Saiva-style lord on it, so neither can be read alone as what the Tamil Sankhyas held.
audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 766's speaker and school are uncertain, as the marker notes.

note: Tirumular makes the five dances the five acts done by grace; the Neelakesi cites the dance and the acts only as the opponent's shield, which 767-775 break.
teaches: The doctrine Tirumular offers as the heart of grace is the very one the Jain debater names in order to refute, and her answer (a god who is all is the author of every harm) is the objection Tirumular's dance never meets.

gains.a: the epic's brief list is shown to be a real Saiva teaching, the dance joined to the five acts, not a straw man
gains.b: the verse gains a hostile contemporary reading that treats the five acts as making god responsible for destruction and harm

audit_text_issue: Marker flagged 766 uncertain; it falls in the Sankhya sarukkam though the doctrine is theist.

note: The Kural's first couplet says the world has the primal Lord as its first; the Neelakesi argues no creator can be first without an endless regress of makers.
teaches: Kural 1 says the Lord is first but never that he made the world, so the Jain regress argument against a creator leaves the couplet standing, which shows why Jain readers could keep it.

gains.a: the epic's attack is shown to be aimed at a maker, not at every claim that a Lord comes first
gains.b: the couplet's simile of the first letter gains a test that sets first apart from creator

note: Sivavakkiyar uses the banyan folded in its own seed as the image of Parabrahman grown within a man; Neelakesi mocks the tall palm said to be already in its seed.
teaches: The tree-in-the-seed image that a Siddhar offers as an insight was, for a Jain debater, the weak point of the doctrine that effects pre-exist, so one image carries a mystic's claim and a logician's refutation.

gains.a: the epic's reductio is shown to bear on a living image of Tamil devotion, not only on a school's technical thesis
gains.b: the Siddhar's image meets an objection it never answers: if the tree is in the seed, why is the hand that holds the seed not holding a tree

note: Against Mokkalan (389) Neelakesi held that a thing's modes perish and arise while the thing stays; against the Sankhya (777) she says a thing is non-existent now and existent later, both at once.
teaches: One Jain doctrine is turned two ways: against the Buddhist's momentary things she stresses what lasts, against the Sankhya's lasting effects she stresses what is not yet, and each answer depends on the other.

note: Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker calls the person the one awareness that knows all; Neelakesi takes the seer and enjoyer as the opponent's own words and gives that knowing to every soul.
teaches: Where the Buddhist epic only records the person as one knowing awareness, the Jain epic uses the same attribute to argue that the Sankhya has already granted a knowing soul in every being.

note: With Arkkachandra (264) Neelakesi offered right vision as the path; with Parasaran (781) the defeated man concedes in his own words and she gives him that vision.
teaches: The Neelakesi ends its debates with a gift and not only a win: the same jewel of right vision closes the Buddhist and the Sankhya sarukkams, so conversion is the form a victory takes.

note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika gives the same six categories (பொருள், குணம், கருமம், சாமானியம், விசேடம், கூட்டம்) and is left unanswered; Neelakesi's opponent gives them in 785 to 788 and she answers them from 791.
teaches: The six-category list was a fixed set piece of Tamil accounts of the schools, and the two epics differ in what they do with it: the Buddhist epic records it and moves on, the Jain epic makes each category a target.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain counts space (ஆகாயம்) as a substance that gives room to all things; in 794 Neelakesi says the Vaisheshika's direction comes down to space.
teaches: Neelakesi's denial of direction is not a denial of space: the Jain list keeps space as a substance, so she can fold direction into it rather than abolish it.

note: In 387 Neelakesi gives Mokkalan the threefold nature of arising, perishing and lasting; in 803 she offers the same three to the Vaisheshika.
teaches: The one triad is aimed at opposite errors: against the Buddhist it adds lasting to momentary things, against the Vaisheshika it adds perishing to eternal substances.

note: The Manimekalai's Jain says each thing is both lasting and passing and has arising, staying and perishing (தோற்றமும் நிலையும் கேடும்); 803 names the three as மும்மை.
teaches: A Buddhist epic's report and a Jain epic's own argument agree on the triad as the Jain signature, which shows the Buddhist account of this doctrine is faithful where the Jain uses it.

note: In 393 Neelakesi tells the Buddhist that quality and bearer are both different and one; in 800 she tells the Vaisheshika that they need no third thing to join them.
teaches: Her 'different and one' answers two opposite opponents: the Buddhist who keeps qualities without a bearer, and the Vaisheshika who keeps a bearer so apart from its qualities that it needs a joining category.

note: In 499 she tells the Buddhist that nothing is ever known except through its qualities; in 802 she tells the Vaisheshika that a quality other than its thing cannot be called its.
teaches: The same principle that a thing is reached only through its qualities is used first to prove a bearer exists and then to deny that the bearer can stand apart from what it bears.
audit_text_issue: 802:3-4 (உதனமு) is obscure; the link rests on lines 1-2.

note: In 393 Neelakesi told the Buddhist that the quality is the qualified thing and that she holds them both different and one; 804 states the same thesis against the Vaisheshika.
teaches: One Jain thesis faces opposite errors: against the Buddhist, who keeps only qualities, she stresses the bearer; against the Vaisheshika, who splits quality from bearer, she stresses their oneness.

note: The opening sermon names standpoints (நயன்) among the doors through which the soul and its qualities are examined; 819 and 820 use the standpoints to settle the quality question and win the opponent.
teaches: The sermon's list of methods is not decoration: the standpoint it names is the very tool that ends the Vaisheshika debate, by making one and different two views of one thing.
audit_text_issue: Both verses are uncertain; 819 'நான்மை' and 'துருநெறி' are unclear and 120 lines 1-3 are hard to divide. | Both verses flagged uncertain; நான்மை and துருநெறி (819) unclear.

note: The sermon promises that in the land of deeds penance drives out dark karma and brings the highest bliss; 807 argues that this needs deeds to be qualities of the soul itself.
teaches: The promise of release in the sermon rests on a metaphysics the later debate supplies: only if karma inheres in the soul can penance change the soul and free it.

note: Before her first debate Neelakesi bows at the Arhat's shrine; at the end of this one she sends the defeated Ulokan to praise the Lord's shrine.
teaches: The debates begin and end in worship at the Jina's shrine, so winning an argument is framed as bringing the loser to the place the debater started from.

note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika closes his account with inherence joining quality and bearer, and the Buddhist epic lets it stand unanswered; 815 attacks that very relation with a regress.
teaches: Read together, the two epics show which Vaisheshika category the rival schools found weakest: the Buddhist work records inherence as the school's last word, the Jain work makes it the first thing to fall.
audit_text_issue: Manimekalai 27:257-261 is compressed and tentative; Neelakesi 815 lines 3-4 are hard to construe.

note: The Manimekalai's Vaisheshika makes generality the first common being that lets substance, quality and action work; 813 says the universal is only likeness between things.
teaches: What the Vaisheshika in one epic treats as the ground of all working, the Jain in the other reduces to resemblance, so the dispute is over whether the common is a thing or a relation.

note: Kural 5 says both kinds of deed, born of darkness, do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise; 807 says good and bad deeds and their fruits are qualities of the soul, or birth and release mean nothing.
teaches: Both count good deeds with bad as what binds, but the Jain debater asks what clinging is: a deed can cling or fall away only if it is a quality of the soul, which the couplet takes for granted.

gains.a: the verse's technical argument is tied to a plain moral teaching that both good and bad deeds bind
gains.b: the couplet's image of deeds clinging gets a stated account of what the clinging is, which it does not give

note: Kural 355 calls understanding the seeing of the true thing in a thing whatever its nature; 819 says thing and quality are one from one standpoint and different from another.
teaches: The couplet separates a thing's nature from its truth and asks us to see through to the truth; the Jain standpoint doctrine holds that the separation itself depends on where one looks.

gains.a: the standpoint method is set against a widely held definition of understanding, showing what it adds: a rule for when nature and thing are to be told apart
gains.b: the couplet's split between a thing's nature and its true being is shown to be one possible view, not the only one

note: In 821 darkness perishes as the disciple understands the three and remembers the Lord's feet; in Tirumanthiram 2293 the malas leave like evening darkness before a flame by grace.
teaches: Both texts end bondage with darkness dispelled, but in the Jain verse the remover is the disciple's own knowledge and remembrance, while the Saiva verse gives the work to grace.

gains.a: the Jain verse's silence about any act of the Lord stands out once set beside a text where the Lord's grace does the work
gains.b: the Saiva image of grace as flame is set against a release with the same image and no giver, which shows grace is its distinctive claim

note: Bhutikan dismisses Neelakesi as a Sudra woman with no competence in the Veda; five verses later the poet names her by her learning (புலமையினாள்) as she argues from the phonetics of the Veda itself.
teaches: The poet answers the Brahmin's caste taunt not with a counter-taunt but by showing the Sudra woman doing the grammarian's and logician's work on the Veda, so the debate's form refutes his premise before its content does.
audit_text_issue: 826 lines 1 and 4 (முன் நான் பயந்த, போத்தந்தியோ) are hard to divide.

note: The Brahmin who opened in anger, calling her an unbeliever, is at the close urged to speak truly, concedes, and is praised by the onlookers as one of the true.
teaches: The Jain poem converts its opponent rather than humiliating him: the man who began by denying her standing ends with standing of his own, praised for yielding to the truth.
audit_text_issue: Verses 845-851 are missing, so the turn to the concession is lost; 826 lines 1 and 4 are hard to divide.

note: The opening sermon praises a land where Brahmins and the rest make up the four flawless varnas, none straying from its path; here the same heroine argues that high and low birth is not real, since no sense can detect it.
teaches: The Jain epic holds two views of caste at once: as a social order it can praise the four varnas, but as a claim of inborn rank it denies it, so its quarrel is with birth as worth, not with the order of occupations.
audit_text_issue: Both verses are flagged uncertain (இரு வேதம், நந்திமிசை சேறல்).

note: The sermon lists the deaths of beasts in Vedic sacrifice among the many sufferings death brings; the debate takes the same slaughter and argues who bears its karma.
teaches: What the sermon offered as an item of compassion for the victim becomes in debate a question of moral accounting for the sacrificer, so the poem moves from pity for the beast to the sacrificer's own liability.

note: In the Manimekalai the Vedic brahmin states that the Veda has no cause, beginning or end, and Manimekalai simply judges that it agrees with no way of truth; here the same thesis is put by Bhutikan as a challenge and answered with five inferences.
teaches: The Buddhist epic records the Veda's beginninglessness and dismisses it without argument, while the Jain epic makes it the hinge of a full debate, showing which of the two heterodox poets chose to argue the point.

note: The Valayapathi fragment says not to accept a dharma joined with killing; Neelakesi applies that rule to the Veda, which she says forbids killing and yet permits limitless killing in sacrifice.
teaches: The fragment's maxim gets a named target: the dharma joined with killing is the Vedic sacrifice, and the Neelakesi adds that such a dharma fails even by its own rule against killing.

note: The couplet ranks not killing one creature above pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices; Neelakesi says the sacrifice itself is the killing and its heavy deed falls on those who perform it.
teaches: Read beside the Jain charge, the couplet's comparison is seen to be the mild form of an argument the debater presses to the end: the Kural weighs sacrifice against abstention, Neelakesi denies the sacrifice any merit at all.

gains.a: Neelakesi's charge gains a widely shared ethical maxim that already ranks abstention above sacrifice, so her conclusion looks like its extension rather than a sectarian novelty
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the oblations it sets aside are themselves animal killing, which sharpens its comparison into an indictment

note: The couplet says a Brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct fails though the Veda can be relearned; Neelakesi says the Veda itself teaches that birth yields nothing yet fixes the four classes and shuts out the Sudra.
teaches: Both put conduct above birth, but the Kural keeps birth as a rank that conduct can lose, while Neelakesi finds the Veda caught between those two and calls the mixture confusion.

gains.a: the verse gains a well-known saying that already ranks conduct above the Brahmin's birth, which makes the contradiction she alleges in the Veda visible in a familiar text
gains.b: the couplet gains a reader who notices that it still assumes a Brahmin's birth as something to be lost, which the Jain argument treats as the very confusion

audit_text_issue: neelakesi:834 flagged uncertain; line 3 சூதித்த தோற்றமும் பிழைப்பென obscure

note: The couplet names tending the ancestors and the gods among the householder's five chief duties; Neelakesi argues that merit done in the name of the eminent dead cannot reach them, or the released would be bound again.
teaches: Set beside the Jain reductio, the Kural's duty to the ancestors is seen to say nothing on whether anything reaches them, which is the question on which the Vedic and Jain views divide.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument gains a respected text whose duty to the ancestors her opponent would cite, so the reductio is seen to strike at ordinary household piety too
gains.b: the couplet gains a sharp question its list leaves open: whether tending the ancestors benefits them or only disciplines the householder

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Neelakesi says a deed of killing done for the gods ripens in the killer as poison in the one who eats it, whoever it was meant for.
teaches: The quatrain's claim that a deed finds its own doer becomes in the debate a weapon against transferred merit, showing that the proverb rules out offering one's deed to gods or ancestors.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument gains a common proverb that already states her premise, so her opponent must deny popular wisdom to escape it
gains.b: the quatrain gains a disputed case, sacrifice offered for another, in which its calf image does real argumentative work

note: Tirumular says there is no dharma that leaves out the Veda, and the wise gave up disputation and recited it to gain release; Neelakesi argues by inference that the Veda is made and, being joined to killing, drives its followers to evil births.
teaches: The two verses disagree both on the Veda and on method: Tirumular sets recitation above argument as the way to release, while Neelakesi makes argument the test that the Veda fails.

gains.a: the verse gains a clear statement of the Veda's claim to contain all dharma, the claim her inferences are built to break
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains a concrete instance of the disputation it tells the wise to give up, and of what that disputation says about the Veda

audit_text_issue: 828 line 2 (குவகொடும்) may be corrupt. | 828 line 2 குவகொடும் is unclear and may be corrupt. | 828 line 2 குவகொடும் may be corrupt.

note: Tirumular says that when steadfast Brahmins pour the oblation sky, earth, the quarters and their gods flourish; Neelakesi says that rites cannot drive off disease or demons and that gods who delight in killing cannot remove the killer's karma.
teaches: Where the Saiva verse gives the rite power to sustain the world and its gods, the Jain debater denies it any power over karma at all, so the two disagree on whether ritual acts on the moral order.

gains.a: the verse gains the full Vedic-Saiva claim for the rite that it denies, which shows how much it is rejecting
gains.b: Tirumular's verse gains an opponent who asks what the oblation can do against a deed already done, a question it does not take up

note: Pattirakiriyar longs to go about without caste, as the agama of Kapila says; Neelakesi argues that high and low birth is unreal because sight, smell, taste and touch find no difference.
teaches: Both reject caste, but on different grounds: the Siddhar appeals to a scripture, while the Jain debater appeals to perception against scripture, which shows that an anti-caste position need not rest on any text.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument gains a later Tamil voice reaching the same rejection of caste, which shows her point outlived the debate
gains.b: the Siddhar's verse gains a reason from the senses that does not depend on Kapila's unidentified agama

note: Both epics give the materialist the liquor figure for awareness arising in combined elements; Manimekalai's lets awareness die like a drum's sound, Neelakesi's sends each element back to its kind and counts space among five elements.
teaches: The liquor analogy was the stock materialist argument in both traditions, but only the Jain epic answers it on its own terms (866, 868), while Manimekalai leaves the doctrine and attacks only its theory of knowledge.

note: Manimekalai asks the materialist whether some have not known a former birth, and he waves it off as the delusion of dreams or possession; Neelakesi points instead to the newborn seeking the breast.
teaches: Set beside the Manimekalai, the Jain choice of evidence shows its point: an infant's instinct cannot be dismissed as dream or a god's delusion, the very escape the materialist used against memory of past births.

note: The Kural says one who denies what the world holds to be will be counted a demon (அலகை); the epic names its materialist Pisasakan, a name that sounds like பிசாசு, and ends the sarukkam by showing him a demon (887-892).
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's label into a plot: the man who denies spirits carries a demon's name and is converted by meeting one, so the Kural's 'demon' becomes both insult and refutation.

gains.a: the name Pisasakan gains an ethical frame, as the stock word for the denier of what all accept
gains.b: the couplet's unnamed blank, what is denied, is filled with a case: the denial of soul, rebirth and spirits

note: The Kural has the five elements laugh inwardly at a deceiver's hidden conduct; Neelakesi argues that no element has theft, lust or generosity as a quality.
teaches: Read together, the Kural's laughing elements must be a figure of moral witness, since the Jain debate shows that moral traits are exactly what the elements cannot bear, and her 'thieving element' mocks any literal reading.

gains.a: her sarcastic 'thieving element' gains a target: a familiar way of speaking in which elements do take moral notice
gains.b: the couplet gains a test of its figure: whether the elements could literally judge conduct is a question the schools argued

note: Neelakesi argues that the ascetic's staff and bowl would be wasted unless a soul survives the body; Tirumular says garb put on the body is not for the soul and falls away with the body.
teaches: Both tie ascetic dress to the body-soul question but draw opposite lessons from it: for the Jain debater the gear presupposes a soul, for Tirumular it cannot reach the soul at all, so outward penance is evidence in one text and irrelevance in the other.

gains.a: the epic's argument gains its limit: the Saiva text denies that outward marks bear on the soul it presupposes
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of garb gains a context in which garb was used as proof of the soul against a materialist

audit_text_issue: The verse has doubtful forms (கட்டில், சுதத்தி) flagged by the marker.

note: Against the Ajivikas Neelakesi argued that a Lord who never spoke left no scripture; here she argues that a school with no teacher freed from deeds has no first book at all.
teaches: Her test of a school's scripture is constant across the debates: authority runs only from an omniscient speaker, and the materialist fails it more completely than the Ajivika, having no such teacher even in claim.

note: Against the Buddha, who denied a soul, she asked who he then was that taught; against the materialist she asks which element is the one debating with her.
teaches: The same self-reference argument serves against both deniers of the soul: the debater's own presence is the counterexample, whether the denial is the Buddhist's no-self or the materialist's mere elements.
audit_text_issue: Neelakesi 568 lines 3-4 are uncertain; the link rests on lines 1-2.

note: Pisasakan says the world has always been only the combining of elements and those who say otherwise are deluded; at the sarukkam's end he says he accepts birth, demons and all she said.
teaches: The epic stages the materialist's claim to permanence of his view in order to reverse it within the same sarukkam, so the debate ends in a conversion rather than a mere victory.

note: In 857 the materialist says the five elements become eye, nose, tongue, body and ear with their five objects; in 879 Neelakesi tells him to give up that very thought and sets up the soul.
teaches: The materialist's derivation of each sense from an element is the exact point Neelakesi chooses to deny, so the soul she proves is defined against a sense apparatus made of matter.

note: In 49 the sage knows she may try to frighten him with her transformations (விகுர்வணை) and fail; in 888 she uses the same power of transformation to frighten the materialist into belief.
teaches: The demon's power to change shape, useless against the Jain sage at the start, becomes at the end the Jain debater's proof of unseen beings, so the same faculty passes from assault to teaching.

note: In 134 Neelakesi likens the sage to a mother who nurses her infant even when it hurts her, and drops her false form; in 891 and 892 she, the demoness, calls herself a mother to the frightened Pisasikan and makes him kin through dharma.
teaches: The work closes its debates by repeating its opening conversion one step down: the demoness who was mothered into dharma now mothers a man into it, so conversion is shown as a lineage passed on.

note: In 7 the poet asks readers not to scorn his work, since people take even a bird's cry as meaningful; in 885 Neelakesi counts the omen of bird cries among the things the elements cannot explain.
teaches: The poem leans twice on the common trust in bird-omens, once to defend itself and once to defeat the materialist, which shows how much of its case rests on what the world already accepts.
audit_text_issue: Verse 7 line 1 is obscure, and the verse is flagged uncertain.

note: Both epics answer a materialist who accepts only perception: Manimekalai shows him that he knows his own parents only by inference; Neelakesi grants his rule and gives him a perception, the sight of a ghost.
teaches: The Buddhist and the Jain epic meet the same Lokayata rule in opposite ways: one turns the rule against itself and leaves the materialist answered, the other satisfies the rule and leaves him converted.

note: Manimekalai asks whether some have not known a former birth, and the materialist dismisses such knowledge as the delusion of the god-struck or the dreamer; Neelakesi offers the reborn man who leads his kin to the treasure he hid.
teaches: The reborn man's found treasure is a check outside his own mind, so it meets the very objection the materialist raised against Manimekalai's appeal to remembered births.
audit_text_issue: 886 line 4 (செத்து வம்மெய்திற் சில்லைமை செய்பவால்) is hard to construe.

note: The Kural says one who denies what the world holds to exist will be set down on earth as a demon; the materialist who denies ghosts is named Pisasikan, the ghost's one, and the demoness claims him as son once he takes the dharma.
teaches: The epic plays the couplet's sentence out and reverses its sting: the denier is indeed reckoned of the demons, but as their adopted kin through dharma rather than as an object of scorn.

gains.a: Neelakesi's pun on the name gains a known moral frame, the denier of common belief as a demon among men.
gains.b: The Kural's unnamed 'what the world holds' gets a content, ghosts and rebirth, and a case where the denier is won back rather than condemned.

note: Neelakesi asks what cause brings the elements together, since they cannot join themselves; Tirumular sets unknowing maya beside the knowing soul and calls the making of elements and senses the fivefold work of grace.
teaches: Both texts deny that unknowing matter assembles itself into a knower, but where the Jain debater leaves the cause in the soul and its deeds, the Saiva verse gives it to grace.

gains.a: Neelakesi's open question gains the answer a rival theist school gives, showing which answer the Jain debater leaves unsaid.
gains.b: Tirumular's assignment of elements and senses to grace gains the opponent it presupposes: the materialist for whom the elements need no cause at all.

audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 1805 line 1 is uncertain (whether ஆயும் அறிவு is the soul). | Tirumanthiram 1805 flagged uncertain.

note: The materialist says that when the elements part, all comes to nothing; the Siddhar says he saw the five elements die and fall and the five senses burn and fall.
teaches: The Siddhar describes as his own experience the parting of elements and senses that the materialist says must end awareness, and he remains to report it, which is the case Neelakesi argues for and does not show.

gains.a: Neelakesi's bare rejection gains a first-person witness who outlasts the falling away of the elements.
gains.b: The Siddhar's vision gains its doctrinal stake: it is the very event the materialist claims would leave no one to see it.

note: Both open by praising the Jain god, but the Cintamani defines him by the bliss he reached by himself and his unceasing qualities, while the Soolamani defines him by the sum of deeds he conquered and by the freeing of those who bow.
teaches: One invocation names what the god is, the other what the god did to deeds, so the Jain epics share a god but each praises a different side of him.

note: Kural 10 has those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; Soolamani 1 has those who bowed at the feet lose their deeds, after a god who conquered deeds himself.
teaches: The Kural says the feet carry one over births, and the Soolamani names a ground for it: a god who has himself overcome the deeds that bind.

gains.a: the departure of the devotees' deeds is set in the crossing-of-births frame that Tamil praise of the Lord's feet already uses, which the verse does not state
gains.b: the Lord's feet get a reason for their power, a victory over deeds, which the couplet leaves unsaid

note: Soolamani 1 praises a god who won the sum of deeds himself and lets those who bow be freed; Tirumanthiram 1649 says by Siva's grace deeds do not cling.
teaches: Release from deeds is credited to a conqueror's own victory in the Jain verse and to the giving of grace in the Saiva one, so the two differ over who removes the deeds.

gains.a: the god is seen as a conqueror who had deeds to overcome, not a giver, set against a Saiva grace that works without such a victory
gains.b: grace is seen against a god who earned the freedom by his own conquest, which makes the Saiva grace read as a gift and not a result

note: Both praise the Jain god as light: the Soolamani's light of the world above after splitting the deeds, the Cintamani's holy form that blazes brighter than flame.
teaches: The Soolamani's light is the result of cutting the deeds, while the Cintamani's is a body brighter than flame and marked with signs, so the same image names an act in one and a form in the other.

note: Both call the Jain god a lamp: the Soolamani's சுடர் that stands as the world's light after the deeds are split, the Neelakesi's ancient lamp of dharma who knows all things.
teaches: The lamp is the Soolamani's god in the world above, the Neelakesi's god as the source of dharma, so the image moves from where he stands to what he teaches.

note: Both poets ask the learned to deal with the flaws of the work, but the Cintamani asks that they wash the flaw out with their wit, while the Soolamani expects the wise to guard the lapses of people like himself.
teaches: One poet asks the reader to correct the flaw and the other to shield it, so the two Jain epics set different tasks for the learned in front of a faulty work.

note: Both place the work before an assembly of the discerning: the Soolamani says the discerning in the king's assembly accepted it, while the Cintamani says it was set out to be told to the assembly of the discerning.
teaches: The Soolamani states the assembly's acceptance as already given, where the Cintamani only offers the story for it, so one poet claims approval and the other asks for it.

note: Both poets answer the fear of fault with the moon's spot: the Neelakesi's poet says even the moon is not spotless and he will own a fault, the Soolamani's says the moon's spot does not stop some from worshipping it.
teaches: The Neelakesi's poet takes the blemish on himself, while the Soolamani's poet asks the good to look past it, so one image gives a confession in one work and a plea in the other.

note: Naladiyar 221 says the faults of those taken as good are kept within, as rice has its husk; Soolamani 5 asks that the poet's fault count for nothing before the good.
teaches: The Naladiyar's rule keeping faults hidden between friends becomes a poet's plea that readers apply it to his own work, which turns a rule of friendship into a rule of reading.

gains.a: the plea to overlook a fault is given a rule behind it, a standing habit of the good to keep faults within
gains.b: the rule of keeping faults hidden is seen applied from a poet to his readers, outside the friendship it was written for

note: The verse praises the land by festival and wealth only; Kural 738 lists freedom from disease, protection and yield as a land's ornaments.
teaches: The epic shows a land's greatness by its splendour alone, so the reader sees what the Kural's list adds that this praise leaves out.

gains.a: A test of what a land's wealth should rest on, which a bare picture of splendour lacks.
gains.b: A concrete land to which the five ornaments can be held up, where the couplet only names them.

audit_text_issue: Line 4 repaired from TSCII leftovers; sense uncertain

note: Women's perfumes weaken even ascetics here; the Thiruppugazh poet confesses his own ruin from craving women.
teaches: The scenic verse already carries the temptation that the poet of the Thiruppugazh later tells in the first person.

gains.a: A named cost of the pleasure it lightly sketches, which the verse itself does not state.
gains.b: An earlier poetic case in which the same allure reaches ascetics, not only a self-confessed sinner.

audit_text_issue: Thiruppugazh 201 opening hard to divide; 11 flagged

note: Both set the regions of the Tamil land together in one country: the four regions mingled here, the tunes and creatures of each region exchanged there.
teaches: Both poems prove a country's wholeness by letting the four regions share each other's things, but the epic only lists them while the Pattupattu ties the mingling to the king's just rule.

gains.a: A political reason for the blend, the king's one umbrella, which the epic's list leaves unsaid.
gains.b: A plain statement that the regions simply lie together, without the court's praise.

note: Both set the cowherds' flute in the evening pastures: a sign of plenty here, a torment to the waiting wife there.
teaches: The same flute is joy in the public landscape and pain in a private heart, so the reader sees how the sound takes its meaning from who hears it.

gains.a: A listener inside the scene, which the epic's description does not give.
gains.b: A public, cheerful reading of the flute against which her pain stands out.

note: Peacocks dance to the clouds' roar here, and in Akananuru 82 the hill is a stage where the peacock is the dancer.
teaches: Both make the hill a stage on which weather and creatures perform together, but the Akananuru names the full orchestra while the epic gives only clouds and peacocks.

gains.a: A fuller account of how the hill's sounds become music, which it only hints at.
gains.b: The same scene shown as ordinary prosperity, free of a lover's longing.

note: Kural 731 names unfailing yield, worthy people and wealthy people as the marks of a land; verse 29 gives only the yield, in stored grain that does not shrink as it is eaten.
teaches: Read against the Kural's three-part definition, the epic's country is first described by what it yields, and the people and the rich come only later, so the poet is building the land from its harvest outward.

gains.a: The verse gets a criterion that shows why grain heaps count as describing a land and not only as a list of crops.
gains.b: The couplet's abstract 'unfailing yield' gets concrete grains stored in houses and not diminishing when eaten.

note: The Pattupattu's mullai is wild woodland of avarai and kaanthal on a hunters' road ending in a meal of roast game; verse 30 gives the mullai as cropland of sesame, avarai and tuvarai pods.
teaches: The same named tract is a place of hunters' hospitality in the older poem and a place of pod crops in the epic, so the epic poet has turned the mullai from forest road to farmland.

gains.a: The verse gets the older mullai as foil and so shows that its pods mark a farmed mullai that the Sangam poem does not describe.
gains.b: The Pattupattu passage gets a later poet who reads its woodland by its yield, which shows that the tract was open to being counted as farmland.

note: Cintamani verse 44 shows ploughmen and buffalo rushing into the fields; Soolamani verse 31 shows the sugarcane and paddy standing with no one in the field.
teaches: Two Jain epics describing the land differ in whom they let in: the Cintamani fills its fields with the labour that makes the crop, and the Soolamani leaves the crop standing alone.

note: In the Pattupattu the fishers sing the kurinji tune, the hill people wear neythal chaplets and the tracts are said to gather under one umbrella; in verse 33 each kind of woman wears the flowers of her own tract.
teaches: Both poems sort a land by its peoples and flowers, but the Sangam poem mixes the tracts to show one king's rule, while the epic keeps each tract's women with her own flower and ends in a catalogue.

gains.a: The verse gets from the Pattupattu the reason such sorting of peoples matters, the unity of a realm under one ruler, which the epic verse leaves unstated.
gains.b: The Pattupattu passage gets the women of each tract, whom it does not describe, as the carriers of the tract's flowers.

audit_text_issue: 33 flower-woman pairing uncertain; flagged uncertain | 33 line 2 கதுப்பயர் கமழும் மேழையம் is obscure

note: Kural 1228 has the herdsman's flute as a weapon that kills the lonely woman at evening; verse 34 has the herdsmen's konrai flute so sweet that the asunam beast sleeps.
teaches: The same herdsman's flute soothes the beast and wounds the parted woman, so its effect lies in the listener's state and not in the music, a point neither verse shows alone.

gains.a: The verse gets a hearer for whom the flute hurts, which shows that its sweet peace holds only for listeners at ease and sets a limit on the land's contentment.
gains.b: The couplet gets a flute that is gentle to those at ease, which shows that the woman's pain is her own separation and not the sound.

note: Verse 36 measures the city against the serpents' world below, and verse 50 against Indra's heaven above.
teaches: The poet bounds the city between the Naga world beneath and Indra's world above, so its praise is a scale with two ends, not one comparison repeated.
audit_text_issue: Verse 50 and 36 are both simple comparisons; 36 line 1 loose construction.

note: Verse 37 makes the city a woman's body and verse 46 fills its ponds with swans that hear her anklets and fear their mates are gone.
teaches: The poet moves from city as woman to a woman's sound as the cause of the birds' fear, so the beauty praised is also felt as loss, which verse 37 does not show.

note: Verse 40 gives the women's eyes rain-dark paint and the wishing tree, and verse 44 shows bees fooled by the same eyes into taking them for flowers.
teaches: The women's eyes are praised once by their effect on lords and once by their effect on bees, so the poet treats the same beauty as ruling men and nature alike.

note: Verse 52 gives Payapati a gentle face for those who come near; Kural 386 says a king easy to see and gentle in speech is praised above others.
teaches: The epic's king is gentle only to those who draw near and hot to foes, so the Kural's single ideal is shown split in two by the king's own enemies.

gains.a: The verse gains a standard that says why being easy to approach counts as praise in a king, which the city-description leaves unstated.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king who keeps his gentleness for friends and is hot to foes, a limit on a rule the couplet states without exception.

note: Tirumanthiram 244 calls the king's share one sixth of the produce and ties it to keeping dharma without lapse; 54 shows the king taking his sixth only as grace.
teaches: The verse puts the one-sixth rule into practice as restraint on both tax and killing, while the Tirumanthiram makes it a step on the road to release and wealth.

gains.a: The verse gains the Tirumanthiram's claim that dharma kept without lapse is the road to release as well as wealth, which its own praise of the king leaves unsaid.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram gains a king who actually takes only the sixth and refuses wrathful killing, so its rule has a figure who keeps it.

note: Kural 550 allows a king to put the cruel to death as weeding the crop; 54 has this king subdue even opponents by bowing them, and not slay in anger.
teaches: The couplet's weeding is the harsher rule, and the verse shows a king who treats killing as what grace avoids, so the two differ on whether death is part of a king's work.

gains.a: The verse gains a rival standard in which a king's killing counts as justified, against which his restraint reads as a choice, not a rule.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king who will not weed even his foes, showing how far a ruler can go without using death.

note: Kural 447 prizes counsellors who rebuke the ruler; 58 shows a court where no one proposes anything except at the king's hint.
teaches: The couplet praises the courtier who dares to rebuke, and the verse depicts a court where none speak unless prompted, which shows what the king gives up by having no one to correct him.

gains.a: The verse gains a measure that reveals its silent court as lacking the correction a ruler needs.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete court of obedient, fearless speakers, showing what its rebuking counsellors would stand against.

note: 53 says the only weapon abroad in his reign was Kama's arrows; 66 shows the same flower-arrowed god working inside the palace to join the king and the two queens.
teaches: The praise of a bloodless reign leads to the place where Kama's arrows land, showing the opening claim as the first note of the palace's own story.

note: 56 says the king guards himself and the earth; 67 has the queens draw his mind from the work of ruling.
teaches: The king whose guarding of the world is praised is shown giving up the work of ruling to the queens' hold on his mind, so the poem sets one claim against the other.

note: Kural 902 says shame follows the man whose desire for his woman makes him careless of other things; 67 has two wives bind a king so that he lets the work of ruling go.
teaches: The couplet speaks for any man and the verse shows the cost to a king, whose neglected work is the world's guarding, so the stakes are larger than shame.

gains.a: The verse gains a verdict on a king set aside by love, which the narrator does not give.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler whose lapse touches a whole realm, which widens its cost beyond personal shame.
