note: 55 puts kings and sages in the shade of the king's umbrella and feet; 69 puts the whole earth asleep under the one white umbrella while the king bathes in the queens' breasts.
teaches: The shade that began as the world's refuge ends as the setting for the king's pleasure, so the umbrella changes from protection to the sign of a wealth enjoyed.

note: Siddhar 1790 scolds the stony mind for wanting to rule the whole earth under one umbrella; 69 closes the king's praise on exactly that single umbrella and his pleasure under it.
teaches: The Siddhar treats the one-umbrella rule as a desire to be given up, while the poem treats it as the king's finished wealth, so the same picture means a trap in one and a reward in the other.

gains.a: The verse gains a rival reading of the one umbrella as the object of craving, against which its praise sounds partial.
gains.b: The Siddhar verse gains a king who has the whole earth under one umbrella, so its warning has a figure who is already there.

note: Naladiyar 3 says that kings who rode under the royal umbrella fall when their deeds turn against them; 69 shows a king at the height of his umbrella-wealth, with no word of what deeds will bring.
teaches: The quatrain says the umbrella's glory lasts only while deeds hold it up, and the verse stops at the glory without the fall, so the reader supplies the warning from the quatrain.

gains.a: The verse gains a condition on its calm, that the king's wealth lasts only while his deeds do.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king in full peace, whose praise stops where its warning would begin.

note: At the princes' birth the clinging moisture of evil deeds is said to dry up for many; Kural 5 says deeds of darkness do not cling to those who delight in the Lord's praise.
teaches: The Kural lifts the hold of deeds through the devotee's own praise, but the epic lifts it for many through the birth of a great being, so each work places the loosening of karma somewhere different.

gains.a: The epic verse gets a stated condition for karma's loosening, the devotee's praise, which it does not state.
gains.b: Kural 5 gets a case where the hold is loosened by someone else's birth and not by the sufferer's devotion, a test of how exclusive its condition is.

note: Both verses close on the princes reaching an age that sets a fire in the women's hearts; 79 puts the cause in their youth, and 84 adds the women's sickness for wealthy lords.
teaches: The repeated line first locates the fire in the princes' youth, then ties it to wealth and rank, so the same phrase shifts what the women are said to burn for.

note: 78 lists conch and discus on the younger prince's palm; in 109 the court names him one who will guard the whole world under one umbrella.
teaches: The body marks listed as ornament in 78 are read, in 109, as a sign of universal rule, which changes how the earlier portrait should be heard.

note: 79 shows youth as a fire kindled in women; Tirumanthiram 180 has a man recall being sweet as cane juice to women and now bitter as the kanjiram fruit.
teaches: The epic shows only the rising stage of desire's arc, and Tirumular supplies the other end, so together they place the princes' present blaze on a curve that ends in the speaker's bitterness.

gains.a: The epic's fire of youth gets the end of its arc, which the verse does not show.
gains.b: Tirumanthiram 180 gets the beginning of its curve, the stage and the women's fire from which its speaker later falls.

audit_text_issue: TM 180 prints only three lines in the packet

note: 80 likens the women's sidelong glances to Kaman's arrows; Naladiyar 17 warns against desiring a woman of spear-like eyes, for she too will lean on a staff.
teaches: The epic shows the glance as a weapon at the moment of its force, and Naladiyar names the later fall of the same weapon, so the pair sets the glance's power against its short life.

gains.a: The epic's glances get a limit it does not state, that the spear-eyed will stoop and walk with a staff.
gains.b: Naladiyar 17 gets a scene of the spear-like glance at work, so its warning is aimed at what the reader has just watched.

note: The astrologer waits on the king's sign and then speaks to show his learning, with a sight of all three times; Naladiyar 52 calls those who prattle of the stars the most foolish of the foolish, set against the thought of death.
teaches: The story rests its plot on an astrologer who is admitted, heard and believed by the whole court, while the quatrain calls his craft folly, so the two give opposite verdicts on the same trade.

gains.a: The poem's own motive line, that he speaks to display his learning, gets an outside judgment on whether that learning is worth the court's trust.
gains.b: The quatrain's charge of folly meets an astrologer who is welcomed by a king, which shows the claim being tested against a trusted practitioner.

note: The astrologer sets aside courtesies, waits for the king's sign and speaks; Kural 696 tells a speaker to know the mood, weigh the time and say what is wanted and not disliked.
teaches: The astrologer keeps the Kural's rule of reading the king and timing his speech, but the poet names his aim as showing his learning, a motive the couplet never allows for.

gains.a: The wait for the king's sign is given a stated rule behind it, so it reads as court craft and not mere delay.
gains.b: The couplet's advice is shown in a scene where the speaker has something the king will welcome, and where the speaker's vanity can still sit under a correct manner.

note: Kannaki's dream of trouble in Madurai, told to Kovalan before he leaves, and the astrologer's dream of an elephant garlanding the young lord are both dreams that foretell what is to come.
teaches: In the Silappathikaram the dream is a warning that cannot turn the course of fate, while here it is a promise that the court at once turns into a plan, so one image serves ruin in one epic and fortune in the other.

note: The astrologer reads a night's dream as true knowledge of what will come; the Siddhar song says all he saw has turned into a dream, like moonlight on a forest.
teaches: One poem trusts a dream to show what is real in the future, and the other uses the dream as the name for the whole of what is seen, so the same word divides prophecy from unreality.

gains.a: The prophetic dream gets a view that holds waking sight itself to be dream-like, which unsettles the court's easy trust in the sign.
gains.b: The Siddhar's figure of dream as unreality meets a dream treated as sure foreknowledge, which shows what the figure is set against.

note: Verse 106 gives the dream of the elephant that garlands the young lord; 107 gives its fruit, a Vidyadhara king's gift of his daughter.
teaches: The astrologer first tells the dream and only then its fruit, so the reader sees a sign turned into a forecast of a marriage and an alliance.

note: The astrologer foretells a messenger with a letter in the Pushpakarandam garden; the ministers propose to set the stone platform in order and post a guard in the garden on his day.
teaches: The court does not wait on the prophecy but prepares the place it names, so counsel here means arranging the ground for a sign the king has only just heard.

note: The ministers propose to place Turumakanthan as guard in the garden; he goes to the garden after bowing to the king.
teaches: The proposal becomes action in two verses, and the guard sets out only after the king's approval, which shows how a counsel becomes an order.

note: Verse 140 faults a mighty king for want of grace to the lowly; Kural 557 says that a king's lack of tender regard is to his people as lack of rain to the earth.
teaches: The epic names one flaw in a king otherwise perfect, so the Kural's claim that lack of regard undoes all else is tested against a ruler praised for everything else.

gains.a: A measure of the flaw's weight, which the verse names without saying how much it costs.
gains.b: A concrete king whose every other virtue stands, so the couplet's rule faces a hard case.

note: Kural 549 counts guarding the people and removing wrongdoing as the king's work and no fault; verse 140 faults a king on the ground of grace toward the lowest lives, which the Kural's list does not ask of him.
teaches: The epic widens the king's duty to grace toward all lowly lives, where the Kural's duty stops at the people and the removal of wrongdoers, so the two hold different measures of a good ruler.

gains.a: A rival standard, the Kural's, by which the king is judged only on what he does to his people.
gains.b: A test of its limit: a king who punishes wrongdoers by the Kural's rule may still lack grace toward lower creatures.

note: Both Jain epics describe a Vidyadhara city by its splendour, this one as a golden city on the southern ridge, the other as a casket of gems opened.
teaches: Both epics fix the Vidyadhara realm in the reader's mind as a city of gems and gold above the plain, so the genre's convention is clear from the pair.

note: In 138 elephant-kings bow to the father; in 159 kings with fierce-eyed elephants bow to the daughter.
teaches: The homage the father wins by victory passes to the daughter by beauty alone, so the poem lets beauty hold the sway that the king's sword held.

note: Verse 161 likens the wealth of the worthless to kongu trees that bloom without scent; Kural 1008 likens the wealth of the unwanted to a poison tree fruiting in the town.
teaches: Both name a tree whose outer splendour fails its purpose, one for giving no scent and one for giving poison, so wealth without worth is shown useless in one case and harmful in the other.

gains.a: A harsher side of the image: wealth without worth does not merely fail to please, it can poison those who come near.
gains.b: A softer case: wealth may leave the others unharmed but unattended, like blossom that no one stops for.

note: Naladiyar 160 says the base follow the rich as their one hope; verse 166 says people leave the rich once their sweetness turns.
teaches: Naladiyar shows the crowd that clings to wealth and the cuckoo shows it is not loyal, since it goes the moment the taste turns.

gains.a: A reason why the followers come: wealth is their only hope, which the cuckoo's simile does not state.
gains.b: A limit: the clinging lasts only while the sweetness lasts, which the quatrain does not say.

note: Verse 187 hails the god as walking above the lotus, as Kural 3 speaks of the one who walked upon the flower.
teaches: The same lotus-walker of the opening couplet appears here as an epic's praised Arhat, so the image carries a Jain form where the Kural leaves the Lord unnamed.

gains.a: The lotus-walker is given an addressee, a congregation that loves him though he feels no pleasure, which the verse's own words alone do not show for any named god.
gains.b: A worship scene in which the image sits within a story of devotees, where the couplet states it as a bare mark.

note: Verse 188 says the god takes no joy in praise yet is loved; Kural 4 says the god without liking or aversion frees those who reach his feet.
teaches: The epic turns the Kural's rule of the one without liking into a devotional posture: love offered without any hope of being pleased.

gains.a: A reason why the worshippers do not need his pleasure, which the verse does not state.
gains.b: A scene of worship that tests the claim that the one without liking cannot be moved by praise.

note: Verse 182 says even calling the Arhat all-knowing does not let one know him; Tirumanthiram 32 says no one knows the lord's nature, and the all-pervading lord is praised only in part.
teaches: Both say naming does not reach the god, but the Jain verse accepts omniscience as a true name while the Saiva verse denies any measure of the lord.

gains.a: The verse's refusal is made sharper: it concedes the epithet and still holds the god beyond it, where the Saiva line denies all naming.
gains.b: A rival that praises by listing epithets, so the lord beyond naming can be seen as a stand against it.

note: Verse 175 draws spring shoots as copies of the women's hands and waists; Naladiyar 48 tells those who praise sandal and garland without knowing the body to look at vultures tearing the carcass.
teaches: A court poet delights in the body's beauty while a moral quatrain holds the same body as carrion, so the same poem tradition holds two views of the body.

gains.a: A counter-voice that sees the beauty it praises as fading.
gains.b: A quatrain's image set against a living scene of pleasure, so its rebuke has a concrete target.

note: Verse 180 says the shrine and its god end births; Kural 10 says only those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births.
teaches: The epic locates the ending of births in the shrine and its god, where the Kural puts it in the devotee's reaching.

gains.a: A statement of what the god gives, not only what the devotee reaches.
gains.b: A place in which the reaching happens, the shrine.

note: Verse 181 praises him who conquered the harsh dust of karma; Kural 5 says the two deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
teaches: The epic names the conqueror of karma whose praise the Kural says keeps deed from clinging, so it names the one the couplet leaves as 'the Lord'.

gains.a: A Lord defined by his conquest of karma, so what the praise protects against is plain.
gains.b: A reader's reason why praise should loosen the deeds' hold.

note: Verse 179 opens the shrine's gem doors at the king's coming; verse 185 shuts them after his praise.
teaches: The worship is bounded by an opening and a closing of the doors, so the whole of the praise lies between them.

note: Kural 351 says the joyless birth comes from a confusion that takes the unreal for real; Soolamani 198 says deeds grow from a seed of lacking true knowledge and ripen into pain through a chain of births.
teaches: The sage supplies a growth path (seed, deeds, ripening, rebirth) for the couplet's bare claim, while the couplet says what kind of knowledge fails.

gains.a: the missing true knowledge is made specific as seeing the unreal as real, a wrong seeing and not just an empty gap
gains.b: the confusion gains the steps by which it ends in birth: a seed that grows into deeds that ripen as pain

note: Kural 361 names craving as the seed that produces unceasing birth; the Soolamani's sage names lacking true knowledge as the seed of the deeds that bind.
teaches: Two Tamil teachers name different seeds of rebirth, so the root of bondage is a question of doctrine and is not common ground.

gains.a: its seed is set beside a rival one, so lack of knowledge is shown as one choice among Tamil answers
gains.b: the couplet's craving gets an older cause to answer, whether craving grows out of not knowing

note: Soolamani 199 has deeds breed deeds until a refuge is reached; Tirumanthiram 120 has a teacher make the seeds of births like seeds touched by fire, which will not sprout.
teaches: Both see rebirth as a growing seed; the Jain verse tells how the chain runs, the Saiva verse how it is cut at the root by a teacher.

gains.a: it gains a picture of how the chain can be stopped at the seed, which the sage only says is by reaching a refuge
gains.b: it gains the chain that the scorched seed stands against, deeds producing deeds through their fruit

note: Soolamani 200 makes the feet of the beginningless Lord the refuge from great suffering; Tirumanthiram 138 says the holy feet are Sivam, Sivaloka and the path, and a refuge for those clear within.
teaches: Both name the feet a refuge, but the Saiva feet are the goal and the way at once, while the Jain verse sets the refuge apart from the state it leads to, described in 202.

gains.a: the refuge is shown as a means only, as the goal is another thing, by contrast with feet that are also the goal
gains.b: the feet as goal and refuge together are shown as one answer among others, since a Jain verse names them only as a refuge

audit_text_issue: 200 lines 1-2 hard (காதியம், போதியங் கிழவர்) | 200 lines 1-2 (காதியம், போதியங் கிழவர்) are hard.

note: Soolamani 200 recommends refuge in the Lord's feet as the cure for suffering; Civaka Cintamani 380 shows Civakan going to the Wise One as a raft because an old deed drove him.
teaches: The sermon says why to take refuge and the story shows why someone does, adding that the going is itself moved by an old deed.

note: Kural 355 says knowledge is seeing the real in whatever thing; Soolamani 201 sets discerning true things as the first of three, followed by knowledge and conduct kept to the text.
teaches: The epic makes the couplet's seeing the start of a sequence that does not end until conduct is kept, not the whole of release.

gains.a: the discerning of true things is placed first and so not enough alone, it must be followed by conduct
gains.b: the couplet's seeing is given a place in a larger course ending in disciplined conduct

note: After taking refuge, Manimekalai's teacher begins on the three jewels of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha; Soolamani 201 gives three things to hold after the refuge in 200: true seeing, knowledge and conduct.
teaches: Both sermons give threes after refuge, but the Buddhist three are what one goes to for refuge and the Jain three are what the follower must hold.

note: Soolamani 202 describes release as a shining form and limitless, unfailing bliss; Tirumanthiram 136 says the soul subsides into Sivam as salt returns to water.
teaches: The two release verses differ on whether the freed self keeps its own form and bliss or subsides into another, if the salt image is read as loss of separate being and the Jain 'shining form' as a kept one.

gains.a: release is shown as a state the freed self keeps as its own, since no one else is named for it to join
gains.b: the salt image meets a Tamil account in which the freed soul keeps form and bliss, so merging is not the only picture of release

note: Kural 352 says that for those of stainless sight darkness leaves and joy arises; Soolamani 203 has the light of knowledge from the sage's words split the darkness of evil deeds in the whole assembly.
teaches: The two verses use darkness and light, but the epic has the light come to a crowd from a teacher's words, while the couplet leaves it to one's own clear sight.

gains.a: the darkness is given as the darkness of evil deeds, and the light comes by hearing a teacher
gains.b: the bare word 'darkness', which commentators read as hell, ignorance or births, is shown in one reading as the darkness of deeds

note: Verse 205 has the king's daughter resolve on a vow and think how to finish it with greatness; verse 212 has her complete the vow of Chakravalam and then wish a great special worship.
teaches: The resolve at the sermon's end is kept here, and it grows into a second act, the worship, beyond the vow.

note: Kural 3 gives the Lord as the one who walked on the flower, at whose feet one arrives; Soolamani 214 gives the girl's hymn to the primal Lord who gave the scripture, who stood on the flower, at whose holy feet she bows.
teaches: The hymn uses a flower-footed epithet close to the couplet's and gives it to the Jain Lord with titles that name him, which the couplet does not.

gains.a: a familiar Tamil epithet for the flower-footed Lord is borrowed as a form of worship, so the girl's praise sits in a shared idiom
gains.b: the couplet's disputed 'one who walked on the flower' appears in a later Jain work applied to the Arhat, one data point on how the epithet was read

note: The king's question in verse 229, which youth is fit for his daughter, is met in verse 238 by sending for the ministers learned in policy.
teaches: The king does not choose the groom himself but turns his open question into a council of treatise-learned ministers, so the epic makes a marriage a matter for counsel.

note: The poet's opening hymn praises the god who conquered the sum of his deeds; the princess's hymn here names what he conquered, desire and Death.
teaches: The invocation praises the god's victory in general terms, while the princess's hymn names the enemies; one is left to see that the poem's single praise is told twice, in two voices.

note: Kural 445 tells a ruler to take counsel from ministers as his eyes; verse 237 says that kings' lives and even Indra's lordship do not flower without counsel.
teaches: The epic widens the Kural's rule from a ruler's prudence to a claim about all rule and even the gods' rule.

gains.a: A statement of the rule as a duty of a ruler, where the verse shows only that counsel is needed.
gains.b: An example from the Brahmanical and divine world that the couplet's own kings never reach.

note: Kural 445 calls counsellors a ruler's eyes; verse 234 pictures a king opening like a lotus by the sun only through the learned who consider.
teaches: The epic gives a picture of how counsel acts, a bloom that opens only at the sun's touch, where the Kural gives a rule that counsel should be taken.

gains.a: A plain rule that counsel is to be taken, behind its picture of the lotus.
gains.b: A figure that shows kingship as a bloom needing the light of the learned.

note: Naladiyar 274 uses a daughter of the house, enjoyed by a stranger, as a figure for wealth that others will use; verse 228 calls a girl the jewel beyond all earthly and heavenly jewels.
teaches: The Naladiyar's picture treats a daughter's going to another house as a thing to be expected, while the epic makes her the treasure whose giving is a king's weightiest care.

gains.a: A plain statement that a daughter's passage to a stranger is as sure as hoarded wealth falling to another.
gains.b: A measure of how much the girl was worth to the one who gives her, which the simile treats as a mere example.

note: Verse 242 has the king say he can grasp subtle things only through the learned treatises; Kural 637 says that even one who knows the method must act by knowing how the world goes.
teaches: The council's first claim makes the treatise the king's only guide, where the couplet warns that a treatise's method must still be tested against the world, so the two disagree on where good judgment is found.

gains.a: A corrective: the books the king defers to still leave him to read the world's own way.
gains.b: A case for deference: why a ruler should hold a treatise above his own sense.

note: Verse 243 says the learned keep blame and fierce deeds from a king whose sceptre is unbent; Kural 547 says justice guards the king if he does not falter in it.
teaches: The epic names who keeps a king from faltering, the learned counsellors, where the couplet names only the law that guards him if he does not.

gains.a: A reason why the sceptre stays unbent: it is kept by the learned.
gains.b: Persons who do the guarding the couplet gives to justice itself.

note: Verse 244 makes the ministers the king's mind, eye, living, strength and sceptre; Kural 445 calls counsellors the king's eyes and says he must take them after testing them.
teaches: The epic widens the Kural's single image of eyes to the king's whole body of rule, while the couplet adds a duty of choosing that the epic leaves unsaid.

gains.a: A rule for choosing: the king must test his counsellors before taking them.
gains.b: A fuller count of what rests on counsellors, from sight to the sceptre itself.

note: Verse 247 makes a king one who acts calmly on what the learned choose and tell him; Kural 638 says the man at the king's side must tell him what is good even if the king knows nothing and spoils wise counsel.
teaches: The epic sets the king's duty to act on counsel beside the minister's duty to give it, where the couplet shows only the minister's duty when the king will not hear.

gains.a: A case where the king refuses counsel and the minister must still speak.
gains.b: A test of kingship: the king's standing comes from acting calmly on the counsel he is given.

note: Verse 248 says counsel, not strength of arm, is the quality of a king; Kural 546 says it is not the spear but the unbent sceptre that gives victory.
teaches: Each puts a different power above the weapon, counsel in the epic and justice in the couplet, so the pair shows that the Tamil tradition names more than one winner of a war.

gains.a: A moral check: counsel that is clever but crooked would still fail the sceptre's test.
gains.b: A practical account of how victory is planned, where the couplet gives only its moral condition.

note: Verse 249 says even what comes like fate shows itself within the counsel of counsellors; Kural 620 says those who strive without flagging see even fate's back.
teaches: The epic puts fate and effort together in the council hall and finds that deliberation is where fate takes shape, while the couplet says effort can turn fate back.

gains.a: A place where fate and effort meet: counsel, not only labour, is the effort.
gains.b: A limit on its boast: effort works through counsel, and counsel is the stage on which fate shows.

note: Verse 249 says what comes like fate takes shape in the counsellors' deliberation; Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
teaches: The epic lets fate arrive through chosen acts of counsel, while the quatrain says the old deed finds its doer whatever he does, so the two differ on how far deliberation shapes what comes.

gains.a: The unavoidable pursuit by an old deed, which the verse softens by placing fate in counsel.
gains.b: A route by which an old deed arrives: through the choices of counsellors.

note: Verse 237 says that without counsel a king's life does not flourish and that even Indra's lordship rests on a thousand counsellors; verse 250 has the king himself rank counsel above his other powers.
teaches: The poet's maxim about counsel becomes the king's own weighing of counsel against his other powers, so the section turns a reflection into a decision.

note: Verse 251 compares a king in love's grip without learned men to a rutting elephant ridden by a fool; Cintamani 9 tells of a king whose dense desire made him refuse counsel and lose to a plot.
teaches: The Cintamani's story gives the cost that the Soolamani's maxim only warns of, a king who would not hear and lost the throne.

note: Verse 252 says failed counsel turns on the king like an angry snake whose charmer's art has failed; Kural 448 says a king with none to rebuke him perishes even without a foe.
teaches: The epic shows a king with counsellors destroyed by counsel gone wrong, where the couplet shows a king destroyed by having no counsellor who dares to rebuke him.

gains.a: A king who had counsellors and still fell: counsel itself can fail.
gains.b: A picture of how the king ruins himself: the instrument turns on the user.

note: Verse 254 has the king thank the ministers for his rule; Cintamani 206 has a counsellor press the king to hear counsel he does not want.
teaches: The Soolamani's council shows a king who welcomes counsel, while the Cintamani shows the counsellor who must speak when the king would not listen, so the ideal depends on a willing king.

note: Verse 140 names the one fault of the Vidyadhara king as want of grace toward the lowly; verse 262 has a minister say that great lords who bear the lapses of the lowly are followed by the whole earth.
teaches: The council offers the remedy for the king's single fault, so the earlier flaw reads as a fault the poem expects the counsellors to mend.

note: Verse 262 says lords who bear the lowly's lapses, like sandal under the rutting elephant, are bowed to by the earth; Naladiyar 66 says the well-born bear the base's stone-like words and let them pass, held back by their lineage.
teaches: The epic names the reward of forbearance in the king's public standing, where the quatrain names its reason in birth.

gains.a: The reward of forbearance in public honour, which the image alone does not name.
gains.b: A political result for the restraint that the quatrain justifies only by lineage.

note: Kural 559 says that when a ruler bends justice the sky bends the rain; verse 263 says that a cruel king is to the world as a sea-scorching sun is to its creatures.
teaches: The Kural names rain as the lost gift, but the epic names the people's suffering as the creatures' in a burning sea, so the ruler's fault is one of heat, not drought.

gains.a: The measure of the loss: not a missed crop but life in a sea turned hostile, which the Kural's line does not give.
gains.b: A different figure for the same fault, in which the injured are creatures with nowhere to go, not a land that goes dry.

note: Kural 389 puts the world under the parasol of a king who can bear bitter words; verse 264 says that a parasol grown hot scorches the cool ponds and groves under it.
teaches: The Kural gives the cool shade as a gift of the king's patience, and the epic gives the reverse: when the king is hot the shade itself scorches.

gains.a: The danger the Kural leaves unsaid: shade turned to heat when the one under it loses his patience.
gains.b: A named cause of the parasol's coolness, the king's duty of guarding, in a parallel to the Kural's patience.

note: Verse 266 says that nothing is better for the world than the shade at the feet of a king who stands in aram and guards the people like his own life; verse 140 faults a king who has every virtue but lacks grace to the lowly.
teaches: The counsellor's ideal king guards all like his life, and the poet's own Vidyadhara king, perfect but lacking grace, shows the ideal cannot be taken as met by any one virtue.

note: Kural 544 says the world holds to the feet of the great king who embraces his people; verse 266 says no one has anything better than the shade of such a king's feet.
teaches: The Kural makes the king's embrace of his people the condition of the world's clinging to his feet, and the epic gives the reason: they cling because men are wounding one another.

gains.a: A cause for the clinging, which is men's mutual harm, where the couplet gives only the condition.
gains.b: A negative picture of what the world is like without the king's feet, which the couplet only implies.

note: Kural 388 calls the king who protects with justice the இறை of his people; verse 267 calls him god-like because he orders a man's lot in both worlds.
teaches: The epic gives a reason for the Kural's word இறை as god: his rule reaches the next world's lot as well as this one's, which the couplet leaves untouched.

gains.a: The ground for calling the king godlike, which is a claim about both worlds.
gains.b: A reading in which இறை means a power over a man's fortune and not only a title of rule.

note: Kural 392 says numbers and letters, learning, are the eyes of living beings; verse 268 names three eyes, the king, learning and the sun.
teaches: The Kural calls learning the only eye of life, and the epic puts learning beside the king and the sun, so what learning sees is made one of three lights the world needs.

gains.a: A rival that sees where learning cannot, the king, the sun's equal in lifting the world's darkness.
gains.b: A list that puts learning's eyes among the world's lights and not only life's.

note: Tirumanthiram 1006 says that worship brings Indra's wealth, then the siddhis, then release; verse 272 says the world of the gods is reached by the true word and great austerity or by unslackening rule.
teaches: The same prize, Indra's world, is reached by worship in one and by one's own austerity or rule in the other, so the paths differ over whether a god's favour is needed; the conflict holds if Tirumular's worship counts as asking his grace.

gains.a: A path that asks for no god: the epic's way depends on the doer's truth, austerity and rule.
gains.b: A way to see worship as one route among several to Indra's wealth, which the epic's king-or-ascetic choice does not need.

note: Tirumanthiram 1464 says kings of the just sceptre and countless great ascetics have fallen; verse 273 says austerity and rule are heavy burdens, harder than lifting a diamond hill.
teaches: The epic stresses how heavy the two burdens are, and Tirumular says that even those who bore both have fallen, so the weight is not the end of the road.

gains.a: A measure of the fall: the ones who fell had borne the hardest burdens.
gains.b: A sense of what the fallen kings and ascetics had carried before they fell.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out the one who did it as a calf finds its mother among many cows; verse 274 says a deed done in a former birth rises into fruit and shows that it was real.
teaches: The epic uses karma's sureness as the model for counsel, so a plan's result is as certain as a deed's fruit, a use of karma that the quatrain does not make.

gains.a: A comparison for the way a royal plan works, which turns karma into a model of policy.
gains.b: A second sign of how settled the doctrine is in Tamil verse, said in passing by a counsellor.

note: Naladiyar 137 doubts that the city of those in the wide heaven is sweeter than learned men gathering and laughing together; verse 279 praises a heaven-like realm that only the meritorious can enter.
teaches: The quatrain tests the heaven the epic praises against the pleasure of a company of the learned, and the epic's heaven is praised for its senses while the quatrain finds its sweetness no better than conversation.

gains.a: A measure to doubt its own claim: a pleasure the Naladiyar sets against heaven's.
gains.b: A full picture of the heaven it weighs, which is the one this verse and its neighbours describe.

note: Verse 129 ends the poet's praise of the ridge by asking what more need be told once its groves are wishing-tree gardens with golden lotuses; verse 282 ends on a question of the same kind.
teaches: The same closing question over wishing-tree groves is first the poet's boast and then the counsellor's pitch to the king, so the ridge's beauty is now used to move a decision.

note: Naladiyar 14 says a once-desired woman, bent and shaking on a staff, torments men who still desire her; verse 286 describes lovers whose desire sprouts without end in a heaven-like city.
teaches: The epic's desire without end belongs to a realm without death (278), so the quatrain's old age has no place there, which shows that the quatrain's argument depends on this world.

gains.a: A world where the quatrain's decline does not happen, and so a limit on the quatrain's lesson.
gains.b: A picture of the endless desire against which the quatrain's old woman is the corrective.

note: Verse 130 names a golden city, Ratanupura-Chakravalam, on the southern ridge; verse 285 names a golden city of Ratna-pallavam in the same realm.
teaches: The counsellor's golden city may be the poet's or a second one, so the king hears of the Vidyadhara country in terms that differ slightly from the poet's own.

note: Verse 304 says the kings paid tribute in fear of his anger; verse 305 says that since the girl was born he has stopped taking it.
teaches: The same overlord appears first as one who is paid in fear and then as one who waives his due, so the girl's birth is given as a political turning and the courting rests on that change.

note: Verse 305 reckons the girl's birth as the moment Asvagriva softened; verse 310 gives the birth as the moment the astrologers set down her horoscope.
teaches: One birth is read twice, by a minister as the cause of a change in the suitor and by an astrologer as the moment her fate was fixed, so the story weighs politics against the stars.
audit_text_issue: 310 flagged uncertain; horoscope content not told

note: Verse 308 vouches for Sachchutan's truth and learning; verse 309 says the speaker saw a fault and will not stay silent.
teaches: The second minister grants his colleague's praise and then withholds assent in the same breath, so agreement on facts does not carry agreement on the verdict.

note: Bhavachutan says that he saw a fault and will speak though the other has praised; Kural 638 says the one at the king's side must speak what is good even if the king is ignorant.
teaches: The couplet binds a minister to speak against a king's folly, and the scene shows the harder case where he speaks against a fellow minister's persuasive counsel.

gains.a: The minister's refusal to join the praise gets a stated rule, so his dissent reads as a duty and not as rivalry.
gains.b: The rule meets a case in which the one to be corrected is a colleague already trusted by the king, not the king himself.

note: The minister lists Asvagriva's army, its order and the food supply among the reasons none equals him; Kural 381 counts army, people, resources, ministers, friends and fort as a king's six limbs.
teaches: The minister's praise follows the Kural's list for army and food but adds the discus, the lineage and learning, so the poet counts as kingly worth what the Kural's checklist leaves out.

gains.a: The speaker's list of army, food and ministers gets a stated standard of what a complete king must have.
gains.b: The couplet's six limbs meet a king whose praise adds lineage, learning and a magic discus, so its checklist is tested against what a court poet values.

note: The minister's praise rests on law-treatise, omen-books and learning; Kural 636 says that natural wit joined to treatises cannot be matched by any scheme.
teaches: The poem's model minister is made by treatises alone, where the couplet gives native wit the first place, so the court poet and the Kural weigh a counsellor differently.

gains.a: The minister's praise gets a measure that asks what books alone can do without native wit.
gains.b: The couplet's pairing of wit and learning meets a counsellor described only by learning, so it is tested against a case where one half is missing.

note: The Vidyadhara kings pay tribute and send word out of fear of Asvagriva's anger; Kural 680 says those of small domains, afraid, bow to the great and take what is offered.
teaches: The kings' tribute is the couplet's counsel carried out, but the minister then asks for the girl to be given, which shows how bowing to a great king can end in a marriage and not only in a payment.

gains.a: The tribute out of fear gets a name in policy: the small bowing to the great for what they can get.
gains.b: The couplet's bowing is shown running on from tribute into the giving of a daughter, a cost it does not name.

note: Verse 289 names the pleasures of lovers as ripe fruits they taste; Tirumanthiram 201 names a man's wife as the ripe jackfruit he will not eat while he toils for the wild date.
teaches: Both speak of sexual joy as fruit, but the poem lets lovers eat it freely in the grove while the Tirumanthiram asks whose fruit it is, so the image carries opposite moral weights.

gains.a: The fruit image gets a question the verse leaves unasked, whose fruit it is and whether it is one's own to eat.
gains.b: The jackfruit image meets a scene of lovers who eat the ripe fruit freely, so the verse is seen against the pleasure it warns about.

note: Verse 314 speaks of the aeon's time running out for Achuvakandan; verse 333 says the words spoken of him match the old words of the aeon.
teaches: The council's reasoning comes back to the same fated end, so the choice of a husband is set under a doom the epic has already spoken.

note: Verse 323 claims no one, not even the red-eyed Tirumal in anger, can harm Arikandan; verse 2 says the tale is of the red-eyed tall one who tore the lion.
teaches: The boast of an unassailable prince is held against the hero the poet promised at the start, so a reader hears the council's confidence as a setup for its overturning.

note: Kural 504 says to examine qualities and faults and take what predominates; the roll of princes names only qualities, and verse 334 ends on a danger.
teaches: The council's list of suitors names only merits and the last verse adds a warning, which shows the Kural's rule to weigh faults was missing from the roll.

gains.a: A named rule by which the one-sided praise of the roll is judged and found short.
gains.b: A court scene in which the praise-only roll of candidates is the failure it warns of.

note: Kural 445 calls counsellors the king's eyes, to be taken after counsel; verse 330 asks that the worthy suitor be examined and then Pavachchuthan's word settles it.
teaches: The epic shows counsel working as the Kural wants, by examining before choosing, but one man's word still carries the room.

gains.a: A standard that says who should do the examining and why his word is valued.
gains.b: A scene in which the eyes of the king are tested by a real choice and the room simply agrees.

note: Verse 11 says the perfumes and flowers of the land are so heavy that even ascetics in good austerity are weakened; verse 350 shows a youth who stands high in austerity while women's glances strike him.
teaches: The poem first lets the land's pleasures unseat ascetics, then offers a youth who stays firm, so the earlier fall is shown as common and not necessary.

note: Naladiyar 11 says that the wise renounce in childhood because they know grey hair will come; verse 351 shows a youth who turns from music, dance and heaven-like pleasure while still young.
teaches: The Naladiyar gives the reason for early renunciation and the epic gives a young man living it, so the reader sees how the reason looks as a character.

gains.a: A reason for the youth's distaste, the argument from coming old age, which the verse never gives.
gains.b: A named young man who has already done what the quatrain says the wise do.

note: Tirumanthiram 634 says those who do austerity become lords of Amaravati and live in bliss by the Lord's grace; verse 354 says a king who leaves his rule for austerity becomes lord of the gods, with no god named as the giver.
teaches: The same heavenly kingship is credited to the ascetic's own austerity by the Jain sage and to the Lord's grace by Tirumular, so the two disagree about who gives the reward.

gains.a: A giver of the reward, which the sage's prophecy leaves out, against which the claim of earned rule can be measured.
gains.b: A path to the same heaven that needs no grace, which tests the claim that grace gives it.

note: Tirumanthiram 258 names austerity and virtue as a boat across the sea of deeds that the Lord makes fruitful; verse 355 says austerity ends all evil and reaches Sivagati, with the god unnamed.
teaches: Both name austerity as what ends deeds, but one adds a god who makes it bear fruit and the other leaves effort alone to do it, so the dispute is over what austerity needs.

gains.a: A second agent, the Lord, against which to weigh the sage's claim that effort alone ends evil.
gains.b: A case where austerity is said to bring release with no god named, which tests how far it depends on grace.

note: Naladiyar 27 praises the firm who see the body as a bubble and resolve to end their wandering; verse 356 says the body's nature of leaving, with austerity and knowledge, brings the mind to the divine seat.
teaches: The quatrain stops at the resolve born of seeing the body pass, and the epic names where that resolve is said to lead.

gains.a: A reason that the body's passing matters: it is the ground of the resolve that leads to the divine seat.
gains.b: A destination for the firm resolve, which the quatrain leaves at the ending of birth.

audit_text_issue: 356 flagged uncertain; கருமச் சுற்றம் is unclear.

note: Kural 380 says that nothing is stronger than fate, which arrives first even when one devises another way; verse 358 says that when they plan, fate gives the result and a strong plan may end otherwise, and Sumantiri still goes on to counsel.
teaches: The couplet gives fate as a rule; the minister uses it as a caution that does not stop deliberation, so the rule is shown as bounding counsel and not replacing it.

gains.a: A use of the fate rule as a counsellor's caution, which the couplet's flat statement does not show.
gains.b: A scene of deliberation where the rule is applied, so its strength is tested against a council that goes on planning.

note: Civaka Cintamani 215 makes a king heedless of a warning because an earlier-formed destiny rose in him; verse 358 has a counsellor name fate as the power over plans and still press counsel.
teaches: One epic makes fate the reason a king ignores counsel and the other makes it the reason counsel must be given with humility, so fate is shown as excusing the king in one and humbling the adviser in the other.

note: Verse 359 puts the question of the yazh-voiced girl's fate to the council, and verse 382 has the astrologer turn to the girl's matter.
teaches: The council's question is carried from counsel to omen-reading across the chapter, so a royal question is settled by two kinds of experts in turn.

note: The counsellors tell the king to go in at once and not let counsel drag; Kural 638 says a minister must tell even a king who has ruined wise counsel what is good for him.
teaches: Here the counsellors' advice is a plain urging of haste that the king accepts, so the Kural's hard case of an unheeding king meets its easy one.

gains.a: A test of what it looks like when counsel is taken without a quarrel, which the verse alone does not discuss.
gains.b: A scene of a minister doing his duty before any failing of the king, which the couplet only imagines after the failing.

note: The time-keepers tell the king the hours that have passed; Kural 482 says acting in season is the rope that binds fortune.
teaches: The epic shows the machinery of a court that keeps its king aware of the hour, which is what the couplet's rule needs before it can be followed.

gains.a: A reason why a king's day is measured and reported, which the verse treats as ceremony.
gains.b: A working instance of how a king could know the season, which the couplet states only as advice.

note: The attendants read the king's sign and withdraw unasked; Kural 701 praises one who reads what is meant before it is said.
teaches: The reading of a sign here serves privacy and not counsel, so the Kural's praise of sign-readers is shown at work in a small court habit.

gains.a: A name for the skill of the attendants who leave, which the verse mentions in a clause.
gains.b: A scene where reading a sign is discretion and not advice, a use the couplet does not mention.

note: Both epics let the washed-off paste and saffron of bathing women thicken a pool, here in the Vidyadhara palace and there in the city's ponds.
teaches: Both Jain epics fix wealth in the cosmetic that the bath washes into the pool, so the image is the genre's mark of luxury.

note: The verse thickens a pool with the washed paste and saffron of women's bodies; Naladiyar 48 mocks those who praise sandal paste and garlands without knowing what the body is.
teaches: The epic's picture of the bath as pure delight is set against a Jain verse on the same bodies as flesh for vultures.

gains.a: A Jain corrective the poet never voices, so the bath scene stands as one the tradition itself would look past.
gains.b: A scene of the very perfumed bodies the quatrain mocks, shown as the epic's own delight.

note: The king ends the day in song and pleasure; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones look to the pain in pleasure and do not cling.
teaches: The chapter shows a whole day of enjoyment with no word of its pain, so the quatrain's test of pleasure is left unanswered by the story here.

gains.a: A measure the narrator does not apply, so the night's pleasure goes unjudged in the verse.
gains.b: A king who is shown enjoying, not a fool, which tests whether the quatrain's contrast of wise and foolish fits a ruler.

note: Verse 385 names the first lord as the light who bore the wheel of dharma (அறக்கதிர் ஆழி); Kural 8 calls the god அறவாழி அந்தணன், where ஆழி can be taken as sea or as wheel.
teaches: A Jain epic uses the words aram and aazhi for a god where the Kural's phrase leaves open sea or wheel, so the same wording is read two ways across the corpus.

gains.a: A much older Tamil praise-phrase for a god, which shows its wording is not a coinage but a shared devotional idiom.
gains.b: A second reading of ஆழி, the wheel an epic plainly bears, which the couplet's own words do not decide.

note: Verse 395 has the world take refuge in the grace of the first lord who bears the wheel; Tirumanthiram 349 says the bright-flamed First gave the discus to Achyuta.
teaches: Both texts make the wheel the sign of a first lord, but one makes it his own dharma-wheel and the other a gift he hands to a lesser god, so the wheel's source is claimed for two rival firsts.

gains.a: A rival claim, in which the discus is given and not borne, against which its own claim that the first lord holds the wheel stands out.
gains.b: A Jain account in which the wheel belongs to the first lord and is not passed to any god, against which its gift of the discus reads as a Saiva claim.

audit_text_issue: ஆழி uncertain in both verses | Tirumanthiram 349 lines 1-2 are uncertain.

note: Verse 396 gives the lord who has no taste of the senses the work of opening doors that end hunger; Kural 225 ranks the strength of those who endure hunger behind that of those who remove it.
teaches: The epic's lord is at once the senses' renouncer and the hunger-remover, so he fills both places the couplet sets in rank order.

gains.a: A test of its claim, since the couplet ranks the ascetic's strength below the giver's, which the epic's lord meets by being both.
gains.b: A figure in whom the ranking does not split, a renouncer who is also the giver the couplet places higher.

note: Verse 402 has the lord foretell that the Kesava will take Ashvagriva's discus; verse 114 has the ministers say the young lord will hold the discus weapon in his hand.
teaches: The ministers' reading of the palm marks is borne out by the lord's own foretelling, which names the discus's source as a rival's own.

note: Verse 406 names the younger of two sons as the purana's hero; verse 78 describes the younger prince as bearing the conch and discus marks on his palm.
teaches: The marks of verse 78 and the purana's foretelling in this chapter are two proofs that the younger prince is the hero, one of the body and one of the story.

note: Verse 2 promises the lion Tivittan tore open; verse 409 is the first time the story itself foretells it, a month away.
teaches: The opening's promise is tied to a named date inside the story, so the lion's killing is something the plot is steered toward, not only the poet's announcement.
audit_text_issue: soolamani:2 line 1 கணிவான்சுடர may be a misprint for அணிவான்சுடர்.

note: Verse 107 has Podanam's astrologer read a dream that a Vidyadhara king will come and give a daughter; here the Vidyadhara king's own astrologer reads the same match from the ridge and adds what the king gains by it.
teaches: Two astrologers on two sides of the sky foretell the same match, and only the ridge's gives the giver's reason, two rows of the ridge.

note: Verse 108 says a man able to speak well will come with a letter into the garden Pushpakarandam; verses 429 and 430 bring Marusi to a grove with that name.
teaches: The astrologer's date is kept by the story's own messenger, so the plot is built on a promised arrival rather than chance.

note: Verse 418 gives the saying that the childless are like trees and the queen's joy at a daughter; Kural 61 holds children valuable only when they come to know what should be known.
teaches: The Kural makes the worth of a child depend on understanding, where the epic king's praise rests only on having a child at all and on her marriage prospect.

gains.a: A measure of children's worth beyond the bare fact of having them, which the verse does not state.
gains.b: A scene where a child is prized for the marriage she will make, which tests the couplet's call for children who know what should be known.

note: Verse 427 chooses Marusi as envoy because he is learned and can put kin and affairs into words; Kural 686 names learning, fearlessness and sense of the time as the envoy's marks.
teaches: The ministers' test for an envoy stops at learning and speech, where the Kural adds fearlessness before hostile eyes and a sense of the moment, so the gaps show what the court has not yet asked of Marusi.

gains.a: Two further qualities, fearlessness and sense of time, that the verse's choice does not name.
gains.b: A court that picks an envoy by the stated learning and speech, which shows how a rule is applied in practice.

note: 447 has the priest foretell the slab; 441 has the keeper offer it as a seat made for the man.
teaches: The offer in 441 is the fulfilment of the foretelling in 447, so the keeper is shown acting from a prophecy and not on his own.

note: 176 draws spring as a copy of women; 451 has the women confuse the peacock with their gait.
teaches: One image runs both ways: spring is drawn from women's bodies in 176, and in 451 women outdo nature, so the poet changes which side is the model.

note: 450 sets the women's eyes above the deer's; Kural 1085 finds the deer, the eye and Death all in one look.
teaches: The epic uses the same deer-and-eye comparison as the couplet but lets the deer lose, where the couplet lets the look hold the deer's frightened shyness as one of its three natures.

gains.a: The women's eyes get the couplet's three-natured look, so the poem's deer is more than a measure of beauty: it is something the look can frighten.
gains.b: The deer-eye comparison shown at work in a procession where a king sends the women out for a purpose, rather than a lover's chance meeting.

note: 453 calls the women's sword-like eyes the mark of every killing art of love; Kural 1083 learns what Death is from a woman's large war-making eyes.
teaches: Both name the glance as a killer, but the couplet is one man's astonished cry and the epic makes it a settled doctrine of the women's whole equipment.

gains.a: A first-person confession that the eyes kill, which the epic's catalogue states only as a fact of their bodies.
gains.b: A general rule about what such eyes carry, given as the sum of breasts, brows and arts rather than the eyes alone.

note: 453 hails the women's eyes as the killing sign of love; Naladiyar 44 refuses the sword-and-lily praise and sees only a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The two cannot both stand: one accepts the eye as a weapon, the other denies the image on the ground that the eye is only flesh, and which holds depends on whether the speaker is praising or renouncing.

gains.a: Its praise of the eyes is shown to rest on a metaphor a renunciant would call blindness.
gains.b: The target of its refusal is given a full, dazzling form in a poem written to enjoy it.

note: 454 shows the women shaping the face's work with glance and smile; Siddhar 10 prays to forget women who show hand, eyes and face.
teaches: The siddhar's prayer names the same tools the epic's women use, as the lure to be forgotten, where the epic presents them as skill.

gains.a: The women's play of face is seen as what the renunciant fears, not only what the poet admires.
gains.b: Its infatuating gestures get a full picture of them performed, which the prayer names but does not show.

note: Verse 458 has men grant that the women's long dark eyes kill and bow to them; Naladiyar 44 refuses to call eyes spears or carp, since he has seen the eye is a scooped-out palm fruit.
teaches: The Soolamani gives the lover's image of the lethal eye a scene of surrender, and the Naladiyar answers with a renunciant who would not give way, so a reader sees the image only works on one who agrees to be struck.

gains.a: A refusal of the image of the killing eye, which the verse alone only enjoys.
gains.b: A scene in which men yield to the very image the renunciant's resolve is set against.

note: Kural 1085 asks whether the young woman's look is Death, an eye or a doe; verse 458 says the women's long dark eyes are skilled at killing.
teaches: The eye as Death is a shared trope of the lover's tradition, which the epic makes the plea of many men at once.

gains.a: The Kural's own line that the look is Death, which sets this plea in a known convention.
gains.b: A crowd of men instead of one man, the Kural's one lover made general.

note: Verse 462 has men blame the Creator for making women, whose beauty they take as the cause of desire; Tirumanthiram 204 turns the same beauty into an etti fruit that looks good and poisons, and tells the heart to hold back.
teaches: The men's wonder at the Creator's sin shows desire as a thing done to them, and Tirumular sets it as a choice of the heart, which marks where the epic stops short of the Saiva remedy.

gains.a: A remedy for the cry of the men, who only blame the Creator.
gains.b: A scene of men who feel the beauty the verse warns against, and who blame another for it.

note: Verse 463 puts a fire of desire within the women that sends up lines like smoke; Naladiyar 89 says desire burns the mind itself and is more to be feared than arrow, fire or sun.
teaches: The epic shows the fire of desire as marks on the body, and the Naladiyar says what the fire burns, the mind, so each supplies what the other lacks.

gains.a: A statement that this fire burns the mind and is worse than outer fires.
gains.b: A body in which the fire shows as smoke-lines of fine hair.

note: Verse 83 says the fire of desire burns women within and none bears it more heavily than the shame-bound; in verse 465 the men voice it aloud to the women.
teaches: The epic first shows desire borne in silence by women and then spoken freely by men, so the burden is set unequally by who may say it.

note: Verse 53 says that in this king's days nothing but Kama's arrows mingled in the land and no killing force troubled it; verse 466 has the women report to Kama their victory over an army of lovers.
teaches: The earlier verse treats Kama's war as the only gentle one, and here it has victims and a victor, which shows the gentle war is still a war.

note: Verse 50 says the golden city seems an Indra's heaven come down to earth; verse 469 has a Vidyadhara, who knows the sky, judge that this is heaven.
teaches: The poet's praise of the city as heaven is confirmed by a sky-dweller who can compare, so the boast is turned into an outsider's verdict.
audit_text_issue: 469 sense uncertain; whether the place is the city of 50 is not stated

note: Kural 84 says a glad face towards good guests draws the goddess of wealth; verse 471 shows the host women doing every service to the guest for the Vidyadhara.
teaches: The Kural's rule is given a court in which welcome is a trained skill and not a feeling, and the Kural shows what the women's service is for.

gains.a: A rule that the welcome depends on the host's face, which the women who set aside their looks only half meet.
gains.b: A setting in which the guest-duty is done by those whose art is desire.

note: Verse 81 says the women swoon with fear that the dark-gemmed prince, who came in a dream, will take their lives; verse 476 has the women faint on the terraces as the princes pass.
teaches: The dream-fear of the women becomes a public swoon, so the epic shows the prince's coming as the fulfilment of the fear.

note: At 427 the ministers choose Maruci as one who can carry what he has learned and say what is fit; at 495 his first act on reaching the princes is to rise and bow.
teaches: The envoy named for his speech opens with a bow and not with the message, so his fitness shows first in manner.

note: The prince at 496 asks why the Vidyadhara bows to them; 500 gives the answer, that those who bow at their feet have done hard penance.
teaches: The bow is first met with surprise and then given a reason, so the envoy's courtesy is shown to rest on a belief about merit and not on mere flattery.

note: At 409 the astrologer's sign says Tivittan will split a lion's mouth within a month; at 497 the envoy meets the two princes and weighs them by the rules of his lore.
teaches: The foretold hero now meets the person who must find him, so the astrologer's sign is put to a test of eyes before the envoy speaks.

note: Naladiyar 17 warns against the woman's spear-like eyes, since she too will age and lean on a staff; at 486 the blue-eyed women pour out their hearts to the princes.
teaches: The epic shows love's pull in full while the quatrain names its price, so the two together show what a reader is warned off and why.

gains.a: A test of the women's rush of feeling against the thought that youth and beauty do not last, which the scene does not raise.
gains.b: A scene in which the beauty it warns against is shown in full, in the women's own act of giving up their hearts.

note: Kural 1183 says the lover has taken a woman's modesty and given her sickness and pallor; at 487 many women grow pale and sigh for men who have only passed by.
teaches: The Kural's single lover is replaced by two princes and a crowd, so pallor from love is shown as a common mark of beauty's reach as well as a private ache.

gains.a: A name for the paleness of the women's shoulders and a cause for it, the lover's taking of their modesty.
gains.b: A scene in which the same paleness comes at first sight of strangers, with no parting that the couplet takes as its cause.

note: Kural 687 ranks highest the envoy who knows the protocol, weighs the moment and place, and speaks after thought; at 500 Maruci opens with a bow and a courtesy that honours the princes before any message.
teaches: The epic shows an envoy meeting the Kural's test of protocol, and shows that what he first says is praise and not the matter of his errand.

gains.a: A standard that names the opening courtesy as part of the envoy's art and not a mere ornament.
gains.b: A scene in which the protocol it asks for is carried out, with praise placed ahead of the message.

note: Verse 108 foretells that a man good at speaking will come down with a letter into the garden Pushpakarandam; here the letter is read in the king's hall.
teaches: The astrologer's forecast of a letter is now met by its words, which turn out to be the offer of a bride that the dream was read to promise.

note: Verse 107 reads the dream as a Vidyadhara king who will come and give a daughter; the letter in 515 gives her as the younger prince's through an envoy, not in person.
teaches: The dream's promise returns as a formal proposal sent by letter, so the prophecy opens a scene of answering and choosing rather than ending in a bare fact.
audit_text_issue: 515 flagged uncertain; who gives and takes in line 4 unclear.

note: Verse 106 tells a night dream that the court takes as a true sign of this match; in 526 the king says that he can take the offer only as a dream. This holds if 526's dream means a thing not to be trusted.
teaches: The same word, dream, stands for a sure sign in the court's mouth and for something too good to be believed in the king's, and the plot rides on that gap.

note: Verse 427 names Marusi because he can say what is fit; in 517 the same envoy answers the king's silence with anger and a rebuke.
teaches: The ministers chose a speaker for fitting words, and the scene tests that skill when he is met by silence and shows how quickly it turns to pride.

note: Kural 685 asks an envoy to speak briefly, to leave out what offends and to say it so that it wins a smile; Marusi's words in 518 to 523 offend the king and end by calling men of the earth unable to know what is fitting.
teaches: A couplet of what an envoy should do is seen broken in a scene where the envoy's anger grows from the court's silence rather than from ill will.

gains.a: 523 gains a standard against which the envoy's pride reads as a failure of his office, not just a mood
gains.b: 685 gains a case where the pressure on the envoy comes from a silent king, so softening speech means bearing silence as well as choosing words

note: Naladiyar 115 says the words of the poor glance off while the rich are heard; Marusi says that anyone who speaks wanting something is slighted, even when he speaks for the stronger lord.
teaches: The Naladiyar finds the cause of being ignored in the speaker's poverty, while Marusi finds it in the act of asking, so a rich lord's messenger can be slighted too.

gains.a: 518 gains the rule it assumes, that how a man is heard follows his standing, which shows Marusi's complaint to be about rank
gains.b: 115 gains a case where the unheard speaker comes from the richer side, so need rather than poverty may be what silences him

note: Naladiyar 27 sets the body as a bubble in pelting rain; 520 calls the human body a frothy hollow. The first uses it to urge ending the cycle of births, the second to bar men from a Vidyadhara's wealth.
teaches: One image of the body as foam serves a teacher of release and an envoy's claim of rank, so the image shows weakness only and takes its direction from who uses it.

gains.a: 520 gains the sense that its froth-body is a commonplace of teaching on impermanence, so using it as an insult turns a lesson into a boast
gains.b: 27 gains a use of the bubble-body to exclude rather than free, showing that the image alone does not call for renunciation

note: Kural 377 says that even those who amass millions enjoy them only as the apportioner has apportioned; verse 527 has the king say that only former deeds strive and later effort does not win what is not due.
teaches: The epic gives the couplet's unnamed apportioner a face, the person's own earlier deeds, and uses it to settle who may marry whom, where the couplet only consoles about wealth.

gains.a: A statement that a lot is fixed by something other than present effort, which the king asserts without a general rule.
gains.b: A case where the rule is used as an argument across a divide of rank, not as comfort about wealth.

audit_text_issue: 527 lines 3-4 hard to construe | 527 lines 3-4 are hard to construe.

note: Verse 528 reads the Vidyadharas' high wealth as the fruit of earlier austerity; Naladiyar 265 reads the wealth of the unjust as the fruit of old deeds.
teaches: The same rule that makes the Vidyadhara's wealth a sign of past austerity makes a rich man's wealth no sign of present merit, so the epic's reasoning holds only for those of known past.

gains.a: A warning that wealth is a poor sign of present worth, which the king does not consider.
gains.b: A group, the Vidyadharas, for whom wealth is taken as proof of earned austerity, which the quatrain gives to no one.

note: Naladiyar 72 says to bear in silence the unfit words of those who are not one's equals; verse 529 has Marusi ashamed because the king bore his unfit words.
teaches: The quatrain shows forbearance as the superior's duty, and the epic shows what it does to the one borne with: shame and a calmed anger rather than a grudge.

gains.a: A rule that explains why the king's patience is praised and why Marusi feels small.
gains.b: An effect of silent forbearance on the speaker who was borne with, which the quatrain does not show.

audit_text_issue: sense flagged uncertain; sentence in lines 1-2 compressed

note: Verse 427 chooses Marusi as one who can say what is fit; in 529 his first words are called unfit and he is ashamed.
teaches: The minister's praise of Marusi's speech is tested at once by a slip, so his later success in 531 is recovery from a fault and not ease.
audit_text_issue: 529 lines 1-2 compressed and uncertain | 529 lines 1-2 are compressed; 427 line 2 is uncertain.

note: Verse 107 has the astrologer say a Vidyadhara king will come and give a daughter to the young lord; verse 530 raises the doubt that Vidyadharas and men do not marry.
teaches: The prophecy skips the custom against such a match, and Marusi's reply is the story's way of making what was foretold pass through argument before it can happen.

note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from work; verse 531 says Vidyadharas are men, distinguished only by their lore.
teaches: The couplet is turned from a general saying into the reason a marriage across a supposed divide may go ahead.

gains.a: A principle that makes sameness of birth the ground, so that the Vidyadharas' lore becomes a difference of work and not of kind.
gains.b: A use of the principle to open a marriage across a boundary of rank, a case the couplet does not take up.

note: Kural 133 says that conduct is nobility of birth; verse 535 has the first lord make the five royal lineages and teach each its conduct and occupation.
teaches: In the epic, lineage is a thing made, with conduct as one of its parts, so the couplet's identity of conduct and birth is the made thing's own mark.

gains.a: A sense that a lineage's standing rests on its conduct, so that it is not simply handed down.
gains.b: An origin story in which lineages are set up by an act of the first king together with their occupations.

note: Kural 4 says those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering; verse 541 sings of the Lord as one who put away every desire and yet gives his servants unfailing bliss.
teaches: The hymn lets the desireless Lord be a giver, which the couplet avoids by saying only that no suffering reaches those at his feet.

gains.a: A statement of what the desireless one does for his servants, which the verse puts as a gift.
gains.b: A hymn in which the desireless one is nevertheless the one who gives, a tension the couplet does not face.

note: Tirumanthiram 1626 says that people who ask for many things get their wealth, but those who do great tapas win the end of birth; verse 547 has Nami ask a god's servant for wealth.
teaches: Nami stands as a case of the first sort, asking for wealth at the feet of a yogi, and the Tirumanthiram supplies a rank by which his wish is lower than release.

gains.a: A standard by which Nami's request looks lesser than a request for release, a judgment the epic does not make.
gains.b: A named person who asks for wealth in the presence of a yogi and gets it, which makes the verse's contrast concrete.

note: Tirumanthiram 670 says siddhis come through eightfold yoga and Shakti's grace; verse 548 has Dharanan hand Nami the sky-going lore and a mountain for the asking.
teaches: In the epic, powers are a gift passed through a go-between to a man who asks for wealth, where the Tirumanthiram sets them at the end of discipline and grace.

gains.a: A contrast showing that a power may be had by asking when it is not had by yoga.
gains.b: A case in which the powers called siddhis go to someone who has done no yoga and wanted only wealth.

note: Verse 408 has the astrologer say that the marriage will bring the king both rows of the ridge; verse 548 tells that the silver mountain was first given to Nami, a man of Kasi.
teaches: The ridge the astrologer promises is shown to have begun as a gift to a man, which supports Marusi's claim that the Vidyadharas are men.

note: Verse 549 judges the match fit because both houses have high lineage and wealth; Naladiyar 195 says high and low caste are only words and that austerity, learning and effort, not famous wealth, make a lineage.
teaches: The two disagree about what equality of houses rests on: the epic points to descent and riches, the quatrain to conduct and learning, and the clash holds only if lineage in 549 means inherited standing.

gains.a: A test of the match by learning and conduct, which Marusi does not apply.
gains.b: A case of a match argued from descent and riches, the very ground the quatrain calls empty.

note: Verse 427 chooses Marusi to put kin and the matter in words; verse 549 is where he does so, naming the line the two houses share.
teaches: The envoy's task of setting out kin is carried out in this closing, where the shared descent from Nami is the reason offered for the marriage.

note: Verse 108 foretells a man who can speak well coming down with a letter; here the Podanam king defines such a man as the voice of the king's body.
teaches: The foretold messenger is received as a part of the other king's body, which the astrologer's foretelling alone does not say.

note: Verse 354 foretells that a youth who gives up rule will reach Indra's world for seventeen oceans of time; verse 560 has an ancestor who gives up rule take kevala and become rare even to the gods.
teaches: The renunciations in the story do not end alike: one ancestor goes past the gods, while the foretold youth first holds a god's seat.

note: Verse 560 makes kevala the bride whom the renouncer takes and by which he rises above the gods; Tirumanthiram 494 calls those who have left the kevala state the Vijnanars, so the same word marks the state to be left.
teaches: The same word names the goal in one text and the soul's first bound state in the other, so the two cannot be read on the same ladder.

gains.a: The epic's kevala gets a rival ranking in which the same name is the bottom, which the Jain verse does not know.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's kevala gains a case where the word is the highest prize, showing that the term's rank turns on the school.

audit_text_issue: both verses flagged uncertain; TM 494 reading is loose

note: Verse 268 says all living beings worship the one who has gained his own self; verse 556 has kings bow at the feet of a man who left a throne and let creepers climb him.
teaches: The beings who worship the self-conquered man in the story are kings and serpents together, as the couplet does not say.

gains.a: The scene gets a stated reason why even kings bow, which is his gaining of himself.
gains.b: The couplet gets a picture in which the worshippers are those whose rank he gave up.

note: Kural 388 gives the title of lord to the king who guards by justice; verse 561 claims the title by a line of kings who never drew reproach.
teaches: A clan's boast of blamelessness is a debt to be repaid in each reign, which the couplet makes clear and the priest's speech blurs.

gains.a: The priest's descent claim gets a test: the line holds only while each king keeps the guarding that the couplet names.
gains.b: The couplet gets a case where the title is claimed through ancestors, and its test then falls on the heir.

note: Verse 561 presents the king's greatness as coming from a high clan; Naladiyar 195 says good and bad caste are words and that austerity, learning and effort make a lineage, which holds if 'clan' is taken to mean birth alone.
teaches: The priest's boast of birth is checked by the poem's own ancestor, who gained his rank by renouncing, which is the test the Naladiyar sets.

gains.a: The epic's clan pride gets a standard it passes only because its founder earned his place by austerity.
gains.b: The quatrain gets an example where a king's lineage is named as the cause of greatness, so its claim is against a living boast.

note: Kural 681 names birth in an honourable family among the first qualities of an envoy; verse 564 comes after the two clan recitals and praises the envoy's knowledge of clans and customs.
teaches: Family is not a bare boast but a thing the host tests by having the envoy recite and understand it.

gains.a: The recital of clans gets a reason: the envoy's family is a qualification the host checks before the message.
gains.b: The couplet gets a scene where family is spoken aloud and judged against the host's own.

note: Kural 685 asks the envoy to speak in brief, remove offence and gain the good; verse 566 has the king bid the envoy show faultless virtues in sifted words.
teaches: The host asks for the craft the couplet describes and does not simply receive it, so the envoy's skill is put on trial at the host's court.

gains.a: The king's bidding gets a named standard of speech: brief, free of offence and sifted.
gains.b: The couplet gets a scene where the host himself demands what it asks of the envoy.

note: Verse 427 chooses Marusi because he can put the kin and the matter in words; here he opens his report by promising the descent, the entry and the host's words, in that order.
teaches: The ministers' reason for choosing him is tested by his first act on return, which is to set out his account in the order it happened.

note: Verse 116 has the ministers post Turumakanthan as guard in the garden for the day the astrologer named; Marusi recalls a bright man with a tight girdle who met him there and bade him come up.
teaches: The ministers' preparation is confirmed from the envoy's own side, which shows the plan worked.

note: Verse 426 resolves to send a messenger to Tivittan's father to settle the match; verse 590 recalls that father speaking kindly, becoming kin and giving gifts.
teaches: The embassy's aim is reached only after a silence and an objection in 588 and 589, so the match is won and not simply given.

note: The king reads the outcome of the errand from the envoy's face before he speaks, as Kural 706 says the face shows what the heart holds strongest.
teaches: The epic extends the couplet from a feeling to a piece of news, so a returning envoy's face can carry the result of a mission before his words do.

gains.a: The verse lacks the reason a king can read success unspoken, which the couplet gives: the face shows what is strongest in the heart.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where what the face shows is the end of a mission, not a mood, and this verse supplies it.

note: Marusi adds, beyond his message, his own eye-witness judgement that no other king he has seen equals the host; Kural 688 asks of an envoy purity, support, resolve and truthfulness in delivering the message.
teaches: The envoy's truthfulness here covers a judgement of the other king that the message does not carry, which is more than the couplet's duty of faithful relay.

gains.a: The verse lacks a standard to test the praise against: the couplet's truthfulness makes the eulogy a testimony that can be trusted or doubted.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case of an envoy who adds his own appraisal of the other king, which stretches truthfulness from relaying words to judging men.

note: Marusi's pairs, fire in command and cool in giving, name two of the four things Kural 390 calls the light of kings: giving and a straight sceptre.
teaches: The envoy's pairs put two marks of the Kural's ideal king into the temperature of one man, so command and giving are shown as tempers, not as separate duties.

gains.a: The verse lacks the standard that makes its pairs more than ornament: the four marks the couplet calls the light of kings.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of how command and giving sit together in one king, which the fire and cool pairs give.

note: Marusi calls the king hard for kings to reach yet easy for his own servants; Kural 386 praises a king who is easy to see.
teaches: The epic limits the couplet's easy access: it is a favour kept for a king's own men and withheld from rival kings.

gains.a: The verse lacks the named virtue behind its claim, easy access, which the couplet makes a ground of a land's praise.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the limit that a king may be easy to some and closed to others, which the verse shows.

note: Marusi says the world would not be without the king's gentle grace; Kural 544 says the world clings to the feet of the king who embraces his people with the sceptre.
teaches: The envoy states the Kural's idea of the world's dependence on the king's grace as a bare condition for existence, and in the mouth of a rival's envoy.

gains.a: The verse lacks a mark of how the grace works, which the couplet gives as the king first embracing his people.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the strong form of the dependence, that without the king's grace there is no world, which the verse speaks.
