note: Marusi describes those under the king's umbrella as learned men bound by love who give their lives; Kural 389 says the world dwells under the umbrella of the king who bears bitter words.
teaches: The umbrella's shelter is filled by learned retainers who die for the king, and the couplet shows what keeps them there: a king who can bear their bitter words.

gains.a: The verse lacks the quality that holds the retainers, which the couplet supplies as a king's patience with bitter words.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of who stands under the umbrella and what they give back, which the verse supplies.

note: Kural 542 has the people looking to the sceptre as the world looks to the sky; verse 598 runs it the other way, with the king glad or hurt as the world is.
teaches: The pair shows rule as a two-way dependence, where the couplet states only the people's need of the king.

gains.a: The verse lacks a picture of the people's side of the bond, which the sky and sceptre image supplies.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the king's felt share in his people's fortune, which the verse adds.

note: Kural 549 says guarding and caring for the people is the king's work and no stain; verse 599 shows that work as sleeplessness.
teaches: What the Kural calls work, the verse shows as a worry that costs a king his sleep.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule saying the guarding is his own task rather than a burden laid on him.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the felt cost of that work, which the verse gives.

note: Verse 53 shows Payapati's land troubled only by Kama's arrows; 599 holds up a king who cannot sleep for fear of failing his people.
teaches: The envoy's praise of the king's sleepless care sits beside the poet's own earlier description of him, whose days were spent among queens.

note: In 407 the astrologer says the girl is fit to rest on the lord's breast; in 603 the envoy asks what austerity earned that seat.
teaches: The woman on the lord's breast first comes as a forecast, then as something already earned, so the prophecy turns into a reward.
audit_text_issue: Both verses flagged uncertain in sense

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed finds its doer like a calf its mother; verse 604 says merit joined this pair.
teaches: The Naladiyar's law of the old deed is shown working for good here, where its examples elsewhere fall on the wicked.

gains.a: The verse lacks the idea that the old deed seeks out its own doer, which gives its merit a mechanism.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a joyful instance, since its law is usually shown on sinners.

note: Verse 108 foretold a man of good speech coming with a letter; in 605 the envoy has come and is paid for his words.
teaches: The astrologer's forecast is kept to the letter, the envoy's reward being the fruit of the arrival it named.

note: Verse 409 has the Vidyadhara astrologer give the month's limit for the lion; 607 has a counsellor give it again to the Podanam king.
teaches: Two courts, with the same date in each, act on one word, so the lion-killing is a shared fate rather than one court's hope.

note: In 427 the Vidyadhara ministers choose the learned Marusi to carry the letter; in 608 Podanam's ministers choose a learned man to answer.
teaches: Both courts treat the embassy as the work of learning, so the exchange between them is a matching of one practice on each side.

note: Kural 920 puts double-minded women, liquor and dice together as the company of the man Fortune has left; verse 615 makes desire itself the liquor.
teaches: The verse folds two of the Kural's three vices into one, so the women's eyes are the cup.

gains.a: The verse lacks a verdict on the man who loses day and night, which the couplet supplies.
gains.b: The couplet lacks an account of how women and drink become one vice, which the verse gives.

note: Verse 402 says Tivittan will take the life and discus of Ashvagriva; 619 shows Acuvakanthan at his ease, unaware of heat or cool.
teaches: The telling that the rival's life will end is set against a scene of his ease, so the reader looks on his pleasure knowing its end.

note: Naladiyar 60 says fools long for pleasure though suffering mounts, and the higher look to the pain in it; 619 shows a king past all noticing.
teaches: A verse of ethics gets a king's case, where the cost is a realm and not one man's comfort.

gains.a: The verse lacks the judgment that pleasure holds its own pain, which it only implies.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks an example from the seat of power, where the fool's pleasure ruins others.

note: Kural 539 bids one swollen with joy think of those ruined by negligence; verse 619 shows Acuvakanthan so swollen.
teaches: The couplet's advice is the thing Acuvakanthan does not heed, so the story reads as its example.

gains.a: The verse lacks the explicit warning that joy breeds negligence, which the couplet states.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a named man to stand for the ruined, which the verse supplies.

note: Kural 389 says the world rests under the umbrella of a king who can bear words bitter to the ear; verse 620 names a king by the opposite temper, striking in anger and unable to bear a word against him.
teaches: The couplet's virtue is given its negative portrait in a ruler whose pride goes with his intolerance.

gains.a: The verse lacks a measure by which this temper counts as a failing, which the couplet supplies.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a figure who embodies the opposite, which the verse supplies.

audit_text_issue: 620 sense uncertain | 620 is flagged uncertain in sense.

note: Kural 617 says the goddess of misfortune lives in sloth and the lotus goddess in the labour of the unslothful; in verse 621 the goddess of fortune takes offence and looks for another place, because the king has not come to her.
teaches: In the Kural fortune leaves a man for sloth; here she leaves a king for his pleasure, so the fault is attention given elsewhere.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule saying what kind of man keeps fortune, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of fortune as a slighted lover, which the verse gives.

note: Tirumanthiram 140 says the five senses come under one's control of themselves once one has met the Lord; verse 624 says a king who has conquered himself is hard for others to conquer.
teaches: The epic gives self-conquest as a ruler's own work with a public reward; the Saiva stanza makes it follow from meeting the Lord.

gains.a: The verse lacks any account of how self-conquest comes about, since it names only its fruit.
gains.b: The stanza lacks a worldly payoff for the mastery it describes, which the verse gives in an unconquerable realm.

note: Kural 385 names a king as one able to create, gather, guard and apportion wealth; verse 626 gives the same four acts and says it is the learned man who becomes the protector of others.
teaches: The couplet's four tasks are tied to learning, so the verse makes the king's wealth-work depend on what he has studied.

gains.a: The verse lacks a compact statement that these four acts define rule, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the condition that only the learned can do it, which the verse adds.

note: Kural 431 says the wealth of those without arrogance, anger and smallness has a dignified quality; verse 627 makes arrogance a frost that destroys the lotus of wealth.
teaches: The couplet says what spoils the dignity of wealth; the verse shows how, with arrogance falling on wealth like frost on a lotus.

gains.a: The verse lacks the positive side, that wealth without arrogance keeps its dignity, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks an image of the ruin pride causes, which the verse supplies.

note: In 627 the astrologer warns that pride falls like frost on the lotus of wealth; in 634 the king, smiling, boasts that his shoulders have beaten the Vidyadhara kings and so he need fear no foe.
teaches: The warning is answered by the very boast it described, so the king's reply is what the astrologer's image forecasts.

note: Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode elephants at the head of armies fall and change when their deeds turn against them; verse 635 has a king boasting that mere men cannot shake him.
teaches: A king's claim of strength is read as the very certainty that, in the Naladiyar, precedes the fall of such rulers.

gains.a: The verse lacks a standard that sets his boast against what happens to powerful kings, which the quatrain supplies.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a living king speaking the boast it warns against, which the verse supplies.

note: In 402 the lord says that because of a girl he will take the life and the discus of Ashvagriva; in 638 the king names that very discus as the power by which he could cut down the shoulders of the gods.
teaches: The weapon the king trusts is the thing the earlier verse says will be taken from him with his life.

note: Verse 409 says the sign about the garlanded one means that within a month Tivittan will split a lion's mouth; verse 639 has the king ask whether the book of omens may be a deceit.
teaches: The king treats as doubtful the omen-book that the other court has already taken as certain, which is the difference between the two courts' fates.

note: Verse 402 says the lord will take the discus and life of Ashvagriva because of a girl; verse 632 has the astrologer call the youngest Podanam prince a foe of old.
teaches: The same prince is named as the threat from the rival's court that the earlier verse named as the taker of his life.
audit_text_issue: 402 line 3 name corrupt; 632 speaker split unclear

note: Kural 445 says counsellors are the king's eyes and he should take counsel; verse 641 has the king, who has already said he will fight regardless, tell his ministers to counsel.
teaches: The couplet's rule is shown with its limit, as counsel asked after the king has made up his mind.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule saying why counsellors matter, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case where counsel is asked only to confirm the king's mind, which the verse shows.

audit_text_issue: 641 sense flagged uncertain | 641 lines 3-4 are hard to construe.

note: Kural 674 says what is left over of a deed or a feud scorches like a fire's remnant; verse 643 draws the same fire but warns of a foe still small.
teaches: The epic's counsellors aim the couplet's fire at an enemy not yet seen to strike, which turns a rule about unfinished business into a case for striking first.

gains.a: The verse lacks the rule that an unfinished enmity is a remnant that will burn, which the couplet states as a general law.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a counsellor's use of it against a foe who has done nothing yet, which the verse supplies.

note: Kural 879 tells the king to cut a thorn tree young lest the hand that cuts it be hurt; verse 644 adds a nail for the sprout and that axe and hatchet fail once it has grown.
teaches: The verse makes the couplet's thorn tree an argument for haste, though Arimanju's reply in 646 to 648 shows the story doubts that the tree is a thorn at all.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's warning that the grown tree harms the hand that cuts it, a cost to the cutter and not only to the tree.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the image of tools failing, which makes the delay one of means as well as of danger.

note: Kural 871 says no one should want enmity even in jest; verse 647 says that making foes of the harmless and trusting the ill-hearted both burn later.
teaches: Arimanju's caution answers the counsellors' haste with the Kural's own rule against courting enmity, so the epic stages two readings of Kural 879 and 871 as rival counsel.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's reason that enmity has no good in it, and gives only its later pain.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the second warning, against counting the ill-hearted as friends, which the verse pairs with it.

audit_text_issue: line 2 of 647 corrupt | soolamani:647 line 2 word for the ill-hearted is corrupt.

note: Verse 304 says that kings of the earth, fearing the rival's anger, paid tribute and sent word; verses 663 to 665 show the same demand arriving at Podanam.
teaches: The tribute that 304 named as the rival's usual power is shown here in the act, and its list shows how much he asks of the one he treats as a vassal.

note: Verse 514 reads the Vidyadhara king's letter to the lord of Podanam, which sends gifts and good wishes; verse 662 reads the discus-king's letter to the same lord, which demands them.
teaches: A letter sealed and read at the same palace first carries a gift and a request and then a demand, so the same act of reading shows two different powers dealing with Podanam.
audit_text_issue: 662 line 3 clipped and line 4 short a syllable; 514 line 2 name and line 4 sense doubtful | 662's last word உரைத்தர் is short a syllable and line 3 is clipped; 514 line 4 is doubtful.

note: Kural 756 counts what falls to the king, customs and what he takes from crushed foes as his wealth; verse 665 lists treasure and royal marks demanded of a king who has not been crushed.
teaches: The epic shows the third kind of the couplet's royal wealth being claimed before any war, by an overlord's letter and not by victory.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that foe-wealth is a king's by right, which would make the demand lawful as the speaker claims.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where such wealth is demanded by letter before any fight, and where the foe is asked to give up his own umbrella.

note: Kural 380 says nothing is stronger than fate, and that it arrives first even when one devises another course; verse 668 has the king put fate's power to use as the ground of giving way.
teaches: The couplet's law of fate is turned by the king into a reason to submit, which the hero rejects in the same chapter.

gains.a: The verse lacks any statement that no counter-plan can outrun fate, which would turn the king's despair from a mood into a rule.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a person who reaches for its truth to excuse giving way, which shows the rule serving as an alibi.

note: Tirumanthiram 2030 gives fate's great strength as the sea-girt earth; verse 668 pictures that strength as fate upsetting a city and handing its wealth to others.
teaches: A one-line claim that fate's power is the earth is shown as a scene of one city's wealth passing to another.

gains.a: The verse lacks a general statement that fate's power reaches the whole earth, which would make the loss of one city an instance of that law.
gains.b: The verse of the Tirumanthiram lacks an enactment, which the epic gives in a king reasoning that his own city may be taken and given.

note: Kural 680 says those with a small domain, afraid of unrest within, bow to the great and take what they are offered; verse 670 has the king bowing on the strength of earlier kings who pleased their overlord.
teaches: The king's submission follows the couplet's prudence step by step, so the prince's later refusal is a refusal of that prudence and not of mere cowardice.

gains.a: The verse lacks a stated policy that a small domain bows to the great, which gives the king's reasoning its general standing.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the felt cost of such bowing, which the epic shows in the king's swallowed insult in 666 and his hiding the deal from the princes in 672.

note: Naladiyar 33 says the fool grieves when the fruit of past deeds comes, while the wise take it as an old desert crossed; verse 670 accepts the fruit of deeds without grief and answers by paying.
teaches: The same calm acceptance of deeds' fruit that the quatrain offers as freedom is here the mood in which a king submits.

gains.a: The verse lacks a way to meet the fruit of deeds without fretting, which the quatrain gives as passing the desert.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a case where such acceptance becomes political submission, which the king's use of it supplies.

note: Verse 670 holds that earlier kings paid and pleased their overlord and that this is the way; verse 685 says that paying tribute would make one's own arms and sword useless.
teaches: The same demand draws the king's resigned precedent and the prince's refusal, so one court holds two ideas of what a king is for.

note: Verse 304 said that kings of the sea-girt earth, fearing Asvagriva's anger, had paid tribute and sent word; verse 680 brings the same demand to Podanam.
teaches: The earlier claim that every king pays Asvagriva becomes a case at Podanam, where it is the prince who first meets it with anger.

note: The house-priest foretold in 446 that the youth would come blazing in anger against the discus-lord; verse 681 shows the first blaze, lit by the word tribute.
teaches: The prophecy of anger is given its trigger, a single word of demand, so the fire that is foretold is also provoked.

note: Kural 894 says a weak man who harms the strong beckons Death with his hand; verse 686 makes the demander, who counts himself strong, the fool who beckons.
teaches: Strength is not settled by who sends the demand, and the couplet's rule can be turned against the one who thinks himself the strong party.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that harming the stronger is a gesture that summons death, which gives the cobra image its warning.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where the apparent strong man is the one deceived about strength, which the epic supplies.

note: Purananuru 73 has the fool who ignored a king's strength as a blind man stumbling on a sleeping tiger; verse 686 has the demander as a fool reaching for the jewel in a cobra's hood.
teaches: Both pictures make provoking the strong a blind mistake, and the epic moves the blame from stumbling to coveting.

gains.a: The verse lacks the Sangam king's gentler half, that he would give even his life to men who come with courtesy, which makes the cobra's rage a reply to manner.
gains.b: The poem lacks an image in which the fault is covetousness and not mere ignorance, which the jewel in the hood supplies.

note: In 304 the kings of the sea-girt earth pay Acuvakanthan tribute for fear of his anger; in 690 the prince says tribute refused has only a trial of force to answer it.
teaches: The prince's refusal reads as a break from the fear that made every other king pay.

note: The minister's trick answers the prince's offer of a method against those who refuse tribute: it will enrage him and make him run to the lion.
teaches: The prince's challenge is turned into the trap that the minister builds in reply.

note: Kural 636 says no over-subtle scheme stands before keen native wit joined with learning; verse 695 rests the scheme on the target's lacking the sense to tell good from bad.
teaches: A scheme's success is shown to depend on how the target is judged, which the couplet alone does not say.

gains.a: The verse lacks a standard by which the minister's contempt for the prince's judgement can later be tested.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a schemer who bets openly on his target's inexperience.

note: In 695 the minister says he will show a magic and set a lion on the youth; in 696 he calls Arikethu and commissions the magic lion.
teaches: The plan of 695 becomes an order, and the instrument is named.

note: Kural 698 warns against belittling a ruler as young; in 703 Acuvakanthan waves off the prince as a child and the story then lets the prince take up his challenge.
teaches: The verse shows the belittling the couplet warns against and what it provokes, a prince who vows rather than withdraws.

gains.a: The verse lacks a measure that names Acuvakanthan's dismissal of youth as the fault it is.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where the belittled youth answers with a vow, not submission.

note: Kural 685 asks an envoy to speak so as to bring a smile and remove what would offend; here the envoys carry the king's taunt whole, because the minister of 700 wants the youth angered.
teaches: The envoys' offence is the lord's chosen means, a purpose the rule for envoys does not allow for.

gains.a: The verse lacks the standard that shows the envoys' unsoftened message as a choice of policy.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case where giving offence is exactly the work the lord sends an envoy to do.

audit_text_issue: Sense flagged uncertain; the purpose rests on verses outside this packet.

note: In 698 the roar of the made lion fills the Himalaya and Sindhu land; in 706 the envoys, who do not say so, describe it as a lion of the gem hill.
teaches: The envoys repeat the false lion as a fact, so the reader sees the trick work on the very messengers.

note: In 409 the speaker says within a month Tivittan will split a lion's mouth; in 707 he swears to split the lion's mouth, on the minister's bait.
teaches: The enemy's trap supplies the occasion on which the earlier sign is to be met.

note: In 703 Acuvakanthan calls the prince a child; in 707 the prince says the king is a child if the lion is not killed.
teaches: The same insult is thrown back, with the prince staking his word where the king staked nothing.

note: Kural 471 says weigh the work, one's own strength, the foe's and the allies' before acting; in 708 and 709 the prince sends away his elephants, chariots and men and goes with no allies.
teaches: The prince's vow sets aside the allies' strength that the couplet counts, leaving the outcome to his own strength.

gains.a: The verse lacks a standard that names the dismissal of the host as the risk it is.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a hero who deliberately gives up the allies' strength to keep his word.

note: The opening verse promises the tale of the red-eyed one who tore open the lion with the gaping mouth; verse 723 shows the tearing.
teaches: The poet's first promise is kept here as a deed in a scene, and the lion in the invocation is now seen as an actual foe.
audit_text_issue: verse 2 flagged uncertain; line 1 may be misprinted

note: Verse 95 sets a fanged beast on the throne gripping an elephant calf as the king's emblem; in 723 the real lion is seized and torn by the prince.
teaches: The royal lion of the throne is an image of power, and this verse puts the prince above the beast the throne imitates.

note: In 109 those in the hall say Tivittan will guard the whole world under one umbrella; in 722 the gods tremble before the lion he is about to overcome.
teaches: What the hall only affirmed of Tivittan's coming rule is tested here by a foe even the gods fear.

note: Tirumanthiram 2026 tells of five lions in a forest whose claws and teeth must be cut before the Lord is reached; verse 723 has a prince seize a lion by the fangs and tear it.
teaches: The same beast is mastered here by force of arm and there by a cutting of the claws, so the lion stands both for an outer foe and for an inner one.

gains.a: The verse lacks any sense of the lion as something within, which Tirumular's five lions give.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse lacks the act itself, a seizing of the fangs and a tearing, which the epic supplies as a deed.

note: Naladiyar 198 holds up the lion's strength as the measure of a man who would die poor rather than shame himself; in 724 the lion is the foe whose strength the gods marvel to see overcome.
teaches: The lion is first the model of honour and then the thing a stronger man destroys, so strength is not a single measure.

gains.a: The verse lacks the use of the lion as a standard of honour, which the quatrain supplies.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a case where the lion's own strength is beaten, which the verse shows.

note: Kural 774 has the warrior laugh as he pulls a spear from his body; in 726 the victor of a harder fight shows neither joy nor wonder.
teaches: The Kural's soldier takes pleasure in the fight and the epic's prince does not, so the same bravery is shown with two moods.

gains.a: The verse lacks the picture of a fighter who delights in the wound, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a hero who is plain after victory and calls it the removal of a harm.

note: Kural 382 names fearlessness, giving, understanding and drive as a king's nature; in 719 the prince taunts a lion in its own cave.
teaches: The couplet's first quality is shown here as a deed done before a foe with no help, so fearlessness is seen at its cost.

gains.a: The verse lacks a general name for what the prince is doing, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a test of fearlessness against a danger, which the verse supplies.

note: Verse 126 has women playing with youths on the Vidyadhara hill until their powder stains the rocks; verse 747 has bangled women at play and petals falling in the lion's mountain.
teaches: The poet reuses one pleasure-on-the-hill picture for two different mountains, so the lion's range is painted as a pleasure ground as much as a hunting ground.

note: Akananuru 84 sets a rainbow on the mountain under rain clouds as the season of return; verse 754 uses Indra's broken bow among dark clouds only as a likeness for blossom.
teaches: The same bow-on-the-hill image works as a season marker in the Sangam poem and as a bare comparison here.

gains.a: The verse lacks any use for the image beyond decoration; the poem shows it can mark a season and a waiting.
gains.b: The poem lacks the Indra's-bow naming that ties the rainbow to a god's weapon, which the verse supplies.

note: Akananuru 38 has the ashoka as the lovers' old swing-tree now empty; verse 757 has the ashoka in red pollen and humming bees, likened to adorned youths.
teaches: The ashoka stands for young lovers in both, one time in their absence and one time as their likeness.

gains.a: The verse lacks the ashoka's use as a trysting place, which the poem gives.
gains.b: The poem lacks the ashoka's red pollen and the likeness to adorned youths, which the verse gives.

note: In 409 the astrologer reads from the horoscope that within a month Tivittan will split a lion's mouth; in 769 the lion's blood is seen running down the hill.
teaches: The prophecy's fulfilment is shown only through its aftermath, the blood stream, so the reader sees the foretold deed by its trace.

note: In 446 the priest names the foe's destroyer as the lion-slaying man; 772 shows the deed that gives him that name.
teaches: The lion-slaying title that the priest later uses against the rival king is shown being earned here as a protective act.

note: Kural 550 likens a king's killing of the cruel to pulling weeds from young corn; verse 772 praises a prince's killing of a beast that preyed on the herds, as a gift of safe sleep to the world.
teaches: The epic carries the weeding rule from criminals to a beast, and gives the reason in the world's sleep, though a Jain poet still has to justify a killing.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that makes the killing of the cruel a king's care for the many, and so answers why a Jain work may praise it.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where the killed is a beast and the killer a prince, which tests how far the weeding image stretches.

note: Kural 388 makes the ruler who does justice and protects an இறை for the people; verse 773 sets the king's sons under the same duty and says it outweighs their own lives.
teaches: The duty to protect reaches the king's sons and is stated as a willingness to lose their lives, which the couplet leaves unsaid.

gains.a: The verse lacks a status that rewards protection, which the couplet states as being counted an இறை.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the cost of protection, the prince's risk to his life, which the verse names.

note: Naladiyar 34 tells one to take the great fruit of a rare body while it lasts; verse 774 says the body yields no fruit if it cannot help the afflicted.
teaches: The body's fruit is named as aid to others in trouble, where the quatrain leaves what the fruit is to the word virtue.

gains.a: The verse lacks the impermanence of the body, the cane refuse that makes using it now urgent.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a concrete form of virtue, the relief of the helpless, that the verse gives it.

note: Tirumanthiram 724 keeps the body alive because true knowledge needs a living frame; verse 775 holds that a man should give even himself to end the world's pain.
teaches: A Jain epic's praise of the body given away for others and a Saiva text's care for the body to win knowledge set out two uses of the same frame.

gains.a: The verse lacks any limit on self-giving, the claim that the body must be kept for the sake of knowledge.
gains.b: The mantra lacks a counter-ethic, the claim that the body may be spent for another's pain, which tests its practical argument.

note: Kural 235 speaks of a death that is really existence, a growth through ruin; verse 776 says the flesh body goes while the form of fame stands.
teaches: The verse supplies the two-body picture that explains the couplet's death that is existence, as the fame body that survives.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's claim that only the skilled manage this exchange, which makes the fame body an achievement.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a plain statement of what survives the death, the form of fame, that the verse gives.

note: Kural 1067 begs the beggars not to beg of those who conceal; verse 784 likens a deer's thirst to a high-born man who begged from a low man's eyes and earned blame.
teaches: The verse makes the cost of begging of the wrong person a stain on rank, where the couplet gives only a warning.

gains.a: The simile lacks the Kural's rule that the fault lies in begging of those who conceal, which names why the noble is blamed.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the sense that the shame falls harder on the high-born, which the verse's noble adds.

audit_text_issue: 784 flagged uncertain; first two lines loose

note: Kural 742 counts a shady forest as one of a fort's four parts; verse 785 shows who holds the forest, men who live by violence and serve the king.
teaches: A forest that guards the realm is held by violent servants, a cost the couplet's list of fort parts does not show.

gains.a: The verse lacks the idea that the forest is itself a defence, which the couplet names.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the picture of who actually keeps the forest, which the verse adds.

note: Akananuru 45 has the lover cross a summer forest with rattling dry pods and a tiger on the waterless track; verse 781 shows the same dry forest, with trees keening like a mourning house.
teaches: The same summer forest is a woman's dread in the Sangam poem and a mourning house in the epic.

gains.a: The verse lacks the human reason for the forest's dread, the parted woman, which the Akananuru poem supplies.
gains.b: The Akananuru poem lacks the image of the forest as a house of mourners, which the epic adds.

note: Verse 781 shows the dry forest in the heat; verse 795 shows the same wooded country green and dancing with peacocks.
teaches: The two verses show that the harsh forest of the first part gives way to a country of plenty as the party travels on.

note: Verse 786 has the moon-hued prince say 'these are yours, see them'; verse 800 repeats the 'see this' as he points to the marutham water.
teaches: The pointing opened at the start of the tour is carried through the whole series up to the farm country.

note: Kural 65 says touching one's children is joy to the body; the king here holds both sons in both arms as soon as he sees them.
teaches: The king's embrace shows a father's bodily joy in his sons coming before any royal question.

gains.a: The verse gives the embrace but not why it is joy, which the couplet names as the pleasure of touch.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a scene of a king, who must rule, undone by the sight of his sons safe.

note: Kural 65 also names the joy of hearing children's words; in 825 the king revives when his son tells him he went along.
teaches: The king's lifting at his son's words gives the couplet's pleasure of the ear a sudden effect on life itself.

gains.a: The verse lacks a general statement that a child's speech alone can be a parent's joy.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where those words carry news of a danger passed, so joy follows relief.

note: Kural 550 likens the king's removal of the cruel to weeding a crop; 824 gives a lion ruining the king's forest, removed by his sons.
teaches: A king's clearing of harm to his land can be done by a beast-slaying prince, which widens the weeding image beyond wrongdoers.

gains.a: The verse lacks any rule that makes the removal of the menace the king's own charge, which the couplet supplies.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a menace that is a beast and not a criminal, and a son who acts for the king.

note: Verse 409 reports the sign that within a month Tivittan will split a lion's mouth; verse 828 brings word that the lion has in fact been destroyed.
teaches: The prophecy is shown fulfilled by a spy's report, so it reaches the Vidyadhara king as news, not as a vision.

note: Kural 381 counts an army first among a king's six limbs, while verse 838 raises the host as a marriage escort, in the likeness of a sea swallowing the world.
teaches: The pair shows an army used for display and escort, a use the couplet's list of royal strengths does not name.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's view that an army is a standing limb of rule, not raised for a single occasion.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case of a host raised for a wedding, where numbers show a king's worth to his allies.

note: Kural 676 says to act only after weighing the finish, the hindrance and the yield; verse 829 has the king consult his kin and then press on with the wedding.
teaches: A king's deliberation can be a formality over a choice already made by the deed of the suitor.

gains.a: The verse lacks any test of the plan's hindrances, since the lion's death has already decided the match.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where counsel follows a settled choice instead of shaping it.

note: Kural 57 holds that guarding women by confinement is no use and their own steadfastness is the best guard; verse 861 sets armed women round the princess.
teaches: The pair shows the guard of arms as outward show beside the inward guard the couplet values.

gains.a: The verse lacks a measure of what really guards the girl; the couplet gives one.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a concrete household that does guard its women by force; the verse supplies one.

note: Cintamani 1344 has jewelled women standing guard round the bride before her wedding; verse 868 posts two thousand armed maidens round the princess.
teaches: Both epics guard the bride with women, but this one makes the guard an armed troop of the magic-learned.

note: Cintamani 1344 has the astrologer fix the day; verse 866 has learned men judge the hour before the girl boards.
teaches: The pair shows the wedding hour as a learned decision in both Jain epics, with the Soolamani making it the king's cue to act.

note: The Silappathikaram sets Kannaki's wedding under a pearl canopy on diamond pillars; verse 852 hangs gems and pearls on a hall.
teaches: The pair shows the same jewelled hall at two scales: a city wedding and a palace one dressed like the gods' own.

gains.a: The Soolamani hall lacks any rite; the Silappathikaram unit gives the fire and the blessing.
gains.b: The Silappathikaram canopy is only a canopy; the Soolamani hall grows into a wishing-tree.

note: Kural 761 calls a complete army the chief of a king's wealth; verse 874 shows the host as a spreading display round a bridal vimana.
teaches: The pair shows that the host here is wealth on show, not strength at work as the couplet rates it.

gains.a: The verse lacks any test of whether the host is the king's strength; the couplet gives one.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the sight of an army spent on a wedding escort; the verse gives it.

note: Verse 875 starts the guide's naming of the lands below; 889 ends the tour at the grove where the host alights.
teaches: The tour is a framed journey that ends with the host's landing at Podanam, so the descriptions serve the arrival.

note: Kural 381 counts the army among the six limbs of a king; verse 898 shows an army encamped with allied kings rimming the forest around the royal banner.
teaches: The camp shows the army as a ring of allies as well as a limb, which the couplet's list of six does not show.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that makes the host a part of kingship, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks any picture of an army in the field with its allies pitched around the king.

note: The maiden-city built in 899 is where the maiden lands in 900.
teaches: The city is built before she arrives, so her descent into it is a planned reception and not a stray landing.

note: Maruci's report in 901 draws the king's reply to him in 906.
teaches: The envoy's report wins a lodging and a reply, so the envoy's word is what sets the king's preparations moving.

note: The soldiers hold that only bound fate may take a life; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate.
teaches: A warrior class that claims only fate may kill makes its own arms the servants of fate, which the couplet's praise of fate's strength never says.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that fate outruns every other plan, which would explain why soldiers can speak of fate as the only killer.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of armed men who put its claim into their own battle-cry and so make Death tremble.

audit_text_issue: sense of 916 flagged uncertain; grammar clipped

note: The prince stocks the city's feast for guests as each desires; Kural 81 says a household exists to tend guests.
teaches: The wedding feast is a state's display and a political courtesy, which shows a limit of the couplet's household hospitality that needs no such display.

gains.a: The verse lacks the moral reason that makes feasting a guest the very point of keeping wealth, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case of hospitality scaled to a royal alliance, where the feast also announces rank and ties.

note: Verse 902 orders gate-arches, gold pots and a decorated city; verse 923 carries the order on to saffron and sandal mud, aloe smoke and gold powder.
teaches: The wedding is prepared in stages, from the frame of the city to its scent, and the second order goes beyond what the first asked.

note: In 917 the king seats Maruci on a gold-fronted elephant before him; in 933 the king himself mounts the dressed elephant.
teaches: The elephant first honours the guest's envoy and only afterwards carries the king, so the ride is a courtesy given in order of rank.

note: Verse 927 shows a keeper who knows the elephant's ways re-roping it and handing it to its riders; Tirumanthiram 2023 sets five rutting elephants in the body that will not come to the post of the Agamas' teaching.
teaches: The same craft of the keeper is both a working skill here and the picture of a discipline that fails without a teaching there.

gains.a: The verse shows a keeper's craft but not why such taming might matter beyond the ride.
gains.b: The verse names the inner elephants but has no scene of a keeper who actually succeeds with one.

note: Verse 934 shows the king's white umbrella raised in the ride that cools the world; Kural 389 says the world lives under the umbrella of a king who can bear bitter words.
teaches: The umbrella cools only for a king who has the character the Kural names, which the display of the ride cannot show.

gains.a: The verse lacks the condition of character that makes the umbrella a shelter.
gains.b: The couplet lacks any picture of the umbrella in its pomp as the world sees it.

note: Verse 934 shows a king riding an elephant under a high umbrella; Naladiyar 21 says kings who rode elephants under umbrellas like the moon over a hill have been carried off.
teaches: The same pomp that the Soolamani shows as the king's splendour is the thing the Naladiyar sets against death, so the display is also a reminder of its end.

gains.a: The verse lacks any hint that the splendour of the ride is brief.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks the scene whose brightness gives its warning weight.

note: Verse 936 gives the roar of pipes, drums and horns at the wedding ride; Naladiyar 23 says the drums that sound for a wedding may sound the same day for the bridegroom's funeral.
teaches: The wedding's noise is the same instrument as the funeral's, so the Naladiyar turns the verse's joy into a warning without changing the sounds.

gains.a: The verse lacks any thought that its music could change meaning.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks the wedding's full noise that makes its reversal strong.

note: Verse 941 shows women along the route losing their composure at the sight of the young men; Kural 1254 says the restraint she boasted of passes beyond concealment into the open.
teaches: The public street is the occasion where the Kural's private breaking of restraint becomes visible to all.

gains.a: The verse lacks the woman's own account of the restraint she once claimed.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the crowded occasion that draws desire out in public.

note: In 901 Maruci goes to the lord of Suramai to announce the Vidyadhara's arrival; in 943 he goes the other way to tell the Vidyadhara king that the lord of Suramai is coming.
teaches: The messenger crosses between the two courts in both directions, so each side is first hosted and then hosting, and the welcome is mutual.

note: Verse 944 gives the host's standing by its look: elephants like hills, banners like streams, warriors like tigers; Kural 768 says an army without striking power still gains standing from its martial bearing.
teaches: A host at a wedding is shown by its bearing alone, which is the standing the Kural says an army can have even before it fights.

gains.a: The verse lacks any statement of what such bearing is worth.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a picture of the bearing it names.

note: Verse 838 has the king raise a host like a sea swallowing the world; verse 949 shows the two hosts meeting as the Ganga and the Yamuna.
teaches: The host first likened to a sea is now the river that mingles with another, so the image turns from size to joining.
audit_text_issue: 949 sense flagged uncertain; whose hosts is inferred.

note: Verse 873 has the host's drums and bells roar like the sea as it leaves; verse 950 turns the sea into the milk-sea of the sky.
teaches: The sea simile follows the host from departure to meeting, changing from noise to something heavenly and calm.

note: Verse 880 has wild elephants mistake clouds for a rival elephant; verse 951 says clouds and young elephants cannot be told apart.
teaches: The mistake of cloud for elephant is the beasts' in one verse and the poet's own wit in the other.

note: Verse 875 has the host go across the sky past seas and hills; verse 948 gives the order to leave the air and walk the ground.
teaches: The sky journey ends in an order of descent, so the aerial tour serves the protocol of a meeting on earth.
audit_text_issue: 948 flagged uncertain; subject only 'he of the mountain'.

note: Verse 866 has learned men fix the hour for the bride to board; verse 958 has the kings meet at the hour the astrologers named.
teaches: The same trust in the astrologers' hour governs the leaving and the meeting.

note: Verse 845 shows Arkakirti standing proudly on his elephant at the head of a host; verse 962 shows him folding his hands to the Podanam king.
teaches: The warlord of one scene is shown as a bowing guest in the next, so his pride is placed beneath his courtesy.

note: Verse 845 puts Arkakirti on his own elephant; verse 963 has the Podanam king raise him onto the king's own young elephant.
teaches: Arkakirti's own elephant is replaced by the host-king's, marking the passage from commander to honoured guest.

note: Kural 680 has a small ruler bow to the great out of fear; verse 960 has the princes fold hands before the king at a meeting arranged for a wedding.
teaches: The bow of a wedding visit is shown as courtesy between equals, where the couplet sees bowing as a way of buying safety.

gains.a: The verse lacks any reading of the bow as a policy, and the couplet supplies the cold case of a bow from weakness.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a bow made freely by allies who gain nothing by it, which the verse supplies.

note: Kural 90 says a guest wilts when the host's face changes on seeing him; verse 963 has the host drink in the guest's beauty and seat him on his own elephant.
teaches: The welcome here is warmer than a kept face, since the host shares his own mount, a test the couplet does not set.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's test that a host's welcome is read from the face.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case of a host who answers by sharing his own seat of rank.

note: Soolamani 107 has the astrologer read a dream as a Vidyadhara king coming to praise the lord and give a daughter; here he arrives at Podanam and says he has come gladly to give her.
teaches: The reading of the dream is kept in the king's own gladness, so the prophecy is borne out as willing consent and not only as outcome.

note: Soolamani 109 has the court confirm that Tivittan will guard the whole world under one umbrella; here Prajapati, holding the bride, says that his earlier austerity is the reason and that the wheel is certain.
teaches: The prophecy gets a cause in Tivittan's earlier austerity, which the court's earlier confirmation lacked.

note: Kural 1251 has the axe of desire break the door of restraint bolted with shame; Soolamani 981 has restraint vanish because desire runs straight on, and puts it in the poet's voice about the girl.
teaches: The Kural gives restraint a lock that desire can break, while the Jain epic says the restraint was not broken but given to the one she loves.

gains.a: The verse lacks a picture of how restraint fails; the couplet gives the door, the bolt and the axe.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where the woman's restraint is not lost to chance but handed to a particular lover, and the poet argues it a worthy gift.

note: Kural 1094 has the man see that when he looks she looks at the ground, and when he does not she smiles; in 982 the lad looks boldly while her modesty holds her back and she melts.
teaches: The Kural gives the lover's inference from the lowered eye, and the epic shows the same shyness from within, as a pull she cannot hide.

gains.a: The verse lacks the timing of looking and looking away that tells the watcher she is moved.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the girl's inner melting and the power of her modesty over her, which the epic shows.

note: Kural 1125 has the man say he would recall her only if he forgot, but he does not know how to forget; 990 has the girl say that if she tried to forget, fate itself would drive her back to remember.
teaches: Both deny forgetting, but the Soolamani lays the compulsion on fate, which the Kural leaves to the lover's nature.

gains.a: The verse lacks the compact logic that remembering needs a prior forgetting.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a cause for the failure to forget; the verse supplies fate, and the girl's inward cry that the world does not know it.

note: Kural 1102 says the cure for a disease is usually other than its cause but this woman is herself the cure for the sickness she brings; Soolamani 991 says love's sickness has no cure and that looking coolly at loved ones only doubles the wound.
teaches: The Kural finds the remedy in union with the beloved, and the epic denies any remedy before the union.

gains.a: The verse lacks the possibility of a cure in the beloved, which the couplet names.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the stage before union, where the girl sees no cure and fear doubles the pain.

note: Naladiyar 47 has the fool call a body of nine seeping openings 'broad-shouldered one, bangle-wearer' because skin dazzles his eyes; Soolamani 987 has Prajapati marvel that the Maker gathered all beauty into one girl.
teaches: The same dazzled look at a woman is a fool's error in the Naladiyar and a bride's honour in the epic, so the epic's praise stands on a view of the body the Jain text refuses.

gains.a: The verse lacks the view of the body as flesh that the epic's praise leaves out.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a case where the praise of a woman's beauty is made by a worldly king and so shows what it attacks.

note: Tirumanthiram 204 tells the heart to turn away from smiling women as the etti fruit is poison under a good look; Soolamani 980 shows a man's looks seize a girl's eyes and holds the pull as natural.
teaches: The epic tells love as a force that wins the heart, and Tirumular gives the warning that such pull is the poison.

gains.a: The verse lacks any warning that the seizing of the eyes may harm.
gains.b: The poem lacks a case that shows the pull working, from the woman's side.

note: Soolamani 155 has her modesty make a flower-vine droop in shame; here modesty is the curtain she draws round the prince she carries in her heart.
teaches: Modesty shifts from an ornament of her beauty into the screen that hides her love.

note: 1001 has Madhavasenai fix the bride's form in her heart and begin to paint; 1010 has her tell the queen the form was beyond any painting and that her hand was steadied by the queen's grace.
teaches: The painter's pride in the likeness turns into modesty when it is presented, so the portrait serves as praise of the bride and of the queen.

note: In 829 the bride's father judges the girl fit only for the lion-killer and begins the wedding rites; in 1012 the groom's mother, seeing only the portrait, welcomes the match as ripened merit.
teaches: The match made by the fathers is accepted by the groom's mother through a painted likeness, so the women make the bride a member of the family before she is seen by the groom.

note: In 445 the keeper reports the priest's word that a Vidyadhara lord would come seeking a bride for the king's son; 1015 is the girl's portrait brought to that son.
teaches: A foretold match is finished not by the prophecy itself but by a go-between's practical acts, here a painter carrying a likeness to the groom.

note: Kural 1274 says something lies within the bud of the girl's smile like scent within a bud; in 1004 the friend reads the bride's silent smile and gives it words.
teaches: The couplet's hidden meaning in a smile is shown here as read and spoken for her by a friend, which makes private signal into public courtesy.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's picture of a smile whose meaning is real but unseen, as scent is in a closed bud.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case where the smile is read aloud by a third person who then acts on what it says.

note: Kural 685 describes the envoy who speaks briefly, removes what would offend, and brings a smile; in 1011 Madhavasenai carries the bride's greeting to the groom's mother as a go-between.
teaches: The same tact of an envoy is shown in a domestic errand between two households, where the greeting claims kinship before the wedding.

gains.a: The verse lacks a stated measure of what makes a message-bearer good, which the couplet gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case of such tact used between a bride's house and a groom's, not between kings.

note: Naladiyar 53 lists beauty among the things that fail to last, which the best renounce; 999 praises the bride's beauty as so bright she cannot be looked at, and says nothing of its end.
teaches: The poet gives full praise to beauty that his school's moral verse calls perishable, so the reader sees the praise and the warning side by side without either answering the other.

gains.a: The verse lacks any limit on the beauty it praises, which the Naladiyar supplies by naming it as one of the things that go.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a concrete case of the beauty it says does not last, set in the full pride of its glow.

note: Verse 1017 asks whose daughter the picture shows; 1018 answers that she is no earth-woman and so the Vidyadhara king's daughter.
teaches: The answer is reached by elimination from the picture's beauty, not from any name, so the maiden's identity rests only on how she looks.

note: Verse 1016 puts the portrait before the youth; 1019 shows love begin as soon as he looks, with Kaman taking aim.
teaches: The poet makes the painted likeness itself the occasion of love, so no meeting has taken place when the wound is given.

note: Kaman's shaft of 1019 has landed by 1021, where the youth himself lets desire swell slowly.
teaches: Love enters by a god's act but is then fed by the lover himself, so the verses show both cause and indulgence in one fall.

note: While the youth in 1020 burns for the maiden's picture, 1035 shows her elsewhere, praised by women, going to worship at dusk.
teaches: The reader sees the youth's fire for a girl who is far away and busy with prayer, so his longing has no answer from her yet.

note: Verse 1037 sets the lotus drinking the feet's glow beside the worshippers; 1038 repeats the figure with bees singing.
teaches: The second verse adds the bees' sound to the lotus image, so the worshippers' bloom is also heard as a hymn.
audit_text_issue: Lines 2 and 3 of each are near duplicates.

note: Both ask whether a woman is a goddess, a rare bird or a human, but in verse 1017 the question is asked about a painted likeness and answered by reasoning.
teaches: The question that Kural 1081 puts as a lover's reeling is here a calm puzzle about a portrait, so the same three-way wonder can come from sight alone.

gains.a: The verse lacks the lover's own giddy heart, which the couplet puts first and which the woman's reasoned question leaves out.
gains.b: The couplet lacks any sense that the wonder can be a deliberate question put to another person about a likeness.

note: Kural 1171's woman blames her eyes for showing her the man; verse 1020's youth melts as his eyes take in only a picture.
teaches: Love through the eyes does not need the person present, so the eyes' guilt in the couplet is wider than a meeting.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's turn on the eyes themselves as the cause of sorrow, which names an instrument for the fire.
gains.b: The couplet lacks any case where the eyes meet only a painted form and still bring the sickness.

note: Kural 1224's parted wife meets evening as enemies at a killing ground; verse 1033 gives a lit, scented evening that burns only those who carry desire.
teaches: The epic locates the pain in the viewer's state ('for those who have it'), while the couplet makes evening itself the attacker.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's starkness, in which evening is a force with an army, not a charming hour.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the verse's detail of lamps, smoke and birds, which show evening pleasant in itself before it hurts.

note: Both verses show evening birds going to their nests and young while one who is away or lovesick suffers.
teaches: Pairing the two shows that the happy birds are used as the measure of the lover's loneliness in both, only here the sufferer is a youth and there it is a wife.

gains.a: The verse lacks the akam frame of a wife whose husband is on his work, which Natrinai 69 supplies and which gives the birds' return a cause for grief.
gains.b: The Sangam poem lacks the wide epic eye that lists the fields, the fish-carrying birds and a generous man's spear-like feeling in one evening.

note: Verse 1029 compares closing lotuses to chaste women whose beloved has left; Akananuru 71 compares bees leaving pool flowers for branch flowers to graceless men.
teaches: The same evening scene casts the flower as a faithful wife and the bee as a leaving man, so each poet gives the figure a different party to blame.

gains.a: The verse lacks the blame that Akananuru puts on the one who leaves, since its simile is only a praise of women's constancy.
gains.b: The Sangam poem lacks the picture of the wife as the shut lotus, which turns the flower into the one who stays loyal.

note: Verse 1036 gives a woman setting lamps, incense, flowers and music before the Jina; Tirumanthiram 1005 sets golden lamps and incense in every direction and promises release.
teaches: A Jain maiden's temple rite and a Saiva verse use the same lamp-and-incense offering, though only the Tirumanthiram names its fruit.

gains.a: The verse lacks any statement of what the offering brings, which the Saiva verse gives as release.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram lacks a person doing the rite, with her doors, garlands and strings, which the epic shows in motion.

note: Verse 1024 narrates the youth's heart burning for a woman's body as the natural course of love; Tirumanthiram 204 tells the heart to turn away from such burning.
teaches: What the epic narrates as an unfolding desire, the Siddhar-side verse treats as a trap, so the two disagree about what the heart should do with beauty.

gains.a: The verse lacks any judgment on the burning, which the Tirumanthiram supplies as a warning.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram lacks the felt scene of a young man wasting with desire, which shows why the warning is needed.

note: Verse 1037 shows lotuses opening in the glow of the feet and worshippers blooming at the Jina's feet; Kural 3 promises long life to those who reach the feet of the one on the flower.
teaches: Both join feet and flowers, but the epic gives the bloom as the worshipper's own joy while the couplet gives a lasting earthly life.

gains.a: The verse lacks a stated reward for reaching the feet, which the couplet names as long life.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the verse's picture of the flower opening in the feet's light, which the worshipper's joy is likened to.

note: In 1040 the maiden prays that the sickness of birth leave her; in 1049 a friend says the love of a united pair outweighs even the state without birth and death.
teaches: The same eve holds two valuations of release, a bride's prayer and a friend's boast, and the poet leaves them standing side by side.

note: 1054 names the wedding day as the day to enjoy good deeds; 1057 uses the passing of good deeds and the coming of evil ones as a figure for night's darkness.
teaches: The same karmic words serve first for a bride's joy and then for the dread of night, so the story's fortune is read through deeds both times.

note: 1053 proposes to beg the moon to bring tomorrow near; 1056 shows the moon shrinking and sinking.
teaches: The moon she meant to petition simply sets, so the night she wished short is shown passing without her asking.

note: 1050 shows birds without mates as fire to the separated; 1061 shows paired birds sheltering mates and young as they sleep.
teaches: The birds that stand for separation in the friends' talk stand for union in the poet's closing picture, which gives the night a second reading.

note: Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one can be sweeter than sleeping on the beloved's soft arms; verse 1049 sets the lovers' union above the state without birth and death.
teaches: The Soolamani friend raises the Kural's comparison from a god's heaven to release itself, the goal her own Jain work teaches.

gains.a: The verse lacks a model for weighing love against the highest good, which the Kural's open question gives.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case where the thing weighed against love is release from birth, not a heaven.

note: Naladiyar 51 says that, as darkness rushes in when a lamp's oil runs out, evil takes its stand when good deeds are spent; 1057 sets the passing of good deeds beside the thickening of darkness at night.
teaches: The Naladiyar teaches the lamp-and-darkness figure as a rule; the epic turns it into a description of night, which shows how common the figure was.

gains.a: The verse gives the darkness-and-deeds figure without a rule, which the quatrain's lamp and oil supply.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a scene in which the darkness is a real night around a sleeping city.

note: Kural 1183 says love has taken the woman's grace and modesty and left sickness and pallor; verse 1045 shows a maiden who tries to hide her sickness and is betrayed by her pallor.
teaches: The epic shows the moment when modesty tries to hold and pallor breaks it, a step the couplet only reports after the fact.

gains.a: The verse lacks a statement that pallor is the price paid for modesty, which the couplet states.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a maiden before marriage who still has her modesty and is losing it.

note: Naladiyar 23 says the wedding drums of one hall can be the funeral drums for the bridegroom the same day; verse 1052 reports a drum sounding tomorrow's wedding.
teaches: Read beside the quatrain, the drum of joy carries the warning of the same drum's other use, which the epic's happy scene does not say itself.

gains.a: The verse lacks any thought that the festive drum could mean loss, which the quatrain supplies.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a drum that is only the announcement of a coming wedding, with no loss in the story.

note: 1068 sends the sun up to see the fire-circling; 1070 reports the rites complete.
teaches: The poet makes the sun a witness, so the unseen wedding is told through daybreak and not in itself.
audit_text_issue: both flagged uncertain; 1070 word division damaged

note: 1071 beats the drums for the worship day; 1075 lays out the stages of the day's procession.
teaches: The festival's religious worship and its marriage procession share one day and one set of stages.

note: Both lay out the city streets full of offering and goods.
teaches: The streets are filled first with sound and incense, then with goods, building one festival picture.

note: Naladiyar 23 sees wedding drums that may be funeral drums by evening; Soolamani 1107 ends the rites with some who leave for the forest and some who go home amazed at the wealth.
teaches: The same festival shows the transience of the day for some and wonder for others, so the Soolamani lets the Naladiyar's lesson be heard only by those who leave.

gains.a: The wedding verse gains a rule of why some depart to the forest, which the verse leaves unsaid.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a scene where its lesson is taken by some and missed by others, which it states only as a rule for the wise.

note: 1040 has the bride praying to the Jina to lose the disease of birth; 1107 ends her wedding with some going to the forest and others returning to enjoy.
teaches: The wedding that the maiden began by praying to be freed of birth closes on the same two answers, release or return.

note: 1101 shows the priest's fire fed while the groom's desire is kindled; Siddhar 147 asks when he will kindle the homa fire inside to cross the sea of desire.
teaches: One fire serves desire on one side and ends desire on the other, so the rite is the same fire put to opposite uses.

gains.a: The wedding fire gains a rival use, as a fire inside the body that ends the desire it kindles in the groom.
gains.b: The Siddhar's inner homa gains the outward rite it turns inward, with a priest's actual oblation set beside the longing.

note: Kural 1011 says true shame is shame at wrongdoing and anything else is only the shame of women; 1103 gives the bride's trembling shyness at the first clasp.
teaches: The bride's shyness is the kind the Kural calls a woman's own and not yet the shame of deeds, so the verse shows what the couplet sets aside.

gains.a: The bride's trembling gains a name for what it is, the shame of the bright-browed that the Kural separates from moral shame.
gains.b: The couplet gains a living case of the shame it sets aside, which it names without showing.

note: 1099 has the hill-king give the bride with water before the fire as god; Naladiyar 56 says marriage is called கடி because it binds the husband even to a faulty wife.
teaches: The giving of the bride before the fire is the act that creates the hardship of binding which Naladiyar names, so the rite explains why the husband cannot put her away.

gains.a: The gift before the fire gains a consequence, the lasting duty it puts on the groom.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the actual rite of water and fire that makes the binding.

note: 1103 shows the bride's shyness at the hand-clasp; 1106 has her scorn herself as shameless when shown the star.
teaches: Her shyness grows from trembling in the body to a spoken reproach, so the poet follows one feeling across the rite.
audit_text_issue: 1106 sense uncertain; speaker inferred from இகழ்ந்தாள்.

note: 1088 bathes the groom with water poured from pots; 1091 bathes the bride with mountain water and flowers.
teaches: Both are bathed before the fire but she is bathed by the Vidyadharas from above and he by kings, so the two sides bring different guests.

note: 1099 has the father give the bride with water; 1102 has the groom lead her round the fire holding her fingers.
teaches: The gift only becomes a marriage when the groom takes her hand and walks the fire, so the two verses give the two halves of the one act.

note: 1104 has both families pour gold and gems on the priests; 1105 names the learned chief priest who gets the greatest rain of wealth.
teaches: The gift is shared out by the priest's learning, so the wealth follows the Veda and not the families.

note: 1111 shows her shame breaking like a cage; 1122 shows her still shy and stranger-like in his lap.
teaches: The bride's shame is not undone in one embrace, and the groom still feels the distance it leaves after the cage is said to be broken.

note: 1112 makes two bodies one heart by ripening; Kural 1122 says the bond is as body is to life.
teaches: The epic gives the oneness of lovers a history of slow ripening, while the couplet states only the result as a bond of body and life.

gains.a: The epic verse gets a measure of how total the oneness is, as between body and life, which its bud-and-fruit figure does not give.
gains.b: The couplet gets a story in which the bond grows from bud to fruit instead of being given.

note: 1111 has the groom's ardour carry her shame off; Kural 1134 has the flood of love carry off the raft of shame and manliness.
teaches: The same flood that costs the secret lover his standing in the Kural is blessed here, because the epic's shame falls away inside a wedding.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the Kural's naming of shame as something love sweeps away, and so as a loss, which its cage image hides.
gains.b: The couplet gets a case where losing shame costs nothing, showing the loss it names depends on love outside marriage.

note: 1113 mixes union, delight and sulking in one daze; Kural 1109 lists sulking, making up and union as love's fruits in order.
teaches: The epic blends what the couplet puts in a sequence, so the sulk is a flavour inside union and not a stage before it.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the Kural's claim that the sulk is itself a reward of love, which explains why it sits in a list of pleasures.
gains.b: The couplet gets a scene where the three do not follow each other but occur together, without any making up needed.

note: 1113 lets the pair dissolve in a daze of union; Tirumanthiram 1960 teaches union in which the bindu is kept and infatuation dies.
teaches: The epic gives the surrender that Tirumular's discipline of union is set against, and the Saiva verse asks what the daze costs.

gains.a: The epic verse gets a question it never asks, whether the daze of union is a loss, and a measure by which a yogi would judge it.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gets the householder's full surrender as the ordinary case its restraint is defined against.

note: 986 says whoever wins the bride must have great earlier austerity; 1117 has the groom claim he did austerity to touch her.
teaches: The groom's claim fulfils the father's prediction and turns the language of penance from release to desire.

note: 1022 has the youth fear her glance as an arrow that will kill him; 1117 takes her eyes as the arrows and his austerity as their reward.
teaches: The same arrow that the fear of the picture-scene dreads is accepted as the prize of the wedding night.

note: 1118 makes the girl both his life and his rare medicine and him her servant; Kural 1102 says she is the cure for the sickness she brings.
teaches: The cure is a bondage in the epic, since the groom who is healed is enslaved by what heals him.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the argument behind its list of titles, that a cure ordinarily differs from its cause but here is the same person.
gains.b: The couplet gets a sequel in which the cure becomes servitude, which its single line leaves open.

note: 1037 compares the lotus and the worshippers of the Jina's feet to the maiden's red feet; 1119 has the groom call worship of those feet enough.
teaches: The poet moves the worship of feet from the Jina to the bride through the groom's mouth and so shows love borrowing a devotional form.
audit_text_issue: 1037 lines 2-3 doubled; feet of Jina or maiden ambiguous

note: 1122 has him gaze unblinking so as not to lose her; Kural 1129 has her not blink lest he be hidden.
teaches: The refusal to blink is common to both lovers, but the epic's reason is that she seems to recede each time he blinks, and the Kural's is that he lives in her eye.

gains.a: The epic verse gets proof that not blinking is a common sign of love, said by the woman in the Kural and by the man here.
gains.b: The couplet gets the groom's reverse case, where the fear is that she herself becomes a stranger at each blink.

note: 986 says the winner of the bride will surely rule the wheel; 1127 calls her the great queen of the wheel-ruler.
teaches: The singers speak as if the father's prophecy were already true, so the wedding is also the first coronation of her place.

note: 1128 warns the kurava tree not to grow as fragrant as the bride, lest it be plucked; Kural 1111 greets the anicham flower and says the beloved is more delicate.
teaches: Praising a girl by comparing her to a flower carries a threat in the epic, where equalling her gets the flower plucked, and only flattery in the couplet.

gains.a: The epic verse gets the Kural's form of speaking to a flower, so that its warning can be heard as a courtly praise.
gains.b: The couplet gets a darker side to the comparison, since a flower that equals her is in danger.

note: 1128 closes the songs' warnings about being plucked; 1129 shows the bride's smile after hearing them.
teaches: The songs tease the groom as the one who plucks, and the smile is the only answer given.

note: 1108 has him climb the tall mansion with the maid; 1130 has him climb the cloud-high mansion again after the grove.
teaches: The two climbs enclose the grove as an interlude, so the chapter starts and ends on the mansion where the wedding night is held.

note: In 707 the prince swears to split the lion's mouth; in 1135 the spy tells that the younger bull has split it and the sky-dwellers shake.
teaches: The vow's keeping is told from the enemy's side, where it is felt as terror rather than triumph.

note: In 704 the envoys carry Acuvakandan's word that the little one cannot kill the lion if he knows his strength; in 1141 he says men's strength is only fear's exaggeration.
teaches: The king's contempt for the prince is stated twice, once before the lion's death and once after, and the death in between has not moved it.

note: In 681 the prince's long-held anger kindles like a fire at the word tribute; in 1147 fire is born in Acuvakandan's eyes at the news of the marriage.
teaches: The two rivals are drawn with the same image of rage as fire, so the coming war reads as two fires meeting.

note: In 770 a speaker says the lion was beyond even the gods and only Tivittan could destroy it; in 1155 the kings say no god or man can match Acuvakandan.
teaches: Each side's champion is raised above the gods in speech, and the story means to test the two claims against one another.

note: In 620 the poet says the king destroys in anger without weighing a matter; in 1149 he says he will gather his people and then decide.
teaches: The king who was drawn as acting without thought now says he will consult, but only after his anger has already taken form.

note: In 306 the counsellor argues that the girl is fit for Asvagriva, whose mind is set and whom the Vidyadharas fear; in 1146 the girl has gone down to earth as wed to another.
teaches: The rejected suit explains why a marriage far away becomes a cause of war against the whole discus-lord's host.

note: In 1139 Acuvakandan shatters a diamond pillar with a blow; in 1151 the arriving kings see it lying burned and tremble.
teaches: The broken pillar is left standing as the proof of rage that the summoned kings read before he speaks.

note: In 695 the minister plans to enrage the prince into running into a lion; in 1136 the same minister hides the lion's death and has the cunning lion himself tell it.
teaches: The minister who used the king's pride against the prince now shelters the king from news that wounds it.

note: In 723 the prince seizes the lion by its fangs and tears it to strips; in 1143 Arikethu, who was set to play the lion at 697, marvels at that tearing.
teaches: The one man in the rival court who has played the lion's part is the first to admire the youth who killed the real one.

note: 1139 shows a king's blow breaking a diamond pillar; the couplet says the ruin of one who prizes anger is sure as a hand that strikes the ground.
teaches: The blow succeeds first, so the couplet's ruin is shown as not yet in sight and the story has to come back to it.

gains.a: the epic's king strikes stone and the stone breaks, which shows how anger can seem to succeed before any cost appears
gains.b: the couplet's ground that never misses gets a case where the blow visibly lands and the ruin it promises is still withheld

note: 1136 shows a minister hiding the lion's death for days; the couplet says the world rests under a king who can bear a bitter word.
teaches: The cost of a king who cannot bear bitter words falls first on his ministers, who delay the news and arrange who tells it.

gains.a: the epic gives a concrete delay and a go-between, where its king has only been called proud
gains.b: the couplet gets a named cost of an intolerant king, the stage-managed late report, which it states only as the world's shelter lost

audit_text_issue: 1136 may still be the spy's report (marker's note).

note: 1144 shows Arikethu holding back his own view and speaking courtesies at the angry king's feet; the couplet says to stay neither far from nor near a quarrelsome king, as with a fire.
teaches: A courtier's distance from an angry king can be a matter of what he withholds, not where he stands.

gains.a: the epic shows how a counsellor keeps from the fire by silence and flattery while holding his own admiration of the enemy
gains.b: the couplet's fire is made literal in a king whose eyes spit flame, and its measure of distance is shown to be one of speech

note: 1149 has Acuvakandan rage and boast, then say he will gather his people before deciding; the couplet faults a king who does not think with his circle and then lashes out.
teaches: Consulting after the rage has set may offer none of the couplet's protection, because the order of anger and counsel is reversed.

gains.a: the epic's king says he will consult yet has already boasted and resolved, so counsel is shown arriving after the anger
gains.b: the couplet gets a case where consulting follows the outburst, which it does not consider

note: In 1153 the kings wonder whether the king rages at Death or at those who rule through the ages; Naladiyar 21 says even kings under umbrellas on elephants are carried off as dead.
teaches: The courtiers imagine his anger reaching Death himself, the very pride the quatrain says Death gathers in.

gains.a: the epic's courtiers show how far a king's pride can be imagined to extend, to Death himself
gains.b: the quatrain's anonymous fallen kings get a living counterpart whose court takes him to be above their end

note: In 1148 Acuvakandan boasts of turning mountains and rolling the world; Tirumanthiram 1686 lists burning with anger and boasting of greatness among what is not the nature of one near the Lord.
teaches: The Saiva list names as marks of the unripe what the epic's rival king shows as his great-hearted rage.

gains.a: the epic's boast is classed by a Saiva text among the faults that mark a man far from the Lord, a reading the Jain narrator never states
gains.b: the list of faults gets a king in whom anger, scheming and boasting of greatness all appear together

note: 1153 asks what is the root of the king's anger; 1156 has the people stop guessing and fall silent.
teaches: The frightened crowd moves from asking the cause to waiting without words, so the dread grows as the cause stays unknown.

note: 1155 asks who would anger a king no demon can match; 1158 gives the cause, a rumoured pledge of a daughter to a human.
teaches: The court's puzzle in 1155 is answered by a rumour the king repeats as fact.

note: 1172 warns that a great king should not march against lowly foes; 1181 has the king ask what kind of war this is.
teaches: The king answers the warning by asking whether this war is human, divine or both.

note: The king is lord of a rutting war elephant and in rage; the Siddhar song kills anger as a mad elephant's rut with the goad of reasoning.
teaches: Anger as a rutting elephant is a royal fact in the epic and a figure in the Siddhar, which shows what the goad of reason would have to stop.

gains.a: The epic's king has a real elephant and a real rage but nothing that checks the rage, which the Siddhar's goad of reason supplies.
gains.b: The Siddhar's elephant of anger lacks a king who actually rides one, which the epic gives.

note: The soldiers eager to carry arms and win; the Siddhar says horses, elephants and infantry shine under the parasol and are nothing without the ash.
teaches: The soldiers' pride in their strong shoulders is set beside a verse that says armies are worth nothing without the right mark, so the epic's boasts are weighed against a Siddhar's measure.

gains.a: The soldiers' boasts lack any measure of what an army is worth beyond winning, which the Siddhar sets in grace.
gains.b: The Siddhar's list of horses, elephants and chariots lacks men who speak, which the epic gives by letting soldiers boast.

note: 1165 calls anger a fire that gives birth to pride and a sword thirsty for blood; Kural 306 calls anger a fire that burns even one's own safe raft of kin.
teaches: The warrior prizes anger as the fuel of his sword, while the Kural counts the same anger as what burns one's own people.

gains.a: The warrior's praise of anger names no cost, which the Kural states as the burning of one's own kin.
gains.b: The Kural's rule has no one who values anger as martial fuel, which the epic supplies by letting a warrior praise it.

note: 1165 makes pride the child of anger's fire; Tirumanthiram 266 says the swollen-headed die without support, fallen into withering anger.
teaches: Pride that grows from anger in the epic is shown by Tirumular to end in a death without any support.

gains.a: The warrior's anger-born pride has no account of its end, which Tirumular gives as dying unsupported.
gains.b: Tirumular's proud man has no face or voice, which the epic gives in a swordsman boasting of his anger.

note: 1169 says a lowly jackal rising against lions would only be laughed at; Kural 500 says a jackal can kill an unflinching elephant in mud where its feet sink.
teaches: The speaker assumes the lowly cannot beat the great, while the Kural says the ground can let a jackal beat an elephant.

gains.a: The speaker's scorn for the jackal ignores the place of battle, which the Kural makes the deciding thing.
