gains.b: The Kural's jackal and elephant have no council that dismisses the jackal, which the epic supplies.

note: 1173 has the king's anger die at his kin's words; Naladiyar 68 says the worthy's anger cools of itself like boiled water.
teaches: The king's anger dies at others' words rather than by itself, so the epic shows a cooling the quatrain says only the worthy manage unaided.

gains.a: The epic king's anger cools only after his kin speak, which the quatrain says the worthy do alone.
gains.b: The quatrain's worthy cooling has no scene of a king and his kin, which the epic gives.

note: 1174 has the king thunder that he is faultless and then go to the council hall; Kural 568 says a king who lashes out in anger without thinking with his circle loses fortune.
teaches: The king rages first and consults after, so the epic shows the order that the Kural warns against, though it ends in council.

gains.a: The thundering king in 1174 shows no sign that the council will check him, which the Kural gives as the test of a king's anger.
gains.b: The Kural's circle that must be consulted is only a principle, and the epic shows a king who enters the hall after his rage has begun.

audit_text_issue: Spy's first-person line 4; sense not tied to anger.

note: 1175 has the minister Arimanju ask the angry king what he now thinks; Kural 445 says a king must take counsel as the counsellors are his eyes.
teaches: The minister's question is the counsel the Kural asks of a king, asked after the king has already raged.

gains.a: The minister's question is put to a king already set on war, which tests whether counsel can still act as the king's eyes.
gains.b: The Kural's counsellor as the king's eyes has no scene, and the epic gives a minister putting the first question.

note: 1179 says a king's justice is to prefer scheming to fighting and see what can be got; Kural 546 says victory comes not from the spear but from the unbent sceptre.
teaches: The counsellor rests victory on scheming and the Kural on the king's justice, so the two name different grounds for winning.

gains.a: The counsellor's rule asks only what can be gained, which the Kural answers with the question of whether the king's sceptre is just.
gains.b: The Kural's sceptre has no scheming rival, which the epic supplies in a council voice that puts craft first.

note: 1181 asks which kind of war to fight; 1200 has the prince take the war upon himself.
teaches: The council's question about the kind of war is answered when the prince claims the fight as his own, after the lords' boasts.
audit_text_issue: speakers in 1181 and 1200 are inferred from neighbouring verses

note: 1183 sorts war into human, divine and mixed; 1185 lets the lecture go and settles on men against men.
teaches: The long taxonomy of war is dropped for a single practical choice, so the lecture serves the decision.

note: Both make a weapon a feeder: the sword drinks demons' blood to still its hunger, the plough turns blood into a sown field.
teaches: Two boasts turn the same thing, blood, from a loss into food or seed, which shows how the council's talk makes killing a work of cultivation.

note: 1204 puts the ultimatum; 1205 shows the prince's heart catching fire at it.
teaches: The envoy's two options provoke an anger the verse shows as fire, so the ultimatum cannot be accepted.

note: The king asks which kind of war to fight; the couplet says weigh the work, one's own strength, the foe's and the allies' before acting.
teaches: The Kural states the weighing as a rule; the epic shows a council doing it by splitting war into human, divine and mixed kinds.

gains.a: The council's question gains a stated rule behind its caution: the choice of war is a weighing and not a taste.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete case where the foe's strength includes divine arts, which its list of four strengths does not foresee.

audit_text_issue: speaker identified only by his banner

note: The king gathers allies after the spy's report; the couplet says a king who does not gather through spies and judge has no victory ready.
teaches: The epic shows a spy's report prompting a council, which is what the couplet calls the ground of victory.

gains.a: The scene gains a reason why the spy's word is repeated before the whole council: the report is the first step in the war.
gains.b: The couplet gains the next step it leaves out, what the ruler does with the report once he has it: he convenes allies.

note: A war of men without trickery is proposed; the Pandya Kudumi proclaims dharma to the weak before battle.
teaches: Both limit war, one by limiting means, the other by sparing those who cannot fight.

gains.a: The proposal gains a second sort of limit, protection of non-combatants, which it does not name.
gains.b: The poem gains a limit on means, no trickery between combatants, beside its limit on who may be harmed.

audit_text_issue: 1186 sense flagged uncertain (line 4) | 1186 line 4 (நஞ்சனாற் குரைப்ப) is doubtful

note: Arkakirti's bowstring is named for shame (நாண்) and he prizes the bow above life; the couplet says the honourable give up life when honour is lost.
teaches: The epic gives the hero's honour a physical thing, the string, that the couplet only states as a rule.

gains.a: The verse gains a statement of the stake: shame at disgrace outweighs life, with the bowstring as its image.
gains.b: The couplet gains an image of honour as something one wears and draws, the warrior's bowstring, instead of the yak's hair.

note: Arkakirti's wrath rains arrows and blood; the couplet says to guard against anger, which kills the one who does not.
teaches: A speech that glories in wrath as war's fuel meets a rule that says it destroys its own bearer.

gains.a: The boast gains a warning it does not hear: the wrath that drives the arrows can also destroy the archer.
gains.b: The couplet gains a counter-case where anger is praised as a duty, so its advice is tested against the warrior's ethic.

note: The envoys give an ultimatum with no softening; the couplet says an envoy speaks briefly, removes offence and gets the good done.
teaches: The envoys act as the opposite of the couplet's envoy, brief but offering only two harsh options, and it shows the rule's cost.

gains.a: The verse gains a measure by which the envoys' manner reads as a failure of diplomacy, not strength.
gains.b: The couplet gains an example where the envoy's brevity serves the sender's pride and brings about war instead of a good result.

note: 681 lights Tivittan with anger on hearing the word tribute; 1206 to 1207 show the same anger spreading through his body at the envoys' second round of words.
teaches: The poet lets the first anger be inward at the demand and the second visible at the insult, so the hero grows from controlled to burning as the embassies go on.

note: 690 sends the envoys back with a defiant word; 1210 again lets them go unharmed, now by naming the custom that protects envoys.
teaches: The hero's first dismissal is only defiance; the second gives the reason, that the envoy is not the one at fault, so he is shown as a lawful and not merely angry fighter.

note: 402 foretells that the Kesava will take the discus and the life of Asvagriva; 1216 sets a divine word that this youth will win and reign.
teaches: The prophecy of the lord's word is echoed as a divine pledge at the moment of the first war-answer, so the battle is told as the keeping of an old promise.

note: 686 calls the tribute-seeker a fool who would take the jewel from a venomous cobra's hood; 1225 gives the cobra's venom to the foe's laugh.
teaches: The cobra moves from the hero's image of the danger the foe courts to the foe's own laughing venom, so the image of the poisonous snake cuts both ways.

note: 1215 asks whether lives or honour weigh more with the enemy kings; 1224 answers that they keep pride though they feel ruin near.
teaches: The ultimatum's question is answered by the kings' choice, which shows honour overriding fear of death in those the poet says were told to bow.

note: 1210 sends away envoys who brought evil words that burned the ears; Kural 685 says an envoy should remove what would offend.
teaches: The envoys fail the Kural's standard of speech and are still protected, so the immunity of an envoy is shown to stand apart from how well he speaks.

gains.a: The epic scene gains a measure by which the envoys' evil words count as a failure of the office, not just of manners.
gains.b: The couplet gains the case of an envoy who offends and yet may not be harmed, which the couplet's ideal of inoffensive speech does not reach.

note: 1224 shows enemy kings holding to pride though they know it brings ruin; Kural 969 praises those who give up life when honour is at stake.
teaches: The couplet's honour is tested on the wrong side of a war the poem says is already decided, so pride that kills is shown as heroic and also as futile.

gains.a: The epic verse gains a named value, honour as a reason to die, for conduct it only calls rage.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where those who would die for honour serve an unjust demand, which the couplet's praise does not distinguish.

note: 1207 shows the hero's anger at petty words in his body; Purananuru 72 turns Neduncheliyan's rage at kings who mocked him as young into a vow with named forfeits.
teaches: The Sangam king binds himself in public speech to avenge a taunt, while the epic hero is let burn first and be confirmed by gods afterwards, so anger at a taunt is lawful in both but sanctioned differently.

gains.a: The epic hero's anger gains a Sangam precedent of a king answering mockery of his youth, which marks it as a king's duty and not temper.
gains.b: The Sangam vow gains a view of the same rage seen from the body and the heavens, and of a hero left to stand on others' pledge, which the vow has not.

note: 1243 has the Vidyadharas' arrows darken the sky; 1246 has the hero's arrows rise, strike their eyes and darken it again.
teaches: The darkness changes sides inside four verses, so the same arrow-shadow that shields the attackers blinds them.

note: 1251 reports the broken army to the proud king; 1255 gives the king's answer, a laugh.
teaches: The king's laugh meets news of ruin with a boast, making defeat into proof of the foe's single-handed skill.

note: The Kural names the army that does not collapse; 1250 shows drums split, crowns sunk and chariots overturned in a collapsing army.
teaches: A rule that an army must not collapse is tested against the detail of what a collapse looks like in a field.

gains.a: A standard to measure the broken host against, so its rout reads as failure of what an army must be.
gains.b: A worked case of collapse, which the definition names but never pictures.

note: The Kural calls an eye that blinks at a flung spear flight; 1247 has whole ranks blind with arrows, puzzled, hiding and falling.
teaches: The Kural counts flinching as flight, but 1247 shows troops struck blind by a dark of arrows, where fear and confusion are not the same.

gains.a: A name for the fear it shows, making the rout a failing of courage and not only of fortune.
gains.b: A case where the eye cannot see, which tests whether blinking is always cowardice.

note: The Kural's warrior laughs as he pulls a spear from his own body; 1255 has a king laugh at his army's rout.
teaches: The laugh of a warrior pulling a spear from his body is a private triumph, while a king's laugh at a lost army is a boast over others' loss.

gains.a: A measure of what the king's laugh costs against the warrior who laughs at his own wound.
gains.b: A contrasting laugh, from a leader and not the wounded fighter, which tests how far the Kural's praise reaches.

note: 1233 sets cloud against cloud and sea against sea as two hosts meet; Purananuru 17 sees the Chera king's host as an army like the sea.
teaches: The sea-army that praise sets at rest as a king's glory here meets another sea, and the figure turns from praise into clash.

gains.a: A source for the sea-army figure, here shown as one sea among two.
gains.b: A second sea set against the king's, so the image of an unopposed host meets its match.

note: 1259 pitches the camp on Arungalam hill; 1266 sets the two armies against one another.
teaches: The poet readies the field in one verse and the clash in the next, so the camp's choice of ground leads straight into the fight.

note: 1261 has the eldest brother vow vengeance; 1265 has the lord, cooled by the brothers' words, send them to fight.
teaches: The brothers' vow of vengeance is turned into their lord's permission and a goal of making their names stand.

note: 1262 has a brother laugh at the humans; 1270 shows the warriors as too great for the world.
teaches: The laughing Vidyadharas misjudge their foe, since the poet next shows those warriors as towering figures.

note: 1280 has victors decline to strike the blinker or shame the fled; Kural 775 calls a blink at a spear flight.
teaches: The epic shows the winners declining to treat a blink as flight, a gentler ending than the couplet's flat verdict.

gains.a: The epic's chivalry is measured against the couplet's strict rule that a blink is already defeat.
gains.b: The couplet's reflex of valour is shown with a winner's answer, mercy to the one who flinches, which it alone never gives.

note: 1279 has warriors who do not fear Death send the fearful away; Kural 765 calls an army one that stands against raging Death.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's test of an army into a selection, since warriors themselves dismiss those who fear.

gains.a: The warriors' call gets a standard for whom to keep, since the couplet names fearlessness before Death as what makes an army.
gains.b: The couplet's standing together is given a speaking crowd who sort themselves, which the couplet itself does not show.

note: 1256 closes that no one finishes an aim except by hard ripening after kings flee; Kural 473 says many who rose on enthusiasm broke midway.
teaches: The epic offers no cause for the kings' failure, while the couplet blames ignorance of one's own strength.

gains.a: The generalising closing lines get a stated cause of ruin, rising without knowing one's strength.
gains.b: The couplet's warning gets a scene of kings who marched and fled, which makes the broken rise concrete.

note: 1283 has Arisenan boast that none can stand against his sword; 1294 has a younger youth cut him in two as he draws back.
teaches: The poet puts the boast and the death a few verses apart, so a name proclaimed before the fight is shown to guarantee nothing in it.

note: 1297 shows Gunasenan roaming like a rutting elephant and tiger; 1304 opens on his falling.
teaches: The praise of Gunasenan's strength is cancelled by his own fall, which turns the new champion's boast into the next test.

note: 1305 brings Kamukan, learned in all arts, with bow and arrow; 1306 shows him ward off the volley and shoot his foe.
teaches: The note that he had learned all the arts is made good in the next verse, so the learning is shown as a fighter's skill.

note: Arisenan names himself and offers the foe the choice to flee; Kural 777 calls the war-anklet an adornment for those who value fame above life.
teaches: The epic shows the cost of the bold stance the couplet praises: the one who proclaims it is among the first to fall in 1294.

gains.a: The boast of 1283 is read against a standard of honour, so the proclamation becomes a claim to fame and not mere bravado.
gains.b: The couplet, which gives no outcome for the bold man, is given a case where the fame-seeker is cut down at once.

note: 1305 sets Kamukan, learned in the arts, with his bow; Naladiyar 386 likens a modest woman's beauty to a sharp sword in a clear-minded hero's hand.
teaches: The epic shows the learned hero whose skill the quatrain only uses as a simile, so a warrior's mind and weapon are tied.

gains.a: The learned bowman is placed in a stock of images where skill governs the weapon, which the verse alone does not state.
gains.b: The comparison gets a concrete clear-minded hero who actually wields the weapon in the next verse.

note: 1286 taunts a rival with a bride won by another; Cintamani 769 taunts rivals with their wives' sulking looks lost after the battle.
teaches: Both epics make a pre-battle taunt turn on the rival's wife or bride, so the insult reaches his private stake and not his strength.

note: The danava pierces Sarthulakan in 1315, and in 1316 the pierced man cuts him down with the trident.
teaches: The wound does not decide the duel; the wounded man's counter-stroke decides it, so the pair shows the fight reversed in one verse.

note: The pierced Sarthulakan fights on and kills the thrower, as in the Kural's warrior who sends his spear off and smiles at the one in his own body.
teaches: The poem makes the Kural's warrior who smiles at a spear in his body into a man who turns the wound into a weapon.

gains.a: 1316 gains a norm that treats a wound received in the fight as a mark of the warrior, not a loss
gains.b: Kural 774 gains an actual wounded fighter who turns the thrown trident on its thrower, not only a smile

audit_text_issue: sense flagged uncertain; who is pierced and who falls is not in the verse

note: Dhumaketu is likened to the Death of the age's end; Tirumular says the Lord's thinkers are beyond Death's messengers.
teaches: The war poem sets Death above all fighters, while Tirumular sets one who thinks of the Lord above Death.

gains.a: 1317 gains a view in which the Death its hero resembles can be turned back
gains.b: Tirumanthiram 176 gains the epic's warrior who becomes Death's own image on the field

note: Dhumaketu's boast in 1318 is repeated clause by clause and turned back by the younger king in 1320.
teaches: The answer uses the boaster's own clauses to cut him down, so the boast is shown to be what ruins him.

note: Dhumaketu's boast of lifting hills and drinking the sea is the kind of word the Naladiyar says the excellent never speak.
teaches: The epic gives the Naladiyar's rule a case in which the boast comes just before a fall.

gains.a: 1318 gains a standard by which its hero's boast marks him as the lesser man
gains.b: Naladiyar 346 gains a warrior's boast whose price is paid in the next verses

note: The younger king's promise that Dhumaketu's match will come is kept in 1325 when Dhumaketu rolls from the field.
teaches: The prediction made in the taunt is fulfilled in a few verses.

note: 1330 gives back 1329's words almost unchanged.
teaches: Giving the same words to both fighters leaves the taunt itself as the thing the poet shows, with neither side ahead.

note: The vow of 1336 to take the earth or the world of the gods is met when the arrow fells Suvarnaketu in 1350.
teaches: The vow of earth or heaven is ended not by either prize but by an arrow, so the warrior's two-sided promise leaves out the third outcome of defeat.

note: 1339 asks whether one may stand aside while another fights; 1341 takes the single fight as the king's custom.
teaches: The duel is argued as a question of courage first and accepted as royal custom second, so the rule is made by the debate and not given in advance.

note: 1345 names the arrow Naama; 1346 shows it cutting bow, arrows and illusion.
teaches: The poet shows the arrow's effect on the magic itself, so the king's last arrow answers the illusion that had outlasted every earlier shot.

note: The fall of the spear-bearer in 1350 is followed by the fall of the golden banner and the rout in 1351.
teaches: The army breaks at the moment its banner-holder falls, so the poet makes the champion's body the whole army's footing.

note: 1355 warns that fleeing warriors will be shunned by women; Purananuru 278 shows a mother who swears to cut off the breast that fed a son she thinks has fled.
teaches: The shame of flight is placed in the women's mouths in both, but the epic's speaker uses it to threaten, while the Sangam mother tests the rumour before she acts.

gains.a: The verse gains a case where the shame of flight is acted on by a woman with a sword, not left as a threat.
gains.b: The poem gains a speaker who turns the same dread of women's contempt into a rebuke before battle, not after it.

note: 1356 spends the perishing body for fame that stands for ever; Kural 233 holds that nothing in the world stands undying except renown.
teaches: The epic's call to a warrior to give up his body for fame puts into action the couplet's claim, and shows who is asked to pay for it.

gains.a: The verse gains the couplet's flat claim that only renown does not die, which it uses as its reason.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene where the price of that renown is a warrior's body in the heat of a rout.

note: 1356 asks warriors to stay and die for fame; Kural 780 calls such a death worth asking for if those who sustained one weep for it.
teaches: The couplet makes the dead man's supporters the judge of the death, which the epic speaker, urging flight not to be done, leaves out.

gains.a: The verse gains the test that the death should be one whose supporters mourn it, not one spent for its own show.
gains.b: The couplet gains a speaker who uses the worth of such a death as a reason to stop a rout.

note: In 1349-1350 the arrow goes through shield and chest and the warrior falls; Kural 774 has a warrior laugh as he pulls a spear from his own body.
teaches: The couplet shows the wound as a thing a brave man shrugs off, and the epic shows the same pierced body falling, so wound-laughter and wound-falling mark two ends of one warrior ideal.

gains.a: The verse gains a standard by which the fall is read: a warrior is judged by how he takes the wound.
gains.b: The couplet gains a body that does fall, the other end of the laughing warrior.

audit_text_issue: Sense flagged uncertain; the fall the note relies on is in 1350, outside the unit.

note: 1357 shames men who run to save life; 1380 calls a swordsman who runs from one man loathsome.
teaches: The rally and the taunt are one argument in two voices: flight is judged first as lost honour, then as disgusting manhood.

note: 1366 shows the hero mounted and frightening all; 1381 shows the enemy kings turning back in fear.
teaches: The terror one rider causes at the start is what finally sends the whole Vidyadhara line home.

note: The falling crown of 1377 is followed at once by the army's flight in 1378.
teaches: The crown's fall is shown as the cause of the rout, not merely its sign.

note: 1378 shows an army breaking at the sight of its king's fallen crown; the Kural says an army needs leaders.
teaches: A fallen crown scatters an army that Kural 770 would call leaderless, showing the leader's role as a matter of sight as much as of command.

gains.a: The rout gains a general rule: the army broke because it had no head to keep it together.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene in which the leader's loss is not death but a crown struck off, and the effect is instant.

note: 1380 calls flight from one man loathsome; Kural 775 says even a blink at a hurled spear is flight.
teaches: The two texts set the line of disgrace at different places: the epic at running away, the Kural already at the flinch.

gains.a: The taunt gains a stricter test: by Kural 775 the Vidyadharas' shame began before they turned.
gains.b: The couplet gains a speaker who shames living men in front of their army, not a rule stated apart.

note: 1380 condemns a fleeing swordsman; Purananuru 278 gives a mother's vow to cut her breast when told her son fled.
teaches: The Sangam poem shows what the epic's taunt costs the one who runs: the family's shame, not only his own.

gains.a: The taunt gains a household that would mourn and punish the runaway.
gains.b: The Sangam poem gains a Jain-epic scene where the same charge of fleeing is thrown at kings in the middle of a battle.

note: 1381 says the mountain Vidyadharas fled from men whom fate has marked; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate.
teaches: The epic gives fate as the one reason a strong flying army can be turned by men with no such powers.

gains.a: The Vidyadhara retreat gains a cause beyond skill or number: the opponents are fated to win.
gains.b: The couplet gains a battlefield instance in which fate beats a stronger force without any scheme being named.

note: 1382 begins the speech that 1379 announces when Kanaka Chitran steps in and speaks.
teaches: The announcement of a speech in 1379 only becomes a taunt of fear and manhood in the verses after it.

note: 1387 shows an unnamed youth in ornaments; 1390 gives his name and sets his kin's host moving.
teaches: The description of the youth and the report of his name together show that one hero is both the sight and the cause of the army's rising.

note: 1390 raises the brothers' host; 1392 shows the younger brothers and kings joining the press.
teaches: One hero's entry draws in kin after kin, so the battle spreads by loyalty rather than by order.

note: 1383 asks whether the flesh body must break for honour's sake; Kural 969 says the honourable give up life when honour is lost.
teaches: The epic's taunt tests the Kural's rule on men who run, showing it as a shaming speech to the living where the couplet states a private resolve.

gains.a: gains a measure for its taunt: honour is set above life as a standard
gains.b: gains a spoken use in battle, where the rule becomes a challenge hurled at cowards

audit_text_issue: Last two lines turn on a rare construction.

note: 1386 has the hero push through slanting spears for honour; Kural 774 has the soldier laugh as he pulls a spear from his own body.
teaches: Both link honour to the warrior's joy in danger, but the epic gives the motive as honour itself and the couplet as the pleasure of the wound.

gains.a: gains the wound-joy of the couplet, which its hero does not show: he is only seen advancing
gains.b: gains a stated motive, honour, which the couplet leaves unnamed

note: 1395 shows the flood of blood and broken tusks as a spectacle; Purananuru 62 asks what victory there can be when both armies have died.
teaches: Set side by side, the epic dwells on the field's carnage without cost where the Sangam poem measures it by the widows and the empty claim to victory.

gains.a: gains the question it never asks: what is won when the field is full of the dead
gains.b: gains the epic's long image of the carnage, which the poem only sketches

note: 1408 sows fame in a field ploughed with the plough; 1415 ploughs open the warriors' chests with the same plough.
teaches: The metaphor of a farmer's field opens as a boast and returns as the literal wound, showing the plough as both sign and tool of the hero's rule over the battle.

note: 1412 cries that the young prince has fallen and the army heaves; 1414 brings the elder brother and the plough and the army roars again.
teaches: The army's despair and its roar are made by one man's presence, so the verses show whom its courage hangs on.

note: 1416 shows Kanaka Naman coming to the fight on hearing of the plough-bearer; 1417 shows him struck on the shoulder.
teaches: The listener who joins a fight because he heard of a rival's feats is also the one who is struck down, so the fame that draws him is what ruins him.

note: 1418 leaves one man burning at the news of defeat; 1419 has Ratna Greevan lift the mountain.
teaches: The news of the defeat is turned into an act, which shows what anger does with grief in the epic's warriors.

note: 1419 lifts the mountain; 1420 shows the Suramai army scattering as he advances.
teaches: The scattering shows that the mountain wins by fear before it falls, so the plough-bearer's earlier victory is reversed here.

note: 1424 brings the messengers' report; 1425 has the king resolve to loose the spell.
teaches: The report is the whole cause of the spell, so the epic ties the world's destruction to one man's grief.

note: 1426 orders the spell to destroy mankind; 1427 has the spell pass the work on to Death.
teaches: The command goes from king to spell to Death, so the epic shows destruction as a chain of obedience with no one pausing.

note: 1427 has the spell call Death; 1428 shows the spirits and the goddess coming and the spell loosed on the army.
teaches: Death's summons is joined by a feast of spirits, which shows the destruction as a gathering that feeds many.

note: 1420 shows an army scattering before a mountain-lifter; Kural 765 sets the standard of an army that stands together even when Death comes at it.
teaches: The scene gives the Kural's test a failure that the couplet only describes as a standard, and shows the Kural's army needs a leader to hold.

gains.a: the unit gains a measure by which the scattering is a failure of the army and not only the fault of one man
gains.b: the couplet gains a scene where the standard is not met, showing what its unbroken army is set against

note: 1425 has a king's grief and anger lead him to loose a spell that destroys the world; Kural 305 says anger kills the one who does not guard against it.
teaches: The epic shows anger as a power that reaches the world and not only the angry man, which limits the couplet's 'yourself'.

gains.a: the unit gains a rule that makes the king's anger the cause of what follows and not only an act of war
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the harm of anger goes outward and the self is not the only victim

note: 1426 has a king order the destruction of all men; Tirumanthiram 238 says an unlearned king who says 'kill' is worse than Death, since Death spares the good.
teaches: Set side by side, the king who commands total death is judged by a rule the epic's own narrator does not state.

gains.a: the unit gains a standard by which its royal order is judged as the act of a king who says 'kill'
gains.b: the verse gains a case of a king with the power to turn Death into his tool

note: 1427 has a spell command Death to finish his work at a king's wish; Tirumanthiram 176 says no one can fight when life leaves and only the thought of the Lord turns Death's messengers.
teaches: The epic's Death takes orders from a spell while the Saiva verse holds Death answerable to the Lord alone, so the two disagree over who commands Death.

gains.a: the unit gains a view in which Death does not serve a king's spell
gains.b: the verse gains a scene where Death is commanded by a human wish, which the verse denies

note: 1435 says the missile cannot be turned back; 1439 shows its deity frightened and returned to its own shape.
teaches: The warning rests on a rule about hate-loosed weapons that the scene then breaks, so a claim of certainty is answered by the hero's greater strength.
audit_text_issue: 1435 speaker of last words unmarked | 1435 and 1439 both marked uncertain; change of speaker in 1435 line 4 unmarked.

note: 1445 is a boast of what the speaker is; 1448 answers that this is talk among his own band.
teaches: Boast and reply are a pair: the boast is judged by where it is spoken, not what it says.

note: Garuda comes as Tivittan's mount in 1443 and as his weapon in the same shape in 1452.
teaches: The bird changes from a helper that arrives to a weapon that is released, showing it as a power he can both ride and shoot.

note: The naga weapon of 1451 is cut down by the Garuda weapon of 1452.
teaches: The duel runs by counters, each weapon answered by its natural enemy, not by greater force.

note: Fire of 1453 is put out by the Varuna arrow of 1454.
teaches: Again the answer is the opposed element, which makes the fight a sequence of matched counters.

note: The sleep arrow of 1455 is undone by the awakening arrow of 1456.
teaches: The last pair completes the pattern: each of Asvagriva's divine weapons has its answer, so none is decisive.

note: 1448 sets brave speech among one's own against facing the foe; Kural 664 says speaking is easy and doing as one has said is hard.
teaches: The epic gives the Kural's remark a speaker and a test: the hilltop boaster must now act, which the next verses show.

gains.a: The rebuke gains a general rule that talk is cheap, so it reads as a measure of action and not only a sneer.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene where the bragger is made to act within a few verses and his weapons fail.

note: 1449 shows anger rising at insult and arrows poured out; Kural 305 says to guard against anger or it kills the one who has it.
teaches: The arrows are beaten away in 1450, so the epic shows the Kural's warning working out in the battle rather than as a rule.

gains.a: The rage gains a cost: the arrows turn back on the shooter's hopes, as the next verse shows.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king with an army whose anger leads him to weapon after weapon that fails.

note: 1437 compares the bow's arrival to a friend won in a former life; Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its doer like a calf its mother.
teaches: The simile gives the old deed a good side: what returns can be a helper in need, not only a penalty.

gains.a: The bow gains a possible source in former good deeds, which the narrator only hints.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the old deed returns as a weapon in a fight, not as suffering.

note: In 1459 the king's discus hides the hero; in 1461 the same discus, hurled back, kills the king.
teaches: The weapon that seemed the king's whole safety passes to his enemy, so the first strike is shown to be only half the story.

note: 1460 shows the discus halting at the youth's side; 1463 explains it by saying a harm aimed at a blameless man returns on its sender.
teaches: The strange halting of the discus is given a moral frame only a few verses later, so the poet explains the marvel by a rule of rebound.

note: 1463 ties the death to the rebound of a weapon sent against the blameless; 1466 says the discus he threw became his own enemy.
teaches: The rebound is first a simile and then a plain statement, so the onlookers read the king's death as his own act turning back.

note: 1462 shows the king falling from the elephant like a cloud struck by fire; 1464 turns the same fall into a moral on impermanence.
teaches: The poet first shows the fall and then lets onlookers draw the lesson, so the doctrine comes from the scene and not before it.

note: The chief queen loses her life in 1470; the other wives fall in 1471.
teaches: The queen's collapse leads the rest of the household, so the grief runs outward from her to all the women.

note: 1473 opens the laments with praise of the king's rule; 1481 closes with a question about his abandoned land and servants.
teaches: The women's laments move from praise of the king to a complaint that he left his duty, so grief ends in a charge against him.

note: 1464 shows a king who rode elephants under the umbrella brought low; Naladiyar 3 says kings on elephants fall when their deeds turn against them.
teaches: The quatrain gives the cause as the king's own deeds and the verse gives the scene, so the pair joins the rule to a particular fall.

gains.a: 1464 states only that glory ends and does not name why; the quatrain supplies deeds that turn against a king as a reason.
gains.b: The quatrain states the rule in general; here a named king in a battle is the case it applies to.

note: 1465 says that the man who came yesterday under the umbrella is felled today; Kural 336 says the world's greatness is that one who was here yesterday is not here today.
teaches: The verse gives a king's fall as the proof of the couplet and adds that the end comes by his own weapon, so impermanence is shown with a cause the couplet leaves out.

gains.a: 1465 shows the fall but lacks the couplet's plain statement that loss between yesterday and today is the world's greatness.
gains.b: The couplet is an abstract rule and gains a king felled by his own discus as a case.

note: 1467 lists strength, wealth and beauty that do not last; Kural 332 likens wealth's coming and going to a crowd gathering and breaking up at a dance hall.
teaches: The verse names what is lost, the couplet gives the image of its loss, and together they show loss as an ending without warning.

gains.a: 1467 gives a list of lost things but no image of how they go.
gains.b: The couplet gives wealth alone and gains strength and beauty with a king's body as the proof.

note: 1463 says a harm aimed at a blameless man returns on its sender; Kural 319 says hurt done in the forenoon returns in the afternoon of itself.
teaches: The couplet makes the return a rule of time, while the epic makes it happen through the victim's own hand turning the weapon back, so the return has an agent.

gains.a: 1463 lacks the couplet's plain rule that wrong done is wrong received; it only has a simile.
gains.b: The couplet gives the return without a means; the verse shows the thrown weapon as that means.

note: 1471 shows wives falling and beating their faces at a husband's death; Naladiyar 25 shows kin wailing as a corpse is carried to the burning ground.
teaches: Both pass from mourners' grief to what it shows about life, but the epic keeps the grief in the scene and the quatrain turns it into a reason to give up household life.

gains.a: 1471 lacks the quatrain's turn from grief to a judgement that household joy is empty.
gains.b: The quatrain gives wailing in general and lacks the specific grief of a king's wives.

note: 1476 asks whether a king who lay on a golden couch with wives rubbing his feet should now lie on an elephant's brow; Siddhar 642 says the throne of pure gold does not go with the body when Yama takes it.
teaches: The epic shows the couch lost by a battle and the Siddhar shows it lost by Yama, so one losing of luxury is told as a war and as the common end.

gains.a: 1476 gives a king's lost luxury but does not say that no luxury could follow him in death.
gains.b: The Siddhar verse speaks to anyone and gains a particular king's fall as a case.

note: 1470 shows the chief queen failing at her husband's body; Cintamani 293 shows women beating their breasts as the king lies dead.
teaches: In both epics the king's death is felt first by his women, so a fall in battle becomes a household loss and not only a political one.
audit_text_issue: 1470 sense uncertain (faint or death); 293 says nothing of the king in its own lines

note: 1466 says the discus he threw became his own enemy; Purananuru 227 calls Death a fool that cooked and ate its own seed by taking Valavan.
teaches: The epic shows the king as the agent of his death while the Sangam poet blames Death as an outside foe, so the two poems disagree on who ends a king.

gains.a: 1466 gives the fall as the king's own deed and lacks the Sangam poet's view that Death is to blame.
gains.b: The Sangam poem blames Death and gains the epic's case where the weapon of the dead man killed him.

note: 1482 has the women's tears put out the victor's wrath like water on fire; Kural 555 says the tears of the afflicted wear away a king's wealth.
teaches: Tears are a force against a king in both, but the epic turns them to a mercy that ends the fire while the Kural makes them a loss that grows.

gains.a: The scene gains a rule: the victor is shown ruled by the weeping, as the couplet says a king should dread.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where the tears act at once and quench, not only wear away over time.

note: 1483 lays a king on a bed of silk and gives him to the fire; Naladiyar 21 says kings under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and called dead.
teaches: The fire takes the proud king as the quatrain says it takes all, and the honour of his funeral does not alter that.

gains.a: The funeral gains the quatrain's lesson that rank is no shelter from death.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a named king whose cotton and silk bed does not save him.

note: 1485 shows the queens barring desire with the fence of chastity and the lock on the senses; Kural 57 calls a woman's own restraint the best guard.
teaches: The epic's widows guard themselves by their own restraint, which is the kind the Kural prefers to confinement.

gains.a: The widows' act gains a test: it is the self-made guard the couplet praises.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case at the point of greatest loss, after the husband's death, where outside guard has gone.

note: 1488 has the beaten Vidyadharas bow in fear; 1489 has the victor answer with mercy and a drum for the dead king's kin.
teaches: The fear of the defeated is answered with grace, which turns a conquest into a settlement.

note: 1493 has the father say he reached fatherhood through penance; Kural 70 says the son's help to the father is the question of what penance he did.
teaches: The father in the epic asks the question the couplet puts in others' mouths, so the son's worth is credited back to the father's penance.

gains.a: The father's remark gains a rule that a worthy son is the world's proof of his father's penance.
gains.b: The couplet gains a father who answers it himself, making the saying his own humble claim.

note: 1499 crowns the hero because the discus won the war; Kural 546 says victory comes from the sceptre that does not bend, not from the spear.
teaches: The epic gives the title to the winner of the weapon, which the Kural would call a lesser ground than justice.

gains.a: The crowning gains a stricter standard: is the discus a better ground than a straight sceptre?
gains.b: The couplet gains a king whose title rests on the weapon, which tests its claim that the spear gives no victory.

note: 1512 shows the hero lifting a gem mountain with both arms; 303 shows him as a youth rolling a rock heap that two hundred elephants might raise.
teaches: The boyhood feat of 303 is the first form of the strength that lifts Kotisilai, so the mountain is the proof of something already known.

note: 1517 shows the hero holding a mountain in one hand; 273 says even a man who could carry a diamond hill finds austerity and rule heavier.
teaches: The hero's lift is the lighter of the burdens that 273 weighs, and rule, not strength, is what he must still carry.

note: 1517 praises a mountain-lifter whom kings and gods hail; Tirumanthiram 350 tells of a lifter of the great mountain who was crushed by the Lord and then given grace.
teaches: The epic stops at homage to the lifter, while the Saiva verse asks what becomes of that strength before God.

gains.a: the epic scene lacks any verdict on mountain-lifting strength beyond the kings' homage, and gains a measure from the lifter who is crushed
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse lacks a lifter honoured and unpunished, and gains one whose feat is a king's proof, not an offence against a god

note: 1510 has the hero without swelling pride at the moment feats are listed; Kural 979 calls greatness the absence of pride.
teaches: The epic shows modesty arising from counting those who came before, a source the couplet does not name.

gains.a: the epic verse lacks a name for the hero's lack of pride, and gains the couplet's term for it as greatness
gains.b: the couplet lacks an occasion in which pride is tempted by lists of earlier deeds, and gains one

note: 1523 shows the pearl parasol bringing joy to the people and the sea-ringed world; Kural 389 says the world rests under the parasol of a king who bears bitter words.
teaches: The epic's parasol is the sign of conquest, while the couplet makes shelter depend on a king's patience with harsh speech.

gains.a: the epic verse lacks any condition on the parasol's shelter, and gains the couplet's test of hearing bitter words
gains.b: the couplet lacks a visible sign of sovereignty, and gains the pearl parasol of a triumphant king

note: 1508 counts a discus-lord's wealth in jewels, treasures, lands, cities and gatherings of kings; Kural 381 counts a king's parts as army, people, resources, ministers, allies and fort.
teaches: The epic's list is of things owned and has no ministers or fort, while the couplet's list names the organs a state cannot do without.

gains.a: the epic list lacks counsellors and defences, and gains the couplet's organs of a state
gains.b: the couplet lacks the epic's treasures and festive cities, and gains a picture of imperial wealth

audit_text_issue: 1508 line 4 hard to read | 1508 line 4 is obscure.

note: 1520 has the kings bow their crowns in fear as the hero holds the mountain; 1530 has kings hail him from their war-elephants as he enters the city.
teaches: The fear before the mountain becomes open praise in the city, so the feat is turned into public kingship.

note: 1541 darkens the streets with incense and gold; 1544 makes the sun give up and set.
teaches: The festival's smoke is first a lamp for the elephant's eyes, then the cause of the sun's flight: the poet builds one hyperbole across two verses.

note: 1547 announces the coronation at dawn; 1550 carries it out.
teaches: The announcement and the crowning make a promise and its keeping, so the festival is a prelude to the crowning, not merely its decoration.

note: 1381 has the Vidyadhara kings turn back from fated men; 1552 says no rival is left.
teaches: The Vidyadharas' flight from the battle is what leaves the prince without an enemy at the wedding; his joy is the victory's late fruit.

note: 1553 shows great treasure arriving and the king drowning in it; Kural 332 compares wealth's coming to a crowd gathering and its going to the crowd's scattering.
teaches: Read together, the epic shows only the gathering of the crowd, and the couplet supplies the scattering that the festival hides.

gains.a: The scene of arrival gains the knowledge that the sea of wealth is a crowd at a show that will break up.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king at the height of his fortune, not an anonymous owner, so the image is tested at its peak.

note: 1552 gives the prince's elation at fortune with no hint of its cause; Naladiyar 93 says wealth gathers when its time comes and leaves when the deeds that sent it run out.
teaches: The Naladiyar supplies a karmic account the epic withholds in these verses: his elation is for a fortune whose source and end are deeds, though the verse says no such thing.

gains.a: The prince's elation gains a limit that the poet does not state: the fortune is held by karma and not by his own act.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where wealth, wife and rule arrive together, so its claim is tested against a complete success.

note: 1556 shows the king settled under the moon-white umbrella; Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode under umbrellas have fallen when their deeds turned.
teaches: The poem sets Tivittan at the top of his glory, and the quatrain supplies the warning that such a place is held by deeds and can be lost.

gains.a: The opening praise gains a measure that the umbrella is no guarantee, so the lord's net of women reads as a risk.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king shown at his height with no fall yet in sight, which is the moment it speaks to.

note: 1559 shows a king with the homage of three realms taking pleasure like Kama; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones see the pain in pleasure and do not cling.
teaches: The poem offers pleasure at its largest scale, and the quatrain asks whether one who has all of it is looking at its pain.

gains.a: The scene gains a standard by which a lord in his harem is judged without the poet having to judge him.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an extreme case of the pleasure it warns about, with gods and kings standing guard over it.

note: 1561 has the chief queen resolve to see the plants wed; in 1564 the king smiles and accepts, and the grove outing follows.
teaches: The queen's wish becomes the king's plan only through the maid's message and his answer, so the outing is shared.

note: 1569 has the jester say his belly is full of many modakas; 1570 has him deny eating any.
teaches: His pain is only greed for a feast to come, so the first claim is turned into a joke by the second.

note: 1571 limits the king's gifts to Vedic brahmins; 1572 has the jester answer that debate-skill will win them.
teaches: The rule meant to bar the jester is met by a claim that skill in debate can stand in for Vedic learning.

note: 1571 has the king test a gift-seeker by Vedic learning; Kural 134 says a Brahmin can relearn the Veda but loses his birth if conduct fails.
teaches: The king's test is of learning, and the couplet's is of conduct, so the jester's comic case falls under both and passes neither.

gains.a: The king's rule gains a rival test, so the gift is shown to rest on a narrow ground.
gains.b: The couplet gains a brahmin who has neither Veda nor conduct and appears at the king's court.

note: 1572 has the jester boast of winning debates; 1573 gives his method, a stick for those who recite.
teaches: The boast gets its method, which shows that his debate is a comic beating, not an argument.
audit_text_issue: 1573 line 3 reading (தடியாலே) uncertain | 1573 line 3 தடியாலே reading is not certain.

note: 1573 has the jester win debate by beating reciters; Tirumanthiram 51 says the wise gave up disputation and recited the Veda to gain release.
teaches: The jester practises debate for a gift and the verse in the Tirumanthiram says the wise leave debate for recitation, so the farce is set against that view.

gains.a: The jester's boast gains a standard against which debating for a gift looks like a caricature of the learned.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's rejection of disputation gains a figure for whom argument has become a way to get food.

note: 1576 has the jester at the fallen fruit with his mouth watering; 1569 has him holding a belly full of modakas.
teaches: The same belly-led jester returns, now drooling instead of groaning, so greed is drawn as his trait and not one joke.

note: 1581 has the jester say the grove has no guard at all; 1582 has the king answer that many warriors keep the wall, so the two contradict each other on the same grove.
teaches: The dispute is settled only in 1583-1584, where the guards turn out to be the monkeys the jester then calls thieves, so the question of who guards is itself the joke.

note: 1591 has the jester ask why the asoka bears red shoots at its foot; 1592 has the king show that they are women's lac-stained footprints.
teaches: The jester's puzzlement is the setting for the king to show how the grove's flowering is linked to women's feet, which 1593 then turns on the king himself.

note: 1592 shows the asoka cured of longing by women's feet; 1593 has the jester say the king too blooms when the queen's foot touches his head.
teaches: The grove lesson becomes a jibe at the king, who is made the asoka's counterpart in his need of a woman's foot.

note: 1594 has the king strike the jester and the jester threaten to tell the queen; 1595 has the king take his hand and promise never to do it again.
teaches: The jester's threat of the queen's knowledge is enough to make the king, lord of the world, give way, which shows who rules in the household.

note: 1597 has the jester claim that a man-eating spirit lives in the stone; 1600 has him see that his own shadow imitates his acts, and he is calmed.
teaches: The claim in 1597 is made through the scene itself, not by argument, and the later verse answers it by showing the fear to have no source outside him.
audit_text_issue: 1597 sense uncertain; 'stone' not in the verse

note: 1600 has the jester shown his own acts in his shadow, which does what he does; Kural 208 compares the ruin that follows evil deeds to a shadow that stays at the foot.
teaches: The shadow that is a comic false spirit here is the same thing the Kural uses as a sign that a person's deeds follow them, so the pairing shows the image in two uses.

gains.a: The scene gains a moral dimension: the shadow that copies the jester is the image the Kural uses for a deed's consequence, and the king's order to see his acts in it points that way.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which the shadow is an object of comic fear, which shows how readily people fear what is only their own doing.

note: 1597 has the jester fear a spirit that is not there; Kural 428 says the knowing fear what should be feared while the fool does not fear it.
teaches: The couplet names the fool who feels no fear where it is due, and the scene shows the other fault, a fear aimed at something unreal.

gains.a: The jester's panic gains a name: a failure to judge what is truly to be feared, not simple cowardice.
gains.b: The couplet gains a counterpart it does not state, in which fear is misplaced on an empty object.

note: 1601 has the king say they will sit and wait for the queen; 1602 has her enter the grove with her maidens.
teaches: The waiting on the stone is a brief pause that gives the jester's fright its place before the queen enters.

note: 1561 has the queen resolve to see the parijata and the Kama creeper wed; 1621 sets the tree as bridegroom and starts the rites.
teaches: The queen's wish is carried out only after a quarrel and its mending, so the wedding is the end of an unplanned scene.

note: In 1609 Madhavan slips away from the angry queen; in 1613 her people trace him into the grove and bring him back by his cloth.
teaches: The jester's flight is undone by the queen's command, which shows who in the household has power over the king's companion.

note: 1576 has the jester's mouth water at the fruit and him call the king to eat; 1618-1620 turn that greed into songs on the fruits of the grove.
teaches: The jester's appetite from the arrival in the grove is now his act for the couple, so his greed is what pays for his pardon.

note: 1556 says the king who has set the world under his umbrella is caught in a net of deer-eyed women; 1624 shows the net at work, with arrows from the women's brows.
teaches: The poem's opening image of the netted king becomes a scene in which the quarrel's cause returns at once.

note: 1608 has the queen burn with anger at the king's praise of a stranger's footprint; Kural 1313 has a woman angry at a wreath she says was worn for another woman.
teaches: The epic gives the wife a real occasion where the couplet's wife sulks on a pretext, and shows the husband pleading as the couplet's man does.

gains.a: The queen's anger gains a measure: the Kural treats the jealousy of love as sulking even when nothing was done, and here something was.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where the husband did give cause by speaking of another woman, so its jest has a dark side.

note: 1616 has the king end the quarrel by embrace and plea; Kural 1304 says that not reconciling those who sulk is like cutting a withered creeper at its root.
teaches: The king's embrace shows what the couplet's warning needs: the sulk is healed by the one who gave cause, and the quarrel comes to an end in a wedding scene.

gains.a: The scene gains a rule behind the king's acts: the Kural says a sulk left unreconciled kills love, so his bow and embrace are what love needs.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king with a crown at his wife's feet, a case where reconciling costs a ruler his dignity.

note: 1614 has the queen, once the king has bowed, smile and turn her anger into a game on the jester; Naladiyar 384 praises the wife who knows when to sulk and relents sweetly.
teaches: The queen relents by moving her anger on to the jester in garlands, which the quatrain's wife does not do.

gains.a: The queen's smile gains a standard: a wife is praised who sulks at the right time and gives way sweetly, and she does so at once.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a wife who is also a queen, whose sulk is ended in a public game that costs a third person.

note: 1611 has the queen turn to leave and the king bow with his crown at her feet; Kural 1302 says sulking is like salt in right measure and a little more ruins it.
teaches: The king's bow comes before the sulk can become too much, so the scene shows the couplet's measure kept.

gains.a: The quarrel gains a gauge: the Kural's salt means the queen's anger is a proper amount of love's seasoning, which the king answers at once.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler for whom the cost of ending the sulk is a bowed crown, making the measure a matter of rank.

note: 1561 has the chief queen resolve to see the parijata wed to the Kama creeper; 1628 has the queens dress the bride and join her to the tree.
teaches: The queen's wish ends in a ritual the women perform themselves, so the festival is theirs and the king only attends.

note: 1628 calls the wealth of sweet-smiling sons sweet to all; Kural 63 says people call children their wealth because their wealth comes through their own deeds.
teaches: The poem's child is a tree that has no deeds, so its sweetness comes wholly from rearing, which tests whether the couplet's reason is the only one.

gains.a: The wedding gains a reason for the parents' joy that lies in the child's own deeds, which the plant cannot supply, so only the rearing is left to explain it.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which the child is a plant and cannot earn anything, so the joy it names is shown to rest at least partly on the care given.

note: 1629 says the lord hides by a stratagem; 1630 shows the stratagem, an art that makes darkness a curtain, with Madhavan beside him.
teaches: The hiding is done by a magic art and with a companion, so the king does not slip away but joins the women's game unseen.

note: 1630 has the king hidden among the women; 1631 has the chief queen guess it and send more women out to play like children.
teaches: The queen answers the hiding by staging the game she thinks he wants to watch, so the women's play is her reply and not only their sport.

note: 1632 builds the women's beauty out of gold, leaves and sprouts to delight the king's eyes; Naladiyar 46 asks which part of the fresh-garlanded woman is she, among entrails, fat, blood and bone.
teaches: The poem makes the body a thing of ornament and the quatrain takes it apart into its parts, so the two disagree on whether the adorned body is a person to be praised.

gains.a: The adorned women gain a test of what is being praised once the leaves, gold and sprouts are taken off.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a body shown at its most dressed and admired, so its question has an object that actually looks like a woman.

note: 1637 has the women paint the king and themselves sulking at him; Kural 1329 has the man wish the woman would go on sulking so that he may go on pleading.
teaches: The women fix the sulk in paint, where no pleading can follow, so the picture keeps the lovers' quarrel without its making-up.

gains.a: The portrait gains the reading that a sulk is something the lover wants, which explains why the women paint it for him.
gains.b: The couplet gains a sulk that is drawn, not spoken, which separates the delight of being sulked at from the pleading that follows.

note: 1642 has the women say a garland bent their slender waists; Kural 1115 has the man say a woman who wore anicham flowers with their stems has a waist too weak for good drums to sound.
teaches: What the couplet gives as a lover's praise of a woman's delicacy the poem gives to the women as their own complaint, so the delicacy becomes something they offer to be noticed.

gains.a: The women's complaints gain a source in the convention of praising a woman's frailty, so they speak in the lover's idiom.
gains.b: The couplet gains women who claim the praised frailty themselves, so the frailty is shown as performance as well as praise.

note: 1627 crowns the groves as kings and hangs jewels on every branch; 1643 says the women conquer the flower-grove with their waists, glances and limbs.
teaches: The grove made a king in 1627 is taken by the women, so the same grove is first a court and then a thing conquered.

note: 1647 has the guards search the caves and thickets and then watch every side; 1630 has the king already hidden among the women by art.
teaches: The guard stands around a king who is already inside the place it guards, so the watch protects the game and not the king.

note: 1646 sets the artificial hill with gem waterfalls as the place the women reach; 1650 makes the same hill answer them and mock them.
teaches: The hill that was scenery becomes a speaker, so the grove ends the run by playing back at the women.

note: 1649 has the women's girdles and anklets answered by the hill; 1650 has the hill take their lisping and answer it as mockery.
teaches: The echo of metal in 1649 grows into an echo of speech in 1650, which turns the sound from answer into jest.

note: 1663 has the king order a god to become an elephant; 1664 shows the god taking the shape and nearing the women.
teaches: The king's order is carried out at once, so the fear in the grove is the king's own design and not an accident.

note: 1666 has the king soothe the frightened woman; 1667 shows him driving off the elephant and adorning her.
teaches: The rescuer is the one who sent the danger, and the comfort completes his ruse.

note: 1635 has the women sing the king's fame; 1659 begins a pounding song whose next verses list his deeds.
teaches: The fame the women only named earlier is now given its content, war and love together, in the song.

note: 1669 sends the king to the pool to see the women bathe; 1674 has the bathing turn into a water-fight with him.
teaches: The watcher he meant to be becomes a target, so the pleasure goes from looking to joining.

note: 1666 ends by saying the king did a great penance that gives him whatever he wishes; Kural 265 gives wish-fulfilment as the reason penance is practised.
teaches: The wish that penance buys here is a prank to win an embrace, which tests whether the Kural's reason for tapas needs any worthy wish.

gains.a: 1666 gets a stated rule behind its claim, that penance pays in whatever is wanted, so the king's power reads as a fruit of tapas.
gains.b: Kural 265 gets a case where the wish bought is a trivial love-ruse, so its 'whatever is wished' is shown to cover small and worldly wishes.

note: 1663 names the rutting elephant with a spread face-cloth; Kural 1087 likens the cloth on a woman's breast to the face-cloth over a rutting elephant's eyes.
teaches: The same elephant's face-cloth marks erotic danger in a couplet and is used as a stage prop to scare women into a man's arms in the epic.

gains.a: 1663 gets the face-cloth read as the sign of a threat that is also desire, so the elephant's fright is a love-device.
gains.b: Kural 1087 gets a scene where such an elephant is actually set before women, showing the image as a danger they flee, not only as a metaphor.

note: 1675 opens the women's spray-war against the king; 1678 has the queens cry that they have beaten him and the pool run dry.
teaches: The water-play is told as a war from first volley to cry of victory, so the king's surrender is the planned end of the game.

note: 1694 has the Vidyadhara drop from the sky and bow; 1697 has the king make him tell the message in his own words.
teaches: The envoy's arrival is the start of an exchange which waits on the king's leave, shown in the order of events rather than said.

note: 1696 has the king give away all but his crown on seeing the letter; 1698 begins the message, which is a suitor's request for a bride.
teaches: The king pays for news before he knows what it asks, so the reward is for coming and not for what is said.

note: 1680 has the king and his wives clinging to a float in the pond; Akananuru 266 has the husband bathing with young women on a float, whose gossip the wife throws back at him.
teaches: The same float-play is a king's marital pleasure in the epic and a husband's scandal in the akam poem, so what makes it fair or shameful is who the partners are.

gains.a: The pond scene gains a measure of the play as a thing that, with other women, would be a wrong, which the epic never states.
gains.b: The wife's reproach gains a version of the same play with no reproach in it, showing that her anger is aimed at the partners and not the bath.

note: 1697 has the envoy take the letter, wait for the king's order and then bow and speak; Kural 687 says the best envoy knows the protocol, the moment and the place.
teaches: The epic shows an envoy in the sequence of bows, seating, gifts and leave to speak that the couplet names but does not show.

gains.a: The scene gains a standard by which the envoy's waiting and bowing read as skill and not only as courtesy.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete order of events in which an envoy shows he knows protocol and time.

note: 1707 leaves the queen trembling and whispering, and 1708 has the king answer by reading her vision as the coming of a son.
teaches: The poem passes the fright of the omen to the king's reading of it, so the vision becomes a promise before the child is born.

note: 1706 shows the moon entering the queen's mouth in union, and 1712 gives the birth of the radiant son the vision announced.
teaches: The moon's entry in the bed finds its fulfilment in the birth, so a reader sees the poem treat the dream as a true prediction.

note: 1713 lets the drums sound for the birth, and Naladiyar 23 says drums that sound for a wedding can sound the same day for the bridegroom's funeral.
teaches: The rejoicing of the birth is set beside the quatrain's warning that the same drum serves joy and death, so the festival is read against impermanence.

gains.a: The drumming for the royal birth gains a darker echo, that what is loud with joy is a loan, which the poem does not say here.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a scene of joy at its height, a king's son born to a palace city, in which its warning has the most to undo.

note: 1706 shows pleasure on the bed as the cause of the longed-for son, while Naladiyar 54 says the wise see pleasure's pain and keep away from household life.
teaches: The poem lets the pleasure that Naladiyar condemns bear fruit in an auspicious child, so the householder's pleasure is not shown as barren.

gains.a: The union gains a measure by which its fruit, a son, is the gain that a renunciant verse never counts.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the pleasure ends in a birth greeted by all, which tests how far its warning holds.

note: 1720 has brahmins, kings and elders praise those who bore the child, and Kural 70 says a son's worth lies in making others ask what penance his father did.
teaches: The epic voices the praise at the newborn stage, before any deed, while the couplet says the praise belongs to the father only after the son has proved himself.

gains.a: The praise of the parents gains the couplet's reason: it is the son's worth that earns the parents' credit, here advanced to birth.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene where the praise is spoken aloud in an assembly of every order, and for a child whose worth is only promised.

note: 1722 gives the newborn the name Vijayan, and 71 earlier tells of the birth of the elder Vijayan at the start of the story.
teaches: The name Vijayan returns in the next generation, so a reader must keep the uncle and the son apart while seeing the name tied to fortune and victory.

note: 1706 has the moon enter the queen's mouth as the sign of Tivittan's son; 1730 has a gem come to the Vidyadhara wife in a dream and swell her breasts.
teaches: The poem uses the same dream of a bright thing entering the mother for two houses, so the Vidyadhara child's birth is told as a parallel of Tivittan's own.

note: 1712 shows Tivittan's son born in saffron-bright radiance; 1732 shows the Vidyadhara boy born with a face to shame the moon.
teaches: The two births are drawn with one image, the lit young body, which lets the later chapters set the two boys side by side as equals.

note: 1735 names the boy Amitatejas for his boundless might; 1791 has the prince Amitatejas enter the swayamvara hall so bright that other kings are dimmed.
teaches: The name given at birth is made good at the swayamvara, so the boy's later outshining of kings is shown as the sign promised at his birth.

note: 1721 has Tivittan show jewels and gold to his guests and invite them to take them; 1737 has him give a share of his treasure to the Vidyadhara messenger.
teaches: The giving at the son's birth and at the nephew's news both follow the same open-handedness, so Tivittan is drawn as a king whose joy is shown by giving.

note: 1743 has Tivittan give his five-year-old son to teachers 'rich in unfailing learning'; Kural 67 says a father's good to his son is to put him first in the assembly.
teaches: The Kural names the goal of a father's care, the seat in the assembly; the epic shows the first step toward it, early schooling in the hands of learned men.

gains.a: The prince's schooling gains a stated purpose, that the father's good lies in the son's standing among the learned, not his wealth.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete first step, a royal father handing a child of five to teachers, which the couplet does not name.

note: 1743 calls the teachers 'rich in unfailing learning' (பொய்யாக் கல்விச் செல்வர்); Kural 400 says learning is the one wealth that does not perish.
teaches: The epic uses the language of wealth for learning, which Kural 400 claims for it alone, but gives it to men who serve a king whose other wealth is shown at length.

gains.a: The teachers gain the Kural's ground for the title 'rich', that their wealth is the one that does not fail.
gains.b: The couplet gains a court where learning and the other wealth stand together, a test of whether learning is the only wealth.

note: 1745 has the father sink in a sea of joy at the naming and the gathering of kin; Kural 69 says a mother is gladder to hear her son called worthy than at his birth.
teaches: The epic's joy comes at the naming and the kin's praise, while the Kural puts the greater joy later, in the son's worth, so the verse's delight is the first joy, not the last.

gains.a: The father's delight gains a measure, that it is the joy of the birth and the Kural counts a greater one still to come.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene of a father's joy at the naming, a joy of the birth that it sets as the lower mark.

note: 1738 has the child grow in the guard of women who tend him; Naladiyar 20 says Death takes even the newborn while the mother wails.
teaches: The poem's guarded growth is the thing the quatrain says cannot be guaranteed, so the child's safety is read against death's stealth.

gains.a: The guarded child gains the quatrain's reminder that guard does not keep death off, which the poem does not say.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a child as well cared for as can be, the strongest case for its warning.

note: 1730 gives the dream of a gem as the sign that the child is coming; Tirumanthiram 453 says the Lord, at the moment of the joining, fixes the span and the earthly life of the child.
teaches: The epic reads the conception from omens and the mother's body, while the Tirumanthiram says the life was fixed by the Lord at the joining, so a sign is read against a cause.

gains.a: The gem-dream gains a view in which the child's fate is already fixed, before the sign comes.
gains.b: The verse of Tirumular gains a conception told as a royal dream, a case where signs are read as promises.

note: 1746 closes with the girl whose name is that of lightning growing up; 1750 shows the young women's ball-play at the swayamvara chapter's start.
teaches: The girl born here grows into the maiden of the later chapters, so the birth is the root of the swayamvara story.

note: 1752 likens the returning balls to lovers who will not be held off; Thiruppugazh 586 asks Murugan not to let the poet waste away over women whose palms ache from ball-play.
teaches: One text enjoys ball-play as courtship, and the other treats the same game as the snare from which a devotee asks to be freed.

gains.a: The epic's lively ball-play gains the devotee's view that this very beauty is what he must be saved from.
gains.b: The Thiruppugazh's brief mention of ball-playing women gains a full scene of what the game is, with its clinging balls and flying powder.

note: 1538 has attendants tie the bride's fine cloth and gem girdle for the wedding; 1753 has her daughter tie the same silk and gem girdle for ball-play.
teaches: The girl's self-dressing repeats her mother's bridal dressing and shows the game as a step toward marriage.

note: 1757 has the parents call the tired daughter from behind the curtain; 1758 shows her letting the ball go and reaching her father's feet.
teaches: The call becomes obedience: the daughter breaks off her play at once, which is how a swayamvara's choice is later left to the father's council.

note: 1759 has the father hold his sweat-brow daughter after ball-play; Akananuru 17 recalls a girl too tired for a ball game who lay in her mother's arms.
teaches: The tired child resting in a parent's arms is the last scene before she leaves for a husband, by public choice in the epic and by flight in the akam poem.

gains.a: The epic's scene of the father holding his daughter gains the foreboding of loss that the akam poem builds from the same picture.
gains.b: The foster mother's memory gains a case where the father arranges the girl's marriage openly, which the elopement she mourns has bypassed.

note: 1760 shows the father seeing his daughter's ripening body; 1762 follows with a council that sets the swayamvara.
teaches: Her ripeness is the unspoken cause of the proclamation: the poem lets the father's look become public policy.

note: 1762 has the king command the drum after council; 1763 has the drum struck.
teaches: The order given in the council is carried out at once in public sound.

note: 1763 beats a drum to announce a wedding; Naladiyar 23 says the drums that sounded for a wedding may sound the same day as funeral drums.
teaches: The same drum that proclaims joy is, for the Naladiyar, the sign of how quickly joy passes into death.

gains.a: The epic's wedding drum gains a shadow: the sound that calls the kings is the sound a worldly man should fear.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the wedding drum is proclaimed with royal pomp for a bride not yet chosen.

note: 1764's herald prays for the king's life, virtue and cool rain and harvest; Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather where the ruler wields his sceptre justly.
teaches: The herald's prayer asks for the rain and crops that the Kural says come as a fruit of just rule, so the blessing doubles as a claim on the king.

gains.a: The herald's list of blessings gains a rule: rain and crops are the sign that the king's sceptre is just.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ceremony in which this wish is spoken aloud as the king's reign is made public.

note: 1766 has the drum summon the world's kings to a marriage open to all; Naladiyar 86 praises a wife married with drums beaten for many to know.
teaches: A marriage announced to all is a mark of honour in the Naladiyar, and the swayamvara pushes the same openness to where the bride is chosen before the world.

gains.a: The proclamation gains a measure: public marriage is thought to guard the bond from later claims.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the drum summons rival suitors as well as witnesses.

note: 1766 has the drum fix the day and call the kings; 1768 shows kings and others arriving round the city.
teaches: The proclamation is answered by the arrival, and the crowd outruns the invited kings.

note: 1782 has the builders finish the hall and the musicians play; 1783 has the herald call the kings in at the auspicious hour.
teaches: The hall is finished before the hour is announced, so the festival's order moves from building to music to the kings' entry.

note: 1783 has the herald call the kings in and the drums sound; 1784 has the first king, of Ayodhya, enter.
teaches: The call is answered at once by named kings entering one after another, so the roll-call of kings is the proclamation's result.

note: 1791 has the prince outshine the other kings; 1792 has the young women's eyes leave the kings for him.
teaches: The brightness the poet claims for the prince is proved by where the onlookers look, not by the poet's word alone.

note: 1792 has the women's eyes already settle on the prince; 1793 has the king then call the maiden to come in.
teaches: The assembly's gaze is decided before the maiden is called, so her choice enters a room that has already leaned.

note: 1783 has conches and a great drum sound the hour of the kings' entry; Naladiyar 23 says the drums of a wedding hall can be the funeral drums of that very day.
teaches: The same drums that open a wedding hold the thought that joy and loss come under one roof.

gains.a: The festival scene gains the quatrain's warning that its drums do not guarantee the happy end it announces.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a hall with real drums and a gathering, set before the bride has chosen.

note: 1790 has kings of five great lines wait with elephants and hosts for the choosing; Naladiyar 21 says kings who rode elephants under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and called dead.
teaches: The kings' show of force at the choosing is the same show that the quatrain says does not save a king.

gains.a: The roll of kings gains a measure by which their armies and elephants seem brief.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the sight of kings gathered in full strength and ready to be seen, at the moment the strength is displayed.

note: 1792 has young women's eyes fall on a handsome prince; Naladiyar 102 says beauty, youth, wealth and awe do not last.
teaches: The pull of the prince's looks is shown at full strength by the very verse that the quatrain would call short-lived.

gains.a: The moment of beauty's pull gains the quatrain's reminder that what draws the eye is passing.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case in which beauty actually moves a whole assembly, so its claim is set against real force.

note: 1797 sets her procession to the sounds of praise and music from all quarters; Naladiyar 23 shows wedding drums in a hall turning to funeral drums for the groom.
teaches: The poem fills the bridal march with music and hope, and the quatrain says the same drums can announce the end of the groom.

gains.a: The procession gains the shadow that its music may not last, which the poem leaves out here.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a wedding at its brightest, before any reversal, which is the moment it warns against trusting.

note: 1798 shows kings' desire swelling as she enters; Naladiyar 17 tells the man not to desire a spear-eyed girl, who will stoop on a staff.
teaches: The poem lets the reader see her with the kings' eyes, and the quatrain supplies what those eyes will not see.

gains.a: The kings' longing gains a limit set by age, which the verse does not state.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a young woman actually seen, so its warning is tested against an entrance that wins every eye.

audit_text_issue: 1798 line 1 'சராவி' uncertain | 1798 line 1 சராவி is a rare or damaged word.

note: 1804 sets this king's glory 'after Bharata'; 397 says the First Lord's grace made a king of the earth Bharata.
teaches: The herald's yardstick, Bharata, is the ruler the earlier verse shows as the First Lord's gift, so the king's glory is measured against a grace-given one.

note: 1809 gives the harp-playing boon-winner of the northern mountain; 543 has Dharanan come at Nami's song, which is how the boon was won.
teaches: What the herald says in two lines is the story told at length at 538-547, so the hall's praise draws on the book's own earlier telling.

note: 1810 praises a king for the line that bred him; Naladiyar 195 says a lineage is made by austerity, learning and effort, not by name.
teaches: The herald's whole mode of praise is descent, and the quatrain offers another test for the same kings, what each has done.
