gains.a: The suitor's praise gains a test the herald does not apply, effort and learning in the man himself.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a hall of kings praised for birth, which shows how common the claim it denies was.

note: 1815 says women who reached this king's chest had done austerity; Naladiyar 31 says present comfort comes from earlier austerity and is lost without more.
teaches: The herald's line puts a marriage on the same ledger of past austerity that the quatrain keeps, and the quatrain adds that it runs out.

gains.a: The praise gains a warning that earlier austerity wears down, which the herald omits.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a new case, a bride's good fortune, where its past austerity pays out in a marriage rather than a house.

note: 1814 puts a moon-line king under a tall umbrella with cloud-like elephants; Purananuru 3 puts the Pandya under a white umbrella like the full moon.
teaches: The poem makes the moon-line king's umbrella the sign of his kind, as the Sangam poem does for the Pandya, so the herald's king reads as the Pandya of that tradition.

gains.a: The verse gains a Sangam picture that fills in the umbrella and moon that it names only in passing.
gains.b: The Sangam poem gains a late epic that keeps its image but brings it to a marriage hall, not a battlefield.

note: 1816 places a king at Urandai among swans, drums and banners; Akananuru 385 uses Uranthai as the standard of a house rich in festival.
teaches: Urandai is the name of wealth in both books, so the herald's list of its splendours carries a meaning already known from the Sangam poem.

gains.a: The epic city gains an earlier use of its name as a measure of richness.
gains.b: The Akam poem gains a king's side of the city, whose wealth it uses only as a comparison.

note: 1824 says the herald's showing was needless because her lot of enjoyment had already ripened; Kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate, which reaches first even when one tries another way.
teaches: A choice that looks free and quick is shown to have been set before the guide's words, which a bare general rule about fate does not show.

gains.a: The verse gains a general rule that fate comes before any human device, which would otherwise be only an aside about her lot.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene in which a formal, careful introduction is overtaken by fate in a glance.

note: 1827 has kings with every means to win her calm themselves because deeds ripen as they will; Kural 377 says even those who have gathered millions enjoy only what the apportioner has apportioned.
teaches: Fate's apportioning is shown over a bride and not over wealth, among men whose rank and army were equal, so the rule is tested where effort was all in place.

gains.a: The kings' calm gains a stated general law behind it, which the verse leaves as their passing thought.
gains.b: The couplet gains a contest in which every competitor had equal means, the case where apportioning alone must decide.

note: 1827 shows kings who lose the bride calming themselves by seeing the loss as karma; Naladiyar 33 contrasts the fool who sighs hotly at the fruit of deeds with the wise who call it old desert.
teaches: The same step from sighing to calm is shown as a group's act on a public loss, where the quatrain gives only the principle.

gains.a: The kings' calm gains a named opposite, the fool who sighs and breaks, which the scene alone does not give.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case of powerful men who choose the wise answer after having sweated and sighed, as 1826 shows.

note: 1839 states for everyone the thought that 1827 reports of the rejected kings: the fruit of deeds is what comes.
teaches: The kings' private resignation is the lesson the poet then gives to all readers, so the swayamvara scene is built to carry it.

note: 1839 bids all remember the fruit of deeds; 1842 shows Payapati reasoning that the pleasure of his grandchildren is the fruit of swollen merit with more seed to sow.
teaches: The poet's general advice becomes a king's own reasoning, which turns the closing moral of one sarukkam into the opening act of the next.

note: 1839 says wealth and heavenly pleasure are the fruit of deeds and bids remembering; Tirumanthiram 267 says joy and sorrow were fixed by earlier acts and that fools who see joy yet do not give know no virtue.
teaches: The poem asks only for remembering the fruit and keeping to the way; the couplet names what that way includes, giving, and what its absence shows.

gains.a: The poet's advice to keep to the way gains one concrete act, giving, as the proof that the fruit has been understood.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a story of fruit at its fullest, a royal wedding and gods' pleasure, set against which its warning to the unmoved has its force.

note: 1842 says more seed must be sown for the austerity that bore present pleasure; 1851 shows those who instead cut the root and die.
teaches: The warning of 1851 is the unsown field that 1842 fears, so the king's wish to sow is shown as the way out of that ruin.

note: 1843 reads the kingship and the bowing kings as the gift of the good-deed deity; Naladiyar 3 says kings on elephants under umbrellas fall when deeds turn.
teaches: Read together, the umbrellas that 1843 credits to past merit are the same ones Naladiyar says a turn of deeds can remove.

gains.a: The grant of kingship gains an explicit reversal: what a good deed gave, a turn of deeds can take back.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an account of why the king rose, through the good-deed god, which it assumes without saying.

note: 1844 calls those who destroy the root of good deeds base; 1851 shows them leaving the root that feeds them sweetly.
teaches: The root of good deeds is a recurring image whose repetition shows the king returning to the same fear from two sides.

note: 1847 concludes that nothing is better than austerity; Kural 46 asks what is gained by going the outside way if household life is lived in virtue.
teaches: The pair turns on whether household virtue is enough: the king answers from the certainty of death, the couplet from the sufficiency of aram.

gains.a: The king's resolve gains the opposing case that a householder who keeps aram may need no leaving.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler for whom death makes household virtue seem insufficient.

note: 1849 shows the adorned body undone by one small prick; Naladiyar 41 says a bit of skin torn off needs a stick to drive away crows.
teaches: Both break the body's finery with a trivial injury, but the epic does it for a king examining his own display, the quatrain to answer a lover's praise.

gains.a: The king's reflection gains the quatrain's crows, which the injury will draw.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a body decked with garland, paste and incense that the injury undoes.

note: 1850 has crows and kites guarded off with a hand stick; Naladiyar 41 has the stick that drives the crows from the torn body.
teaches: The same stick appears for two different speakers, a king guarding himself and a poet mocking the lover, which shows how fixed the picture was.

gains.a: The verse gains a second use of the stick and the crow, as a rebuke of those who call the body lovely.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king speaking of his own body in the same terms.

note: 1850 turns on the body's filth to set aside kingly pride; Thiruppugazh 146 describes the same filth as a house of diseases and asks Murugan for grace.
teaches: The Jain king ends his disgust in a plan to leave and seek sages, while the Thiruppugazh ends the same disgust in a plea for a god's feet.

gains.a: The verse gains a different exit from the body's foulness, a god's grace in place of the sage's feet.
gains.b: The poem gains a king who draws the opposite practical conclusion from the same catalogue.

note: 1856 tests whether any statecraft can escape Death; Naladiyar 6 says none here has leapt clear and bids the wealthy give.
teaches: The king tries the four expedients the quatrain never names, and by their failure the quatrain's rule is shown by a ruler's own attempt.

gains.a: The question gains the rule that no one leapt clear, so the ministers' failure is not their own.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a ruler who actually tries every device of power to escape.

note: 1859 shortens the term to a blink before Death; Kural 334 calls the day a blade that saws the life.
teaches: The epic shortens the quantity: the couplet measures life as days, the verse measures it by the blink the minister names.

gains.a: The blink gains the blade as an image for time's cutting.
gains.b: The couplet gains a minister who counts the cut in a blink.

note: 1860 asks for a refuge beyond Death; 1862 answers that none exists but the austere sage's feet.
teaches: The question and the answer divide the council's work: the king asks, the minister names the sage's feet.

note: 1862 names the austere sage's feet as the only refuge from Death; Tirumanthiram 2 praises Siva who kicked Death and became king of the south.
teaches: The two refuges differ in kind: a teacher's feet to be reached by one's own austerity, against a god who defeated Death himself.

gains.a: The sage's feet gain a rival refuge in a god who has already defeated Death.
gains.b: The invocation gains a Jain-framed answer that makes the sage, not Siva, the shelter.

note: 1864 gives the order to sound the drum for the festival; 1868 shows the drum sounded and the whole city rising in joy.
teaches: The order and its carrying out show a king's single word turning a whole city to festival, so his authority is shown at its greatest before the sarukkam's later turning away.

note: 1867 promises the festival-goers a celestial form; 1882 shows the procession wearing their deeds away.
teaches: The promised heaven of 1867 is fed by the dying of deeds in 1882, so the festival works as a means of release in the ledger of karma, not a mere celebration.

note: 1869's people hear the drum as the sign of a long life and a blessing; Naladiyar 23's wedding drums turn to funeral drums the same day.
teaches: The same drum is a promise of long life in the epic's crowd and a warning of death in the quatrain, and the pair shows how a listener's state decides what it announces.

gains.a: The citizens' blessing gains a shadow of death that they do not see but the king, who has just asked whether anything beats Death, does.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case in which the drum's joy is not reversed into mourning but turned to a king's resolve to leave.

note: 1870 piles up festoons, banners, drums and conches that drown the sea; Kural 34 calls virtue the mind's spotlessness and the rest a noise (ஆகுலம்).
teaches: The epic lingers on the din of worship while the couplet measures a rite by the mind within, so the pair asks whether the festival is aram or only clamour.

gains.a: The festival's din gains a standard the poet does not apply in this passage: the mind of the worshipper.
gains.b: The couplet gains a full, glittering example of outward worship against which its charge of mere noise can be tried.

note: 1866 makes the Lord the foe of deluding deeds and rewards the festival's onlooker with the world of merit; Kural 5 says both kinds of deed do not cling to those who praise the Lord.
teaches: The epic ends in merit's world, a reward the couplet's two-fold deeds would also refuse to cling to, so the pair shows two ways of reading what freedom from deeds amounts to.

gains.a: The promise of a world of merit gains the couplet's reminder that good deeds too are bonds to be shed.
gains.b: The couplet gains a public act, the royal festival, through which a community pays the Lord's praise.

note: 1880 sets the king under his umbrella with fly-whisks at the head of his army; Naladiyar 3 says those who rode in such state fall when deeds turn.
teaches: The quatrain's fall of the umbrella-borne is forced by deeds, while the epic king's glittering display is the height from which he will walk away by choice.

gains.a: The parade gains the quatrain's warning that its splendour is borrowed from deeds that can turn.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king whose descent is not a loss to enemies but a renunciation he has already chosen.

note: 1886 has offered flowers falling in a rain at the king's approach; 1897 has a divine rain of flowers burying the golden ground at the Lord's appearance.
teaches: The same flower rain is first the king's offering and then the heavens' answer, so the worship and its reception share one image.

note: 1902 has the crowned king bow until the gem-crown touches the earth; Kural 9 says a head that does not bow at the feet of the eight-quality one is a useless organ.
teaches: The couplet's useless head becomes the crowned one of a king who sets power on the ground, which shows what the bow costs a ruler.

gains.a: The king's bow gains a stated reason, that a head which will not bow is as dead as a sense that does not sense.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler whose head carries a crown, so the bow costs a pride the couplet's speaker does not mention.

note: 1903 asks whether the Lord's red feet are reddened by lotus petals or by their own rays; 181 has the king praising the red lotus feet of him who conquered the dust of deeds.
teaches: The red feet appear in both shrine hymns, first as a fact and then as a riddle of cause, so the later hymn plays on the earlier plain praise.

note: 1904 says the Lord cut off the dark garlands of fierce deeds; Kural 5 says the two deeds born of darkness do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's true praise.
teaches: The Lord is shown in 1904 as the one who has already done what the couplet promises his devotees, so the cause of their freedom is his own freeing.

gains.a: The hymn gains a stated result for the praiser, that the two kinds of deeds will not cling to him.
gains.b: The couplet gains a named doer who has cut his own deeds, which it leaves unsaid.

note: 1904 says those who do not grasp the Lord's greatness quarrel and are bound by a quarrel of deeds; 182 says that even when called the knower of all the Lord is hard to truly know.
teaches: The earlier verse says why the Lord is hard to know and the later says what follows from not knowing him, which is the quarrel that binds.

note: 1906 says there is no other god to count, and the Lord is easy for those who worship his feet; Kural 7 says only those who reach the feet of the one without a peer can remove the mind's anxiety.
teaches: The hymn names its peerless one by what he does to living things, while the couplet leaves the feet unnamed and so open to any tradition.

gains.a: The hymn gains the couplet's claim that the anxieties of the mind are removed only by those feet.
gains.b: The couplet gains a candidate for the one without a peer, whose peerlessness is given as harmlessness and ease of access.

note: 1906 says no one but the Lord, who harms no life, can be counted as god; Tirumanthiram 1451 says there is one God in all ten directions and bids us take refuge in his feet to dry up the sea of deeds.
teaches: Both hold one God whose feet end the deeds, but they name different ones, and the pair turns on whether the one at whose feet deeds are shed is a Jina who gave up his own, or a God who gives grace.

gains.a: The hymn gains a rival that makes the same demand, to take refuge at one pair of feet, but on the strength of a different god.
gains.b: The verse gains a Jain claim that the Lord who deserves such refuge is the Jina, who has no part in creating or ruling.

note: The ministers of 1916 ask the sage to turn aside the tangled births; 1920 lists what he will teach in answer.
teaches: The sage's list of topics shows that the answer to a plea for escape from births is first a map of the births themselves.

note: 1921 says four states turn the souls; 1922 names them as hell, beast, man and god.
teaches: The four are named at once, so the turning wheel is shown to carry a soul as easily into hell as into heaven.

note: 1844 says those who cut the root of good deeds will be kings in the hells; 1923 counts the layers and dwellings of those hells.
teaches: The hells of the earlier threat are shown to be a ranked place with room for every kind of fallen king.

note: 1923 counts the lower hells in all; 1926 narrows to the first and its thirteen levels and thirty lakh pits.
teaches: The sage's numbers are first given as a whole and then broken down hell by hell.

note: 1910 praises the Lord as one who has struck down fierce deeds and lit the lamp of knowledge; 2 hails him as light of the world who split fierce deeds.
teaches: The king's praise repeats the poet's opening praise, so the king's worship matches the epic's own account of the god.

note: 1921 turns the soul like a cart wheel through four states; Naladiyar 2 turns wealth like a cart wheel, never level with anyone.
teaches: The same cart wheel is used for what turns beneath a person in Naladiyar and for the person who is turned in the Soolamani.

gains.a: The wheel of 1921 gains a lesser double: the turning of wealth within one life as a small copy of the soul's turning through births.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a larger turning behind its wheel: wealth turns like a wheel because the one who holds it is turned by deeds from birth to birth.

note: 1930 says sufferers entered the pit by their own earlier striving and no one comes when they cry; Tirumanthiram 165 sends those who do not worship Siva to the seventh hell where they cry out.
teaches: The cry in hell is answered by neither text, but the Jain verse locates the cause in deeds and the Saiva verse in worship withheld.

gains.a: The cry of 1930 gains a Saiva counterpart in which a withheld act of worship, not a deed's weight, is the cause of the same crying.
gains.b: The Saiva hell gains a Jain rival in which no rescuer is named because no god sits above the deeds.

audit_text_issue: TM 165: ஏழா நரகு and மாயன் are uncertain.

note: 1931 has tormentors tell sufferers to take the fruit of their own deeds; Tirumanthiram 198 has Death's servants bind killers and drive them with the very commands they gave.
teaches: Both hells have punishers who echo the victim's own deed, but only the Saiva servants act for Death, while the Soolamani's act for no one.

gains.a: The tormentors of 1931, named only by their trade, gain a Saiva figure to compare with: a servant who acts for Yama.
gains.b: The Saiva hell gains a Jain counterpart in which the punishers speak only of the deed the sufferer sowed.

note: 1931 has the sufferers receive the fruit of former deeds; Naladiyar 33 says the fool sighs hotly when the fruit arrives, and the wise who treat it as old debt pass beyond confusion.
teaches: 1931 shows the fruit received with no way to reinterpret it, which is the state Naladiyar 33 says the wise avoid.

gains.a: The hell scene gains the stance it lacks: the sufferers receive their deeds' fruit without the calm that frees.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a concrete picture of the fool it describes, shown in the pit rather than only named.

note: 1920 promises the way of conquering deeds as a thing the sage will teach; Tirumanthiram 219 says the fire worshipped burns up the many ills of deeds.
teaches: The Jain sage treats conquering deeds as a teaching to be given, while Tirumular treats it as a rite whose fire burns them.

gains.a: The sage's 'way of conquering deeds' gains a rival method, burning by rite, against which the Jain way can be read.
gains.b: The fire rite gains a Jain counterpart in which deeds are conquered by teaching and austerity, not by offering.

note: 1851 says those who did evil take its seed and sow it and die wanting pleasure; 1939 shows the harvest as impalement and splitting, named the fruit of deeds.
teaches: The king's earlier fear of sowing evil gets its full price here, where the sage's list shows what the sown seed becomes.

note: 1939 gives hell as the ripening of the sufferers' own deeds with no one allotting it; Tirumanthiram 2544 says the Lord set hell and heaven for souls by grace.
teaches: The same pain is explained once by deeds ripening and once by a lord's grace, which marks where the Jain and Saiva accounts of hell part.

gains.a: The sage's verdict gains a rival answer to who stands behind the ripening, which its last line leaves unnamed.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gains a picture of what hell contains and a cause in the sufferer's own deed, neither of which it gives.

note: Both make the adulterer embrace a figure of red-hot copper in hell.
teaches: Two Jain epics share the same matched punishment, but only 1932 begins from the secret night-visit and the wardens' mocking words.

note: 1932 stages lust's punishment as a forced embrace of fire; Siddhar 450 has the pit of hell say it will eat the lustful and the loins say they will ruin him.
teaches: A Siddhar's warning in the speaker's own body becomes in the epic a scene of wardens and figures, so the same fear is placed inside and outside the sinner.

gains.a: The embrace of fire gains an inner meaning, that desire itself is what the pit feeds on.
gains.b: The Siddhar's threat gains a literal staging, in which the loins' ruin is acted out as an embrace.

note: Both set hell's dogs on the victims; 1933 adds that the wardens raised them in cages and that the victims flee up a tree of thorns.
teaches: The dog and the thorn tree recur as fixed parts of the Jain hell, while 1933 shows the dogs as reared for the work.

note: Both feed flesh-eaters molten metal; the Cintamani calls them to come, 1934 shows them the 'flesh' first.
teaches: The shared molten-metal meal marks flesh-eating as a fixed offence of the Jain hell, with 1934 adding the mocking offer of food.

note: 1935 carves and feeds back to meat-eaters their own limbs; Kural 255 ties eating flesh to hell.
teaches: The Kural's single claim about meat and hell becomes a punishment that mirrors the meal, limb for limb.

gains.a: The carved-and-fed vision gains a general rule that makes meat itself, not cruelty only, the ground of the penalty.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete form of the hell it names, in which the eater's own body becomes the dish.

note: 1937 tears out the tongue of those who slander their betters; Kural 183 says death is better than living by backbiting and falsehood.
teaches: The couplet's preference for dying over slander assumes death ends the matter; the epic says it does not and takes the tongue after death.

gains.a: The torn tongue gains an ethical comparison that sets the slanderer's life against death before any hell is shown.
gains.b: The couplet gains an afterlife in which the death it prefers is not an escape.

note: Both give the thirsty a false drink: poison pools here, water that turns to pus in the Cintamani.
teaches: Relief that destroys the sufferer is a standing device of the Jain hell, shown with different liquids in each epic.

note: 1946 gives the hell-beings' body size in a measure of bows and cubits; Neelakesi 92 gives the dark hells' beings as five hundred bows.
teaches: Two Jain epics share a table of hell body-sizes, so 1946's hard measures may be read against the Neelakesi's figure.

note: 1951 names those who leave their wives for others' as falling into deep sorrow; Naladiyar 84 lists disgrace, a cut leg and long suffering in hell for the adulterer.
teaches: Naladiyar counts the worldly penalties before hell; the epic puts only hell and gives the torment in detail.

gains.a: The adulterer's fate gains the earthly costs of disgrace and mutilation that the sage's hell leaves out.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the long torment that it names only as hell, shown in the verses before.

note: 1951 and the following verses give conduct as the ground of hell; Tirumanthiram 165 puts those who do not worship the Lord's form in the seventh hell.
teaches: The sage's list of sins contains no failure of worship while Tirumular's contains little else, so the two define the sinner differently.

gains.a: The sage's conduct list gains a contrast in which hell's gate is worship, which none of its sins names.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gains a list of acts of harm and greed that earn hell without any lack of worship.

note: 1953 puts those who hoard without householder's dharma and die hard-fisted in hell; Naladiyar 273 says the hoarder is laughed at by his own wealth.
teaches: The miser is mocked in life by the wealth he stored and punished after death for it, two sanctions for one fault.

gains.a: The hell verse gains the earthly shame of the miser, which it omits.
gains.b: The quatrain gains the afterlife penalty it does not mention.

note: 1956 grades animal births by the number of senses from one to five; Neelakesi 77 splits animals into fixed and moving and counts five kinds of the fixed.
teaches: The sense-ladder of the Soolamani and the fixed and moving divisions of the Neelakesi are two cuts of one Jain classification of life.

note: 1962 names the flesh-seller, the one who crushes and the hunter as the animal's killers; Neelakesi 104 names battle, the chase for food and the nets.
teaches: Both Jain tellings draw on one stock list of the animal's torments, so the list is a teaching form and not a poet's own picture.

note: 1962 gives the animals' pain at the killers' hands; Siddhar 269 gives the killers' own end, when Death seizes them for the sake of the body's pot.
teaches: The Siddhar says the killer will answer to Death, while the Soolamani implies what answering means: birth as the beast he hunted.

gains.a: The animals' sufferings gain a reckoning: the Siddhar shows who comes to answer for them, at death.
gains.b: The Siddhar's threat of Death gains a content: the Soolamani says what follows death, rebirth among the beasts.

note: 1965 lists animals killed as offerings to deities among their torments; Kural 259 weighs a thousand oblations against not killing one creature and eating.
teaches: The Kural ranks abstention above sacrifice, and the Soolamani shows from the victim's side what the offering costs.

gains.a: The sacrificed animal gains a ranking: the Kural says the rite is worth less than leaving the animal alone.
gains.b: The Kural gains the victim's side: the epic puts the offered animal among the beasts' sufferings, a cost the couplet leaves unsaid.

note: 1967 says that those who take austerity and then practise deceit are born as beasts; Kural 274 pictures the false ascetic as a hunter hidden in a bush, snaring birds.
teaches: In the Kural the hypocrite hunts the innocent, and the Soolamani turns him into the hunted: the same fault, paid back in the animal's birth.

gains.a: The hypocrite's rebirth gains an image of what he did: the hunter in hiding whom the Kural names.
gains.b: The Kural's hunter gains a sequel: the epic says what becomes of him, since it is the beast's form.

note: 1967 sends the false ascetic to an animal birth; Tirumanthiram 1659 sends those of false austerity to hell and says austerities hold only through true knowledge.
teaches: Jain and Saiva texts agree that false austerity is punished and differ on the place: a beast's birth in the one, hell in the other.

gains.a: The false ascetic's fate gains a rival account, hell for the Saiva text, that shows the animal birth is a Jain choice.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's hell gains a Jain counterpart in which the punishment is a rebirth that can still be left.

note: 1970 sends those who deny soul and rebirth to the nigoda state; Tirumanthiram 2558 sends those who say there is no higher state to hell.
teaches: Both texts answer denial with a bad end and not with argument, but one end is a lower birth and the other is hell.

gains.a: The Jain threat gains a Saiva twin, showing that sending the denier to a bad end is a shared habit of polemic.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's denial gains a content: the Soolamani says what is denied, the soul, rebirth and the difference of good and bad.

note: 1975 says that a people is human only in the bare fact of birth and otherwise animal for want of shame and conduct; Kural 1071 says the base look just like human beings.
teaches: The Kural tests humanness by conduct in each person, while the Soolamani ties the same test to a whole island people's birth.

gains.a: The island people's humanity gains a conduct test: the Kural makes the difference lie in what a person does, not in a land.
gains.b: The Kural's resemblance gains a case where the look-alike is a named people, not a type of person.

note: 1973 puts the Milechchar of the islands among the animals; 1977 adds that even those of human form among them, who live by cruelty, are brought down.
teaches: The classing with animals in 1973 is widened in 1977 to cover people of human form, so the test shifts from form to livelihood.

note: 1982 refuses the name 'people' to those without discernment; 1984 adds the eunuch, the blind and woman's birth to those not counted as fully human.
teaches: The speaker's two tests of being human are discernment and the kind of birth, and the second does not follow from the first.

note: 1989 shows household love bringing sufferings with its ties; 1990 offers vows as the one lasting course for those born in this state.
teaches: The sage sets vows as the answer to the pain that household desire cannot remove, which 1989 only states.

note: 1998 refuses merit to giving harmful things to evil-doers; 1999 compares such a giver to one who feeds the cruel and asks their service.
teaches: The comparison turns a moral rule about giving into a plain foolishness, so a listener sees harm to the giver and not only a fault.

note: 1992 grades gifts into best, middle and lowest by receiver, giver and gift; 2000 says gifts of one who knows the principles are not placed within three grades.
teaches: The gift of the knowing giver is said to go beyond the three-grade scheme, so the grading does not describe the highest case.

note: 1843 has Payapati say that his umbrellas and bowing kings are a gift of his good-deed deity; 1997 says the givers of food become kings with armies and umbrellas.
teaches: The earlier remark that kingship is earned acquires a stated source: a gift of food to the hungry becomes the umbrella.

note: 1992 grades a gift by the receiver's fault-lessness, the giver and the gift; Tirumanthiram 508 sends giver and receiver to hell if the receiver does not bow in worship of the Lord.
teaches: The two ask what makes a receiver worthy and give different answers, so one cannot tell from either how to judge a fit receiver.

gains.a: The Jain scheme lacks a test of worship: it names no receiver whom a gift would harm the giver by reaching.
gains.b: The Saiva verse lacks a grading of gifts and a role for the giver's own qualities, which it reduces to the receiver's bowing.

note: 1992 treats giving as graded with a lowest grade; Tirumanthiram 505 says gifts to those without conduct and vows are like milking a barren cow.
teaches: The lowest grade of giving may still be a gift, and the Tirumanthiram says that at some point there is no crop.

gains.a: The grading gains a limit below which a gift is wasted, which 1992 does not name.
gains.b: The barren-cow image gains a scale: the poem shows that giving is not simply worth or not worth, but graded.

note: 2000 says the gifts of one who knows the true principles lead him among the best gods; Tirumanthiram 1867 says charity to tireless ascetics sinks deep karma and becomes the golden world.
teaches: One text places the fruit of giving in a higher birth, and the other in the removal of karma, which are different ends.

gains.a: The Jain verse gains a different reward, since removal of karma is not what it names, only a birth among gods.
gains.b: The Saiva verse gains a condition: here the giver's knowledge of the principles is part of the reward, not only the receiver's austerity.

note: 1988 pictures pleasure as honey tasted by a man hanging above a pit with an elephant and a snake; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones see the pain in any pleasure and do not cling.
teaches: The parable explains why fools do not renounce: the honey is real, and the danger is out of sight while one tastes it.

gains.a: The parable gains a statement of what the wise do while the honey drops, which the image does not give.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an image for the fool's blindness, so that his not renouncing is shown as enjoyment of a real sweetness.

note: 1985 says only those who hold firmly to good karma come to the human body, out of eighty-four lakh births; Naladiyar 34 says to take the great fruit of the rare body.
teaches: The epic gives the count and cause of the rare body that the quatrain only calls rare, so the urgency has a reason.

gains.a: The count of births gains a use: the rare body is to be pressed for fruit like cane.
gains.b: The 'rare body' gains a measure and a cause: eighty-four lakh births and firm good karma.

note: 1987 draws childhood, youth and old age as a wilderness ending in another state; Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood, knowing grey hair would come.
teaches: The epic shows what lies past old age, another birth, and so the quatrain's renunciation at the start is not a mere fear of aging.

gains.a: The wilderness of life gains an answer: renounce early, before the other state.
gains.b: Old age gains a sequel in another birth, which the quatrain's staff and grey hair do not name.

note: 1997 promises the giver of food a later kingship; Kural 222 says that even if there were no higher world, giving alone is good.
teaches: The epic's giving is promised its fruit, and the Kural says it is worth doing without one, so the reward is a bonus to a duty and not its ground.

gains.a: The promise of kingship gains a test: would the giving stand if there were no later birth.
gains.b: The Kural's 'even if no higher world' gains a case of the world's usual motive, the later kingship.

note: 1862 has the minister name the austere sage's feet as the only refuge; 2003 is the sage's first reply, that austerity is hard to say even for sages.
teaches: The refuge sought in 1862 answers only by admitting that the thing sought is hard to put into words, so the king must be taught in steps.

note: 1842 has the king ask for more seed to sow for austerity; 2005 calls the harvest of austerity a wealth that grows in kinds.
teaches: The sage turns the king's idea of sowing into a promise that the austerity crop multiplies, so the vow rests on growth and not only loss.

note: 2002 offers the vow of not killing to kings as one that leaves no conquest out of reach; Kural 325 ranks not-killing highest among those who renounced.
teaches: The epic recasts non-killing as a king's way to win, where the couplet ranks it only among renouncers.

gains.a: The sage's claim for kings gains a ranking from the Kural, which sets non-killing above every other renunciation.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ruler as its audience: a king who keeps the vow and still seeks conquest, which it never considers.

note: 2009 defines compassion as melting for another's life and counts a moist heart where rescue fails; Kural 315 calls understanding useless without guarding another's pain as one's own.
teaches: The pairing shows compassion as both the test of understanding and a state that stays even when help fails.

gains.a: Compassion gains a test, since understanding is judged worthless without it.
gains.b: The couplet gains an allowance for failure: the moist heart still counts where the pain cannot be removed.

note: 2010 asks equal calm toward abuse, praise and neglect; Kural 151 asks the bearing of scorn only.
teaches: Level calm includes praise, so the couplet's forbearance covers only half of what the sage asks of the clear-minded.

gains.a: Equanimity gains the image of the earth that bears the digger, a reason to take scorn without answer.
gains.b: Forbearance gains the other side, praise, which also stirs the heart and needs the same steadiness.

note: 2014 makes hearing the meaning of the texts a lamp that clears delusion; Kural 423 makes wisdom seeing the true thing in whatever is heard.
teaches: The sage trusts the text as source, where the couplet makes the hearer's seeing the test of any source.

gains.a: Knowledge from hearing gains a check, seeing what is true in the words and not trusting the speaker.
gains.b: The couplet gains an end for its seeing: the clearing of the darkness that binds one to deeds.

note: 2014 calls knowledge from the texts a lamp; 2018 calls seeing the true thing a lamp of vision that ends the dark.
teaches: One lamp is lit twice, once by hearing and once by seeing, so the sage joins the two as stages of one light.

note: 2018 has the lamp of vision end the darkness of deeds; Naladiyar 51 has the lamp of austerity end sin as darkness dies, and darkness return when the oil runs out.
teaches: The lamp's light is credited to vision in the epic and to austerity in the quatrain, with only the quatrain saying the light can fail.

gains.a: The lamp of vision gains the warning of the oil, that light can go out unless fed.
gains.b: The quatrain's lamp gains a source in the knowing of the true thing, where it names only austerity.

note: 2018 has vision destroy karma's darkness by itself; Tirumanthiram 116 has Nandi remove the malas as fire rises from bamboo, out of grace.
teaches: Release by one's own seeing, without any god, meets release by a lord's grace, and the same fire-and-darkness language serves both.

gains.a: The lamp of vision gains a rival cause, grace, for the same burning away of the dark.
gains.b: The grace-fire gains the Jain demand that the soul's own seeing bear the work, so the cause is not left wholly with the lord.

note: 2015 sorts meditation into four kinds by their fruit, two bad and two leading to heaven and release; Tirumanthiram 598 gives three objects of meditation, Shakti, the Supreme and Siva as guru.
teaches: The two works sort meditation differently, by moral fruit in the epic and by the divine object in the Saiva text.

gains.a: The fourfold sorting gains named objects, since it never says what is to be fixed upon.
gains.b: The Saiva list gains a test of fruit, that some meditation leads astray as well as upward.

note: 2017 says those with the lamp of vision reach heaven or the bliss without return even without vows; Kural 356 says those who learn and see the true thing reach the path of no return.
teaches: The epic loosens the couplet's chain, holding that sight alone, even without vows, opens heaven or release.

gains.a: The vowless seer gains a precedent, since the couplet already gives seeing the true thing the path of no return.
gains.b: The couplet gains the claim that vows are not required, which it never says, and the lesser reward of heaven.

audit_text_issue: line 3 ஆட்சி கரிதன்று அமருலகு is compressed; the sense is uncertain

note: 2024 ranks beings best, middle and lowest by the fruit of earlier good deeds; Kural 37 points to the bearer and the rider of a palanquin as the visible proof of virtue's fruit.
teaches: Rank that Kural 37 reads from one palanquin is stretched in 2024 into a ladder of births, so one visible difference becomes a whole order of worlds.

gains.a: The ranking of beings gets a plain proof from daily sight, the palanquin, in place of a bare claim about the fruit of deeds.
gains.b: The couplet gains a longer horizon: the difference it sees between rider and bearer is only the near end of a graded series of births.

note: 2031 has the youth's lotus-like eyes and the girl's blue-lily eyes meet and press; Kural 1082 has the girl's answering look strike like an army.
teaches: The same meeting of eyes is a fated, gentle union in the enjoyment land but a conquest in the Kural's world of passion.

gains.a: The meeting look gains the sense of an attack that ends the other's resistance, which the epic's soft image of lilies leaves out.
gains.b: The couplet gains a setting where the look leads to fulfilment with no cost and no shame, unlike the pain the Kural's lover goes on to feel.

note: 2033 gives the pair unbroken pleasure for their whole span; Naladiyar 16 says the joy of youth is fleeting like the lamb eating the garland before the slaughter.
teaches: The epic can promise pleasure that lasts a full span only by moving it out of this world, which is exactly what the Naladiyar's warning denies is possible here.

gains.a: The long pleasure gains a warning that without a world apart it would end as the lamb's does, which the verse's calm account does not say.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a counter-picture: a place where youth's joy is not a trap, though it too ends in the next verses with the pair's rise.

note: 2034 says the painless pleasure is the fruit of what was given to austere kings; Kural 42 makes the householder the support of those who have let go.
teaches: A householder's gift to renouncers, a duty in the Kural, is shown in the epic as the cause of a later birth in a land of ease.

gains.a: The pleasure gains a stated cause in an act of giving that any householder can do now, not only in a distant rank of merit.
gains.b: The couplet gains a reward beyond the support of the renouncer: the giver's next birth, which the couplet leaves unsaid.

note: 2035 has the human pair rise to heaven after their span; 2038 says the beasts and birds of the same land rise to the kalpa world as well.
teaches: The rise of the pair is not a human privilege: the land's own merit carries even its animals up, so the climb belongs to the place.

note: 2060 says heaven's pleasure comes by austerity yet ends, and that something is higher; Kural 346 says one who cuts off 'I' and 'mine' enters a world above the gods'.
teaches: The couplet's 'higher than the gods' is given a reason in the epic: the gods' world has a measured end, so only what lies above it can be a goal.

gains.a: The vague higher state is given a means, the cutting of ownership and the self, which the verse leaves unnamed.
gains.b: The couplet gains a ground for ranking the gods' world below renunciation: its joys are counted in years and end.

note: 2060 says heaven's wealth ends; Tirumanthiram 184 says time cuts down both the heaven-bound and the deed-bound.
teaches: Both deny that heaven is lasting, but the epic counts the ending in fixed spans of seas and tells of a state beyond, while Tirumular makes time's cutting a general law with no way out in that line.

gains.a: The ending of heaven gets a law of time that reaches everyone, in place of a bare statement of limit.
gains.b: The cutting down by time gets a scale, from a palya to thirty-three seas in 2061 to 2063, and a way above it by austerity.

note: 2051 itemises the gods' mansions, couches and cars as the whole of heaven; Kural 50 says the one who lives life as it ought to be lived will be counted among the gods.
teaches: What the couplet offers as the reward of right householding is shown by the epic as a list of comforts and then, in 2060, as a reward that has an end.

gains.a: The gods' world gets a stated goal in a householder's right life, which its inventory alone does not give.
gains.b: The couplet gains content for 'among the gods' and a limit on how far the reward goes.

note: 2052 lists the gods' play, Indra's company and jewelled terraces as heaven's whole stock; Naladiyar 137 asks whether heaven's city is sweeter than the gathering of learned men.
teaches: Naladiyar weighs heaven against the company of the learned and finds it no sweeter; the epic describes the gods' pleasures as only entertainment and ranks them below the teaching of 2067.

gains.a: The gods' amusements get a human measure by which they look modest.
gains.b: The comparison gains a full picture of what heaven's pleasures consist of, so the contrast is not left abstract.

note: 2065 says the highest gods have no lord over them and none greater; Tirumanthiram 266 says the ripened see the Lord's feet and the resolute rule his heaven.
teaches: The epic's top heaven stands under no ruling god, while Tirumular's heaven is the Lord's own; the conflict depends on reading கோனிலா as 'with no king above' and on taking 'his heaven' as lordship, not only as place.

gains.a: The claim of no lord over the highest gods meets a rival picture of a heaven that belongs to a Lord and is entered by grace.
gains.b: The Lord's heaven meets a counter-picture where beings of the highest rank answer to no one.

note: 2000 says gifts made by one who has grasped the true principles raise the giver among the best of the gods; 2047 names who these are: householders who give, avoid wine and flesh and stay true to the beloved.
teaches: 2047 widens the ground of 2000 from giving alone to abstinence and faithfulness, so the householder's whole conduct is what raises him.
audit_text_issue: Both flagged uncertain; 2047 line 3 construction unclear

note: 2057 says right vision is easy for the great and rare for others; 2067 says that standing in right vision with austerity keeps one from hell and animal births.
teaches: 2067 turns the rarity of right vision into a promise: who holds it with austerity escapes the lower births and keeps unfailing wealth.

note: 2060 hints at a state above heaven's ending joy; 2068 shows the sage, once the heavens are told, setting out how to reach endless bliss.
teaches: The hint of a state beyond heaven's end becomes, in the sage's closing, the thing the teaching moves toward: bliss that has no end.
audit_text_issue: 2068 line 1 doubtful (உறுதிகணன்) | 2068 line 1 உறுதிகணன் is a doubtful word.

note: 2070 traces how birth turns to desire and hatred toward sense objects, heaps up deeds and brings the same nature back after death; Kural 349 says that the very moment attachment ends, births are cut.
teaches: The couplet's moment of cutting is shown in 2070 to be the point where the chain from senses to desire to deed to return is broken.

gains.a: The chain of sense, craving, deed and rebirth gets a plain statement of where it ends, which 2070 leaves unsaid.
gains.b: The couplet gets the working of the births it cuts: attachment makes deeds, and the deeds are what bring the return.

audit_text_issue: line 3 வாயிலா is a compressed phrase; the sense is uncertain

note: 2072 has the hero reach release by his own vision, knowledge, mastered mind and long meditation; Tirumanthiram 126 has the freed ones climb the thirty-six tattvas as a ladder to release, enter the light of bliss and see Sivam.
teaches: Both texts describe release as a climb by stages, but 2072 ends in a world of release won by the self's own effort while Tirumular's ladder ends in seeing Sivam.

gains.a: The hero's path gets a counter-picture in which the top of the ladder is a seen god, which the verse, with no god in it, does not have.
gains.b: The ladder gets a way of release in which the climber is complete without the vision of a lord, which the couplet does not allow.

note: 2074 uses three pleasant senses, jewel-light, sandal coolness and flower scent, for the bliss of release, which it calls சிவகதி; Tirumanthiram 325 uses a drink, the nectar of Siva's bliss in samadhi, for the same kind of state.
teaches: Both reach for sensory pictures of a state they say is beyond the senses, but the Jain verse's சிவகதி names a state of release while Tirumular's Siva is the god whose bliss it is.

gains.a: The comparison to light, cool and scent gets a drink image that shows the bliss as unbroken from sitting to lying, which 2074 does not say.
gains.b: The drink of bliss gets a calmer set of images that carry no hint of the intoxication Tirumular is guarding against in this chapter.

note: 2075 has the king resolve, after hearing the teacher, to strive for the final world; verse 355 has the counsellor repeat the sage's word that the hero will not be dazzled by kings' wealth and will reach the state of release by austerity.
teaches: The sage's early prediction that the king will refuse kings' wealth is kept in 2075, where the king himself declares the resolve.

note: 2018 names the lamp of vision as seeing the true thing and says that, once lit, the darkness of deeds cannot stay; 2072 shows the path in which vision and knowledge, with meditation, lead on to the world of release.
teaches: The lamp of vision in 2018 is a first step; 2072 sets out what must follow it before the deeds are gone and release is reached.

note: 2079 has the king's own ministers urge him to give up the crown for the austerity that ends the disease of birth; Naladiyar 53 says the best people, seeing that home, youth, wealth and strength do not last, renounce them without delay.
teaches: Naladiyar 53 describes a person giving up a house and wealth, but 2079 shows the same renunciation asked of a king, where the crown and a kingdom's charge must be laid down.

gains.a: The ministers' plea gets a general rule, that the wise renounce on seeing that things do not last, to rest on.
gains.b: The quatrain gets a case in which what is given up is a kingdom and its cost to others, which a householder's renunciation does not show.

note: 2082 makes wealth a woman who leaves the men she has joined and always wants someone new; Kural 332 says great wealth comes like a crowd gathering at a dance hall and goes like the crowd breaking up.
teaches: The couplet's crowd goes without any reason in itself; in 2082 the going has a will, the goddess who tires of her man and wants another.

gains.a: The goddess's leaving gets an image of a crowd that comes and goes for its own reasons and owes the owner nothing.
gains.b: The crowd gets a person with a wish behind its going, so wealth's departure reads as desertion and not only as an end.

note: 2083 compares the departing goddess of wealth to courtesans who leave the penniless; Naladiyar 371 says harlots' friendship ends when the hand is empty, as a lamp's light ends when the oil is gone.
teaches: The epic turns the Naladiyar's warning about courtesans into a figure for wealth itself, so a man is asked to see in his fortune the same cold arithmetic.

gains.a: The goddess's leaving gets a plain reason, that the love was only for what the hand held, which 2083 leaves implied.
gains.b: The warning about courtesans gets a larger target: the same trade-friendship is shown to run through wealth and fortune, not only through women.

note: 2086 tells the sons not to trust the goddess and to love the learned, whom she scorns; Tirumanthiram 169 calls bewildering wealth a waning moon and bids the reader seek the king of the gods, who becomes great wealth like a rain cloud.
teaches: Both give up trusting wealth but name different things to trust in its place: the Jain king names the learned, Tirumular names a god who is himself wealth.

gains.a: The advice to attach to the learned gets a rival answer, a lord who stays, so a reader sees that the choice of refuge is itself a doctrine.
gains.b: The rain-cloud wealth of the Lord gets a worldly alternative in which the refuge is people, not a god, and it is held without worship.

note: 2088 says the earth has enjoyed countless men and left them, and has not stayed with the next; Siddhar 286 says crowned kings are burnt to a fistful of ash and become earth.
teaches: The two reverse the same image: the king thinks he holds the earth, but 2088 says she leaves him and the Siddhar says he is returned into her.

gains.a: The earth that deserts kings gets an ending, that the kings she leaves are laid in her as ash, which the verse does not state.
gains.b: The Siddhar's ash gets a living figure for earth, the woman who goes from king to king, so the fact of burning is given a reason.

note: 2093 has the king say his own days are few and he has resolved today; Kural 342 says renounce while there is time.
teaches: The Kural's urgency to renounce in time becomes, in the epic, a king's own reckoning of his remaining days against those of his people.

gains.a: The king's haste gets a rule from outside the story: the time to renounce is limited and it is wiser to act before it runs out.
gains.b: The couplet gains a person who is at once a ruler and a father, whose leaving has to be explained to those he leaves.

note: In 2094 the princes ask what fault they have done; in 2106 they call their quarrelsome prattle foolish and bow to the lord's grace.
teaches: The sons' first grief as a charge against themselves turns, after the sages' consolation, into acceptance of the king's act as grace.

note: 2096 has the ministers put down the heavy burden they bore through the disease of birth; Kural 345 says that for those set on cutting off births even the body is excess.
teaches: The burden of the body in the epic is lifted by a king's grace, whereas the couplet lays it on the renouncer's own will.

gains.a: The ministers' burden gets a stated reason, that the body itself is surplus when one wants to end births.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene of a king's court letting go together, where the renouncer is no lone figure.

note: 2098 has gods carry the king's crown and cast it into the milk sea; Cintamani 3035 has gods lift the tray with Civakan's hair and let it fall into the milk sea.
teaches: Both Jain epics end a royal career with the same act, gods taking the shed sign of rank to the milk sea, so the image reads as a convention for a king's completed renunciation.

note: 2099 has a king give army and earth to his sons and put off his crown by choice; Naladiyar 21 says even kings under umbrellas have been carried off as dead.
teaches: The same fall of a king from rank that Naladiyar reads as death's work is here done by the king's own hand while alive.

gains.a: The king's laying aside of the crown gets the contrast of what happens to kings who wait to be taken by death.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king who is not carried off but leaves before he must.

note: 2099 has the king leave wealth, army and earth to his sons; Tirumanthiram 168 says join the true wealth before the elephants, chariots and wealth pass to others.
teaches: Both tell a king to leave his wealth while he lives, but the epic hands it to sons and takes no god, while Tirumular names the one to join.

gains.a: The king's giving of the realm to his sons gets a rival reading, in which the wealth should be exchanged for the lord, not left to heirs.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gains a case where the same urging is met without a god, by a vow and a handing over to the next generation.

note: 2101 shows the princes wailing as the crown falls from the lord; Kural 347 says griefs hold those who hold attachment.
teaches: The princes' grief shows the couplet's point from the other side: the renouncer is free while those who still cling to him suffer.

gains.a: The princes' sorrow is named as the cost of their own attachment, not only of his act.
gains.b: The couplet gains persons whose grief arises from clinging to another renouncer, not to things.

note: 2109 posts five great captains of the vow-army against incoming karma; Kural 343 says the domain of the five must be crushed and all desire let go.
teaches: The epic's five are vows that hold karma back, not the five senses of the couplet, so the same number is taken from two different disciplines.

gains.a: The five vows gain the older frame of crushing the five senses, which shows what they guard against.
gains.b: The couplet gains a Jain version in which the defence is a set of vows and an army, not a single act of crushing.

note: 2111 shuts the five sense-gates of a fortress and posts guards; Naladiyar 59 names the five gates (body, mouth, eyes, nose, ears) and promises release to one who can guard and steer the craving that comes through them.
teaches: Guarding the senses is shown as one wall among several defences and not a lone act, so restraint looks like the start of a campaign and not its end.

gains.a: The gates, which the fortress leaves as an unnamed row, are named as the five organs through which craving enters.
gains.b: The rule that guarding the gates leads to release gains walls, armed guards and a mind kept within, so sense-restraint is pictured as part of a larger war.

note: 2113 has the lord ride the elephant of knowledge with a diamond goad that is awareness; Kural 24 guards the five with the goad of firmness.
teaches: The same goad turns from a means of guarding the senses to a means of driving the army that kills the karmic enemy.

gains.a: The goad is no longer a guard against the senses but a driver of an assault, which the couplet leaves out.
gains.b: The couplet's goad gains the elephant it only implies, and gains a battle for the elephant to carry the rider into.

note: 2115 has the lord draw the sword of unbroken meditation soaked in samadhi; Neelakesi 86 says that humans of the land of deeds see their dark karma leave by penance.
teaches: Both Jain epics say karma is removed by the ascetic's own effort, and one gives that effort a face as a sword.

note: 2117 kills anger and its fellows one after another in a fixed sequence; Siddhar 87 asks when anger, speech and action, the 'I' and the mind will die so that release can be reached.
teaches: The Jain epic gives a battle order for the passions where the Siddhar only longs for them to die all at once.

gains.a: The passions, which 2117 names but leaves as figures in a rout, are made into an ordered list the seeker must wait out, with the mind and the 'I' added at the end.
gains.b: The Siddhar's longing gains a plan, in which anger falls first and the others follow in turn, in place of a single wish for the end of all.

audit_text_issue: 2117 reading flagged uncertain; the figures are unexplained

note: 2124 throws away the sword of meditation once the karmic kings are dead; Kural 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one who has none, so as to let clinging go.
teaches: A useful hold, whether the sword or the clinging to the unclinging one, is to be dropped at the end of its work.

gains.a: The throwing away of the sword gives the Kural's paradox of a last clinging a scene in which the tool is dropped and an entry follows.
gains.b: The couplet's holding that lets go gains a picture of the very moment the tool is dropped, and of what comes after, an embrace and a city.

note: 2124 has the liberated one embrace the maiden called முடிவு; Cintamani 3117 has the king embrace the maiden Kevala with unblinking eyes.
teaches: Both Jain epics speak of release as a bride, but the Soolamani's bride is the end of birth and the Cintamani's is knowledge.
audit_text_issue: 3117 flagged uncertain; 2125 has stray ங் but 2124 clean

note: 2125 has the freed soul swallow the world and non-world together once the coverings are gone; Cintamani 3082 has the hero swallow the three worlds and the world of non-world after the four enemy kings fall.
teaches: The same formula for omniscience appears in both Jain epics, and only the Soolamani names the removal of coverings as its cause.

note: 2125 places the liberated soul in the state called சிவகதி and wins it by its own meditation; Tirumanthiram 6 says apart from the Lord there is no hard penance that can achieve and no way into his city.
teaches: The two texts both speak of an unreturning state but disagree on whether penance alone reaches it or only the Lord opens the way.

gains.a: The state of release, which the Soolamani reaches by effort alone, is set against a view in which that effort is useless without the Lord.
gains.b: The claim that no penance achieves without him gains a rival case in which a hero wins release by his own meditation with no god acting.

note: 2127 has Death and Desire flee the hero who wins by full knowledge; Tirumanthiram 345 tells of burning Death in the fire of yoga at Kadavur.
teaches: Both texts have Death beaten, but one by a man's own knowledge and the other by a god's fire.

gains.a: Death's defeat, which the Soolamani gives to an ascetic's knowledge, is set against a defeat worked by the Lord.
gains.b: The yoga-fire gains a human counterpart who beats Death without any god, so the Kadavur tale is no longer the only way to beat Death.

note: 2127 calls the lord who has conquered his enemies the crest-jewel of the world; Soolamani 1 opens by praising the one who conquered the whole sum of his deeds and now stands as a shining form.
teaches: The close of the poem answers its opening, so the praise promised at the start is now earned by the war just fought.

note: 2130 shows the dark and white princes worshipping under the lotus feet of the liberated lord; Soolamani 2 says the story is of the one who in an earlier day went to him for refuge.
teaches: The refuge sought at the beginning becomes the festival of worship at the end, which gives the story a completed arc.

note: 2121 has the sky filled with the gods' regalia, flowers, sandal and powder; Cintamani 3090 has the gods rain flowers, coloured sandal and incense that fill the quarters.
teaches: The same festival of gods is set at the end of the war in the Soolamani and at the teaching in the Cintamani, so it honours victory in one and instruction in the other.

note: 2129 has Tirumal lift a straight sceptre with the gods guarding him; Kural 547 says the king guards the world and justice guards him if he does not falter.
teaches: The guard of a king comes in the epic from the gods and in the couplet from his own justice, so the pairing asks what really protects a ruler.

gains.a: The gods' protection, which the epic gives as a plain fact, is made to depend on the rule of a straight sceptre.
gains.b: The couplet's guard of justice gains a mythic setting in which the gods are the guards.

note: 2115 has samadhi give the sword that cuts the foe; Tirumanthiram 121 has the Siva-yogi cut bonds and remain with the body as if dead.
teaches: Samadhi is a weapon of conquest in the Jain epic and a quiet stillness in the Tirumanthiram, so the same state is used for opposite pictures.

gains.a: Samadhi gains an aggressive purpose, in which it is the sword, where the Tirumanthiram uses it for rest.
gains.b: The still, deathlike state gains a battle in which it is the weapon that ends the enemy.

note: The poet bows to a named tirthankara; the couplet praises the feet of one free of liking and aversion without naming him.
teaches: The Jain epic gives a name and a seat under the pindi tree to the one the Kural leaves unnamed, so the same freedom from liking and aversion can be read as a particular lord.

gains.a: the invocation gets a stated quality of the one worshipped, freedom from liking and aversion, which the verse leaves unsaid
gains.b: the couplet gets a named, seated figure that it never gives

note: Both poets ask the learned to take a flawed work for its worth, using a gem as the image.
teaches: A gem image serves the Jain poets as a standing apology, one for flaws washed off and the other for plain wrapping carrying value.

note: The Naga poet's lamp kept despite its smoke is the same plea for lenient reading.
teaches: The minor epics repeat the formula of asking that a work's worth outweigh its faults, each choosing a different household object.

note: Both open with the shedding of former deeds; this verse adds the order and ripening.
teaches: The Jain account of karma shedding that the Naga poem states in a line is here set out as an ordered ripening.

note: The verse allows deeds to be shed in order, where the couplet says fate gets there first whatever one devises.
teaches: The Jain verse leaves room for undoing deeds that the Kural's fate overrides, though the dispute is over what one can do to a deed.

gains.a: the shedding of deeds is set against a strong claim of fate that it must answer
gains.b: the couplet gets a doctrine on which fate can be worn down

note: The seizing bird that threatens the queen in verse 13 is shown in verse 14 to set her down unharmed.
teaches: The bird's danger in 13 is answered in 14, so the abduction is told as a passage to the hermitage and not as an injury.

note: The lute the youth receives from the sage in verse 18 is the instrument that tames the elephant in 19.
teaches: The gift of grace in 18 is shown working at once, so the lute is the means by which Udayanan wins allies.

note: The elephant that bows at his lute in verse 19 pledges itself to him in a dream in verse 20.
teaches: The taming ends in a bond of loyalty, so the music wins a companion and not only a mount.

note: Vikraman's resolve to take up ascetic life in verse 22 is carried out in verse 23 when he goes into the forest.
teaches: A resolve voiced in one verse is kept in the next, with the kingdom handed over first.

note: Vikraman's grief at having no child (verse 21) meets the Kural's praise of children who know what should be known, and the epic gives him a sister's son in place of his own.
teaches: The epic shows that the heir the Kural praises can come by a sister's son, not only by birth, and that the want of a child can lead to renunciation.

gains.a: The verse's grief at being childless gets a standard by which an heir is valued, which the epic's king only feels as loss.
gains.b: The couplet's praise of knowing children gets a case where the lack of one's own child is answered by taking a nephew as heir.

note: Vikraman gives up his kingdom and goes to the forest, as the quatrain's best of men renounce home and wealth on seeing they do not last.
teaches: The epic shows a king doing what the quatrain says, with the order of arranging his heir first and then leaving, which the quatrain does not mention.

gains.a: The epic's king gets the reason for his act, the failing of home and wealth, which the verse does not say.
gains.b: The quatrain's renouncer gets a concrete case, a king who provides for his kingdom before he goes.

note: Vikraman leaves his kingdom to a nephew he has just found, while the Cintamani's Lokamapalan sets his young son on the throne and takes the ascetics' guise.
teaches: Both epics tell of a king handing over rule and turning ascetic, but here the heir is a sister's son and the turn follows childlessness, where the Cintamani's follows the setting up of his own son.

note: Sathanikan crowns the heir first and then turns ascetic, in the order the Cintamani's chariot-king lays down: guard the kingdom, give it to a worthy son, and only then renounce.
teaches: The Cintamani states as advice the order that this king follows in the story, and the epic adds that he passes over his two named sons for Udayanan.

note: Sathanikan gives up the throne while living, where the quatrain says kings under the umbrella on elephants are carried off as dead.
teaches: The epic's king keeps his rank by choosing to leave it before death, which the quatrain does not allow for.

gains.a: The king's leaving gets a sharper meaning, since the quatrain says death is how all kings finally lose the umbrella.
gains.b: The quatrain's claim that none escape gets a qualification: one can leave the throne by renouncing before it is taken.

note: Veeranathan's rain of virtue in verse 5 is set beside the Kural's rain that comes where the king rules justly.
teaches: The epic gives the rain to the tirthankara's teaching, where the Kural makes it the reward of the ruler's sceptre.

gains.a: The epic's rain of virtue gets the Kural's older idea that rain follows the justice of the ruler.
gains.b: The couplet's rain of justice gets a second source: the lord's dharma, not the king, brings the fall.

note: Udayana orders the land searched for his vanished divine elephant; the hunters, seeing the decoy, think it is our lord's elephant and run to him.
teaches: The search for the lost elephant is what makes the decoy believable, since his own people hurry to bring him the news.
audit_text_issue: 46 sense uncertain; no decoy in verse

note: The ministers settle on taking an elephant by showing one; Udayana walks into the grove and sees the false elephant.
teaches: The ministers' choice of lure in 38 is fitted to a king who is hunting for his elephant, which verse 47 shows working.

note: The ministers name his elephant-taming and his veena as his glory; in 48 he plays the veena at the decoy.
teaches: The skill that makes a man formidable is also his weak point, since his veena is what carries him to the trap.

note: The ministers list Udayana's merits to temper the king; the king answers by raging and ordering him seized.
teaches: Telling an angry king a rival's merits does not calm him, it sends the ministers toward a plot.

note: Ninety-six armed men are put inside the machine in 40; in 49 they break out as it becomes a fighting host.
teaches: The machine of 40 is shown to be a hiding place for troops, and 49 is the moment it is turned into one.

note: The Kural's picture is of binding a rutting elephant by means of an elephant; verse 40 builds an elephant of wood and hide, filled with ninety-six men, to take a king.
teaches: The ministers use the Kural's own method in a worse form, a false elephant with men inside and a king as the catch.

gains.a: a rule for the ruse: using one thing of its own kind to take another, here a false elephant to catch a king who tames real ones
gains.b: a case where the stand-in is a built shell with armed men inside and the quarry is a ruler, not a beast

note: The Kural ranks the slackness of great joy below anger as a cause of ruin; in 47 the king goes on though omens and Vayantakan warn him.
teaches: The Kural's slackness is not ignorance: Udayana is told and warned, and in the verse it is his gladness at sight of the elephant that wins.

gains.a: a case where the heedless one has both omens and a friend's warning, so slackness is a choice made in delight, not a lapse of knowledge
gains.b: a story in which joy's slackness is shown over a few verses, before the trap closes on a king and a friend who knew better

note: The Kural makes it the duty of a minister at the king's side to tell him what is good for him; in 36 the ministers tell Pradyota of Udayana's merits.
teaches: The ministers do speak, as the Kural asks, but to a king in anger the truth ends in a plot, so the duty to speak does not guarantee it is heard.

gains.a: a case in which ministers do speak in the king's presence and yet are turned aside
gains.b: a test of the duty to speak when the king, angry, has no wish to be told good of his enemy

note: The Kural says a king who does not think matters through with his circle and then lashes out in anger sees his fortune shrink; in 37 Pradyota rages after the ministers have spoken.
teaches: The king here has taken counsel and yet his anger still rules the outcome, so the Kural's warning is about whether counsel is heard, not just whether it is asked.

gains.a: a king who does hear his circle and still gives way to rage, which the Kural's rule does not cover
gains.b: a scene in which the king's anger leads at once to a plot rather than to a loss of fortune, as the couplet only warns

note: The Naladiyar gives it as a rule that kings who rode in state are carried off and spoken of as dead; here a king's sword snaps and he is seized, but he is afterwards to be rescued.
teaches: The Naladiyar's rule of the ruined proud king is true of the captive here, but the epic makes the ruin a seizure to be undone by a minister, not a final end.

gains.a: The epic scene gains a general statement that kings in elephant-borne state are carried off, so the seizure reads as one case of the rule.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a named king whose fall is not final, which the quatrain's claim that none are left over does not show.

note: Yugi falls as if speared (65) and then rises and sets his plan; the couplet's strong in mind who do not give way where things fall apart.
teaches: The couplet's firm elephant is a person who stays upright; Yugi shows the other half, a man who is struck down and then gets up to act.

gains.a: The epic verse gains a measure for Yugi's rising: not stoicism but the strong mind that recovers and acts.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which firmness does not mean never falling, since its elephant stands under arrows and Yugi first collapses.

note: Yugi removes the king's kin to safety, appoints rulers and plans to answer force with guile, which are three of the minister's skills in the couplet: dividing, holding his own side close, bringing back those who left.
teaches: Kural 633 lists a minister's skills as bare terms; this verse shows one minister doing them in order at a moment of loss.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the Kural's name for what Yugi is doing, a set of skills and not one clever act.
gains.b: The couplet gains a minister at work in a defeat, which its three terms give no scene for.

note: The false death that frees Yugi to act (69) leaves his own lands to be taken once they think him hidden or dead.
teaches: Guile that saves the plan has a price paid by the realm, which verse 69 alone does not count.

note: The couplet wants a spy in a guise that raises no suspicion; Yugi's mad guise draws every eye but carries speech meant for one hearer, the king.
teaches: A disguise can be conspicuous to everyone and still be a secret to all but one, which the couplet's rule of unsuspected appearance does not allow.

gains.a: The epic verse gains the Kural's test of a disguise as one that does not draw suspicion, so Yugi's loud madness stands out as a deliberate exception.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where the disguise is meant to be seen, because the message is in the madman's talk and not in being unseen.

note: Vasavadatta's dream foretells a taking-away by a man, read by experts as a marriage; Kannaki's dream foretells the carrying off of her husband and a false charge.
teaches: A dream in these epics gives the story's course in advance, but the same image foretells a bridegroom in one poem and a ruin in the other.

gains.a: The Udayana verse gains a contrast in which a dream's reading is joyful and its reader is an expert, as against Kannaki's dread.
gains.b: The Silappathikaram passage gains a second story where the dream is read by others and comes true, so its dread is one case of a convention.

note: The ministers say the elephant cannot pass the king's vina; verse 97 shows it coming and bowing at his feet.
teaches: The poem lets the ministers' claim of music's power be tested by what the elephant does in front of the crowd.

note: The mantra and smoke that free the elephant at the post become its killing run through the keepers.
teaches: What looked like a rescuer's stratagem shows its cost at once, on men who were only keepers.

note: Yugi uses the king's own rutting elephant to break the king's hold, as the couplet binds a rutting elephant with another.
teaches: The Kural's image of one task serving another is shown as a plan that also costs lives.

gains.a: the stratagem is named as a type: a means turned on its owner, with a price the couplet does not state
gains.b: the couplet's image of an elephant bound by an elephant is acted out with a real elephant and a real rescue

note: The freed elephant kills the keepers who try to enclose it, as the quatrain says an elephant may kill even its keeper.
teaches: The epic shows the quatrain's keeper-killer elephant as a weapon someone else has deliberately loosed.

gains.a: the keepers' deaths read as a known risk of the beast, not as an accident of the rescue
gains.b: the quatrain's general warning is given a scene where the elephant is not merely ungrateful but sent

note: Yugi and Vayanthakan wait for the right hour and rope, as the couplet says nothing is hard for one who knows time and means.
teaches: The rescue is built on the couplet's rule, but at the cost of others, which the couplet does not weigh.

gains.a: the choice of hour and means is shown as the rule that makes a prison break possible
gains.b: the couplet's claim is tested by a case in which the same skill harms the innocent

note: The king fears the blame of sending a captive before an elephant but admits the capture was by a lie.
teaches: The king dreads the stain of one act and ignores the one before it, which the couplet's test of fame would catch.

gains.a: the king's fear of blame is shown to cover only the last act, not the deceit that made it needed
gains.b: the couplet's warning against acts that win neither renown nor good is shown failing to bind a king who counts only visible blame

note: The rutting elephant is stilled by the vina's song; Tirumular's five elephants are held by the goad of five letters.
teaches: The same picture of a raging elephant brought to rest differs in who tames it, music held by a captive or a mantra held by the self.

gains.a: the elephant's bow reads as a taming of the passions in the bystander's eye, not only a feat of music
gains.b: the inward elephants of the verse get an outward counterpart, a beast whose rage is visible to a city

note: Verse 105 shows Vasavadatta with the arts that verse 103 had her taught.
teaches: The lute lessons planned in one verse come out as proof of mastery in the next, so the teaching is shown as having worked.

note: The fire in the town carries out the trick Yugi sets in verse 109.

teaches: In the Cintamani the dog must consent and think on the words, while here the elephant is simply spoken to and the change is at once.

gains.b: the couplet gets a case where deceit serves loyalty, which tests whether its warning covers it

gains.a: the defence gets a name for the quality shown, steadiness when things fall apart
gains.b: the couplet's image gets a man who stands and answers where the elephant only stands

note: Udayanan, a captive, rides in triumph on the elephant; the quatrain says kings who rode elephants fall when their deeds turn.

gains.b: the quatrain gets a case in which a fallen man rises on an elephant by skill

gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which the fault is not mended by the husband's restraint but by an outside plan, which the couplet never considers.

note: Kural 638 makes it the minister's duty to tell a king what is good for him; Yugi, given a king who will not hear, chooses a trick.
teaches: The couplet assumes the king can be told, while the poem shows a minister who judges telling useless and acts in secret.

gains.a: The epic scene gains the name of a duty that Yugi both keeps in aim and breaks in method.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where the minister's duty to speak is overtaken by deceit for the king's own good.

note: Kural 539 bids a man remember the ruined when swollen with joy; the king of verse 124 forgets even his own ruin.

gains.b: The couplet gains a king whose own loss, not another's, is the ruin he forgets.
