gains.a: The epic's image of desire as a sea gains a bounded end in the quatrain's picture of age.
gains.b: The quatrain's warning gains a living king who does not heed it and pays with his land.

note: The fire set in verse 136 has its effect in the king's collapse in 139.
teaches: The tunnel and fire are not an end: their purpose is the king's belief, and verse 139 shows him believing it.

note: The minister's hidden guest of 137 is the one he asks a boon of in 138.
teaches: The reader sees that the queen is brought to the minister not by chance but to be asked for her consent to the parting.

note: The fire in the town of verse 110 is again a fire here, now a stage prop.
teaches: The same device of fire serves Yugi twice: first to free the fugitives, now to fake a death, so it is his habit and not a one-off.

note: The king's vow to die in 140 is turned aside by counsel in 146.
teaches: A king's wish to die with his queen is checked by minister's counsel, which is the work of a minister in the epic's picture of rule.

note: The journey in 150 carries out the plan Vayantakan puts in 149.
teaches: The reader learns that the long mourning ends with an act, as the king follows the counsel and sets out.

note: The ministers' counsel to a grieving king meets Kural 638 on a minister's duty to speak to a king who will not listen.
teaches: The Kural rule covers a king who destroys good counsel, but the epic shows a king who accepts counsel and is still deceived because the advisers' facts are false.

gains.a: the ministers' speech gains a named duty, so that their advice reads as a minister's task and not only comfort
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which good counsel is taken and yet rests on a false premise, a test the couplet does not make

note: The king mourning a body that was never found is set against the town that wails, buries and forgets in Tirumanthiram 145.
teaches: One poem shows grief for a real death that is quickly ended, the other grief for a false death that the king cannot end, so lament is shown to follow belief and not fact.

gains.a: the king's lament gains the ordinary course of mourning the song describes, against which his unfinished grief over a lie stands out
gains.b: the song gains a case of mourning for someone not dead, showing that a staged death can draw the same grief as a real one

note: The brahmin's promise of the lost queen meets the king's hope in verse 152.
teaches: The promise is aimed at a hope the king already holds, so the deceit works because it answers his grief.

note: In both verses the king sees the dead queen in something else, first flowers and then Padmavati.
teaches: A habit of seeing her likeness in things turns from a poet's sorrow into a real mistake that begins the new marriage.

note: The treasure the king searched for in verse 162 is shown to him in verse 163.
teaches: The king's loss is turned into Urumannuvan's service, so the search sets up the trust that follows.
audit_text_issue: speaker of 163 unnamed; line 4 (பானலங் கிளவி) hard

note: The seven kings named in verse 164 now make their demand and march on the land.
teaches: The list of names becomes a real threat only when they refuse tribute, which is what makes the stratagem necessary.

note: The disguise as merchants carries out the stratagem Urumannuvan promises in verse 165.
teaches: The stratagem is a trade, not a battle, which tells the reader how Urumannuvan means to win.

note: Disguised ministers sell jewels in an enemy camp, as the Kural describes a spy who takes an unsuspected form.
teaches: The epic's spies are the king and his own minister, and gems are the means, which the Kural's spy has no word for.

gains.a: The verse gains a rule, a spy's form must raise no suspicion, which shows why the jewel trade is chosen as the disguise.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which king and minister both act as the spy, which its plain listing of the spy's duties does not offer.

note: The spies' bare report in 169 is followed in 170 by the minister's own telling of Udayanan's deed.
teaches: The king's judgment in 169 rests on spies alone, and the minister's account in 170 is what turns it into joy.

note: The king's vow in 171 to remove the foes is carried out in 172 by Udayanan's army.
teaches: The vow is kept by the guest and not by the host, so the alliance in this chapter runs on Udayanan's arms.

note: The victory in 172 is repaid in 173 with the king's sister as bride.
teaches: The marriage reads as the price of the war: the bride is paid for the battle won.

note: In both epics a prince wins a battle for a king and the king rewards him with a bride (Gunavati there, Padumai here).
teaches: The reward-bride after a won battle is a pattern the Jain kavyas share, which marks the match as a convention and not one king's habit.

note: The ministers, army and friend the king adds to the dowry in 176 are the same things the Kural counts among a state's six parts.
teaches: A king who has lost a state can rebuild its parts by marriage, which the Kural's list of parts does not say.

gains.a: The bride's gift reads as the means by which the exiled Udayanan regains the army and ministers of a ruler.
gains.b: The list of six parts gets a case in which allies and ministers are acquired by a marriage gift and not by long building.

note: The spies' report in 169 is confirmed in 170 by a second voice, the minister's.
teaches: The king rejoices only once a second voice agrees, which suggests the second confirmation is a habit of a court and not only a rule.

gains.a: The shift from spy to minister shows how a second source is found at a court, which the verse alone does not name.
gains.b: The rule of confirming a spy's finding gets an instance in which the second source is a friendly minister, not another spy.

note: The errand to the Panchala king in 179 is carried out in 180, where the kings are driven off and the Panchala army comes on.
teaches: The errand is meant as stratagem and ends in open battle, which shows the plan did not remove the war.

note: The mounting arrows of 180 end in the ruin of 181.
teaches: The sky-darkening arrow exchange is the cause of the field's ruin, so 181 reads as the cost of the fight in 180.

note: The jackals and ghouls feeding on the slain in 181 are the carrion eaters the Siddhar names when each claims the body as its own.
teaches: A battle's bodies are the same flesh the Siddhar tells us is only meat for jackals and kites, so the glory of the field is also the end of the body.

gains.a: The field's feast of jackals is read as the fate of every body, not only of the slain king's soldiers.
gains.b: The Siddhar's abstract claim that the body is prey gets a scene in which the body is the price of a king's glory.

note: The killing of the beaten king in 182 is followed in 183 by the order to stop the war.
teaches: The order to stop comes only after the enemy king is dead, so the killing ends the war and not the king's mercy.

note: After the victory by arms, the king in 185 tends the wounded and rewards them, which is the work of a ruler's rule and not of the spear.
teaches: The epic shows victory first by the sword and then by care, so the Kural's claim is borne out only in the part after the battle.

gains.a: The healing and gifts after the battle are given a name as the sceptre's work, which the verse does not claim.
gains.b: The couplet's contrast of spear and sceptre gets a case in which both are used one after the other.

note: Padumai asks for the lute lessons that verse 103 gave Vasavadatta.
teaches: The lute lessons that began Vasavadatta's tie to Udayanan are now claimed by a second wife, so the same craft becomes a place where two wives are measured.

note: Both verses have a dream read by the wise as a promise of union.
teaches: In each, the dream is read aloud by experts and then fulfilled, but here the reader names the lady's survival while verse 63 names a groom to come.

note: Vasavadatta arrives at Kausambi as the sages in verse 192 foretold.
teaches: The sages' reading is shown to be true when the lady the king thought dead walks into the grove.

note: They leave Jayanti, the refuge reached in verse 120, for Kausambi.
teaches: The safe city reached at the end of the flight is only a stage; the return to the king's own capital is what completes it.

note: The plot confessed here is the trick of Yugi set out in verse 109.
teaches: The trick is described in its working in verse 109, but only here does its author call it a departure from the treatises and ask pardon.

note: The king ends his queen's sulk by praise and an embrace, which is what the couplet urges for a sulker.
teaches: The couplet says not to leave the sulker unembraced, while the scene adds that he first praises her beauty and wins her mind.

gains.a: the verse gains a rule that makes the embrace more than lust, an answer owed to someone already hurt
gains.b: the couplet gains a concrete order of acts: praise first, then the embrace, with a king as the one who must yield

note: Quarrel (201-202), making up (203) and union (204) run in the order the couplet gives.
teaches: The couplet lists the three as a gain of love, and the run of verses shows them as one evening in a king's house.

gains.a: the verse gains a naming of its sequence as love's reward, not merely a king's pleasure
gains.b: the couplet gains a plot in which the quarrel is caused by a second wife and made up by flattery

note: The letter owns the elephant that Pradyotan's side made in verse 39.
teaches: Pradyotan's own letter turns the trap of verse 39 into an offer of kinship, which shows how a captor explains his trick afterwards.

note: Both verses use the lion bound in a spider's thread for Udayanan's capture.
teaches: The image first comes in Vayantakan's report of the capture and returns in the captor's own letter, so the same fall is told once by the losers and once by the winner.

note: The letter looks back at the seizure of the garlanded king in verse 57.
teaches: The capture shown in battle is later acknowledged as a fault to be pardoned, which is not said in the fight itself.

note: Yugi swore in verse 66 to destroy Ujjain, and in this verse its king gives him two brides.
teaches: The vow of vengeance ends in a marriage gift from the enemy, so the plan to destroy is replaced by a bond of kin.

note: Salankayan, who showed the false elephant in verse 41, now speaks of dharma texts with Yugi.
teaches: The minister who ran the trap is now Yugi's friend in learning, so the quarrel is shown to end between ministers before it ends between kings.

note: Udayanan divides towns among those who served him; the couplet names apportioning as one of a king's tasks.
teaches: The poem shows apportioning as reward to friends who risked themselves for the king, which the couplet names without saying to whom the share goes.

gains.a: the grants of towns are seen as the king's last duty of rule and not as favour alone
gains.b: the couplet's word for apportioning gets a scene where the shares go to those who served in the captivity

note: The letter softens the wrong of the seizure with words of pardon; the couplet asks the envoy to remove what offends.
teaches: A letter that must confess a seizure can keep to the couplet's rule of avoiding offence only by naming the fault and asking for pardon in the same breath.

gains.a: the letter's gentle admission of fault is seen as the envoy's craft of removing offence
gains.b: the couplet is tried against a message that carries a fault of the sender, where removing offence is hard

note: Pradyotan pleads the tie of uncle and nephew; the couplet tells a man not to presume on kin degree with a king.
teaches: Here the stronger party pleads kinship and not the lesser, which shows the couplet's warning running the other way once the king has wronged his kinsman.

gains.a: the plea of kin is seen as a way to cover a wrong and not as a sign of equal standing
gains.b: the couplet is tested where the one pressing kin degree is the king himself

audit_text_issue: line 1 hard to construe; flagged uncertain | 212 line 1 is hard to construe

note: The king says that without such counsellors there is no kingship; the couplet makes counsellors the king's eyes.
teaches: The couplet asks the king to choose counsellors after counsel, but the verse shows a king recognising the worth of a minister who had worked against him.

gains.a: the king's praise of Yugi gets a rule that counsellors are his eyes, which makes the praise a statement of need
gains.b: the couplet gets a case where the counsellor praised belongs to the other side and has beaten the praiser

note: Verse 230 brings in Mananigai, named in verse 228, to meet Dattai's defeat.
teaches: The newcomer introduced by name and rank as a chaste princess in verse 228 first acts only in verse 230, when she steps in to answer the defeated Dattai.

note: Mananigai's eight thousand strikes answer the despondency of Dattai's party in 228.
teaches: The gloom with which Dattai sits defeated in 228 is not lifted by Dattai herself but by a stranger's play, which shows the poem making skill the cause of reversal.

note: Her eight thousand outdoes Ariyai's three thousand, the score that had silenced Dattai's side.
teaches: Ariyai's three thousand is shown as the peak only until Mananigai's count, so the contest's score is a ladder and each verse's number is meaningful only against the one before.

note: In 239 Dattai, angry in 238, comes with flowers to worship the king and the second marriage is completed.
teaches: Dattai's anger at the news is not allowed to stand; the next dawn shows her worshipping the king anyway, so the epic treats a first wife's resentment as a passing mood rather than a break.

note: The four chaste women of 241 are Dattai, Padumai, Mananigai and Virisikai; Virisikai's marriage in 240 completes the number.
teaches: The count of four in 241 only makes sense once 240 adds Virisikai to the three queens, so the closing contentment is the sum of the marriages.

note: Both verses list the tricks of ball play, hiding the ball in a garland and making it dance like a snake.
teaches: Two Jain epics share one catalogue of ball tricks, so the hidden-in-garland and snake-dance play is a conventional set of skills, not either poet's invention.

note: Both show a queen's resentment at a king's divided heart, but Dattai's anger ends in worship and the Pandya queen's sulk ends in the king's blindness.
teaches: The Silappathikaram makes a queen's sulk the opening that lets the goldsmith's lie in, while here the first queen's anger is quickly absorbed; the same domestic feeling has opposite consequences.

note: Both close on a king with tribute-paying kings around him, but Civakan turns away from it in dharma and Udayanan stays in it.
teaches: The same picture of a king whom others serve ends in renunciation in the Cintamani and in enjoyment here, so the minor epic's close is not the great epic's close.

note: The Kural's wife calls her husband a philanderer because all women feast on him with their eyes; Dattai's anger at his second marriage is the same grievance.
teaches: The epic shows what the Kural's grievance leads to when the husband is a king who really does take another wife, so the complaint is tested rather than only voiced.

gains.a: Dattai's anger is given a name and a ground that the verse itself leaves unspoken.
gains.b: The wife's complaint, which in the Kural stays a lovers' quarrel, is carried to a real second marriage and a quarrel that is settled by her bowing.

note: The queen's longing named in 242 is given its object in 243.
teaches: The vague longing of 242 is shown to be a wish for flight in the sky, which sets the plot of the next verses in motion.

note: The mantra the god gave in the hunt is now used.
teaches: The god's rescue is not only a past kindness: it left a means to call him, so the gift becomes the tool for the present trouble.

note: In both epics a god gives a hero a spell to call on, and a later need brings him.
teaches: Both Jain epics let a god leave a gift of spells that later serves the hero, so the helping god is a recurring structure of the genre.

note: The Kural's friend clears distress at once; the god's help waits to be called.
teaches: The god's reproach shows a friend's help can be bound by the call, which limits the Kural's picture of friendship that acts in the moment of trouble.

gains.a: The god's ask-and-answer scene shows that friendship with a god runs on being remembered, and that the king neglected it until now.
gains.b: The couplet's friend who acts unasked gets a counterexample: help that needs a call, and stays silent through prison and war.

note: The cause of the queen's longing is given and the means of flight supplied.
teaches: The longing for the sky is explained as the doing of the being in her womb, so the flight is both a cure and a sign of the child's nature.

note: The birth closes the pregnancy that began with the longing for the sky.
teaches: The longing, met by the flight, is followed by an easy birth and gifts, so the god's help is shown to have ended the trouble as well as quieting it.

note: Sight in 256 becomes union in 257.
teaches: The ball-play scene is not an end in itself: the sight of her carries at once into union, which makes her loss in 258 sharper.

note: The Kural's bewildered first sight is here mutual and immediate.
teaches: The epic carries the Kural's bewilderment through to union within a single verse, with no doubt, no gossip and no delay, so the bewilderment is a path to union and not a state of suffering.

gains.a: The verse shows both lovers bewildered, and it leaves out the mourning and doubt that the Kural's chapter dwells on.
gains.b: The couplet's lone man, unsure whether she is goddess, peahen or woman, gets a case in which the sight is answered and the doubt never has time to arise.

note: The captor confines her and then tries to break her steadfastness; the Kural says only her own firmness guards a woman.
teaches: Here the confinement works as the couplet says it must: the captor holds her body, yet only her silence and thought of her husband stand in the way, so the guard is inside her.

gains.a: The abducted girl's silence and memory show what the guard inside a woman is made of in practice, which the epic otherwise leaves unnamed.
gains.b: The couplet's claim that confinement guards nothing gets a hard test: she is truly confined, in the house of a king who wants her.

note: The one sent to break another woman's firmness is overcome by desire herself.
teaches: The plan to ruin Madanamanjikai's steadfastness reverses: the agent of the attack is the one who loses control, which turns the test of one woman into the downfall of another.

note: Vegavati's trick in 261 is carried out as a disguise in 262.
teaches: The guile that was only named in 261 is shown as taking the very form of the woman Naravahanan is looking for, which turns his search into the means of her plan.

note: Desire breaks through the restraint of the one who was to be the tempter.
teaches: Vegavati was sent as the instrument of a plan, and she meets desire the Kural says does not stop to ask whether one is firm in restraint, which makes the plan itself the thing that fails.

gains.a: The verse shows desire overcoming the person of the plan, a case the couplet's general remark does not name.
gains.b: The couplet's general claim that love ignores restraint gets a case where it defeats an agent with an assigned task, not only a lover who is open to it.

audit_text_issue: 261 line 1 desire subject not fixed by grammar

note: The sage's reading of the dream in 282 answers the dream the girl tells in 279 and 280.
teaches: The dream's lion, fish and curse stay riddles until the sage names a bridegroom and an empire as their meaning, so the reading is the dream's fulfilment.

note: Two prophecies by sages, one for the youth's Vidyadhara rule, one for his marriage and earthly rule.
teaches: The youth's promised rule is told from his side by one sage and from the bride's side by another, so the two prophecies fit together into a single destiny.

note: The youth's fall into the forest in 267 brings the sage's rescue in 268.
teaches: The brother's cruelty ends not in the youth's death but in an encounter that sets his future, which turns the fall into the start of his rise.

note: Manasavegan, who had seized the pair in verse 266, is the one whose mind is afraid at the wedding.
teaches: The rival who once held the hero captive now fears him, so the wedding shows the rivalry turning in the hero's favour.

note: The sage's saying that the groom will rule the earth with the wheel is met by the wheel and nine treasures.
teaches: The sage's prophecy is fulfilled step by step, so the reader sees how the promised wheel comes to him through Indra's grace.

note: The sage promised the silver mountain's realms under his feet; here the Vidyadhara lords are brought under them.
teaches: The promise of the sage's earlier words is kept in the same terms, which marks the conquest as foretold, not chance.

note: The epic makes merit's fruit a throne and pleasure in this life, where the couplet calls virtue the companion that stays when you die.
teaches: Merit gathered earlier is repaid here as sovereignty, so the couplet's 'companion' is shown paying out in the same life it began.

gains.a: the verse's merit gets a test against the Kural's claim that virtue's worth is what survives death, which the verse alone does not state
gains.b: the couplet gets a case in which virtue's reward comes while the doer lives, a limit it does not state

note: At the height of empire and eight thousand queens, the Naladiyar says kings on elephants under umbrellas are carried off like all others; the next kandam is a renunciation.
teaches: The peak of enjoyment is set right before the work's renunciation kandam, so the Naladiyar's warning is the story's own turning point.

gains.a: the list of queens gets the Naladiyar's warning of what such splendour is worth, which the verse never voices
gains.b: the quatrain gets a case of a king's splendour at its height, which gives its warning a particular king to fall on

note: Verse 308 gives the reflection behind the turn verse 304 announces.
teaches: The earlier verse only says the vow is taken; the later one shows the king's disgust with pleasure and his seeking out the teacher as how it comes about.

note: The women's show of desire comes as the vow of verse 304 begins.
teaches: A vow is tested at once by the thing it gives up, so the renunciation is shown to cost the king something.

note: The elephant shaking off its foot-fetter may picture the king shedding the delusion the women offer.
teaches: If the elephant is read as the king's image, the same verse turns a rampage into a picture of release, which neither verse says plainly.

note: The teaching the ascetics arrive to give in 318 is heard in 323.
teaches: Verse 318 only names the ascetics' skills and arrival; verse 323 shows what their teaching says, that life is a fearful bondage.

note: Verse 324 shows the feast of birds that the killings of 314 leave.
teaches: The elephant's violence in 314 is followed by its leaving a feast, so its cost is seen in what scavengers gain.

note: Udayanan turns from pleasure after reflecting on past penance; Civakan turns from kingship after hearing the dharma.
teaches: The two epics give a king's renunciation different starting points, one from his own reflection and one from a sermon, and this shows how the Jain epics motivate it.

note: Both name the Charanas as a class of ascetics, one by their powers of flight and one at the mountain where they wash away karma.
teaches: The class appears with its powers in one epic and its purpose, washing karma away, in the other.

note: The Charana appears as a teacher who reads the travellers' minds in the Silappathikaram and as a flier in Udayana.
teaches: One epic shows the Charana's mind-reading and the other his flight, so the powers attributed to him go beyond either.

note: The king's vow follows earlier merit, as the couplet says austerity comes only to those who already have it.
teaches: The couplet's circular rule is shown working in a life, with the vow following earlier merit.

gains.a: the king's turn to a vow gets a ground in earlier merit rather than seeming sudden
gains.b: the couplet's circular rule gets a story in which it works

note: A king of full worldly success leaves pleasure behind, which tests the couplet's question about going outside.
teaches: The couplet asks what is gained by leaving the household that keeps virtue, and the story answers with a king who leaves out of disgust at its pleasures, not out of failure.

gains.a: the king's turn gets a standard against which his leaving can be judged
gains.b: the couplet's question gets a case of a successful householder who leaves

note: The couplet makes austerity and giving depend on the sky's rain; here the ascetics themselves send the rain.
teaches: The dependence of austerity on rain in the couplet is reversed in the unit, where the austere supply the rain.

gains.a: the sages' power is placed within the dependence of giving on rain, so the rain relieves the very distress that would stop giving
gains.b: the couplet's one-way dependence on the sky meets a case where austerity feeds the sky

note: The quatrain praises those who see the body as a bubble and resolve to end wandering; the unit shows a sermon only heard.
teaches: Hearing a sermon on suffering is not yet the resolve the quatrain praises, so the unit stops short of its conclusion.

gains.a: the sermon's claim that life is a bondage of suffering gets an image, the body as a bubble that forms and bursts
gains.b: the quatrain's resolve gets a scene of its audience hearing the teaching, though not yet acting

note: Verse 4 states in the abstract that a deed binds and ripens; verse 326 gives a case, killing and its fruit.
teaches: The opening claim about deeds that ripen is given a concrete case here: a named deed, its sorrow and its hell.

note: The king's question in verse 342 about his love for the elephant is answered by a past birth in verse 346.
teaches: The king's love for the elephant is answered by a birth he cannot recall, not by anything in the elephant.

note: Both give hell as the fruit of the deed; the verse adds animal rebirth to it.
teaches: The epic widens the couplet's hell into an order of fruits that includes animal birth, which the couplet does not name.

gains.a: the sermon's hell is borne out by an old rule that links it to killing for food
gains.b: the couplet's hell gets a longer road of sorrow and animal birth before it

note: Both warn that women and liquor ruin a man; the verse follows the ruin past this life.
teaches: The couplet counts the loss in fortune; the story counts the loss in the next birth, so the harm reaches beyond this life.

gains.a: the brahmin's fall gets a rule that names his company as the mark of a man whom fortune has left
gains.b: the couplet's ruin gets a case in which the cost is a birth as an elephant

note: The verse promises release for gifts to ascetics; the couplet says giving is good even if there is no higher world.
teaches: The verse pays giving in release, while the couplet holds that giving is good without any reward, so the two differ on why one gives.

gains.a: the promise of release for giving is tested by a rule that gives without any reward
gains.b: the couplet's giving for its own sake meets a doctrine that fixes a reward

note: The verse sheds heavy deeds by right vision; Tirumular burns the many ills of deeds by worship of the fire.
teaches: The deed is shed by sight and understanding in one and burnt away by worship in the other, so the means of release is what they dispute.

gains.a: the shedding of deeds by sight gets a rival that burns them by rite
gains.b: Tirumular's fire gets a rival in which no worship is needed and sight alone is enough

note: The Siddhar asks when darkness will leave births as grass, beast and worm; the verse shows one man made a beast.
teaches: The Siddhar names the beast-births without saying why; the verse supplies a cause in a life of drink and lust.

gains.a: the elephant's rebirth gets the Siddhar's longing to escape every such birth
gains.b: the Siddhar's list of births gets a case with a stated cause

note: Both set knowledge and trust before conduct in the sage's teaching.
teaches: Both Jain sages put conduct after discernment of true things, though the Soolamani gives it as three steps and this verse buries it in a long list.

note: The she-elephant that falls bleeding in 114 becomes a god at the king's mantra, and the elephant of 354 becomes a god through its own samadhi.
teaches: An elephant's rebirth as a god is first something the king does for it in a crisis, and in 354 something its own discipline wins for it, so the king learns to treat release as a person's own work.

note: Naladiyar tells the listener to do what good he can at once, because Death comes; the king acts at once on the news of the elephant.
teaches: Naladiyar's warning comes with no figure to act on it; the king gives up a throne, a wife-court and his lands within a verse of the warning, so the rule is shown at its full price.

gains.a: the king's turn gets a general rule behind it, that what seems to stand does not, and that good must be done before Death
gains.b: the quatrain gets someone who pays a kingdom's worth for it at once, instead of only urging it

note: Naga Kumara's king crowns the young prince and rises to austerity; Udayanan crowns Gomukhan, not the son he has just called.
teaches: In the Naga Kumara story the crown goes down the family line, and here it goes outside it, so Udayanan's renunciation is not a settling of an heir but a handing of the realm to whoever can rule it.

note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by going outside if the household is led in virtue; the king takes his queens and ministers with him.
teaches: The Kural weighs the household against leaving it, while the king's whole household leaves together, which tests whether renunciation is abandoning dependants.

gains.a: the king's exit gets a standard, that a virtuous household needs no leaving, against which it must justify itself
gains.b: the couplet gets a case in which the household itself, and not one man, chooses the outside way

note: Kural 126 praises drawing in the five senses like a tortoise; the verse lists holding the five senses as one item of a numbered discipline.
teaches: The couplet states restraint as a single act with a reward over seven births, and the verse sets it as one part of a long catalogue, so restraint becomes one limb of a trained life.

gains.a: the catalogue gets a single plain image and a reward for restraint, which a bare list of numbers does not give
gains.b: the couplet gets the full scheme in which restraint is one of many practices, not a stand-alone virtue

note: Both works end by saying the sage overcomes the two deeds by meditation and reaches liberation.
teaches: Two Jain epics close on the same formula, the two deeds overcome by meditation, and so show it as the fixed ending of a Jain life-story and not a feature of one work.

note: Kural 5 says the two deeds do not cling to those devoted to the Lord's praise; the verse says they are burned in meditation.
teaches: The couplet makes freedom from the two deeds a gift of praise, and the verse makes it the fruit of effort, so the cause of release differs while the word for the two deeds is shared.

gains.a: the verse gets an older line that the two deeds can be shed, so its claim is not a private doctrine
gains.b: the couplet gets a story of how the deeds actually end, by burning in meditation and not by devotion

note: Tirumanthiram 219 says the fire worshipped and risen burns the deeds of ages; the verse says meditation burns them.
teaches: Both texts burn the deeds with fire, but in one the fire is the Lord's, worshipped, and in the other it is the sage's own meditation, which shows where Jain and Saiva release part ways.

gains.a: the verse gets a Saiva statement that deeds can be burned by fire, which shows its own fire is the sage's meditation and no god's gift
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram verse gets a case where the same burning is done by the sage alone and no deity helps

note: The Yasodhara's opening praises the omniscient lord whose feet teach release by leaving karma; the Naga hymn praises him as all-knowing and as the one who burned every old deed.
teaches: The Jain epics' praise of the lord is the same act twice, here as a promise of teaching and there as a list of what the lord has already done to his own karma.

note: Verse 1 says release is taught by leaving cruel deeds behind; Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas burn only when the sun-like Lord appears, as the sunstone burns cotton.
teaches: Whether release is something the one freed does by shedding deeds or something the Lord does by his presence is the exact point where the Jain and Saiva ways part.

gains.a: the Jain opening gains a rival account of what burns away karma, which it states without answering
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram image gains a contrast, a teaching in which the omniscient lord is only the one who shows the way and does not burn anything

note: Both poets answer the flaw in their verse with the lamp and its smoke, and ask hearers who grasp the matter to accept the work.
teaches: The Jain epics share an apology formula in which the poem's worth lies in its meaning, and each poet hangs a different request on it.

note: The Kural says the two deeds do not cling to those who praise the Lord's true fame; verse 4 promises a poem that shows the fruit of deeds, good and bad, as they actually ripen.
teaches: A story shows karma bearing fruit in merit and fear, which limits the couplet's picture of deeds that simply do not cling to the devout.

gains.a: the Yasodhara plan gains a Tamil ethical text which holds that devotion keeps deeds from clinging
gains.b: the Kural couplet gains a case where deeds do bear fruit in birth after birth for those not freed, which the couplet's statement leaves unshown

note: The turtle in the heated pot plays on unaware of its end, as the king and city sit in wealth without seeing release.
teaches: Both place the danger in comfort that blinds, but the Naladiyar names death as the one waiting, while the epic leaves the danger as the loss of the road to release.

gains.a: the king's ease is shown as a dangerous state like the turtle's warm water, not a harmless background
gains.b: the turtle's image is given a named case, a whole city and king, and a consequence in a scene that follows

note: The townspeople tie sickness to the goddess's anger and ask for worship to prevent it; the Siddhar says the offering of goat and cock at the shrine does not stop the sickness and the family deity is not its cause.
teaches: The two disagree on whether a deity's anger causes disease, so the epic's chain from the goddess's anger to the king's sacrifice rests on a belief the Siddhar rejects.

gains.a: the people's fear is seen as a belief another voice in Tamil rejected, so it is not simply the setting
gains.b: the Siddhar's mockery of the goat and cock offering gets a case where the same belief ends in a human sacrifice

audit_text_issue: Siddhar verse sense uncertain, possibly ironic

note: Tirumular says an unlearned king blind to dharma says 'kill'; the king here, without clarity in dharma, takes the people's advice and goes to the goddess's shrine.
teaches: The epic shows how the unlearned king's killing begins: he is led by piety and the people's fear rather than by anger, so the rule applies to a devout king too.

gains.a: the king's choice is read as the failure of learning that Tirumular names, not as cruelty
gains.b: the rule gets a king who kills out of religious duty and not out of tyranny

note: The Naladiyar's lamb nibbles the garland in the slaughter ground; here pairs of animals are brought together at the shrine as victims.
teaches: The quatrain uses the victim's unawareness as an image for the thoughtless, and the epic shows the gathered victims themselves, so the image can be read back onto the sacrifice.

gains.a: the gathered animals are seen as victims who do not know their end, which the verse does not say
gains.b: the lamb's image is tied to an actual rite and its scale: pairs of five kinds, then humans

note: The king holds that worship of the goddess is rightly done by killing, beginning with humans; the Kural says refraining from killing and eating one creature is better than a thousand sacrifices.
teaches: The two rank sacrifice and non-killing in opposite orders, and if the Kural is read as applying to blood offering as well as to oblations, the king's rite is the very thing the couplet ranks lowest.

gains.a: the king's claim is set against a Tamil rule that puts non-killing above every rite
gains.b: the couplet's comparison of sacrifices with non-killing gets a case where the sacrifice is of humans

note: The king orders a pair of human children brought for sacrifice to avert the goddess's anger; the Kural says not to do a deed that takes another's life even if one's own life be lost.
teaches: The king takes lives to avert harm to his city, whereas the Kural allows no exception even for the life of the one who decides, so the scene tests the rule against the case of a ruler who thinks he acts for his people.

gains.a: the order is seen as the act the Kural forbids even to save oneself, and here is done to save a city
gains.b: the couplet's absolute rule is tested against a ruler's duty to protect, which it does not mention

note: The king sends Chandakarma into the city to seek the twin children, and the youth and maiden in ascetic dress enter that city.
teaches: The search for victims and the entry of the pair meet in the city, so the dress of renunciation, put on in verse 27, is what brings them into the king's hands.

note: The king's order to Candakarman to bring a pair of humans for the goddess is carried out here as the two are seized.
teaches: The poem sets an officer's seeing the pair's gentleness against the order he serves, and the order wins, which shows duty to the king ruling over mercy.

note: The king holds that offering a pair of humans at the sword is a fitting rite; the brother holds that harm to the body is no harm to the self and so no loss.
teaches: The same act of killing is a gain to the king's worship and no harm to its victims in their own account, so the doomed two defuse the rite's meaning by their view of the body.
audit_text_issue: 32 line 4 syntax unclear | 32 line 4 (மங்கையாம் அதனை) is syntactically unclear.

note: The epic says fear can neither stop the coming harm nor do anything but add pain and fresh deeds; the quatrain says the fool sighs when the fruit arrives while the wise take it as old desert.
teaches: Fear is shown as a new cause of karma before the fruit comes, which extends the quatrain's advice on taking fruit that has arrived.

gains.a: the quatrain's picture of fruit taken calmly as old desert, which the brother states only as the uselessness of fear
gains.b: a case of the advice under the nearest threat, two captives of a sacrifice, where calm is hardest to keep

note: The brother recalls births among animals driven by old deeds; the Siddhar asks when he will say enough to births as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass.
teaches: The recalled animal births become the very cry of 'enough' that the pair will act on, so the epic gives the Siddhar's wish a remembered cause.

gains.a: the first-person plea to end the lower births, which in the epic is only recounted as past
gains.b: a stated cause of those lower births, old deeds that drive the soul among beasts, with the siblings' own kin as the killers

audit_text_issue: yasodhara_kaviyam:34 line 1 மன்னை is doubtful (perhaps அன்னை).

note: The epic says deeds whirl the soul like a wheel through the four states; the couplet names craving as the seed of unceasing birth.
teaches: The epic gives the wheel's driver as deeds and the Kural gives craving, so the two books hold different roots of the same round of birth.

gains.a: a named seed of the wheel in craving, which the verse leaves unsaid
gains.b: a picture of the wheel itself, four states and births past counting, which the couplet states only as 'birth'

note: The epic says even Indra-like lords of the gods lost their forms; the quatrain says kings on elephants under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and no one is left over.
teaches: The quatrain's visible proof that kings die is stretched by the epic to the gods, so no rank in any world offers refuge from loss.

gains.a: a human instance to rest the claim on, kings borne off whom a reader has seen, where it offers gods only by doctrine
gains.b: a reach beyond the visible, to ranks above the world of men, so heaven too is no way out

note: The epic likens death and birth to putting off a cloth and leaving a house for another; the couplet likens death to sleep and birth to waking.
teaches: The epic's cloth and house are things a person does and leaves, while the Kural's sleep is something that happens to one, so the two images differ on whether the change is in the soul's hands.

gains.a: a figure of death as a daily act with no break in the one who lives on, to calm a frightened girl
gains.b: a purpose beyond mere statement, a comfort spoken at the moment of arrest, where the couplet only describes

note: The brother's thought is that women's minds lack firmness; the Kural names firmness, called karpu, as the greatest thing in a woman.
teaches: Both books turn on a woman's firmness, but the epic locates it in renunciation and the Kural in chastity, so firmness is not the same virtue in the two.

gains.a: a firmness of mind that is not wifely, here set on leaving life, which the Kural's word does not reach
gains.b: a rival test of the same word, a woman who stands firm in leaving the world and not in keeping her husband

note: The brother bids his sister think of the soul as other than the body and leave it in the victors' refuge; the couplet likens the tie of body and life to a bird flying off from its nest.
teaches: The couplet calls the tie light and the epic makes it a choice to be carried out, so the same lightness is turned into an act of leaving.

gains.a: the idea that the tie to the body is a loose one, which makes its giving up no loss
gains.b: a pair who act on the image, two who choose the departure and say where they go

note: The poet says the soul is stainless and other than the body and that its karma is not its own nature; Tirumular says the stains go only when the sun of grace stands over them.
teaches: The epic leaves the stain's end to the soul's own knowledge of itself, while Tirumular needs a light from outside, so the two give opposite sources for the freeing.

gains.a: a rival account in which the stain leaves only when an outside light appears, which shows how much the epic leaves to the soul's own knowing
gains.b: a case of a stainless soul known apart from the body with no god's presence in the account

note: Kural 259 ranks refusing to take and eat one creature's life above a thousand oblations; verse 58 shows the rite at its far end, a man led to the goddess's place with the king's sword drawn.
teaches: The couplet weighs a ritual's merit against one life in general; the epic puts the weighing at the altar, where the offering is a man and the weigher is the king holding the sword.

gains.a: the sacrifice is seen to be what a Tamil couplet already ranks below a single creature's life
gains.b: the couplet's thousand sacrifices gain a concrete victim and a king's hand

note: Naladiyar 16 sets a kid nibbling the leaf garland before it in the fierce ritual ground; verse 59 sets two youths at the place of killing, smiling.
teaches: The kid is glad because it does not know where it stands, while the youths' smile at the same kind of place rests on knowing, so the doomed creature's calm turns from ignorance to composure.

gains.a: the youths' smile is read against a stock image of unknowing gladness and shown to be its opposite
gains.b: the kid's gladness gains a counter-case, one who sees the killing ground and is not shaken

note: Bhadragiriyar longs for the day he will stop killing and eating lives and hold them as his own life; in verse 60 the two at the killing ground wish the king to spread mercy to every life.
teaches: The Siddhar states mercy as a vow about his own food and conduct; the epic has it spoken as a blessing by the victims to the one holding the sword.

gains.a: the blessing is shown to carry an ethic a Siddhar names as the aim of his tapas, so mercy is the road and not a courtesy
gains.b: the Siddhar's wish to see lives as his own gains a scene where the victim does so for the man about to kill him

note: Verse 36 grieves over the bodies taken in each birth; verse 63 gives the youth's cause for the suffering, harm done to living bodies.
teaches: The earlier verse only laments births; this one names harming living creatures as what the sufferings come from.

note: Naladiyar 101 says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother; the youth traces the pair's sufferings over many births to harm done to living bodies.
teaches: The quatrain gives the deed's aim but not its kind; the epic names the kind, injury to living beings, and spreads its return over many births.

gains.a: the youth's account is given a Tamil image of how a deed finds its doer
gains.b: the old deed gains a named kind, harm to living bodies, and a span of many births

note: Pattinattar confesses to killing and eating many lives and trusts the Lord to bear the fault; the youth holds that harm to living bodies brings suffering through births.
teaches: Whether the guilt of killing can be borne by another turns on whether a god stands in the account: the verse sets a chain of sin and suffering with no pardoner in it, while the poet's plea counts on one.

gains.a: the youth's law of deeds is set against a pardon a Saiva poet counts on
gains.b: the poet's trust in the Lord is seen as a step outside a doctrine where the harm simply follows the doer

note: Verse 46 asks whether there is fear in leaving this life of fearful births; verse 62 shows the youths without trembling at the killing ground.
teaches: The earlier fearlessness was a resolve made in a garden of talk; here it is tested at the place of death.

note: In verse 58 the king draws his sword at the goddess's place; in verse 67 he puts the sword in his hand aside.
teaches: The same sword marks the king's turn: first the instrument of offering, then what he sets down when the youth's mercy reaches him.

note: Verse 70 says hearing the dharma checks karma's influx and sheds it; Tirumanthiram 1527 says grace comes as the guru and, when one's own doing ends through the knowledge it gives, the three impurities end.
teaches: Both make a teacher's word the means of release, but in one the hearer's own checking and shedding does the work, and in the other his own doing must cease and grace does it.

gains.a: the Jain account of release by the hearer's own stopping and shedding is set against a rival where grace comes as a guru
gains.b: Tirumular's 'when one's own doing ends' meets a doctrine where one's own effort is the whole means, sharpening what it denies

note: Naladiyar 46 breaks the woman into entrails, fat, blood and bone to cure desire; verse 71 calls the body a hut of filth and the dharma what ends desire for sense-pleasure and the cruelty of killing.
teaches: The quatrain cures desire by looking at the parts; the epic ties the same look to a dharma that also ends killing, so the contemplation of foulness shares a root with the mercy that stays the king's sword.

gains.a: the body-as-filth gains a concrete inventory of parts, which the epic names only as filth
gains.b: the quatrain's disgust is set in a system joining it to non-killing and release, not only restraint of lust

note: Neelakesi 859 gives the materialist's own words, that the world is only the elements and belief in a soul only makes fruitless quarrels; verse 72 gives the denial in one summary and calls it ignorance.
teaches: The same opponent appears as a speaker in one poem and as a target in the other, so the epic's verdict can be set beside the debating poem's long hearing.

note: Verse 49 holds the soul to be other than the body that joins it; verse 72 reports those who say the dead are not reborn.
teaches: The denial in 72 is the denial of the premise 49 had stated, so the dismissal there rests on a claim made earlier in the book.

note: The white hair seen in the mirror is the cause of the king's crowning of his son and departure.
teaches: The poem lets one sign of age carry a whole renunciation, so the choice to leave is the king's own and no teacher's.

note: In both works a king's own greying body is held up as the plain proof that youth does not last.
teaches: In the Silappathikaram a sage says the king need not be told since he sees his grey frame, whereas Asokan draws the conclusion himself and acts on it.

note: Naladiyar praises those who renounce in childhood for foreseeing grey hair; Asokan renounces only after he sees it.
teaches: The king meets the Naladiyar's test late but still before the staff, so renunciation after the first white hair counts as wise, not foolish.

gains.a: The epic gets a measure for the king's timing: the quatrain says the wise act before grey hair, and he acts only at the first strand.
gains.b: The quatrain's warning of the staff gets a person who is shown acting at the first strand, which the verse alone never describes.

note: Both set grey hair and the loss of women's regard against the pleasure of Kama.
teaches: The Siddhar's youth who spends everything on women ends with a staff in his hand, while Asokan reads his first white hair in time to leave, so the two verses show the same fall averted and unaverted.

gains.a: The king's fear that women will turn away gets the full course of a man who ignored it, which the verse only hints at.
gains.b: The Siddhar's ruined youth gets a counter-case, a man who is warned by the first sign and leaves.

note: Both argue that the days before age are few and that austerity should be taken up before it arrives.
teaches: The Saiva verse points to the mountain of great austerity as the use of youth, while Asokan turns to the forest mountain and has no god to appeal to, only the fleeting of youth and kin.

gains.a: Asokan's leaving gets a Saiva statement of the same urgency, with a named goal of austerity beside the forest mountain.
gains.b: Tirumular's advice to hurry gets a case of a king who actually hands over the throne and goes.

note: The father leaves because youth and kin do not last; the son, once king, lives for wealth and pleasure.
teaches: The father's lesson on impermanence does not pass to the son, so the story shows wisdom as personal and not inherited.

note: Kural 32 says there is no ruin greater than forgetting virtue; verse 86 says the cause: pride of wealth turns the prince to forget it.
teaches: The Kural names forgetting as the worst loss but not its cause, and the epic gives it as the pride of wealth.

gains.a: The verse's forgetting of dharma gets named as the ruin greater than any other.
gains.b: The couplet's forgetting gets a cause, the swelling pride of wealth in a young king.

note: The king's plunge into a sea of pleasure is set beside the quatrain's lamb eating the garland before its slaying.
teaches: The epic scene only lists pleasure's delights and the quatrain adds the shadow of the slaughter ground over them.

gains.a: The scene of delight gets the foreboding the verse itself does not state.
gains.b: The lamb image gets a concrete king, wealthy and at ease, who is as unaware as the lamb.

note: Amritamati in a guarded palace chamber is moved by a song from the stable: the confinement fails and her own steadfastness is the real guard.
teaches: The Kural says that only a woman's own steadfastness guards her, and the epic shows the guard fails through the ear, not the door, so steadfastness is a matter of the mind.

gains.a: Her wavering gets read against a test the Kural states: guarding is by the self, and her self is the one that gives way.
gains.b: The couplet's claim gets a case where walls hold and the guard within breaks at a voice.

note: In 103 the friend is glad that the keeper's form will end the queen's passion; in 111 the same friend carries the queen's desire to that body.
teaches: The sight meant to cure the queen's desire turns into the errand that fulfils it, so loathing proves no barrier once the friend takes the queen's side.

note: The keeper first refuses from fear of the king, and the friend's persuasion turns him to count the queen's love a prize.
teaches: His boast of reward is bought by overcoming the very fear he voiced, which shows how little weighing of cost enters the match.

note: In 97 the queen is alone in thought while the king is by; in 117 she leaves the sleeping king for the keeper.
teaches: The inward desire of the first night becomes the act of the night the king watches, so the poem takes her from thought to deed.

note: In 106 the friend urges the queen to shut up her restraint and drop the keeper; in 110 she resolves to go to him.
teaches: The friend's refusal gives way within a few verses, so the poem shows restraint offered by an attendant as only as strong as her pity.

note: The friend asks the queen to confine her restraint; the couplet says desire breaks that bolted door.
teaches: The couplet's door of restraint is shown here as one a friend urges the queen to keep shut and which the queen has already broken.

gains.a: the plea to imprison restraint is shown as too late, since the couplet says desire already breaks the door it names
gains.b: the couplet, spoken in a woman's voice, gets a case where another woman tells a queen to hold the door and cannot

note: The friend answers desire by loathing the body's foulness, as the quatrain does with every body.
teaches: The remedy of disgust works in the quatrain as meditation and fails in the story, where one repellent body cannot cool a mind already taken.

gains.a: her appeal to the keeper's sores and deformity is shown as a kind of the meditation, but aimed at one man, so it lacks the quatrain's reach
gains.b: the quatrain's instruction to see the body as a bag turned inside out is tried on a real person and is found weaker than the desire it was meant to quiet

note: The quatrain weighs great fear against small pleasure and counsels against another's wife; the keeper, who has just said the king will kill him, then calls the queen's love his best reward.
teaches: The quatrain's reckoning of fear against pleasure is tested on a man who does the sum and then goes ahead.

gains.a: the keeper's boast is set against the king's sword he named in 112, so his reward reads as a risk he has chosen to ignore
gains.b: the quatrain's prudence gets a speaker who has done the sum and gone past it, which the plain rule does not allow for

note: The queen leaves the king for the keeper, as the verse says men leave the ripe jackfruit for the thorny date.
teaches: The poem uses the Tirumanthiram's choice of poor fruit over rich fruit for a woman, and for a far more extreme pair.

gains.a: her turning from the king is named as a choice of the worse fruit, which the epic's narration leaves to the reader
gains.b: the image of the jackfruit and the date, spoken of men, is shown to hold for a woman and for the sharpest contrast of rank and body

note: The poet says a desiring mind outruns counsel; the verse says even learned men and yogis cannot turn a mind once bewildered.
teaches: The queen's fall is made one case of a general weakness that knowledge and attainment do not guard against.

gains.a: the queen's loss of restraint is set beside the learned and the yogis, which makes her case a human one and not only a woman's
gains.b: the verse's claim that attainment gives no protection gets a case where even a queen with every comfort is undone by one night's song
