note: The man who is her chosen lover beats her to the ground; the husband she betrayed holds the sword and refuses to strike.
teaches: The two scenes set the lover's blows beside the husband's restraint, so the reader sees whose hand the woman was safer in.

note: The king takes up the sword to follow her and, at the climax of his anger, his hand is stopped.
teaches: Carrying the sword in verse 118 makes the check in 123 a choice taken with the means to kill in hand, not a failure of means.

note: The king has the power to strike and the cause, and holds his anger.
teaches: The couplet separates guarding anger where it can take effect from guarding it where it cannot; the king's stand is the first kind, with a sword drawn.

gains.a: The story shows anger held when the means to act are in hand, which is the couplet's hard case.
gains.b: The couplet gets a king for whom guarding anger is a stayed sword, not a mood.

note: The king spares the woman and the man, but for reasons of sex and rank, not because life is dear.
teaches: The couplet bars killing even to save one's own life without exception; the king's reasons here are narrower, and only at 139 does he come to the couplet's rule.

gains.a: The story shows how an unprincipled restraint falls short of the rule it is made to meet.
gains.b: The couplet's absolute rule is tested against a husband's provoked rage, which it does not itself mention.

note: The king lists what desire destroys; the couplet says pain ends when desire, anger and confusion lose even their names.
teaches: The couplet states the cure; the king's list shows what it costs when desire is not removed, and he begins the cure by leaving the court.

gains.a: The king's list of damage remains a mood until a doctrine says desire can be removed.
gains.b: The couplet gets a concrete account of what the removed desire costs a man who was ruled by it.

note: The Siddhar blames a deceiving demon in woman's form; the king blames desire itself and has just spared the woman.
teaches: The Siddhar locates the theft of understanding in the woman, while the king locates it in desire, and so he can leave her alive.

gains.a: The king lacks the Siddhar's picture of desire as a demon that robs understanding.
gains.b: The Siddhar's blame of the woman lacks the king's separation of the woman from her desire.

audit_text_issue: Siddhar 259 text is cut off at the end ('கச்')

note: The king takes the nature of women as a reason to leave; the quatrain says no guard will keep them from fault.
teaches: The quatrain says guards cannot hold women's conduct; the king's answer is not a stronger guard but his own departure.

gains.a: The king's remark on women's nature is given as a general rule that others also hold.
gains.b: The quatrain's counsel of guarding gets a different answer from a husband who has seen guarding fail.

note: The king's disenchantment with the court and the queen leads him to leave the throne; the Siddhar lists town, kin, women, glory and wealth as things that do not last.
teaches: The Siddhar states what does not last; the king shows the grief and betrayal through which a man comes to accept it.

gains.a: The king's resolve gets a doctrine of impermanence that makes it more than hurt pride.
gains.b: The Siddhar's list gets a worked case in which the loss of a wife and rank is lived, not recited.

note: The mother tells him to kill a kid to protect himself; his answer is that no life may be taken to guard his own.
teaches: The mother and the son give opposite answers to one fear, and the poem lets the son's answer stand.

note: A mother asks for one killing as an offering to a goddess; the couplet says not killing beats a thousand offerings.
teaches: The couplet compares not killing with great offerings, while the story puts the offering on a mother's lips as a cure for her son's fear.

gains.a: The story shows the offering asked at a moment of personal fear, which the couplet's comparison lacks.
gains.b: The couplet gives the king's refusal a ground in a rule above the king's own reasoning.

note: The mother asks a kid for Chandikai; the Tirumanthiram describes Chandika as holding the four directions, without an offering.
teaches: The Tirumanthiram gives Chandika a cosmic form and no offering, while the epic shows how a mother worships her.

gains.a: The epic shows the offering practice and not her cosmic form.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's Chandika gets the folk offering that the epic makes the king refuse.

note: The poet said he would teach release through leaving cruel deeds; the king's refusal is the first such act in this story.
teaches: The opening promise of the poem is enacted in the first refusal of killing, long before any release.

note: The king refuses to kill even to save his own life, and gives the cost in the next world and the shortness of this one.
teaches: The couplet gives the rule alone; the king adds the reason that makes it bear on a man whose own life is threatened.

gains.a: The king's refusal is shown to rest on a known maxim, not only on his temper.
gains.b: The couplet gets a man whose own life is truly threatened and who must pay for obeying it.

note: After the king says no life may be taken, his mother offers a flour cock in the same breath.
teaches: Placing the loophole next to the refusal shows the poem is testing whether a made likeness of life counts as a life.

note: The king says no one can turn back the ripening of deeds, then agrees to the rite meant to ward off the dream's evil.
teaches: The king's own words deny the rite he accepts, which shows his consent as weakness, not belief.

note: The king asks who can turn aside the ripening of deeds.
teaches: The couplet says fate outruns any other device; the king acts that out, trying the mother's device and finding the fruit still comes.

gains.a: The king's question gets an authority that answers it before the story does.
gains.b: The couplet gets a scene where a device is tried and fate comes first.

note: The king consents to the flour-cock offering his mother proposes.
teaches: His doubt in 144 shows the loophole of 142 does not satisfy even the one who takes it, which prepares the cry at 146.

note: The flour cock cries and falls under the sword, answering the king's fear that a likeness is like killing.
teaches: The king's disgust at a likeness of life in 144 is borne out by the cry at 146, which shows his instinct was sound against his mother's argument.

note: The goddess's slaughter-place recurs, once for the two youths and now for a flour cock struck by the king.
teaches: The same altar shows the poem's shift: from killing living victims to a substitute that still cries out, so the question is not only the victim but the act.

note: The king asks what the cry of the flour cock means and fears the sin.
teaches: His question turns the marvel at 146 into doctrine: the cry is read as the sign of a sin that binds to births.

note: The king's wish to give up the kingdom was real; the queen offers the same renunciation as bait.
teaches: The poem sets sincere and false renunciation in the same words, so the reader sees renunciation can be counterfeited by one who means murder.

note: The king and his mother enter the animal state at death, and the youth at 34 tells of wandering among animals and being killed by kin.
teaches: The animal birth at 153 is the state whose pains are told later in the youth's account, so the ripening is followed across births.

note: Hurt done in the forenoon returns in the afternoon of itself, as the king's offering returns on him through the poison.
teaches: The couplet says the hurt returns of itself; 153 shows it returning through a third person's crime, so the doer suffers without being punished by the doer's own victim.

gains.a: The poison is seen as the late fruit of an earlier act of harm.
gains.b: The couplet gets a case where the returning hurt comes through another's crime, not the victim's hand.

note: A deed that seeks out the one who did it, like a calf finding its mother in a herd.
teaches: The quatrain's image says deeds find their doer; 153 shows how: they come in at the hour of the poison and ripen into animal births.

gains.a: The deeds that 'came in' are given an image of seeking the doer out.
gains.b: The quatrain gets a death in which the deed ripens by an unrelated hand.

note: The king had judged that women are not fit to be killed and spared the queen.
teaches: His mercy at 124 is read here as the cause of his death, so the poem asks whether sparing the guilty was a fault or a virtue.

note: The mourners link the king's death to the flour cock he struck.
teaches: The mourners trace the poison back to the offering at 145, a reading the narrator does not himself make.

note: The mourners say he took no part in dharma and has no good death; the king had refused to kill even to save his own life.
teaches: The mourners judge by what they saw, but 139 shows the refusal that belongs to the king's dharma, so their verdict is incomplete.

note: The king says no one can turn the ripening of deeds from him; the queen uses the same words to excuse her own deed.
teaches: The same doctrine from a victim and from the poisoner shows karma can be spoken as comfort or as an excuse.

note: The poem opens by saying it will show how deeds ripen, and the teller here draws that lesson for Maridattan.
teaches: The closing lesson at 160 answers the promise at 4, so the reader is told that the whole tale was an argument about deeds.

note: The teller says that understanding that events arise from deeds gives true companions and joy; the Siddhar says the body is the enjoyment of deeds and joins those who think of Siva's feet.
teaches: The epic makes understanding the nature of deeds the first step; the Siddhar names grace at the feet as what takes one beyond them.

gains.a: The epic's lesson meets the Saiva claim that a god's feet, not understanding, release one from deeds.
gains.b: The Siddhar's body-as-deeds gets a long case in which deeds ripen through poison and rebirth.

note: The king's cry at 147 that his deed calls him into a garland of births is answered here: the garland is now told birth by birth.
teaches: The lament and the account together show that the foreseen chain was real and also how it runs, which the foreboding alone does not.

note: The Jain epic says the fruit of deed cannot be overcome; Tirumular says a teacher's fire makes deed-seeds that do not sprout into births.
teaches: Set together they show the epic's karma as a debt that must be lived through, against the Tirumanthiram's karma that grace can scorch before it grows.

gains.a: the epic's rule that deed's fruit cannot be beaten meets a rival school that says it can be burned
gains.b: Tirumular's seeds that will not sprout gain the stubborn picture of a fruit that must be eaten, which his claim opposes

audit_text_issue: Tirumanthiram 120 is obscure; fire-touched seeds is a reading.

note: The quatrain says kings under the umbrella fall when their deeds turn; the epic shows the fall as the same soul living on as a timid bird in his son's house.
teaches: The couplet's fall of kings is made concrete: the king does not end, he is reborn lower, and at his own son's door.

gains.a: the frightened bird gains a general rule that explains why the great fall
gains.b: the quatrain's fall gains an afterlife it only hints at, the same soul continuing in the palace

note: At 123 the king in human form held a sword and let it fall; the bird, with only a beak, strikes the lover's eyes.
teaches: The restraint of the man and the blow of the bird together show that the epic does not make the king's patience a trait of his soul but of that one body.

note: A calf finds its mother among many cows as an old deed finds its doer; here the mother, now a dog, finds the son in a bird's body and kills him.
teaches: The quatrain's mother-finding image is turned over: the deed that finds the doer wears the face of a mother meeting her child.

gains.a: the dog's attack is shown as the finding of a doer by an old deed, not a chance of the hunt
gains.b: the quatrain's calf-and-mother simile gains a case where the finder and the found are in fact mother and son

note: The king at 139 refused to end one life to save another; his son, not knowing, beats the dog who is his grandmother.
teaches: The father's vow against taking life does not pass to the son, so harm continues through ignorance, not malice.

note: The kural's evil that follows the doer like a shadow that never leaves is shown in the snake who becomes a crocodile and follows the fish into the river.
teaches: The pursuit shows that the shadow of deed can pass through the animal births, which the couplet's one life does not show.

gains.a: the mother's following through snake and crocodile is seen as deed's shadow, not mere hatred
gains.b: the couplet's shadow gains a path across several births and species

note: Chandramathi urged her son to cut down a kid to the goddess; the crocodile that was she is now cut and torn by killers.
teaches: The cutting that she asked of the king is returned on her own body, so the offering she urged is the cost she herself pays.

note: The couplet says pains rest on those who caused pains; here the crocodile's pain comes but at the hands of men who themselves do harm.
teaches: The epic shows deed's return working through the very cruelty of new doers, so the rule is true but puts another debt on those who carry it out.

gains.a: the crocodile's torn body gains the rule that explains why it suffers
gains.b: the couplet's rule gains the complication that the one who punishes is himself adding to his own account

note: The grandson king orders the crocodile killed, while his father at 139 would not take one life even to save his own.
teaches: The son does the very thing the father's last words forbade, which shows how a vow dies when its meaning is not handed down.

note: The goat born to the outcaste hamlet in 183 becomes the womb in which the king is reborn as her son.
teaches: Reading 183 and 187 together shows that the doe of the births is the mother and the new kid her own husband's former son, a link neither verse states.

note: The son kills a buffalo as an offering to the goddess; the father refused to take one life to save his own.
teaches: Setting the son's offering against the father's refusal shows that the king's act in 191 undoes the very standard his father kept at 139.

note: The kid eaten for the sake of heaven is the father who would not kill a kid even to save himself.
teaches: The father who would not purchase his safety with a kid's life is bought into 'heaven' by his son as that kid, so the rite of 196 turns his own refusal into its victim.

note: The brahmins' blessing on the dead king is answered by the eaten animal's recognition of its own son and city.
teaches: The pair shows the rite's claim failing in its own scene: the one blessed is the one eaten, and he knows it in 197.

note: The couplet ranks not killing and eating above a thousand sacrifices; the epic's rite of the dead is a sacrifice whose flesh is the dead man.
teaches: The couplet states the rule; the epic's story shows its cost to the rite's own beneficiaries, so that the rule is tested by a case where the dead eat the dead.

gains.a: The rite of 196 gets a stated standard against which a brahmin's flesh offering is shown to be worse than none.
gains.b: The couplet's contrast of ritual and abstention gets a story in which the sacrifice's own beneficiary is the victim.

note: The brahmins here claim a fresh-killed buffalo for the rite and eat it as holy; Tirumular names flesh-eaters as vile ones seized by Yama's messengers.
teaches: The two texts judge the same act in opposite voices, one by merit and the other by hell, so the reader sees that the epic leaves the verdict to the story and not to a threat.

gains.a: The brahmins' claim of merit meets a Saiva text that calls the same eating base and punishable.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's threat of hell meets a case where the eaters think they earn heaven for the dead.

note: The Siddhar wishes to see the lives he might kill as his own life; the kid in 197 is, literally, the king's own father.
teaches: The Siddhar's stance of 'thinking of them as my own life' is a wish; the epic gives it a literal case, where the creature eaten is the eater's kin.

gains.a: The recognition in 197 gets a Siddhar's name for the habit of mind that would have stopped the rite.
gains.b: The Siddhar's 'as my own life' gets a story where it is literally true of the victim.

note: The lamb in the slaughter ground nibbles the garland unaware; the kid in 197 knows its fate and its son.
teaches: The Naladiyar's lamb stands for the heedless; the epic sets beside it a lamb that knows, so the reader sees what the heedless have lost.

gains.a: The kid's awareness of 197 gets an older picture of the slaughter-ground lamb that is unaware.
gains.b: The lamb of the quatrain gets a counter-case in which the victim recollects who it was.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf seeks its mother; the kid in 199 is a king found by his own deeds.
teaches: The quatrain gives the mechanism and the epic gives the case: the doer is found even across births and in a lower body, and still hears the deed named as its own.

gains.a: The kid's line 'the fruit of the deed I produced' gets an image for how the fruit finds the doer.
gains.b: The calf-and-mother image gets a doer who is a king reborn as a kid under his own son.

audit_text_issue: Line 4 இன்னதே ambiguous between wealth and fallen state.

note: The youth at 35 describes beings spun by their deeds through births without number; the kid in 199 speaks from one of those births.
teaches: The doctrine told by the youths in 35 is borne out in the king's own case, so that the reader sees it as lived and not as preached.
audit_text_issue: 199 line 4 is ambiguous between the wealth and the fallen state as the fruit.

note: The onlookers name the fruit of a woman's cruelty as leprosy, coming to her body; the couplet says only that harm returns of itself.
teaches: The epic shows the return of harm as a long delay in which the doer is first shown eating and then rotting, which the couplet's afternoon-for-forenoon image cannot show.

gains.a: the unit gains a plain rule that harm to others comes back to the doer, without needing a past birth
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which the return takes years, passes through a body and is read by onlookers as karma

note: Both say a deed finds its doer; the epic adds that it outlasts her death.
teaches: Putting 217 beside the calf-and-mother image shows that the Jain epic makes the deed's claim reach past the doer's body, a step the quatrain does not take.

gains.a: the unit gains an image of how the old deed finds her, as a calf picks out its mother
gains.b: the quatrain gains a limit case, where the deed still stands after the body has failed

note: Amirthamathi once defended her fortune as the fruit of an earlier deed; the same law now explains her disease.
teaches: The queen's own argument for her desire turns on her: she cited former deeds as the source of what one has, and her sickness is that source's other side.

note: The king reasoned that desire wastes the body and fame; the queen's body is wasted.
teaches: His reasoning from the night of the tryst is borne out on her body, which turns a private resolve into a visible fact.

note: The Siddhar's woman is a pit of sores by nature; here the sores come on one woman as the result of what she did.
teaches: The epic places the body's foulness in a deed and its time, where the Siddhar places it in woman's nature, so the two verses disagree on its cause.

gains.a: the unit gains a rival account of the foul body in which the foulness is a lure, not a punishment
gains.b: the song gains a case that says the sores follow a deed, which unsettles blaming woman as such

note: The couplet says sin, fear and blame never leave one who crosses into another's home; here a wife crosses, and the fruit falls on her.
teaches: The couplet is spoken to a man; the epic carries the same four ills onto a wife and adds the one the couplet lacks, the disease of her own body.

gains.a: the unit gains a stated rule that the crossing carries its own ruin
gains.b: the couplet gains a woman as the one who crosses, and a bodily fruit beyond blame

note: The couplet asks how one who eats another's flesh to fatten his own can hold to compassion; here the flesh is possibly her victim's.
teaches: The epic turns the couplet's general 'another creature' into a creature that may be her own victim's next body, which sharpens its question.

gains.a: the unit gains a rule that eating flesh is a failure of compassion in itself
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the flesh may belong to someone she wronged

note: Tirumular puts the flesh-eaters' pain in hell, after death; the epic spends its verses on the animal's pain first.
teaches: The epic puts the pain first on the animal and sets the eater's suffering later in this same life, where Tirumular's punishment lies only after death.

gains.a: the unit gains a Saiva voice that also holds flesh-eating to be punished
gains.b: the verse gains the animal's side of the pain, which it does not describe

note: The couplet calls a king who torments his people crueller than a killer; here the king seizes merchants' goods over a horse.
teaches: The epic's king acts from a sudden anger, not from habit, so it shows how the couplet's cruelty can come from one incident and an unexamined report.

gains.a: the unit gains a rule by which the seizure can be called cruelty
gains.b: the couplet gains a case of tyranny arising from one angry order, not a settled vice

note: The earlier king calls a king the shield of all living beings; this king's order falls on merchants and an animal.
teaches: One king's rule that a ruler guards every life is set against his successor's order that brings pain on innocent persons and a beast.

note: The sage's rubbed-wood fire answers the executioner's claim that a cut body shows no life.
teaches: The story gives the materialist test and the Jain reply side by side, so the reader sees the argument as one of method: whether failing to see a thing on cutting shows that it is absent.

note: The conch and its sound answer the weighing and the sealed pit that Chandakarman offered as proof.
teaches: The reply meets each of his tests by name, so the reader sees that his proof depends on the soul being a thing that could be weighed or seen leaving.

note: Verse 50 gave the youths' knowledge of the soul as other than the body; verse 238 gives it to the man who denied it.
teaches: The same doctrine, first held by ascetics going to their death, is now put as the answer to a man's disproof, so the reader learns it was framed to meet doubt as well as to console.

note: The fivefold conduct the first teachers spread in verse 54 is here set out as the five vows and three abstentions.
teaches: The earlier verse only names the fivefold conduct, and this one says what the five are.

note: Both give knowledge, faith and conduct as the triple discipline; Neelakesi makes it a medicine against rebirth.
teaches: Neelakesi's frame of birth as a disease for which the three are the cure is not in the Yasodhara, which rather lists their by-fruits of heaven and rule beside release.

note: Right faith as clarity and joy in the Jina's dharma here, against right faith as eight limbs and longing for the one with eight excellent things in Neelakesi.
teaches: The two Jain epics define the same faith differently, one by an inward state and one by a list of acts and freedoms, so the reader sees how a school could teach one term more than one way.
audit_text_issue: 241 sense uncertain; the third term may be faith or a part of it

note: The Jain five vows and flesh, honey and toddy against the Buddhist ten evil deeds of body, tongue and mind.
teaches: The two lists overlap on killing, theft and lust and differ on the rest, so the reader sees which wrongs the two faiths treat as common ground and which they do not.

note: Verse 243 puts truth after not killing and gives each its fruit, as the couplet puts not lying second to not killing.
teaches: The couplet only names the order of the two virtues, and the verse adds what each is said to yield.

gains.a: A ranking that puts not killing before truth, which the verse's list of five leaves unspoken.
gains.b: A fruit in this life for each of the two virtues, which the couplet leaves out.

note: The couplet says a life lives on not eating flesh and keeps hell closed; the verse adds worldly beauty, victory and birth.
teaches: The couplet gives the reason for not eating flesh as fear of hell, and the verse gives a gain in this life, so the reader sees two arguments for one abstention.

gains.a: A reason for the flesh ban drawn from the Kural's own side, the closing of hell, which the verse lacks as it offers only rewards.
gains.b: A reward in this life, of radiance, beauty and victory, which the couplet lacks as it argues from fear of hell.

note: Both speak of eight qualities, here a freed soul's own, there the Lord's.
teaches: The Jain verse makes the eight the property of any soul that is freed, and the Saiva verse makes them the Lord's, so the reader sees where the two schools put the one list.

gains.a: A rival owner of the eight qualities, a god, against which its claim that the freed soul has them unaided can be seen.
gains.b: A school that gives the eight to a freed soul with no god, which tests the Saiva claim that they are the Lord's.

audit_text_issue: 233 line 2 திருமல நித்தமாகி is not sure.

note: The couplet pictures the life as a lodger in the body; the verse argues it by the conch's sound.
teaches: The couplet takes the soul's separateness for granted and the verse offers a reason for it, so the reader sees what the couplet's picture assumed.

gains.a: A figure, the lodger in a body, for the thing that the cut and weighed body fails to show.
gains.b: A reason for the lodger's separateness, which the couplet only assumes.

note: The king says life would fall apart if harming stopped; the sage answers that even a killing in intent alone sends the killers to hell.
teaches: The pair puts the king's claim that rule needs killing beside the sage's reply that killing costs the killer more than it gives, which neither verse shows alone.
audit_text_issue: speaker of 245 tangled between sage and king

note: In 139 Yasodharan refuses to kill a living thing even to save his own life; here he and his mother are said to have killed a cock of flour with a sword.
teaches: Set side by side, they show a stated rule and the later act that breaks it, with 250 giving the cost that carries through every birth.

note: The cocks take the vow and the nectar of dharma, and in 257 the arrow that kills them still sends them into human birth.
teaches: The vow in 255 is what makes 257 a rebirth and not a fall, and the arrow shows how far the vow's protection reaches.

note: The twins are born to Yasomathi after the cocks' death; the youth in chapter 4 says his sight of dharma came from knowing his own births.
teaches: Read together, they let the reader see that the cocks of this chapter are the youth who is telling the story, an inference the poem does not state outright.

note: The sage says kings who kill to keep the body last only a few days and then sink in rebirth; the couplet forbids taking a life even to save one's own.
teaches: The couplet gives a bare ban; the sage supplies the reason that the life one kills to save is brief and the killing makes the next birth worse.

gains.a: The verse finds in the couplet the absolute rule its argument from the body's brevity is trying to reach.
gains.b: The couplet gets a reason against killing to save oneself that it does not itself give.

note: The couplet says all pains rest on those who caused pain; the sage says the pain of killing returns to the killers birth after birth.
teaches: The couplet states the return of pain as a rule; the verse shows it falling across births on two named kin who thought their killing was only a rite.

gains.a: The verse gets a general rule that makes the long suffering of the king and his mother a law and not a freak.
gains.b: The couplet gets the cases of kin reborn as birds, which show how far its rule is meant to reach.

note: Naladiyar says even kings who rode elephants under the white umbrella have been carried off and no one is left over; the verse says kings who kill to last also die and then sink in rebirth.
teaches: The quatrain ends at death; the verse adds that for a king who killed to last, the end is only a sinking into more births.

gains.a: The verse gets the common picture of kings carried off as a witness that the body's span cannot be bought by killing.
gains.b: The quatrain gets a destination after death and the cause that sends a king there.

note: The sage makes feeling another's pain as one's own the base of the chief vow; the Siddhar wishes to think of the lives he would kill and eat as his own life.
teaches: The Siddhar offers this as a wish on the way to completing his tapas, while the verse makes it the support without which the vow of not killing cannot stand.

gains.a: The verse gets a voice from a different tradition that reaches the same rule and ties it to a seeker's tapas.
gains.b: The Siddhar's wish gets a Jain statement that names the pity that must come first and the restraint beside it.

note: The sage says the king's father and mother went into animal births because of their deeds; the Siddhar asks when he will say enough to the births he has had as stone, tree, fish, bird and grass.
teaches: The Siddhar mourns the animal births without naming a cause; the epic traces the animal birth to a particular killing and makes it the fruit of a deed.

gains.a: The verse gets from the Siddhar the weariness of the rebirth it only reports as a fact.
gains.b: The Siddhar's lament gets a case in which an animal birth is the named fruit of a killing and not simply a stage to be escaped.

note: The cocks say that the teacher's dharma has freed them from the fever of rebirth; Tirumular's guru makes the deeds into burnt seeds that will not sprout into seven births.
teaches: Both free through a teacher, but in the epic the cocks' own vow and memory do the work while in Tirumular it is the guru's act that burns the seed, and no god is named in the epic's verse.

gains.a: The verse gets a Saiva picture of how a teacher's act ends rebirth, which it only reports as a result.
gains.b: Tirumular gets a case of a being freed by teaching and its own vow, without a god's act.

audit_text_issue: sense of 255 flagged uncertain; the speaker is inferred

note: The sage says the suffering of births ends only by good dharma; Tirumular names austerity and virtue the boat across the sea of deeds, which the Lord makes fruitful.
teaches: The Jain verse makes dharma sufficient to end the fruit of deeds; Tirumular makes the Lord's act the thing that gives austerity and virtue their effect.

gains.a: The verse gets a rival account in which dharma needs a god's act to bear fruit.
gains.b: Tirumular gets a Jain case where dharma alone is said to end a deed's fruit, which tests his added condition.

note: The hounds loosed in 265 to seize flesh are shown in 279 not coming near the ascetic.
teaches: The weapon that the king relied on is turned back by the very one it was loosed on, so the story shows his force failing before his remorse begins.

note: In 67 and here a king puts down the weapon in his hand under pressure of a speech; in 67 it is the victim's own sermon, here a third party's plea.
teaches: The two scenes show that the sword is laid down for different reasons: there the king is moved by what the victim teaches, here by what a friend says of the victim's greatness.

note: In 273 the king puts down the weapon but scorns the dust-grimed man; in 283 he bows so that his crown-flowers touch the ascetic's feet.
teaches: The king's change is made in two steps, so the first (weapon) does not yet carry the second (reverence).
audit_text_issue: 283 last line cut short; flagged uncertain

note: 274 says he ruled the whole land alone like a lion; 276 has him cast off that land, women and army.
teaches: What the king of Kalinga gives up in 276 is given its size by the merchant's earlier account of how entirely he held it.

note: In 82 Asokan reasons that greater merit now may win Indra's world; in 284 the ascetic says Asokan reached a divine world by earlier penance.
teaches: Asokan's reasoning about merit is shown to bring about the heaven he had thought of, only now told by another.

note: 81 says youth and kinship are fleeting and the mind should leave them; 275 adds wealth and pleasure and ends with the pleasure-rich heaven as the aim.
teaches: The same impermanence argument that leads one king to give up the kingdom is shown aiming at heaven rather than release, in both.

note: 280 has the king resolve to offer his own head; 281 says that to destroy one's own life is not grace.
teaches: The rule against killing is used here to forbid an act of reverence by the doer on himself, and so it does not give way to atonement.

note: In 270 the fruit follows honour or scorn though the ascetics hold neither favour nor anger; in Tirumanthiram 36 grace comes in the measure of the praise.
teaches: One text lets the result come from the one who honours without any granting, the other makes the Lord answer; the two differ over whether anyone grants the fruit.

gains.a: The epic verse lacks any figure who gives the fruit, and the Saiva verse shows what the ascetic's indifference excludes: a giver.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse lacks the Jain case in which a reverence has result with no one pleased by it.

note: 271 says the ascetic thinks of pain inflicted as his own deed; Naladiyar 58 says the worthy grieve for those who scorn them, fearing the hell that will follow.
teaches: Together they show that holding hurt as one's own deed does not leave the ascetic cold: Naladiyar adds the pity for the offender that 271 omits.

gains.a: 271 gains a feeling for the offender that its karma explanation leaves out.
gains.b: Naladiyar 58 gains a king with dogs as its case: the scorner is shown at the moment before the fall it fears for him.

note: 272 grounds 'all lives are like my own' in an ascetic's grace and a result beyond karma; Kural 315 tests understanding by guarding another's pain as one's own.
teaches: The epic puts the rule into a speech to a hunting king, so that guarding other lives has a named cost to him: his hounds and spear.

gains.a: 272 gains the Kural's plain test: understanding that does not guard another's pain is empty.
gains.b: Kural 315 gains a person who does the opposite, a king hunting with a pack.

note: Kural 327 forbids taking another's life even to save one's own; 281 forbids the king to take his own life even to atone.
teaches: The couplet's rule against killing is shown to cover the doer's own life, which the couplet does not say.

gains.a: 281 gains a forceful general rule against taking life, with no exception for need.
gains.b: Kural 327 gains the opposite case, where the life endangered is one's own, to be spared in atonement.

note: 278 has the ascetic hold neither 'I' nor 'mine' nor even benefit; Kural 346 says cutting off 'I' and 'mine' reaches a world above the gods.
teaches: The epic adds a third term, benefit, to the Kural's pair, so letting go includes even what one might claim as one's own good.

gains.a: 278 gains the Kural's statement that this giving up has a result beyond the gods' world.
gains.b: Kural 346 gains a figure who has done it, a king turned ascetic.

note: Naladiyar 53 has the best renounce home, youth and wealth at once to save themselves; 275 renounces for the pleasure-rich heaven.
teaches: The epic shows that the same reflection on impermanence may end in heaven rather than in release.

gains.a: 275 gains Naladiyar's view that the point of renunciation is saving oneself.
gains.b: Naladiyar 53 gains an instance in which the reflection leads to a heaven of pleasure, not release.

note: Kural 28 says the greatness of those whose word is full shows in their hidden words; 269 says what such ascetics will comes about, even the cloud, and puts this under fate.
teaches: The epic places the ascetic's power in his will and under fate, where the couplet puts it in the word.

gains.a: 269 gains the Kural's claim that greatness is known through the word.
gains.b: Kural 28 gains a kind of proof, rain and destruction at the ascetic's will.

note: The wife's hell is reckoned at ten and seven oceans, the father's heaven at ten.
teaches: Counting both fates in oceans of years shows one standard measuring the reward and the punishment, with the wife's term the longer.

note: The queen who offered the low man her whole love is the woman who plots with the old mother to poison the king.
teaches: The poisoning and hell here are the fruit of the passion the earlier verse shows only beginning.

note: The youth said that harm to living bodies brought them birth after birth of pain; here the muni names the first harm and the beasts.
teaches: The muni's account gives the cause the youth's earlier remark leaves unnamed: a single killing carried through many beast births.

note: The king who refuses to take a kid's life to save his own is the same Yasodharan that the muni names as caught in beast births for killing.
teaches: The refusal in verse 139 does not hold in the story's end; the reader sees that a good stand can still be overturned and then paid for.

note: The poison she meant for the king is poured back into her mouth in hell.
teaches: The punishment copies the crime, so the reader sees the hell as the working out of her own deed.

note: In both, the flesh the eater took from another is answered in the eater's own body: the crab-eater's fingers rot, the queen's limbs are cut off for her to eat.
teaches: Together they show the deed answering in kind, once in a diseased human body and once in a hell where the body will not die.

gains.a: The epic shows the same retribution in a hell with a tormentor's speech, where the quatrain gives only a result on earth.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a longer, harsher case in which the eater is made to eat herself, not merely lose a limb.

note: The Kural says that for the flesh-eater hell does not open its mouth; here the flesh-eater is told 'you ate' and hot copper is forced into her mouth.
teaches: The couplet's closed mouth of hell becomes a scene in which hell feeds the eater, and the penalty is shown to match the eating.

gains.a: The epic gives the couplet's warning a named sufferer and a tormentor's reproach.
gains.b: The couplet gets a mechanism: the penalty copies the meal rather than being a general threat.

note: Tirumanthiram has Yama's messengers seize the flesh-eaters and break them in fire-mouthed hell; here the dwellers of hell burn and split her with no god's order named.
teaches: Both fill hell with fire and breaking, but only the epic leaves the tormentors without a lord, which shows how little each needs a judge.

gains.a: The epic's hell has no named judge or messenger, only its own dwellers.
gains.b: The Saiva verse's Yama's servants stand out as one way of staffing hell, not a necessity.

note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother; here the old deed 'stands and burns' the queen in hell.
teaches: The calf's search takes the deed to its doer, and the epic shows what the deed then does once it has arrived.

gains.a: The epic shows the deed after it has found the doer, still burning her.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a case where the deed, once arrived, does not leave until spent.

note: Tirumanthiram has old deeds following the subtle body into a new body; the muni gives the bodies one by one for the king's father, with a vow taken in the cock's body turning the chain upward.
teaches: The epic shows that the following deed can be altered by a vow made in a beast's body, which the Saiva line says nothing of.

gains.a: The epic names each body and the vow that changed the course.
gains.b: The Saiva verse's general passing of the old deed gains a concrete life, a beast birth by beast birth.

note: The quatrain has mother seeking mother through the world; here father, mother, son and daughter change places among themselves across births.
teaches: One shows kin passing the world on, the other shows kin turning into each other, so grief for kin has no fixed object.

gains.a: The epic's twins and king have actually been one another's father, mother and children.
gains.b: The quatrain's general chain of mothers gets a family that names its members.

note: The Kural says all pain falls on those who caused pain; the king reads his own life as a ripening of the pain he gave his father and mother in their births.
teaches: The couplet's rule becomes a confession in which the doer sees the pain return across several births.

gains.a: The king applies the rule to himself and to kin in earlier births.
gains.b: The couplet gets a speaker who feels the rule falling on him.

note: The Kural names not killing as the chief virtue; the king names the lack of mercy joined to seeking wealth and pleasure as his fault.
teaches: The king adds the motive of wealth and pleasure to the couplet's plain count of killing, so greed becomes part of the fault.

gains.a: The king's lament names the greed that drives the killing.
gains.b: The couplet gains a cause for the killing it forbids.

note: The king who put aside his sword in verse 67 now asks the twins to forgive his earlier wrongs.
teaches: The softening at the altar is only a first step; the king completes it by asking pardon and taking his own refuge.

note: Asokan takes the vow with fifty-two kings; Maridattan renounces with kings and a merchant.
teaches: The tale that began with a king's renunciation among kings ends with a former sacrificer doing the same, so the vow is shown to reach even the cruel.

note: The youth said fear of what is due gains nothing; here the disciples fear the ripening of deeds and that fear drives them to austerity.
teaches: Fear of karma is useless as dread but useful as a reason to act, so the earlier advice is limited by what the fear is turned toward.

note: Naladiyar 4 tells the hearer to do good at once because Death comes in anger; verse 317 grades austerity to each one's strength.
teaches: Urgency in the quatrain is made practicable by the epic's graded vows, which say how those not yet able to renounce fully are to begin.

gains.a: the verse lacks the sense that time is short and delay is costly
gains.b: the quatrain lacks any ladder of vows for those who cannot yet give up everything

note: The youth said harm once done to bodies brought sufferings in birth after birth; here the flour cock killing is the instance.
teaches: The general claim of verse 63 is given its measured example, in which even an effigy's killing is followed for lives.

note: Kural 321 calls not killing the first of dharma and says killing brings every other kind of deed; verse 321 shows one killing without a real life still following across births.
teaches: The couplet's rule is tested at its smallest case, the effigy, which shows how far the epic extends the rule beyond the couplet.

gains.a: the verse lacks a general statement that killing leads on to all other wrongs
gains.b: the couplet lacks the story of a symbolic killing whose pain still lasted through births

note: Tirumanthiram 200 counts killing as a mountain-sized sin that is put away by reaching Siva's feet; verse 321 says the killing's result cannot be undone by anything given, and only the dharma's austerity loosens it.
teaches: The Saiva text frees one from the sin by reaching the Lord, while the Jain verse leaves the deed to be worn away by conduct alone.

gains.a: the verse lacks any Lord whose feet remove the sin
gains.b: the quatrain lacks an account of how long one killing travels through births

note: In verse 49 the brother bids his sister give up the body in the refuge of the victors; verse 325 shows them doing it.
teaches: The plan made under threat of the sword is kept after the threat ends, which shows it was a choice and not only a reaction to danger.

note: Tirumanthiram 499 has karma bring the soul to wombs and then knowledge reach Siva; verse 329 says the dharma holds karma off and leads on to release.
teaches: Both give heaven or birth as a stage, but one reaches release through the Lord and the other through the dharma's own power.

gains.a: the verse lacks a Lord who brings the soul to release
gains.b: the quatrain lacks a way of holding back karma by conduct

note: Kural 360 says pain perishes when even the names of desire, anger and confusion perish; verse 330 names dharma, giving up anger, knowledge and the vow as what to do.
teaches: The couplet names what must perish and the epic's last verse names the practices that make it perish.

gains.a: the verse lacks the three faults of desire, anger and confusion that the couplet names
gains.b: the couplet lacks the practices of dharma, knowledge and keeping a vow
